packets.name: Handshake
packets.desc: The very first packet sent by the client. Initiates the connection and requests a protocol state transition.
packets.notes: Determines whether the connection enters STATUS or LOGIN state. Sent by GuiConnecting.java during server connection, Minecraft.java for local singleplayer, OldServerPinger.java for server list pinging, and RealmsConnect.java for Realms. The requestedState field is critical: value 1 enters STATUS (used by server pinger), value 2 enters LOGIN (used for actual gameplay).

writeup.p: The handshake is the first packet of every connection: a single serverbound C00PacketHandshake carrying the protocol version, the server address as a length-prefixed string, the destination port, and an int state (1 = status, 2 = login). It is sent exactly once, before any encryption, and its state field selects which protocol machine the server runs next. Nothing in the 8 reference clients constructs or intercepts it at runtime; the MCP code path that builds it lives in GuiConnecting.attemptHandshake and the integrated-server path skips it entirely.

writeup.h: Why clients do not touch it
writeup.p: grep of all 8 reference sources (Memeware 7.3, Nekoware v1 private, Rise 5.99, Rise 6.1.30, Rise 6.2.4, Sigma 4.11, Spicy, Tenacity 6.0) returns zero module references to C00PacketHandshake. The reasons are structural: it is sent once before the game world exists, so there is no per-tick module hook active; the vanilla client builds it from GuiConnecting state that modules never influence; and the server trusts its fields for routing only. The one place clients historically touch it is a server-list pinger spoofing protocol version 1 (or 0) to enumerate servers, which these 8 clients do not implement.

NetHandlerHandshakeTCP.processHandshake reads the state int. State 1 routes the connection to the status handler (NetHandlerStatusServer), state 2 to the login handler (NetHandlerLoginServer). Mojang's version of the packet also carries a second address string (the 'hostname the client thinks it is connecting to'), which proxies and BungeeCord-style setups use for server routing. The server compares the protocol version against its own and answers with a disconnect or LoginDisconnect if the client is too old or too new.

Because the packet is unencrypted and fully client-controlled, its real abuse is server-side: protocol-version lying (clients claiming an older version than they speak), hostname injection for proxy routing, and state-flip confusion (sending state 1 then 2) which some anti-bot plugins used to fingerprint scanners. For a client cheat, the packet is a dead end: no timing, no per-tick value, no server-side math to abuse. This is why every one of the 8 clients leaves it to vanilla.

implementation.overview: The one-shot connection preamble: protocol version, hostname, port, and target state. None of the 8 reference clients touch it at runtime, because it is sent once before any module hook exists and carries no per-tick state to exploit.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerHandshakeTCP.processHandshake validates the protocol version against the server's registered versions and selects the next state machine from the state int (1 = status, 2 = login). A mismatched version produces an immediate disconnect (S00PacketDisconnect in login state) or a protocol-error kick. The embedded hostname is used by proxy frontends to route the connection; vanilla singleplayer and most offline servers ignore it.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: VarInt protocol version, String server address (VarInt length prefix), Unsigned Short port, VarInt next state. Sent over an unencrypted, uncompressed channel. The 1.8.9 protocol version is 47. After this packet the connection switches state machines, and the next serverbound packet must match the chosen state.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats almost never inspect the handshake because it arrives before the play state and before any player entity exists. The relevant detection is proxy/ban management: plugins (AntiVPN, server-list bots) fingerprint scanners by protocol-version lies or by abnormal status-then-login sequences. None of the 8 clients participate in that game.

anticheat.overview: The handshake is the first packet on the connection and arrives before any anticheat pipeline exists, so no check in the corpus runs on it. The corpus hits are keyword noise from the proxy and Bungee search terms: chat-component imports, proxy registries and config flags. The only real processing is at the packet-library level, where Artemis decodes GPacketHandshakeClientSetProtocol in ArtemisDecoder.handleHandshake and routes the next-state field into the player profile, and Negativity intercepts PacketType.Handshake.IS_SET_PROTOCOL in its channel inbound handler. Both are infrastructure that establishes protocol state, not checks.

wiki_notes: The vanilla server does not use the Server Address or Server Port fields for anything; they exist for proxies and server routing, so address spoofing only matters on BungeeCord-style setups.
By convention a client pinging only to determine the server version should send protocol version -1 in the handshake.

The handshake should be sent immediately after opening the TCP connection or the server may disconnect, and servers should also still accept the legacy 0xFE server list ping which uses a nonstandard non-length-prefixed format.

MCP 1.8.9 C00Handshake implements Packet<INetHandlerHandshakeServer> dispatching to INetHandlerHandshakeServer.processHandshake; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readStringFromBuffer, readUnsignedShort, readVarIntFromBuffer.
1.8.9 callers: Minecraft.? sends new C00Handshake (line 2338) +4 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/Minecraft.java

packets.name: Keep Alive (Response)
packets.desc: Response to S00PacketKeepAlive. The client echoes back the server's keep-alive ID.

fields.name: key
fields.desc: The keep-alive ID received from the server

packets.notes: If the client doesn't respond within ~30 seconds, the server will disconnect them.

writeup.p: Keepalive is the protocol's liveness and latency probe. The server sends S00PacketKeepAlive with a monotonically increasing key (server tick-based), the client must echo it back as C00PacketKeepAlive with the same key. NetHandlerPlayServer.processKeepAlive compares the echoed key to the stored field_147378_h and folds the round-trip time into the player's ping EMA: ping = (ping * 3 + delta) / 4. It is the only packet in the play state whose sole purpose is timing, which makes it the backbone of ping spoofing, disconnect-detection, and timer-based disabler modes.

Client side, NetHandlerPlayClient.handleKeepAlive immediately echoes: `this.addToSendQueue(new C00PacketKeepAlive(packetIn.func_149134_c()));`. Server side, processKeepAlive is a pure timing check: if the key matches, it recomputes ping; otherwise it silently ignores. Note there is no per-connection timeout in vanilla 1.8.9 server code for a missing keepalive response; timeouts are enforced by the network layer (read timeout) or by anti-cheat plugins. This asymmetry is exactly what ping-spoof modules exploit.

The 8 clients show three distinct families. (1) Ping spoofers (Rise 5.99 PingSpoof, Rise 6.x PingSpoofComponent, Sigma 4.11 PingSpoof, Spicy PingSpoof) buffer the packet and release it late. (2) Disablers (Memeware 7.3 Disabler, Sigma 4.11 Disabler, Rise 6.x KeepAliveDisabler/DynamicPVPDisabler/LunarDisabler/Verus2Disabler, Spicy Disabler, Tenacity 6.0 AdvancedDisablerModule) cancel or mutate the key to break server-side timing heuristics on specific anti-cheats. (3) Movement modules that need to reset the server-side timer or cancel all stateful packets (Nekoware v1 Fly, Spicy Bhop/BackupFly/Fly, Rise 5.99 Fly/LongJump/Speed, Sigma Blink, Spicy Blink, Rise BlinkAntiVoid/WatchdogAntiVoid).

Delaying the echo inflates the server's measured ping. Mutating the key (Memeware's Mineplex Combat mode subtracts a random 3..127 from the key) makes the server's key comparison fail, so the ping EMA is never updated, freezing the displayed ping and confusing plugins that use keepalive gaps to estimate lag or detect timer. Cancelling keepalive outright is the crude version: safe only while the server has no keepalive timeout, which is why disabler modes pair the cancel with periodic re-sends (Sigma's Erisium mode re-sends lastKey every 1500 ms).

implementation.overview: The timing backbone of the play state: server sends S00 with a key, client echoes it, server folds round-trip into a ping EMA. Ping spoofers delay the echo, disablers cancel or corrupt the key, and a surprising number of movement modules (Fly, Bhop, Blink) cancel it as collateral when they need to stop all stateful traffic.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerPlayServer.processKeepAlive (line ~1015 in the bundled 1.8.9 sources): if packetIn.getKey() == field_147378_h, ping = (ping * 3 + (now - lastPingTime)) / 4. No response to a wrong or missing key: the packet is simply ignored. The client handler echoes unconditionally. Because wrong keys are silently dropped, mutating the key is undetectable from the packet stream alone: the server just never updates ping.
implementation.protocol_notes: Serverbound C00 and clientbound S00 share the same int key field (writeVarIntToBuffer / readVarIntFromBuffer in 1.8.9 MCP; the key is a plain int). S00 is sent roughly every second of play time (server tick counter). C00 must be sent on the same connection before the next S00 for the ping EMA to converge. In practice modules intercept C00 in PacketSendEvent and S00 in PacketReceiveEvent.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: NCP and AAC track keepalive timing to distinguish real latency from timer abuse; a frozen or wildly inflated ping is a classic timer/fly flag. Verus-era servers (the Rise 6.x Verus2Disabler, Memeware's 'Latest Verus' mode) correlate keepalive gaps with transaction (C0F) gaps, so disablers buffer C00 and C0F together and flush them together after a fixed delay. The risk trade-off: pure delay is stealthy but does nothing against servers that timeout dead connections; cancellation is strong but requires knowing the server has no keepalive timeout.

modules.name: PingSpoof
modules.purpose: Inflate the player's measured ping by delaying keepalive (and transaction) echoes.
modules.how_it_works: Intercept S00 on receive; on the send side, cancel C00 (and usually C0F) and park it in a map keyed by release timestamp; on each pre-motion tick, flush entries whose delay has elapsed via sendPacket (bypassing the event bus).
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketSendEvent (cancel + park), PreMotionEvent (flush), PacketReceiveEvent (S08 resets the timer).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Pure delay is low-risk: the server only sees late echoes. Pairing C0F with C00 keeps transaction order consistent, which matters because modern anti-cheats correlate the two gaps.
modules.variations: Sigma 4.11 and Spicy implement the same buffer-and-release pattern on their own event buses. Rise 6.x moves this into PingSpoofComponent used by both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4. LiquidSense Dev's PingSpoof parks C00 and C0F together in a packetsMap with a random MinDelay/MaxDelay release time and flushes through addToSendQueue from an ignoreCondition UpdateEvent, skipping buffering while the player is dead or below one health.

modules.name: Disabler
modules.purpose: Break anti-cheat timing heuristics that use keepalive as a latency reference.
modules.how_it_works: Mode-dependent: cancel the echo entirely, corrupt the key so the server silently drops it, or re-send a stale key on a timer. Memeware's Mineplex Combat mode corrupts; Sigma's Faithful/Erisium/SagePvP/ColdNetwork modes cancel and Erisium re-sends lastKey every 1500 ms; Rise 6.x splits this into KeepAliveDisabler, DynamicPVPDisabler, LunarDisabler and Verus2Disabler, each tuned to a server family.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketOutEvent (cancel or mutate the live packet object).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Key corruption is stealthier than cancellation because the server's response is identical to a dropped packet: ping just stops updating. The random 3..127 offset keeps the mutation from looking like a fixed-value spoof.
modules.variations: Sigma 4.11 (Faithful/Erisium/SagePvP/ColdNetwork modes), Tenacity 6.0 AdvancedDisablerModule, and the Rise 6.x per-server disabler suite (KeepAliveDisabler, DynamicPVPDisabler, LunarDisabler, Verus2Disabler). LiquidSense Dev's Disabler keeps separate queues for C00 and C0F, cancels them on PacketEvent, and re-sends spoofed keepalives with an incremented keepAliveId on a randomized C00-Base delay while the watchdog sequence runs.

modules.name: Fly (timer reset)
modules.purpose: Cancel keepalive as collateral when a movement exploit needs to stop all stateful serverbound traffic.
modules.how_it_works: Movement modules that spoof position or use damage tricks cancel every packet the server treats as stateful (C0F, C00) and reset their own timer. Nekoware v1's Fly cancels C0FPacketConfirmTransaction and C00PacketKeepAlive together; the point is not ping spoofing but keeping the server's view of the player frozen while the client replays position packets.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Blunt but effective on servers without keepalive timeouts. The visible side effect is a frozen ping on the tab list, which staff can notice.
modules.variations: Spicy's BackupFly, Bhop, Fly, AutoLog and Blink all reference C00PacketKeepAlive with the same cancel pattern; Rise 5.99's Fly, LongJump, Speed, Freecam and BlinkAntiVoid touch it via their own packet handlers.

modules.name: Blink / AntiVoid
modules.purpose: Buffer-and-release: keepalive is one of the packet types held while the client 'blinks' (stays frozen server-side).
modules.how_it_works: Blink cancels all serverbound packets including C00 while enabled, then releases them in order on disable. AntiVoid variants (Rise 6.x BlinkAntiVoid, WatchdogAntiVoid) do the same but release early if the player would fall into the void. The keepalive is included so the server keeps receiving a steady stream when the blink window is short.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Long blink windows flag on every serious anti-cheat; the keepalive handling here is incidental, not the point of the module.
modules.variations: Rise 6.x implements it as BlinkComponent used by Blink, BlinkAntiVoid and WatchdogAntiVoid in both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4.

modules.name: Fly (keepalive mode)
modules.purpose: Fly mode that sends a fresh C00PacketKeepAlive every tick while flying at vanilla speed, using keepalive spam instead of position mutation to hold the server's movement checks.
modules.how_it_works: The keepalive case in the mode switch sends an empty C00PacketKeepAlive (default key 0) via addToSendQueue, sets isFlying false, zeroes motion, and strafes at vanillaSpeed; jump and sneak keys add vertical motion. The same module carries aac3, flag, minesecure and other modes that do not touch C00.
modules.vanilla_hook: UpdateEvent / PacketEvent on LiquidBounce's event bus; send via mc.getNetHandler().addToSendQueue.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Keepalive spam with key 0 is a known NCP-era anti-flag: the server sees a steady keepalive stream while movement is handled purely client-side, so timer and fly checks that depend on keepalive timing never see a gap.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus sends C00 from a Fly module; the other Fly-family hits cancel it.

modules.name: LuaEventPacket
modules.purpose: Expose the packet to November's Lua scripting API as an id plus direction pair, so scripts can filter on C00 without touching obfuscated class names.
modules.how_it_works: The static initializer maps C00PacketKeepAlive.class to 0x00 in a packetIds table (the table exists because obfuscation makes reflection unusable); the wrapper constructor reads the id via getOrDefault and sets direction to 'out' or 'in' from the EventPacket type.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.Out / EventPacket.In routed through the scripting bridge; scripts read packet and direction.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None; this is a read-only mapping, the script payload is the risk surface.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent (serverbound C00) and PacketReceiveEvent (clientbound S00) on every client; Rise 6.x uses its component system (PingSpoofComponent, KeepAliveDisabler). LiquidSense Dev and November Recode 2.0 hook the same PacketEvent/EventPacket surfaces; November additionally exposes C00 to Lua scripts via LuaEventPacket.
implementation.client_variations: Classic clients (Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy) mutate or cancel the packet object inside the event. Rise 5.99 and 6.x replace the packet on the event (event.setPacket) or flush via PacketUtil.sendPacket, which bypasses the event bus entirely. LiquidSense Dev sends via mc.getNetHandler().addToSendQueue and cancels via PacketEvent.cancelEvent; November Recode 2.0 wraps the packet in LuaEventPacket for scripting and uses its own EventPacket.Out bus.

anticheat.overview: The keepalive echo is the anticheat's latency reference. Serious anticheats issue their own keepalives (Frequency TickManager, FlopAC KeepAliveHandler) or track the vanilla ones, and fold the C00 round-trip into a ping value that movement checks read. Ping spoofers delay or duplicate the echo, so ping-spoof checks compare keepalive RTT against transaction RTT (Frequency PingSpoofA) or validate the echoed ID against the list of server-issued IDs (Grim BadPacketsO, Hydro BadPacketsE/F). Because a frozen or inflated ping breaks timer discrimination, timer checks gate their acceptance on keepalive confirmation (Frequency TimerA) and NCP rate-limits keepalive replies outright.

checks.name: PingSpoofA (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Cross-checks the keepalive round-trip against the transaction round-trip to catch ping spoofers that delay keepalive echoes.
checks.how_it_works: On every flying packet, compares the ping computed from keepalive echoes (playerData.getKeepAlivePing()) with the ping computed from transaction echoes. If the transaction ping exceeds the keepalive ping by more than 50 ms, outside the first 10 ticks and the lag/teleport/TPS exemptions, the check fails. The premise: a ping spoof buffers C00PacketKeepAlive and flushes it late, so the keepalive ping stays artificially low while transaction traffic reveals the real latency.
checks.detects: Ping spoofers that delay the keepalive echo, and clients that fake a low tab-list ping.
checks.variations: Azure PingSpoof measures the delay between the client's last move packet and its keepalive reply and flags anything above roughly 150 ms. Hydro PingSpoofA, FlopAC PingSpoofA-D and Artemis PingSpoofProtocol, PingSpoofDuplicate and PingSpoofIdDupe implement the same cross-signal idea on their own trackers. FrequencyPlus and Degrade carry near-identical copies of the Frequency check.

checks.name: BadPacketsO keepalive ID validation (Grim)
checks.purpose: Rejects keepalive replies whose ID was never issued by the server, catching fabricated echoes, key-mutating disablers and duplicate replays.
checks.how_it_works: Records every server-issued keepalive ID in a linked list on the send side, then on each C00 reply scans the list for the echoed ID and drains entries up to the match. A reply that matches no pending ID is flagged and cancelled. Listening to both directions lets the check tell a legitimately delayed echo from a fabricated one: a real echo always corresponds to an outstanding server ID.
checks.detects: Ping spoofers that fabricate keepalive IDs, disabler modes that corrupt the key so the server silently drops it, and duplicate-echo replay.
checks.variations: Hydro BadPacketsE flags keepalive IDs that were never sent and BadPacketsF flags a duplicate of the current ID; Azure BadPacketsG flags a keepalive arriving more than 550 ms after the last move packet; Frequency BadPacketsP and Artemis PingSpoofIdDupe and PingSpoofDuplicate do the same ID bookkeeping on their own packet wrappers.

checks.name: KeepAliveFrequency (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Limits the rate of keepalive replies and maintains the lastKeepAliveTime reference that the net and godmode checks use to separate real latency from timer abuse.
checks.how_it_works: The ProtocolLib KeepAliveAdapter records every incoming C00 reply with its ID shape and updates data.lastKeepAliveTime; the check itself buckets reply timestamps into a frequency bucket model and cancels when the first bucket exceeds 1, with modeled-boundary exceptions so two replies timestamped in the same millisecond do not flag. A startup delay after join and duplicate-ID handling suppress the false positives that join-time bursts would cause.
checks.detects: Keepalive floods, duplicate or spoofed keepalive spam, and disabler modes that fire extra echoes to reset server-side timing heuristics.
checks.variations: Fight GodMode reads lastKeepAliveTime with CheckUtils.guessKeepAliveTime as fallback; Artemis ConnectionPreProcessor and AntiHaxerman ConnectionTracker maintain equivalent per-player keepalive ping state that their timer and lag checks consume.

checks.name: TimerA (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Detects timer speed by measuring movement packet cadence against the 50 ms tick, gated on keepalive confirmation that the server tick actually ran.
checks.how_it_works: On each flying packet, computes the delay since the previous one, feeds it into a 20-sample MovingStats deviation model, and accumulates an allowance of +50 ms per expected tick minus the observed delay. The check only runs when the current server tick has a matching keepalive echo in ConnectionManager, so lagged or desynced connections are excluded. A persistent deviation under the 7.07 threshold with a positive allowance balance flags.
checks.detects: Timer cheats that raise the client game speed, and indirectly ping spoofing, because a spoofed low ping keeps the keepalive acceptance gate open.
checks.variations: Grim Timer and TimerLimit use the same balance concept with a packet-type whitelist that deliberately excludes keepalive from the count; FlopAC TimerA/B and Artemis TimerBalance, TimerGladUrBad and TimerReverse add statistical scoring; Azure Timer and TimerB average timer speed over a deque; TruthfulAC TimerA keeps a nanosecond timer balance; AntiHaxerman TimerA runs a balance system on the Artemis packet wrapper.

wiki_notes: 1.8.9 key is a plain int coded as VarInt (readVarIntFromBuffer/writeVarIntToBuffer), not a long.
PLAY serverbound 0x00; client echoes the S00 key and the server folds RTT into a ping average, ignoring mismatched keys.
Server issues S00 about once per second; a missing echo leads to read-timeout disconnect, not an instant kick.
MCP 1.8.9 C00PacketKeepAlive implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processKeepAlive; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: GuiDownloadTerrain.updateScreen sends new C00PacketKeepAlive (line 44) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/gui/GuiDownloadTerrain.java

packets.name: Login Start
packets.desc: Starts the login process by sending the player's GameProfile (username) to the server.

fields.name: profile
fields.desc: Player's GameProfile containing the username (UUID is null at this stage)

packets.notes: Sent immediately after C00Handshake (with state=LOGIN). The GameProfile has a username but the UUID is null — the server fills in the UUID from Mojang's auth servers and returns it in S02PacketLoginSuccess. This is the first step of the login handshake after the initial HANDSHAKING state.

writeup.p: C00PacketLoginStart is the first packet of the LOGIN state, sent immediately after C00Handshake with nextState=2. It carries a GameProfile whose username is the only meaningful field; the UUID is null at this stage and the server fills it in from the session service. The vanilla client fires it from three places: GuiConnecting on connect, Minecraft.java's direct networkmanager path, and RealmsConnect for realm joins. The server answers with S01PacketEncryptionRequest on online-mode servers or S02PacketLoginSuccess on offline-mode servers. Everything after this packet is gated on the server's decision in processLoginStart.

NetHandlerLoginServer.processLoginStart validates the currentLoginState is HELLO via Validate.validState, stores the profile, then branches on server.isServerInOnlineMode() and whether the channel is local. Online mode moves to KEY state and sends S01PacketEncryptionRequest; offline mode jumps straight to READY_TO_ACCEPT. The username arrives as a VarInt-length-prefixed UTF-8 string; the client enforces the 16-character limit at the login screen, and the packet itself does no re-validation beyond reading the string.

Three families in the corpus reference this packet. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 BlinkComponent list C00PacketLoginStart in a five-class exemption set that is returned untouched by the blink buffer. Spicy Blink, Fly and BackupFly use an identical three-way guard (C00PacketKeepAlive, C00Handshake, C00PacketLoginStart) in their EventSendPacket handlers so the handshake always flows while the module cancels everything else. LiquidSense Dev is the one client that rewrites the packet: MixinGuiConnecting overwrites the vanilla connect method and, when an MCLeaks alt session is active, sends C00PacketLoginStart with a GameProfile built from MCLeaks.getSession().getUsername() instead of the launcher profile. The 8 classic clients treat the packet as untouchable plumbing; the 1.8-era Gugustus NameSpoof pattern never reappears in this corpus.

The packet is sent before encryption, so the username is visible to any MITM during login, and on offline-mode servers the name is trust-on-first-use: impersonation is a server configuration weakness, not a packet bug. The MCLeaks variant in LiquidSense Dev reuses that trust model, since the swapped username is what the server stores on offline-mode joins. Client-side abuse is otherwise limited to cancellation, which stalls the login at HELLO until the server's connection timeout fires. The only real engineering concern for module authors is accidental swallowing: a blink module that buffers C00PacketLoginStart breaks every future join, which is exactly why both Rise's component and Spicy's modules hard-code the exemption.

implementation.overview: The login opener: username-only GameProfile sent right after the handshake. BlinkComponent (Rise 6.x) and Spicy's Blink/Fly/BackupFly exempt it from packet buffering so the handshake survives while they hold everything else; LiquidSense Dev's MixinGuiConnecting is the only corpus hit that rewrites the username, swapping in the MCLeaks alt profile when an alt session is active.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerLoginServer.processLoginStart: Validate.validState(HELLO), store loginGameProfile, then either send S01PacketEncryptionRequest and move to KEY (online mode, non-local channel) or move straight to READY_TO_ACCEPT (offline mode or local channel). No username validation beyond the wire read; the server trusts the client's login-screen limit of 16 chars.
implementation.protocol_notes: Sent in LOGIN state only, id 0x00. Single String field: VarInt length + UTF-8 bytes. UUID in the GameProfile is null until the server resolves it via the session service. State must be LOGIN after the C00Handshake; a C00PacketLoginStart in any other state is a protocol violation that the server's Validate check rejects.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat parses this packet: it carries no position, timing, or interaction data and the player entity does not exist yet. Serverside plugins and proxies (auth plugins, BungeeCord) consume the name for pre-auth bookkeeping, but nothing in the 8 clients interacts with that. The packet is a non-surface for flagging, which is why modules only need to avoid breaking it.

modules.name: BlinkComponent
modules.purpose: Exempt C00PacketLoginStart (and the other four pre-play serverbound packets) from blink buffering so the login handshake always reaches the server while blink is active.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketSendEvent listener at VERY_LOW priority returns without cancelling when the packet is C00Handshake, C00PacketLoginStart, C00PacketServerQuery, C01PacketPing or C01PacketEncryptionResponse. Any other packet is parked in the static queue and cancelled, unless it matches the per-module setExempt list. The queue flushes via PacketUtil.sendNoEvent when a C03PacketPlayer arrives, the player dies, or the world changes.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the packet is returned untouched, so wire behavior is identical to vanilla. The exemption exists purely to prevent self-inflicted login stalls, not to evade anything.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the byte-identical file at com/alan/clients/component/impl/player/BlinkComponent.java; both versions use the same five-class instanceof list and the same 100ms exemption window.

modules.name: Blink / Fly / BackupFly (login allowlist)
modules.purpose: Keep the handshake alive while the module cancels and buffers all other serverbound packets, so blink and Hypixel-mode fly cannot kill the login sequence.
modules.how_it_works: EventSendPacket pre handler returns early when the packet is C00PacketKeepAlive, C00Handshake or C00PacketLoginStart. Every other packet is added to a static ArrayList and cancelled. Blink flushes the queue through mc.getNetHandler().addToSendQueue on disable; Fly's Hypixel mode applies the same guard before rewriting C03PacketPlayer fields and parking packets in its own buffer.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat relevance: the guard only prevents the module from breaking its own connection. The interesting detail is that the exemption is identical across three modules, which suggests a shared template in Spicy's codebase.
modules.variations: Fly.java repeats the same three-way instanceof guard at lines 398, 818 and 1032 in its Hypixel mode, and BackupFly.java at lines 356 and 725; both additionally rewrite C03PacketPlayer on-ground/moving flags after the guard.

modules.name: MCLeaks / MixinGuiConnecting
modules.purpose: Swap the login GameProfile for the MCLeaks alt session so the server records the alt username instead of the launcher account.
modules.how_it_works: @Overwrite on GuiConnecting.connect reimplements the connect thread: it sends C00Handshake, then C00PacketLoginStart whose GameProfile is built from MCLeaks.getSession().getUsername() when MCLeaks.isAltActive() and from mc.getSession().getProfile() otherwise. A second @Inject at the C00PacketLoginStart NEW allocation that would do the same swap via networkManager.sendPacket sits commented out, leaving the overwrite as the live path.
modules.vanilla_hook: No event hook: a Mixin @Overwrite replaces the vanilla connect method body; the send goes through the raw NetworkManager.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat reads the login state; the swap matters only to the server's offline-mode name storage. The packet is sent before encryption, so the alt name is visible on the wire to any MITM.
modules.variations: Rise 6.x and Spicy only exempt the packet from buffering; LiquidSense Dev is the single corpus client that actually rewrites the profile field, and only when an MCLeaks alt is active.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent / EventSendPacket on the classic clients; Rise 6.x routes through its component system with @EventLink listeners. LiquidSense Dev hooks the send site itself via a mixin overwrite instead of the event bus.
implementation.client_variations: Rise uses a central BlinkComponent with an explicit class allowlist and sendNoEvent flushing. Spicy implements the guard inline in each module's EventSendPacket handler with instanceof casts on the raw Packet. LiquidSense Dev replaces the vanilla send site entirely and conditionally picks the GameProfile at construction time.

anticheat.overview: LoginStart is invisible to server-side anticheats: the player entity, world and timing state do not exist yet, and the packet carries only the username. The two corpus hits are packet-library plumbing: FlopAC ChannelHandlerAbstract and intave TinyProtocol both declare the PACKET_LOGIN_IN_START class constant and route it through their channel handlers, and intave's handleLoginStart dispatcher serves the plugin's own cloud-control channel, not a check on the Minecraft login packet. No anticheat flags anything on it.

wiki_notes: On offline-mode (authentication disabled) servers encryption is skipped entirely and Login Start is directly followed by Login Success.
The vanilla server derives offline-mode UUIDs as UUID version 3 of the string OfflinePlayer:<player name>, though the protocol itself accepts any UUID the server sends in Login Success.
MCP 1.8.9 C00PacketLoginStart implements Packet<INetHandlerLoginServer> dispatching to INetHandlerLoginServer.processLoginStart; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readStringFromBuffer.

packets.name: Status Request
packets.desc: Requests the server's status (MOTD, player count, favicon, protocol version). Empty packet with no payload.
encoding: Completely empty packet — just the 0x00 packet ID
packets.notes: Sent immediately after C00Handshake when the nextState is STATUS (1). The server responds with S00PacketServerInfo (JSON status). Used by the multiplayer server list screen (OldServerPinger.java).

writeup.p: C00PacketServerQuery is the STATUS-state request that opens the server-list ping exchange. It is a completely empty packet, just the 0x00 id. OldServerPinger sends it immediately after C00Handshake with nextState=1, and the server answers with S00PacketServerInfo carrying the JSON status blob (MOTD, version, player counts, favicon). RealmsServerStatusPinger uses the same packet for the realms screen. The exchange exists entirely outside gameplay: it runs while the server list is displayed and no world or player entity exists.

NetHandlerStatusServer.processServerQuery is a one-liner: it responds with S00PacketServerInfo(server.getServerStatusResponse()), and the status object is generated on demand by the dedicated server. There is no rate limiting, no state machine, and no validation beyond the handler dispatch. OldServerPinger sends the query on a fresh NetworkManager whose direction is already pinned to the STATUS state by the handshake, so any packet other than S00PacketServerInfo or S01PacketPong on the reply side closes the connection as a protocol error.

Only Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 BlinkComponent reference this packet, and only to exempt it from blink buffering, exactly like C00PacketLoginStart. No exploit module in the 8 clients sends or mutates it. The status query is invisible to gameplay-oriented modules because their event buses are wired to play-state packets and their logic assumes a loaded world. Spicy's Bhop.java carries a C00PacketServerQuery import with no usage anywhere in the file, a dead import that does not count as a module hit.

The abusive use of this packet is server scanning: flood C00PacketServerQuery over many connections to enumerate hosts or measure their response latency. None of the 8 clients ships such a scanner, and the STATUS state is not even reachable from module code in most of them because the event system only fires packet events after world join. The practical consequence is that this packet is a non-surface in the corpus: the only code touching it is the defensive exemption in BlinkComponent.

implementation.overview: The empty STATUS-state opener for the server-list ping. No module in the 8 clients sends or mutates it; the only corpus hit is BlinkComponent's exemption list, which keeps the packet flowing while blink buffers everything else. Spicy Bhop's import is dead code.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerStatusServer.processServerQuery responds immediately with S00PacketServerInfo(this.server.getServerStatusResponse()). No rate limit, no state validation, no per-player tracking: the status is generated fresh for every query and the connection is expected to be closed by the client pinger afterwards.
implementation.protocol_notes: STATUS state only, id 0x00, zero payload bytes. Must follow a C00Handshake with nextState=1. The server replies S00PacketServerInfo; the client pinger then sends C01PacketPing and waits for S01PacketPong before closing. RealmsServerStatusPinger sends the same query on realm connections. Sending it in any other state fails protocol validation at the handler dispatch.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures this packet: there is no player, no world, and no timing value the server folds into anything persistent. Status queries are a reflection/scanning surface for server owners (they reveal MOTD and player counts to anyone), but that is a server exposure, not a client module concern. The 8 clients contain no scanner, so the packet never appears in their gameplay traffic.

modules.name: BlinkComponent
modules.purpose: Exempt C00PacketServerQuery from blink buffering so the server-list ping still completes while the blink queue is armed.
modules.how_it_works: The PacketSendEvent listener returns early for a hard-coded list of pre-play packets that includes C00PacketServerQuery alongside C00Handshake, C00PacketLoginStart, C01PacketPing and C01PacketEncryptionResponse. The packet is never parked in the blink queue, so OldServerPinger's query reaches the wire even when blinking is on.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the packet is passed through unmodified. The only observable effect is that the server list still works while blink is enabled.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 is byte-identical. No other client in the corpus touches this packet with real code; Spicy's Bhop.java has an unused import only.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent in Rise 6.x BlinkComponent; no other client wires the STATUS state into its event bus.
implementation.client_variations: Classic clients (Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity) never reference this packet outside the bundled vanilla OldServerPinger, so their event systems do not even see STATUS-state packets.

anticheat.overview: The status query is a zero-payload packet that arrives before login, so no anticheat check touches it. The corpus contains only declarations: FlopAC NMSObject and Packet define the START constant for PacketStatusInStart, and Artemis wraps it as PacketStatusClientStart in its packet library. Server-list scanners are the only abuse surface, and that is a proxy-level concern, not a check domain.

wiki_notes: The status can only be requested once, immediately after the handshake and before any ping; the server will not respond otherwise.
A client interested only in latency may skip the status request entirely and send a Ping Request instead.
MCP 1.8.9 C00PacketServerQuery implements Packet<INetHandlerStatusServer> dispatching to INetHandlerStatusServer.processServerQuery; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via .

1.8.9 callers: OldServerPinger.onDisconnect sends new C00PacketServerQuery (line 177) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/network/OldServerPinger.java

packets.name: Chat Message
packets.desc: Sends a chat message or command from the client to the server.

fields.name: message
fields.desc: The chat message or command (commands start with /)

writeup.p: The serverbound chat packet carries one String message (max 100 chars client-side, 32767 bytes wire-side). The vanilla client sends it through EntityPlayerSP.sendChatMessage, which runs the client command parser first: any message starting with '/' is a command, otherwise a chat packet is sent. The server's processChatMessage in NetHandlerPlayServer validates length, checks mute/cooldown state, and feeds the message to the server command dispatcher or chat pipeline. For modules this is the single most-intercepted serverbound packet: it is how command systems, spammers, AutoGG, chat bypasses, and login helpers all move data to the server.

NetHandlerPlayServer.processChatMessage: rejects empty messages, trims whitespace, applies the chat cooldown (10 ticks between messages for regular players), and routes to the command handler if the message starts with '/'. The server-side chat pipeline then runs the message through filters and broadcasts. Client-side, the interesting hook is EntityPlayerSP.sendChatMessage: client commands starting with '/' never become packets, which is why clients that want dot-prefixed commands must intercept the packet itself.

Five families in the 8 clients. (1) Command systems: Memeware and Nekoware Commands.java intercept every C01, cancel it if the message starts with '.', and dispatch to client-side commands, so dot-commands never reach the server. (2) Chat bypasses: Rise 5.99/6.2.4 ChatBypass rewrites the message with invisible/combining characters to dodge filter plugins. (3) Auto-login: Rise 5.99 AutoAuthme cancels /register and /login packets and sends the stored credentials itself. (4) Auto-spam: Sigma AutoGG, Rise AutoGroomer/AutoHypixel, Memeware Spammer/DeathInsult send canned messages. (5) Client utility: ChatUtil.sendChat_NoFilter in Sigma sends C01 directly, bypassing the vanilla sendChatMessage command parsing. November Recode 2.0 dominates the new-client side of this packet: CommandExecutor cancels dot-prefixed messages and dispatches client commands, IRCChatModule redirects '#'-prefixed messages to an IRC socket, AutoPlayModule re-sends the win or loss click command, and PhaseModule explicitly exempts C01 from its cage-phase packet buffer. LiquidSense Dev has no chat module: its only C01 reference is an unused import in AntiBot.java.

The chat cooldown is client-enforced on most servers; the packet itself carries no timestamp, so sending faster than the cooldown is only detectable server-side by counting packets, which is why spam modules are trivially flagged. The real depth is in rewriting: filter-bypass via Unicode combining characters (Rise's char[] table), and the fact that the server cannot tell a human-typed message from a packet-injected one. ChatBypass is also a privacy edge: it proves the client can rewrite what the user typed before it leaves the machine.

implementation.overview: The most-intercepted serverbound packet in the 8 clients. Command systems cancel it for dot-prefixed client commands, chat bypasses rewrite the payload with Unicode tricks, AutoAuthme hijacks /login and /register, and a fleet of AutoGG/Spammer/Groomer modules inject canned messages. Everything funnels through one String field and one event.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerPlayServer.processChatMessage: trims the message, rejects it if empty or over-length, enforces the player's chat cooldown (10 ticks), then routes to the command dispatcher when the message starts with '/'. A serverbound chat packet can never carry a client-side command, so dot-prefix command systems must intercept before the packet leaves the client.
implementation.protocol_notes: Single String field: VarInt length prefix + UTF-8 bytes, 32767 byte cap on the wire; the vanilla client GUI enforces 100 chars. Sent in PLAY state only. Messages are unencrypted-in-transit only before TLS; in practice the whole stream is encrypted (after C01PacketEncryptionResponse).
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats do not flag chat packets themselves; anti-spam and filter plugins do, and they operate purely on content and rate. The detectable surface is the rate: spam modules sending 20+ messages/second trip cooldown and mute systems instantly. Unicode-bypass text is caught by plugin-side normalization (strip combining marks, then compare). The client command hijack (cancelling C01 for dot-commands) is invisible to the server because the packet never exists.

modules.name: Commands (client command system)
modules.purpose: Intercept chat packets so dot-prefixed messages dispatch to client commands instead of the server.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketOutEvent handler checks every C01: if the message starts with the prefix ('.'), cancel the packet and run the local command dispatcher. Memeware's implementation splits the message on whitespace, strips the prefix, lowercases the first token, and switches over command names (bind, etc.). The 'say' flag lets the user force a message through to the server when needed.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Invisible to the server: the cancelled packet never exists. The only visible effect is that dot-messages never appear in chat, which looks like a client chat filter to observers.
modules.variations: Nekoware v1 private ships the same pattern in its own Commands.java; both clients also expose ChatUtil.printChat for local feedback.

modules.name: ChatBypass
modules.purpose: Rewrite outgoing non-command messages so server filter plugins cannot match banned words.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketSendEvent, if the packet is C01 and the message does not start with '/', rebuild the string: for every character append the character plus a random invisible Unicode character (from a ~500-entry table of combining/zero-width chars), repeated three times. The Hypixel mode uses a fixed combining char 'ˌ'. The rewritten packet replaces the original via event.setPacket.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketSendEvent; mutates the packet and re-sets it on the event.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Filter plugins that strip combining characters before matching defeat the Normal mode; the Hypixel mode survives because the server-side chat renderer collapses the combining char visually. No anti-cheat flags this as movement/combat abuse.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4 ships the same module in its module/impl/other tree; Rise 6.1.30 does not reference C01PacketChatMessage in ChatBypass form.

modules.name: AutoAuthme
modules.purpose: Automate /register and /login on auth-me servers using stored credentials.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketSendEvent, if not yet logged in and the outgoing message is exactly /register or /login, cancel the packet and fire the stored credentials via the module's own send path. Credentials come from a per-server login file loaded at startup.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Sending credentials faster than a human can type is the only tell; most auth-me servers do not rate-limit login packets. The cancelled /register and /login packets never reach the server, so the server never sees the double-login attempt.
modules.variations: Rise 6.x keeps the feature in other forms (AutoGroomer, AutoHypixel reference C01 in 6.1.30/6.2.4).

modules.name: AutoGG / AutoGroomer / Spammer
modules.purpose: Inject canned messages after events (game end, kill) or on a timer.
modules.how_it_works: Sigma AutoGG listens for death/win indicators (S02PacketChat patterns) and calls ChatUtil.sendChat("gg"). Sigma's ChatUtil has two paths: sendChat goes through vanilla sendChatMessage (client command parsing applies), while sendChat_NoFilter pushes a C01PacketChatMessage straight into the send queue, bypassing the client command parser. Rise's AutoGroomer and AutoHypixel send their own scripted message sequences on world join.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketSendEvent on other modules; ChatUtil call from AutoGG's chat receive handler.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat flags 'gg'. The interesting engineering detail is sendChat vs sendChat_NoFilter: going through sendChatMessage means a message starting with '.' would be eaten by the client command system, so auto-message modules use the NoFilter path to guarantee delivery.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99/6.x AutoGroomer and AutoHypixel; Memeware 7.3 Spammer and DeathInsult; Sigma Sigmeme command injects a random meme phrase via a raw C01.

modules.name: CommandExecutor (dot-command dispatch)
modules.purpose: Intercept every C01 and dispatch dot-prefixed messages to the client command registry, so client commands never reach the server.
modules.how_it_works: The EventPacket.Out listener checks each C01; messages not starting with '.' pass through untouched. Dot messages are cancelled, trimmed, split on whitespace, and the first token is looked up in the CommandRegistry; dispatch runs with the remaining args, and syntax and argument exceptions are printed to chat. A command not found prints an error instead of sending the message.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Invisible to the server: the cancelled packet never exists on the wire. The registry-based dispatch with exception reporting plays the same role as Memeware's Commands switch, but organized as a standalone executor class subscribed to the bus.
modules.variations: November also ships IRCChatModule and AutoPlayModule on the same C01 surface; the eight classic clients implement command dispatch as a module, November as a separate executor.

modules.name: IRCChatModule (IRC bridge)
modules.purpose: Redirect messages starting with '#' out of the game chat and into November's private IRC socket.
modules.how_it_works: The EventPacket.Out handler matches C01, and when the message starts with '#', cancels the packet and sends the substring after the prefix through November.socket().sendIrcChat. The enable message tells the user the prefix. Messages without the prefix pass through untouched.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling before the wire means the IRC traffic is invisible to the server; the module is a chat utility, not an exploit, and carries no anti-cheat surface.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus bridges chat packets to an external IRC socket; Sigma's Sigmeme command is the closest (injects a random meme as a raw C01).

modules.name: AutoPlayModule (auto /play)
modules.purpose: Automatically send the next-game command after a loss or win by replaying the chat click-event command as a C01.
modules.how_it_works: The EventPacket.In handler scans S02 chat for the 'You won! Want to play again?' or 'You died!' line, walks the chat component siblings for a RUN_COMMAND click event, and stores its value. On EventUpdate, once the delay elapses, the stored command is queued as a fresh C01 via addToSendQueueSilent. BLOCKS_MC mode instead finds a paper item in the hotbar and sends C09 held-item change plus C08 placement.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The replayed command arrives after a human-like delay; sending it silently bypasses the client command parser so a '/play ...' value is never eaten client-side. No anti-cheat surface.
modules.variations: This is the auto-command family that Sigma's AutoGG and Rise's AutoHypixel cover in the classic clients; November's version extracts the exact RUN_COMMAND value from the chat component tree.

modules.name: PhaseModule (cage phase buffer)
modules.purpose: While phasing through the glass cage, buffer every outgoing packet except C01 chat, so the chat stream stays live during the phase.
modules.how_it_works: CAGE_PHASE mode removes the glass block client-side when the player stands on BlockGlass with 20 or more ticks since the last S08 setback, then the EventPacket.Out handler cancels and queues every packet while cagePhasing is true, with an explicit early return for C01PacketChatMessage so chat always passes. On disable the queue is drained via addToSendQueueSilent and the glass block is restored from the saved state.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.Out (buffer with C01 exemption), EventPacket.In (S08 setback counter, S02 cage messages), EventUpdate (state machine).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The C01 exemption is the corpus hit: chat is deliberately not buffered because a missing chat stream during the phase would look dead to the server; everything else is held and replayed in order.
modules.variations: November's phase buffers the whole stream and restores the block client-side; the classic clients' Phase modules use teleport or collision edits instead.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent is universal. The vanilla send path is EntityPlayerSP.sendChatMessage; modules that want to bypass client-side command parsing construct C01 directly.
implementation.client_variations: Memeware/Nekoware mutate or cancel the packet inside the event. Rise 5.99/6.x call event.setPacket to swap in a rewritten packet. Sigma routes through ChatUtil helpers so the rest of the client never touches packet construction. November Recode 2.0 intercepts C01 on EventPacket.Out across CommandExecutor, IRCChatModule, AutoPlayModule and PhaseModule, and queues generated chat via addToSendQueueSilent; LuaEventPacket maps C01 to id 0x01. LiquidSense Dev's only C01 reference is an unused import in AntiBot.java, whose addChatMessage calls are client-side chat text, so it contributes no chat packet module.

anticheat.overview: The chat message packet carries every chat line and command the player types, which makes it the input surface for chat spam, captcha systems and text-based exploit attempts. Server-side anticheats split into two families: event-based chat systems that hook the Bukkit chat pipeline, and raw packet checks that validate the message bytes before the server processes them. The packet also carries the commands that log4j and similar exploits are delivered through, so payload scanning of chat is a standard mitigation.

checks.name: ChatB (Grim)
checks.purpose: Rejects chat messages and commands that the vanilla server would never accept, closing the spigot antispam bypass.
checks.how_it_works: PreViaPacketReceiveListener that decodes CHAT_MESSAGE, CHAT_COMMAND and CHAT_COMMAND_UNSIGNED. A chat message is invalid if it is empty, has leading or trailing whitespace, or starts with / on 1.19+ where commands have their own packet. Commands are invalid if they carry trailing or surrounding whitespace. On flag it cancels the packet and calls onPacketCancel so downstream state stays consistent. The comment notes click-event edge cases can false flag on badly configured servers.
checks.detects: Empty or whitespace-padded chat messages, spigot antispam bypasses that smuggle text via formatting, and malformed command packets.
checks.variations: BetterAnticheat ImpossibleMessageCheck flags empty and space-prefixed messages, Photon ImpossibleChat flags chat while sprinting or in an inventory, and Kauri Log4J scans the message for JNDI syntax.

checks.name: ChatListener (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: The classic chat pipeline: captcha, text spam, command spam, relog and login-rate checks dispatched from the Bukkit chat events.
checks.how_it_works: CheckListener that wires the Captcha, Commands, Logins, Text and Relog checks and registers ChatConfig and ChatData. AsyncPlayerChatEvent at LOWEST priority runs the Text check and cancels spam; PlayerCommandPreprocessEvent at LOWEST runs the command checks with left-trimmed messages and command alias resolution; PlayerLoginEvent runs captcha reset, fast relog and login-rate checks. It also records teleport-like commands for the net checks and maintains prefix trees for ignored and chat-handled commands.
checks.detects: Chat spam, command spam, captcha evasion, fast re-logging and login flooding.
checks.variations: Photon ImpossibleChat runs on AsyncPlayerChatEvent too, Grim and BetterAnticheat validate the raw packet instead, and Kauri filters JNDI patterns from the chat stream.

checks.name: ImpossibleMessageCheck (BetterAnticheat)
checks.purpose: Flags chat messages that cannot exist: fully empty or space-only strings and messages starting with a space.
checks.how_it_works: handleReceivePlayPacket reads WrapperPlayClientChatMessage and checks the raw string: a trim that is empty fails with the code emp, a leading space fails with the code spc. Failures are recorded through the check base with the short codes as data.
checks.detects: Empty chat packets and space-prefixed messages used to bypass spam filters.
checks.variations: Grim ChatB also requires the message to be trim-equal and rejects / prefixes on modern versions; Photon ImpossibleChat covers the behavioral side instead.

checks.name: Log4J (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Scans chat messages for the JNDI lookup syntax used by the log4j exploit and cancels the packet.
checks.how_it_works: WCancellable bound to WrapperPlayClientChatMessage. It compiles the pattern \$\{.*} and, if the whole message matches, flags 'Tried to use JNDI exploit' and returns true to cancel; otherwise it debug-logs the message and lets it through.
checks.detects: Log4Shell payloads delivered through chat.
checks.variations: Intave filters the same syntax in its CommandFilter and Log4JExploitFilter modules; Grim and BetterAnticheat validate chat shape rather than content.

checks.name: ImpossibleChat (Photon)
checks.purpose: Flags chat sent while the player is in a state where the client physically cannot be chatting: sprinting, sneaking, blocking, dead, or inside a long-open inventory.
checks.how_it_works: EventListener on AsyncPlayerChatEvent. If the user is sprinting, sneaking, blocking, dead, or has had an inventory open for over a second, it flags with +25 VL and cancels the event at the configured cancel VL (default 75). Violation management decays 25 VL every 600 ms.
checks.detects: Chat modules that send messages while the client is in an impossible state, and inventory-based chat bypasses.
checks.variations: Grim ChatC flags moving while chatting from the raw packet stream; NoCheatPlus runs its Text and Captcha checks on the same event.

wiki_notes: The server rebroadcasts an accepted chat message to all players that have chat enabled, including the player that sent it.
MCP 1.8.9 C01PacketChatMessage implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processChatMessage; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readStringFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerSP.sendChatMessage sends new C01PacketChatMessage (line 298): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/entity/EntityPlayerSP.java

packets.name: Encryption Response
packets.desc: Responds to the server's encryption request with the shared secret (RSA-encrypted with the server's public key) and verify token.

fields.name: sharedSecret
fields.desc: Encrypted shared secret (AES key encrypted with server's RSA public key)

fields.name: verifyToken
fields.desc: Encrypted verify token (random challenge encrypted with server's RSA public key)

encoding: Encrypted with server's RSA public key
Encrypted with server's RSA public key

writeup.p: C01PacketEncryptionResponse is the second LOGIN-state packet and the last plaintext packet on the connection. The client generates a random AES secret, RSA-encrypts it together with the verify token from S01PacketEncryptionRequest using the server's public key, and sends both byte arrays. The server decrypts with its private key, checks the nonce, and enables symmetric AES encryption on the channel from that point on. In 1.8.9 this is where the session service join happens: the server hashes server id, public key and secret, and calls hasJoinedServer to resolve the profile UUID.

NetHandlerLoginServer.processEncryptionResponse validates the state is KEY, decrypts the verify token with the private key, and throws IllegalStateException('Invalid nonce!') unless it matches the stored field_147330_e. It then stores the secret key, enables encryption on the NetworkManager, and spawns a 'User Authenticator' thread that computes the server-id hash and calls getMinecraftSessionService().hasJoinedServer. A null profile closes with 'Failed to verify username!'; a success moves to READY_TO_ACCEPT and sends S02PacketLoginSuccess.

Two clients reference this packet, for opposite reasons. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 BlinkComponent list it in the pre-play exemption set, again as a buffering exemption: blink must not hold it because the server sits in KEY state until encryption is enabled. LiquidSense Dev reimplements the send itself: MixinNetHandlerLoginClient intercepts S01PacketEncryptionRequest and calls ClientUtils.sendEncryption, which builds C01PacketEncryptionResponse and sends it with a callback that enables encryption on the NetworkManager. No module in the corpus cancels, mutates or replays the packet, and there is no field worth spoofing: the nonce is server-issued and RSA-protected, so a tampered secret simply fails the nonce check or produces garbage decryption server-side. The 8 classic clients treat encryption as untouchable infrastructure; their disablers and ping spoofers all operate in the PLAY state where the stream is already encrypted.

The genuine abuse vector lives on the other side of the exchange: a malicious server can present its own RSA key in S01PacketEncryptionRequest and the client will happily encrypt the session to it, enabling MITM for session hijacking. That is a phishing problem, not a packet-level one, and no module in the corpus touches either side. The only client-side interaction is defensive: blink must not buffer this packet, because holding it would leave the server waiting in KEY state until the login timeout.

implementation.overview: The RSA handshake closer: client sends encrypted AES secret plus verify token, server nonce-checks and enables symmetric encryption. Corpus hits are Rise 6.x BlinkComponent's exemption and LiquidSense Dev's mixin-driven reimplementation of the send; no module cancels or spoofs it because there is nothing to gain and everything to lose.
implementation.server_handling: processEncryptionResponse: Validate.validState(KEY), decrypt verify token with the private key and compare against the stored nonce (throw on mismatch), store the AES secret, enable encryption on the channel, then authenticate asynchronously via hasJoinedServer with the server-id hash. Failures close the connection with 'Failed to verify username!'.
implementation.protocol_notes: LOGIN state, id 0x01. Two VarInt-length-prefixed byte arrays: the RSA-encrypted AES secret and the RSA-encrypted verify token, both PKCS1-padded by CryptManager. Must follow S01PacketEncryptionRequest; sending it without a pending KEY state throws. Immediately after this packet the entire stream switches to AES/CFB8, so every later packet is opaque on the wire.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not an anti-cheat surface at all: no gameplay data, no timing hooks, and the exchange is protected by the server's own nonce. Proxy setups (BungeeCord with forced hosts) use the secret to key their own encryption layer, but nothing in the 8 clients interacts with that. The practical flagging surface is zero, which is why only BlinkComponent's defensive exemption appears in the corpus.

modules.name: BlinkComponent
modules.purpose: Exempt C01PacketEncryptionResponse from blink buffering so the encryption exchange always completes and the connection actually becomes encrypted.
modules.how_it_works: The PacketSendEvent listener's hard-coded pre-play exemption list includes C01PacketEncryptionResponse; the packet returns untouched and is never parked in the blink queue, so the login continues to the READY_TO_ACCEPT state normally.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the packet is untouched. The exemption is structural, keeping blink out of the login state machine entirely.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 is byte-identical. No other client in the corpus references this packet from module code.

modules.name: ClientUtils (encryption helper)
modules.purpose: Centralize the encryption handshake send so the login mixin can enable AES on the channel without duplicating the vanilla NetHandlerLoginClient logic.
modules.how_it_works: sendEncryption(networkManager, secretKey, publicKey, encryptionRequest) builds the C01PacketEncryptionResponse from the already-generated AES secret, the server's RSA public key and the request's verify token, sends it through networkManager.sendPacket and enables encryption on the same manager inside the completion callback. The static helper is called from MixinNetHandlerLoginClient's intercept of S01PacketEncryptionRequest.
modules.vanilla_hook: No event hook: a mixin on NetHandlerLoginClient calls the static utility; the packet goes through the raw NetworkManager with a GenericFutureListener callback.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the wire payload is what vanilla sends. The mixin exists to route the flow through LiquidBounce's utility layer, not to alter the handshake.
modules.variations: Rise 6.x only exempts the packet from blink buffering; LiquidSense Dev is the one corpus client that constructs and sends it outside the vanilla login handler.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent in Rise 6.x BlinkComponent; LiquidSense Dev hooks the login handler via mixin instead of the event bus.
implementation.client_variations: All other clients leave C01PacketEncryptionResponse to the bundled vanilla NetHandlerLoginClient, which sends it inside a GenericFutureListener callback after the secret key generation; LiquidSense Dev diverts it through ClientUtils.sendEncryption from its login mixin.

anticheat.overview: The encryption response closes the RSA handshake and is the last plaintext packet on the connection, so anticheats never flag it. Corpus hits are registrations: Negativity lists ENCRYPTION_BEGIN_IN and ENCRYPTION_BEGIN_OUT in its PacketType enum, Artemis maps PacketLoginClientEncryptionBegin in its PacketRepository, and intave's ServerboundConfirmEncryption belongs to Intave's own cloud-control channel with its own cipher pipeline, not to the Minecraft login exchange. After this packet the stream is AES-encrypted and every later anticheat sees ciphertext.

wiki_notes: LOGIN serverbound 0x01; two VarInt-length byte arrays: RSA-encrypted AES secret plus encrypted verify token.
Server decrypts with its private key, checks the nonce, then enables AES/CFB8 so later traffic is opaque.
Valid only in KEY state after S01; a bad nonce or failed auth closes the connection instead of joining.

MCP 1.8.9 C01PacketEncryptionResponse implements Packet<INetHandlerLoginServer> dispatching to INetHandlerLoginServer.processEncryptionResponse; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByteArray.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerLoginClient.handleEncryptionRequest sends new C01PacketEncryptionResponse (line 86): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/network/NetHandlerLoginClient.java

packets.name: Ping
packets.desc: Sends a client-side timestamp for the server to echo back. The client calculates round-trip latency from the difference.
packets.notes: Sent after receiving S00PacketServerInfo. The server echoes the exact same long value in S01PacketPong. The client computes latency as receiveTime - sentTime.

writeup.p: C01PacketPing is the STATUS-state latency probe. After S00PacketServerInfo arrives, OldServerPinger sends it with a single long field, and the server echoes the exact value back in S01PacketPong. The client computes the row latency as receiveTime minus sentTime, averages it over the last few samples, and displays it in the server list. RealmsServerStatusPinger sends the same packet with Realms.currentTimeMillis() on realm connections. This is the only ping in the protocol that exists outside the PLAY state; the tab-list ping later comes from the C00/S00 keepalive pair.

NetHandlerStatusServer.processPing is a pure echo: it sends S01PacketPong(packetIn.getClientTime()) with no transformation and no state change. OldServerPinger tracks a counter (field_175092_e) incremented per ping cycle and sends C01PacketPing with it; the pong handler then computes the round-trip against the stored send time. The packet's long value is opaque to the server: it never reads it beyond echoing, which is why the value can be any client-chosen timestamp.

Only Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 BlinkComponent reference C01PacketPing, in the same pre-play exemption list as the other handshake packets. No ping-spoof module in the 8 clients targets it: every PingSpoof implementation operates on C00PacketKeepAlive in the PLAY state, where the server folds the round-trip into the tab-list ping EMA. Spoofing the STATUS ping would only fake the user's own server-list readout, which is a purely local number, so no module bothers. The corpus confirms the packet is otherwise untouched vanilla plumbing.

There is no meaningful exploit surface. The value is client-chosen and server-echoed, so a client could lie about its own latency, but the result is displayed only to itself on the multiplayer screen and vanishes on join. Server scanners could skip the ping to save a round-trip per host, but none of the 8 clients implements one. The only code interaction is defensive: BlinkComponent must not buffer this packet, or the pinger's latency sample would stall and the server row would show a stale or zero ping.

implementation.overview: The STATUS-state latency probe: client sends an arbitrary long, server echoes it, client measures the round-trip for the server list. No module spoofs it, because the result is a local display value; the sole corpus hit is BlinkComponent's exemption list.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerStatusServer.processPing sends S01PacketPong with the same long value, no validation, no rate limiting, no state change. The status handler is stateless by design: it answers queries and pings and expects the client to close the connection.
implementation.protocol_notes: STATUS state, id 0x01, one 8-byte long. Must follow C00PacketServerQuery and S00PacketServerInfo. The server never interprets the value; it is a client-chosen timestamp (OldServerPinger uses a counter, RealmsServerStatusPinger uses currentTimeMillis). The same field name family (C01) collides with the LOGIN-state C01PacketEncryptionResponse and the PLAY-state C01PacketChatMessage, so id-based dispatch depends entirely on the connection state.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures the STATUS ping: it carries no player identity, no timing that persists, and no gameplay state. Anti-cheat plugins only ever see PLAY-state traffic. The only consumers are the server-list UI and reflection tools, neither of which is a flagging surface.

modules.name: BlinkComponent
modules.purpose: Exempt C01PacketPing from blink buffering so the server-list latency sample completes while blink is armed.
modules.how_it_works: The hard-coded pre-play exemption list includes C01PacketPing alongside C00Handshake, C00PacketLoginStart, C00PacketServerQuery and C01PacketEncryptionResponse; the PacketSendEvent listener returns before the blink queue logic, so the ping always reaches the wire.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: passed through unmodified; the STATUS exchange is invisible to anti-cheats by construction.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 is byte-identical. No other client in the corpus has a module-level reference.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent in Rise 6.x BlinkComponent only.
implementation.client_variations: All other clients use the bundled vanilla OldServerPinger/RealmsServerStatusPinger, which send C01PacketPing directly on the status NetworkManager with no module involvement.

anticheat.overview: The status ping is a pure echo probe used by the server list, and the corpus index is effectively empty of checks: FlopAC defines the PING constant for PacketStatusInPing in NMSObject and Packet, and Artemis wraps it as PacketStatusClientPing. The value is client-chosen and server-echoed for a local display, so no anticheat measures it. Anti-cheat timing only exists in the play state, through the C00 keepalive pair.

wiki_notes: STATUS serverbound 0x01 with one 8-byte long clientTime; server echoes it verbatim in S01 pong.
Value is opaque to the server; vanilla sends currentTimeMillis or a counter and measures list latency locally.
Server-list probe only; shares id 0x01 with LOGIN encryption and PLAY chat, routed by connection state.
MCP 1.8.9 C01PacketPing implements Packet<INetHandlerStatusServer> dispatching to INetHandlerStatusServer.processPing; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readLong.
1.8.9 callers: OldServerPinger.? sends new C01PacketPing (line 151) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/network/OldServerPinger.java

packets.name: Use Entity
packets.desc: Player interacts with (attacks or right-clicks) an entity.

fields.name: hitVec
fields.desc: Target position on the entity (for INTERACT_AT)

packets.notes: ATTACK sends damage to the target entity. INTERACT opens inventory/rides. INTERACT_AT is for hitting specific entity hitboxes (like Armor Stand limbs).

writeup.p: C02PacketUseEntity is the only serverbound channel in 1.8.9 by which the client tells the server it interacted with an entity. The wire form is a VarInt entityId, a VarInt enum action (INTERACT, ATTACK, INTERACT_AT) and, for INTERACT_AT only, three floats for the hit position on the target. Every attack, mount, item-frame edit and armor-stand manipulation goes through it. Because the packet carries no position, rotation or timestamp, the server validates it purely against its own copy of player and entity state, which is exactly what makes it trivial to spoof from a modified client.

NetHandlerPlayServer.processUseEntity resolves the target from the packet's entity id, then enforces a distance gate: squared distance must be under 36.0 (6 blocks) when the target is visible to the player, or 9.0 (3 blocks) when it is not. INTERACT routes to playerEntity.interactWith, INTERACT_AT to the per-vector entity handler, and ATTACK first kicks the player for targeting EntityItem, EntityXPOrb, EntityArrow or self ("Attempting to attack an invalid entity"), then calls attackTargetEntityWithCurrentItem. There is no rate limit and no attack-cooldown validation; the 1.8.9 swing cooldown is enforced only client-side in PlayerControllerMP and EntityPlayerSP.

All eight clients ship combat modules that live on this packet. Aura and KillAura variants send ATTACK in every client: Memeware and Nekoware split Single/Multi/Hypixel/Switch auras, Rise 5.99 and 6.x use Aura and KillAura, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity each have Killaura modules. Criticals exists in Memeware, Nekoware, Rise 5.99, Sigma and Spicy, injecting C04 offset packets before the ATTACK. TPAura and TeleportAura in Memeware, Rise 5.99, Rise 6.x and Tenacity walk the server-side player to the target before attacking. ComboOneHit (Rise 5.99 and 6.x) floods ATTACK packets, and Spicy's TriggerBot and Wtap round out the combat surface. Freecam (Rise), Infinite (Rise 5.99), WorldGuardRegen, GodMode and AntiFireBall (Rise 6.x), PlayerHacks (Rise 5.99) and Sigma's AntiFreeze all filter or forge C02 as a secondary effect. The two new research clients extend the same surface. November Recode 2.0 ships KillAuraModule and WTapModule on its EventPacket bus: the aura queues C02 ATTACK directly when Keep Sprint is enabled and filters outgoing ATTACK packets in its WATCHDOG autoblock mode, and the wtap module reacts to outgoing attacks with sprint resets. LiquidSense Dev contributes the Hypixel movement family (HYTFly, HYTHighJump, HYTLongJump, HYTRun) which cancels and buffers C02 inside a blink window, plus the LiquidBounce Blink and Fly Zoom modes that hold C02 and release it with the rest of the buffer.

The server trusts three things: the entity id, the distance, and the action. Attack rate is unbounded, so ComboOneHit's 50-1000 packet bursts are legal wire traffic. INTERACT_AT's hitVec is client-chosen and unvalidated, which is why Sigma and Spicy Killaura spam INTERACT_AT with random hitVecs plus INTERACT as a disabler sequence, and why Rise 5.99's BedwarsTP can mount entities from outside reach. Friend protection is purely a client courtesy: Rise 5.99's Aura consults its friends list, Sigma's Killaura checks FriendManager.isFriend, Tenacity's KillAuraModule checks FriendCommand.isFriend, but nothing server-side knows about friends, so a client that skips the check can hit anyone. Anti-cheats counter with reach math, attack-rate caps, rotation-motion correlation, and ghost-interact detection.

implementation.overview: The combat funnel of 1.8.9: a VarInt entity id and an action enum are all the server needs to apply damage. KillAura family targets and attacks, Criticals injects C04 fall arcs ahead of the ATTACK, TPAura teleports the server-side player to the target first, ComboOneHit floods the channel, and TriggerBot/Wtap automate the last bits of the attack loop. Friend protection exists only inside the aura target filters, never as a standalone module, across the 8 clients.
implementation.server_handling: processUseEntity runs on the main thread via PacketThreadUtil and calls markPlayerActive, which resets the idle-kick timer. The entity lookup uses packetIn.getEntityFromWorld(worldServerForDimension(player.dimension)). Distance is checked as squared distance: 36.0 when canEntityBeSeen passes, 9.0 otherwise, with no horizontal/vertical split and no per-axis clamp. For ATTACK the invalid-target kick fires before any damage is dealt. There is no vanilla per-tick attack limit: the swing cooldown and the 20-tick hit cooldown live in client-side code (PlayerControllerMP.attackEntity and EntityPlayer.attackEntityAsMob), so a forged client can emit arbitrarily many attacks per tick and the server will process them all.
implementation.protocol_notes: The action is serialized with readEnumValue/writeEnumValue, a VarInt ordinal (0=INTERACT, 1=ATTACK, 2=INTERACT_AT). INTERACT_AT adds three floats read after the enum; the other two actions carry no payload, so the packet length varies by action. The Entity-based constructors resolve the entity id at construction time (entity.getEntityId), so modules that queue C02 after the target dies or unloads send a stale id that the server resolves to null and silently ignores. The Vec3 constructor always selects INTERACT_AT. The packet is registered at 0x02 in the SERVERBOUND play state table.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: NCP flags reach by comparing the server-side player position against the target at ATTACK time and tracks hit rates per second; ComboOneHit-style floods are its primary target. Rotation-aware checks flag attacks whose preceding C05/C06 rotation does not point at the target, which is why Memeware-style auras that send ATTACK without a rotation packet get flagged on newer anti-cheats while rotation-injecting auras pass. The INTERACT_AT plus INTERACT disabler sequence (Sigma, Spicy) is detected by anti-cheats that count ghost interacts. TPAura is trivially caught by movement checks, because the unconfirmed C04 walk trips the vanilla 'moved too quickly' math when the path is skipped. Friend checks are invisible to the server and exist purely as client-side target filtering.

modules.name: Aura / KillAura
modules.purpose: Select a target within reach and emit C02 ATTACK packets at a controlled rate, with optional autoblock around the attack.
modules.how_it_works: Target selection from client-side entity lists (CombatUtil.getTarget in Memeware, PlayerUtil.getEntities in Rise), aim injected into the motion event so the outgoing C05/C06 carries the rotation, then ATTACK fired through the client's packet path. Memeware's SingleAura alternates C07 RELEASE_USE_ITEM and C08 placement at a fake BlockPos to block between attacks. Friend filtering happens inside target selection: Rise 5.99 checks its friends list, Sigma checks FriendManager.isFriend, Tenacity checks FriendCommand.isFriend.
modules.vanilla_hook: UpdateEvent (aim + attack trigger); the attack itself goes through PacketUtil.sendPacket so PacketOutEvent listeners see it.
