modules.anti_cheat_notes: The C16-open + click + C0D-close triplet is the same shape InvMove modules produce, but here it is bounded to one short burst per swap, which reads as legitimate GUI use to servers that mirror container state.
modules.variations: LiquidSense Dev's auto armor is the only one in the corpus that closes with a bare C0D() after faking the open; Sigma and Spicy use their own inventory managers.

modules.name: KeepContainer
modules.purpose: Reopen a previously closed container anywhere by cancelling the client's own C0D and keeping the cached GuiContainer around for an INSERT-key reopen.
modules.how_it_works: ScreenEvent caches any GuiContainer (excluding GuiInventory); PacketEvent cancels every outgoing C0DPacketCloseWindow so the container object stays alive, and tracks S2EPacketCloseWindow to drop the cache when the server closes the window. onDisable sends a real C0D with the cached windowId as cleanup. Pressing INSERT re-displays the cached GUI.
modules.vanilla_hook: ScreenEvent, KeyEvent, PacketEvent (send and receive sides).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling C0D is the same state-consistency flag as InvMove: the server never sees the window close while the player moves. The S2E tracking keeps the local container in sync so a server-initiated close does not desync the cache.
modules.variations: No equivalent reopen-container module in the other clients; Rise 6.x buffers C0D in blink queues instead.

modules.name: InventoryUtils
modules.purpose: Utility closeCurrentInventory() that sends C0D with the live windowId, used by November's inventory manager and modules to close the server-side window after silent interactions.
modules.how_it_works: closeCurrentInventory() pushes new C0DPacketCloseWindow(windowId()) into mc.thePlayer.sendQueue; windowId() reads the player's openContainer and returns 0 when null. A companion openInventory() sends C0B OPEN_INVENTORY for the paired open.
modules.vanilla_hook: No event hook; a static helper called from inventory code paths.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Using the live windowId keeps the close packet valid for whatever container is open, which avoids the stale-id edge cases of hardcoded C0D(0).

modules.name: LuaEventPacket
modules.purpose: Expose C0D to November's Lua scripting API as id 0x0D with a direction, letting scripts intercept window closes.
modules.how_it_works: The static packetIds table maps C0DPacketCloseWindow.class to 0x0D; the wrapper constructor copies id and direction ('out' for serverbound) from the EventPacket so Lua scripts can match on the numeric id.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None; read-only mapping.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent on all clients. Rise 6.x pairs it with BlinkComponent.dispatch and the sendUnregisteredPacket raw path. Tenacity's PacketUtil counts C0D among packet types that bypass the send queue filter.
implementation.client_variations: Classic clients cancel via event.cancel() or setCancelled. Rise 5.99 re-sends rewrapped packets via PacketUtil.sendPacketWithoutEvent. Rise 6.x distinguishes send (event bus) from sendUnregisteredPacket (raw NetworkManager). Spicy tracks open state and emits C0D from module methods rather than event interception. LiquidSense Dev sends C0D via mc.getNetHandler().addToSendQueue (bare constructor) and cancels it via PacketEvent.cancelEvent; November Recode 2.0 closes with the resolved windowId through InventoryUtils and exposes 0x0D to scripts.

anticheat.overview: C0D is the one serverbound packet in this batch, and it is a state signal: closing a window flips the server-side inventory-open state, which is what inventory-move and chest-stealer detection keys on. Real consumers are Azure InvTweaksA (close while sprinting), Daedalus ActionProcessor (close clears openInventory), Intave InventoryTracker (close state plus the beacon special case) and Kauri's PacketHandler (both directions). The rest is wrappers (Artemis GPacketPlayClientWindowClose, FlopAC WrappedInCloseWindowPacket, BendEye-Perus isCloseWindow) and one keyword hit that never reads the packet: FlopAC InventoryC is a click-delay chest-stealer check driven by WINDOW_CLICK events.

checks.name: InvTweaksA (Azure)
checks.purpose: Classic inventory-tweaks detection: closing a window while sprinting is the walking-with-inventory-open tell.
checks.how_it_works: InvTweaksA hooks the inbound packet stream and checks the type: when PacketPlayInCloseWindow arrives while the Bukkit player is sprinting, it calls onViolation with a 60000 ms cooldown. Azure's PlayerStats also records the close-window type in its per-packet stats.
checks.detects: Inventory-tweaks and chest-stealer clients that close the GUI and keep sprinting, plus the walk-while-inventory-open pattern generally.
checks.variations: Azure is the only classic anticheat with a dedicated close-window check. Its PlayerStats counter (line 68) records the type in the same hook. No other classic anticheat in the corpus flags the close packet directly.

checks.name: ActionProcessor close-window state (Daedalus)
checks.purpose: State sync: a close-window packet clears the openInventory flag that Daedalus's inventory and movement checks read.
checks.how_it_works: ActionProcessor is fed by PacketListeners, which wraps the inbound close-window packet (line 103) and calls the update overload. The close-window overload sets openInventory = false, paired with the C0B OPEN_INVENTORY branch of the entity-action overload that sets it true. Checks that must know whether the player has a GUI open read the flag.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: state bookkeeping. It makes GUI-state-dependent checks such as inventory move and click timing accurate.
checks.variations: Kauri PacketHandler wraps both directions: the inbound CLOSE_WINDOW branch sets inventoryOpen false immediately (lines 271-273), and the server CLOSE_WINDOW branch defers the same write to a keepalive action (lines 538-540) so the state lands at the client's tick.

checks.name: InventoryTracker close-window state (Intave)
checks.purpose: Track the player's inventory-open state from the close-window packet, with a workaround for the beacon window that never sends one.
checks.how_it_works: InventoryTracker subscribes to the CLOSE_WINDOW inbound packet at LOW priority and closes the inventory: receiveCloseWindow calls closeInventory, which flips InventoryMetadata's open state to false. On the open side it special-cases the beacon container: since the client never sends a close packet for a beacon window, opening one skips the open-state update entirely, so the tracking never gets stuck with a stale open inventory.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: state tracking. The open and close state feeds the inventory-analysis checks, including the ChestStealer violations that the /intave history command reports.
checks.variations: FlopAC's InventoryC flags chest-stealer behavior from click-delay statistics but never reads the close-window packet; its C0D corpus hit is the flag message text only. Artemis's GPacketPlayClientWindowClose and FlopAC's WrappedInCloseWindowPacket are wrappers, and BendEye-Perus exposes isCloseWindow as a generic packet predicate.

wiki_notes: Vanilla clients send a close-window packet with window ID 0 to close their own inventory even though no open packet is ever sent for it.
MCP 1.8.9 C0DPacketCloseWindow implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processCloseWindow; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerSP.closeScreen sends new C0DPacketCloseWindow (line 332): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/entity/EntityPlayerSP.java

packets.name: Click Window
packets.desc: Player clicks in an inventory window. Handles item moves: pickup, shift-click, number key swap, middle click, drop, drag init, and double-click.

fields.name: clickedItem
fields.desc: Item in slot before the click

packets.notes: The server validates every click against its own inventory state — actionNumber must match. If validation fails, S32PacketConfirmTransaction(accepted=false) reverts the client's inventory via S30PacketWindowItems. Almost NO module constructs C0E directly — they call mc.playerController.windowClick() which sends C0E internally. Rise 6.0 BufferAbuseInventoryMove and RektSky B5 ChestStealer are exceptions that construct C0E directly.

writeup.p: C0E is the inventory click packet: windowId, slotId, usedButton, mode, clickedItem (the server's copy of the stack being clicked), and an action number. The server runs openContainer.slotClick and confirms with S32PacketConfirmTransaction only when the clicked-item copy matches; otherwise it re-sends the whole container. It is the only way to move items programmatically, so every inventory automation module funnels through it, either by constructing it directly or through PlayerControllerMP.windowClick.

processClickWindow verifies the window id matches the open container and that crafting is allowed, then runs slotClick(slotId, button, mode, player). If the returned stack equals packetIn.getClickedItem() it confirms with S32 (accepted = true) and resyncs; otherwise it stores the action number in a pending map, sends S32 accepted = false, and force-syncs the container. The windowId 0 check matters: clients must match the current window or the click is silently dropped.

In the 10-client corpus C0E is used by inventory managers (Sigma InventoryManager via PlayerControllerMP.windowClick), inventory-move modules (Rise 5.99 InvMove cancels and re-wraps C0E with C16+C0D), the Rise 6.2.4 BufferAbuseInventoryMove exploit (sends empty C0E packets to abuse the transaction buffer), captcha bots (Rise 5.99 Auto clicks the Redesky captcha item), and Tenacity NoSlowModule (clicks the armor slot to swap the held item). Note that ChestStealer and AutoArmor in this corpus route through C16 open-inventory status, not C0E clicks. LiquidSense Dev overwrites PlayerControllerMP.windowClick to fire a cancelable ClickWindowEvent before every C0E send, and November Recode 2.0 registers C0E in its Lua scripting packet-id map (0x0E) so scripts can observe and cancel it, but ships no click module of its own.

The action number and clicked-item echo are the attack surface. Sending clicks with a stale or forged clickedItem makes the server resync the container, which some disablers use to flood the transaction pipeline. BufferAbuseInventoryMove exploits the server's transaction accounting by sending clicks the server must answer, delaying watchdog's transaction-based checks. The windowId mismatch is a silent drop, which InvMove uses to cancel clicks and re-send them under a fake open-inventory state. LiquidSense's windowClick overwrite computes the container transaction id and then discards it, sending (short) -1; the server never validates the action number against a counter, it only echoes it in the S32 reply, so the click confirms the same way a real id would and the client container counter is left stale.

implementation.overview: The programmatic inventory click. Inventory managers click through it, InvMove re-wraps it, BufferAbuseInventoryMove floods it, and a captcha bot clicks with it. Its confirm/resync loop is what makes it both reliable for automation and exploitable for transaction flooding. LiquidSense Dev adds the ClickWindowEvent mixin that lets any module veto clicks, and November Recode 2.0 exposes the packet to Lua scripts.
implementation.server_handling: processClickWindow: windowId must equal openContainer.windowId and crafting must be allowed. slotClick mutates the container; on clickedItem match the server confirms (S32 true) and resyncs, on mismatch it stores the action number, sends S32 false, and force-syncs all slots. Crafting players get a full container resend instead of a click.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields: windowId byte, slotId short, usedButton byte, mode byte, clickedItem (ItemStack or null), actionNumber short. Window 0 is the player inventory; chests start at 1. The clickedItem must be the exact stack the server last sent for that slot, which is why clients cache S2FPacketSetSlot/S30PacketWindowItems state.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats track click rate and window state. Inventory move (clicking while moving) is detected by comparing C0E timing against movement packets; CancelInventoryMove in Rise 6.2.4 exists to cancel the C16 open-inventory status so the server never learns the inventory is open. Transaction flooding via C0E is a disabler vector against Watchdog, which uses transaction gaps to time its checks.

modules.name: InventoryManager
modules.purpose: Automatically equip the best armor and tools by clicking the inventory container.
modules.how_it_works: Sigma InventoryManager scans the container slots, computes protection/weapon scores, and performs shift-clicks and hotbar swaps through mc.playerController.windowClick, which internally constructs C0EPacketClickWindow with the current windowId and the next transaction id. The module guards against concurrent modules (e.g. AutoArmor yields when InventoryManager is on).
modules.vanilla_hook: EventTick-driven with a Timer; windowClick wraps C0E.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Inventory managers are low-risk; the detectable part is click speed and moving while the container is open, which anti-cheats measure per-window.
modules.variations: Only Sigma ships a C0E-referencing InventoryManager; Spicy's InventoryManager uses C09/C16 instead.

modules.name: InvMove (packet re-wrap)
modules.purpose: Allow movement while an inventory GUI is open by re-sending clicks under a fake inventory-open state.
modules.how_it_works: In packet mode, InvMove cancels C0DPacketCloseWindow and C0EPacketClickWindow, then replays the click preceded by a C16 OPEN_INVENTORY_ACHIEVEMENT status and followed by a C0DPacketCloseWindow, all via sendPacketWithoutEvent so the server sees a coherent open-click-close sequence while the player keeps moving.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The re-wrap makes the server believe the inventory opened and closed cleanly, hiding the fact that clicks happened while the player moved. Watchdog and newer NCP track open/close sequences, which is why the C16/C0D pair must be exact.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4/6.1.30 ship CancelInventoryMove (cancels C16/C0B-OPEN_INVENTORY/C0D entirely) and BufferAbuseInventoryMove as separate modes.

modules.name: BufferAbuseInventoryMove
modules.purpose: Abuse the server's transaction buffer by sending C0E clicks while the inventory is open, delaying watchdog's transaction-based movement checks.
modules.how_it_works: Sends empty C0EPacketClickWindow packets (no-arg constructor) on a tick cycle while an inventory screen is open, and cancels legit C0E so the client's own clicks do not leak. The flood keeps the server's pending-transaction map busy so its confirm-based timing checks lag.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The no-arg C0E has windowId 0 and null item, which vanilla processes as a click on the player inventory; anti-cheats that do not validate the click's item echo will process it and queue a transaction, inflating the buffer. Very detectable by servers that count clicks per window.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the same module; the WatchdogDisabler in 6.2.4 also watches C0E windowId to decide when to send C16 status.

modules.name: Auto (Redesky captcha click)
modules.purpose: Automatically click the Redesky captcha item and send register/login commands on login.
modules.how_it_works: Intercepts S2FPacketSetSlot; when a slot's item display name contains 'aqui', sends C0EPacketClickWindow(windowId, slotId, 0, 0, item, 1919) via the send queue, confirming the captcha. A companion register/login routine sends C01 chat commands on world join.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Server-specific bot; the captcha is designed to be clicked by humans, so the module just automates a UI action. No movement flags involved.
modules.variations: Unique to Rise 5.99 in this corpus.

modules.name: NoSlowModule (armor-slot click)
modules.purpose: Bypass use-item slowdown by swapping the held item to an armor slot with a window click instead of a C08 use packet.
modules.how_it_works: While using an item and not in a GUI, send C0DPacketCloseWindow(0) followed by C0EPacketClickWindow(0, 36 + currentItem, 0, 6, null, nextTransactionID). Mode 6 with button 0 swaps the held item into the armor slot, ending the use state server-side without the slowdown, then the item is swapped back. A 'Watchdog' mode toggles this per-AC.
modules.vanilla_hook: SlowDownEvent cancel + MotionEvent; PacketReceiveEvent to cancel S2F echoes.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The armor-swap click is an unusual pattern; servers that validate windowId 0 clicks against the open container accept it (window 0 is always the player inventory). Watchdog mode exists because the swap timing is AC-sensitive.
modules.variations: Only Tenacity uses the click-window variant; other clients use the C08 use form.

modules.name: MixinPlayerControllerMP (ClickWindow event)
modules.purpose: Route every inventory click through a cancelable ClickWindowEvent before the C0E is queued, so LiquidBounce modules can veto or observe clicks.
modules.how_it_works: @Overwrite of PlayerControllerMP.windowClick: build ClickWindowEvent, call it on the client event manager, return null if cancelled; otherwise run slotClick locally, then addToSendQueue(new C0EPacketClickWindow(windowId, slotId, mouseButtonClicked, mode, itemstack, (short) -1)). The computed getNextTransactionID value is discarded.
modules.vanilla_hook: PlayerControllerMP.windowClick @Overwrite (mixin); ClickWindowEvent on the LiquidBounce event bus.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The hardcoded -1 action is echoed back in S32 unvalidated, so clicks confirm normally; the quirk only shows in the client's own container transaction counter going stale.
modules.variations: Click-cancel modules consume the same event; no other corpus client fires a pre-click event above the packet constructor.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent (InvMove, BufferAbuse), PacketReceiveEvent (Auto, NoSlow), tick/update loops for click scheduling, PlayerControllerMP.windowClick in Sigma. LiquidSense Dev fires a cancelable ClickWindowEvent from its windowClick @Overwrite, which modules can veto before the C0E exists.
implementation.client_variations: Sigma goes through playerController.windowClick. Rise 5.99 uses PacketUtil.sendPacketWithoutEvent to replay clicks. Rise 6.2.4 uses PacketUtil.sendNoEvent and EventLink listeners. Tenacity uses addToSendQueue directly. Spicy references C0E only inside CsgoSpinbot and YawAndPitchSpoof for packet-spoofing sequences, not for inventory automation. November Recode 2.0 registers C0E in the LuaEventPacket scripting id map (0x0E) so scripts can match and intercept it; LiquidSense Dev intercepts at the mixin layer, above the packet constructor.

anticheat.overview: The click window packet is the only inventory interaction the server sees: window id, slot, button, action number and the dragged item. Anticheats use it to police click cadence and protocol correctness (Frequency InventoryA, NCP InventoryListener with FastClick and Gutenberg), and to catch movement while an inventory is open, the inventory-move cheat domain (CheaterDeleter InventoryMoveCheck, Negativity InventoryMoveProtocol). Because the packet is also the acknowledgement channel for server transactions, it feeds NCP's window-click and frequency bookkeeping.

checks.name: InventoryA (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Classic statistical inventory-click check: legit clicks arrive with variable spacing, clicker clicks do not.
checks.how_it_works: Samples the number of flying packets between WrappedPlayInWindowClick packets when fewer than 5 movements separate clicks and the player is not teleporting. At 5 samples it computes the standard deviation and outlier count; a deviation below 1 with zero outliers fails the check.
checks.detects: Inventory clickers and auto-totem/auto-armor modules that click slots at mechanically constant intervals.
checks.variations: InventoryB in the same package adds delay-pattern scoring; Degrade's InventoryA and azure's InvTweaks checks use the same low-variance template.

checks.name: InventoryMoveCheck (CheaterDeleter)
checks.purpose: Modern Fabric-side inventory-move check: position changes while a screen handler is open must agree with the player's velocity.
checks.how_it_works: A CDModule listening to movement, packet and damage callbacks. While the current screen handler is open and the player is not flying or in a collision cluster, position-change packets are validated: vertical rises with downward velocity flag immediately, and horizontal deltas that grow from a zero-velocity baseline flag after the 500 ms grace window. Closing the screen or taking damage resets the deltas.
checks.detects: Inventory-move cheats that walk or sprint while the inventory is open, including ghost-inventory movement spoofing.
checks.variations: CheaterDeleter's MovementModuleManager registers the check alongside SpeedCheck and PhaseCheck; Grim's CompensatedInventory and TickInventory simulate the same window state on the server.

checks.name: InventoryMoveProtocol (Negativity)
checks.purpose: Inventory-move scoring protocol: movement while an inventory is open is compared against the baseline captured at open time.
checks.how_it_works: Arms on InventoryClickEvent and InventoryOpenEvent, then on PlayerMoveEvent accumulates an alert amount: starting to sprint or sneak since the inventory opened adds points, and covering distance at or beyond walk speed since open adds more. When the inventory has been open for 3 ticks and the amount exceeds 2, it alerts with a confidence based on time open.
checks.detects: Inventory-move cheats that sprint, sneak or walk while an inventory is open, and velocity desync during inventory use.
checks.variations: Frequency's BadPacketsJ/M and Rammelkast's InventoryListener enforce the same no-movement-while-open rule on raw packets; Photon's InventoryMove module is the modern equivalent.

checks.name: InventoryListener suite (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: The canonical window-click check set: FastClick, InstantBow, Gutenberg, MoreInventory and Open, driven by inventory events and the click window packet.
checks.how_it_works: A CheckListener registering the inventory checks with per-player config and data, fed from Bukkit inventory events and the ProtocolLib InventoryAdapter wrapping PacketPlayInWindowClick. FastClick limits clicks per window per second, InstantBow flags bows fired without a charging period, Gutenberg caps creative item spam, MoreInventory catches rapid item nuking, and Open limits how often windows can be reopened.
checks.detects: Inventory clickers, instant-bow cheats, creative item spam, inventory nuking and window-open cycling.
checks.variations: AntiCheatPlus's InventoryListener and DynamicDev's InventoryListener expose the same fastclick idea on 1.7-1.8 servers; Frequency's InventoryA/B are the statistical descendants.

wiki_notes: The server ignores any click targeting a window ID other than the currently open one, including window 0 while another window is open. Right-clicking an odd-sized stack picks up half and leaves the smaller half in the slot, and the mode and button fields jointly encode left, right, shift-click, number-key, drop-key, drag-painting and double-click operations with slot -999 meaning outside the window.

MCP 1.8.9 C0EPacketClickWindow implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processClickWindow; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readItemStackFromBuffer, readShort.

1.8.9 callers: PlayerControllerMP.windowClick sends new C0EPacketClickWindow (line 538): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/multiplayer/PlayerControllerMP.java

packets.name: Confirm Transaction
packets.desc: Client confirms receipt of a S32PacketConfirmTransaction (server inventory transaction).

fields.name: uid
fields.desc: Transaction UID matching the server's confirm packet

writeup.p: C0F is the client's acknowledgement of a server transaction: windowId, action number (uid), and accepted boolean. It exists to keep container actions and the server's movement/state checks in sync. Because the server sends S32PacketConfirmTransaction after inventory actions and certain checks, the client's C0F echo is the server's clock for latency and state. That makes C0F the backbone of disablers (break the transaction stream), ping spoofers (delay the echo), and velocity filters (spoof the echo to desync the check).

processConfirmTransaction is tiny: it looks up the pending action number for the open window and only re-enables crafting if the uid matches and the window matches. Vanilla itself does not time out or penalize missing confirmations; the NetHandlerPlayClient normally echoes S32 back as C0F automatically. This leniency is what disablers exploit: cancel C0F and the server-side container logic stalls without kicking.

Every client in the corpus has a Disabler that cancels, delays, or forges C0F (Memeware, Nekoware, Rise 5.99, Rise 6.x suite, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity). PingSpoof (Rise 5.99, Rise 6.x PingSpoofComponent) parks C0F together with C00 and releases them late. Velocity modules (Rise 5.99 Velocity, Rise 6.2.4 VulcanVelocity) cancel the S32 trigger and answer with a forged C0F so the server believes the transaction completed while the velocity was removed. Rise 6.2.4 Timer parks C0F on the ground to freeze watchdog's transaction clock, and NoVoid/AntiVoid modules cancel C0F while falling. The two new research clients add two more families. November Recode 2.0 mutates C0F on its EventPacket bus: DisablerModule rewrites the uid to Short.MAX_VALUE in its BLOCKS_MC mode, and VelocityModule cancels the C0F echo whose uid matches a cancelled velocity transaction under GRIM, or one C0F per hit under VULCAN. LiquidSense Dev parks C0F in queues (Disabler, PingSpoof), forges a C0F(0, -1, false) sentinel in the Tp and LastestHypixelFly enable sequences, and overwrites the vanilla S32 handler in MixinNetHandlerPlayClient so the echo always fires through the modified send path.

The accepted boolean and uid are forgeable. Memeware sends C0F(Integer.MIN_VALUE, Short.MAX_VALUE, true) to poison the server's transaction map; Spicy swaps the uid to desync; VulcanVelocity alternates uid 1/-1 to break Vulcan's velocity transaction tracking. The detection surface is the timing: a server that tracks C0F gaps (Verus, Watchdog) flags when the echo arrives outside the expected window, which is why disabler modes pair C0F with C00 delays and flush them together.

implementation.overview: The transaction echo that disablers live on. Cancel it to stall container logic, delay it to spoof ping, forge it to break velocity checks, or park it to freeze timer-based anti-cheats. Vanilla barely validates it, so the entire game is timing and uid correctness.
implementation.server_handling: processConfirmTransaction: look up the pending action for openContainer.windowId; if the uid matches and crafting was disabled, re-enable crafting. No timeout, no kick, no penalty for a missing or wrong C0F in vanilla. The client handler echoes S32 automatically, and modules hook PacketSendEvent to cancel or mutate that echo.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields: windowId byte, actionNumber short, accepted boolean. Window 0 (inventory) transactions are sent frequently during normal play. The uid counter is per-container; S32PacketConfirmTransaction carries the same windowId/uid the server expects echoed. Clients that cancel C0F must still answer S32 for window clicks or the container desyncs.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Verus and Watchdog use C0F (and C00) gaps as a latency reference for timer and fly checks. The Rise 6.x disabler suite (TransactionDisabler, DynamicPVPDisabler, Verus2Disabler, WatchdogDisabler, LunarDisabler, UniversoCraftDisabler, MMCReachDisabler, ExperimentalDisabler, TestDisabler, ConvertMovingPacketsDisabler) is one mode per AC family. The trade-off: forging uids breaks the container logic visibly (items snap back), delaying keeps containers working but is detectable as a constant lag offset.

modules.name: Disabler
modules.purpose: Cancel, delay, or forge C0F to break anti-cheat transaction-based checks.
modules.how_it_works: Mode-dependent. Memeware's Transaction/Latest Verus modes cancel C0F and periodically re-send forged ones (C0F(Integer.MIN_VALUE, Short.MAX_VALUE, true) for the autoban channel); Sigma's SagePvP/ColdNetwork modes cancel C0F when id==0 and accepted; Rise 5.99's Disabler has a dozen modes (vulcanCombat, ncp, verus, etc.) that cancel C0F in specific packet windows; Rise 6.x splits this into per-AC disabler modules; Tenacity AdvancedDisablerModule cancels C0F in specific states.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket send/receive; event.setCancelled(true) on the C0F.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling C0F for window 0 freezes the player's inventory transactions visibly; the modes pair it with C00 cancellation so the anti-cheat's latency reference is also broken. Verus-based modes in Rise 6.x (Verus2Disabler) also send C0B sneak/sprint to shape the state.
modules.variations: Memeware Disabler (forged uids, queue-based), Nekoware Disabler, Rise 5.99 Disabler (mode matrix), Rise 6.2.4/6.1.30 per-AC suite (TransactionDisabler, WatchdogDisabler, LunarDisabler, DynamicPVPDisabler, UniversoCraftDisabler, MMCReachDisabler, ExperimentalDisabler, TestDisabler, ConvertMovingPacketsDisabler), Spicy Disabler (C0F packet buffer), Tenacity DisablerModule/AdvancedDisablerModule. November Recode 2.0's DisablerModule adds a BLOCKS_MC mode that rewrites every C0F uid to Short.MAX_VALUE during the first 120 ticks after join, cancelling a single C06 as the second step of the same mode.

modules.name: PingSpoof
modules.purpose: Inflate measured ping by delaying the C0F (and C00) echo.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 6.2.4 PingSpoofComponent cancels C0F and C00 on the send event, parks them in a queue with a timestamp, and flushes them from PostMotionEvent once the delay elapses. The component API (spoof/blink) lets other modules request the delay for specific packet classes.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Delaying C0F+C00 together keeps the two gaps consistent, which is the tell Verus uses to separate lag from spoofing. A constant delay shows as a fixed ping offset; varying it looks like jitter.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 PingSpoof.java parks C0F+C00 in a ConcurrentHashMap with per-packet release times; Rise 6.1.30 uses the same component.

modules.name: Velocity (transaction spoof)
modules.purpose: Remove knockback while keeping the server's transaction bookkeeping consistent.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 6.2.4 VulcanVelocity cancels S32PacketConfirmTransaction when hurtTime == 10 (the knockback window) and answers with a forged C0F alternating uid 1/-1, so Vulcan's velocity check believes the transaction completed and the knockback was legitimately absent. Rise 5.99 Velocity cancels C0F/S32 pairs in its own modes.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (S32 cancel), PacketUtil.send for the forged C0F.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The alternating uid keeps the server's transaction map from desyncing while the velocity check is fooled. Wrong uid parity causes the inventory to lock and the AC to flag a transaction mismatch.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 Velocity.java; Rise 6.1.30 VulcanVelocity.java; WatchdogVelocity/RedeskyVelocity in 6.2.4 use C0B sprint actions instead of C0F for their velocity modes.

modules.name: Timer (transaction parking)
modules.purpose: Freeze the server's transaction clock by parking S32/C0F on the ground so timer-speed movement is not caught.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 6.2.4 Timer, in watchdog mode, cancels S32PacketConfirmTransaction while on the ground and queues it for later replay, so the server's transaction-based timing reference lags behind the client's accelerated timer. Tenacity TimerModule imports C0F for the same purpose.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketSendEvent (S32 park) + PacketReceiveEvent (velocity cancel); PacketUtil.TimedPacket queue.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Watchdog measures timer via transaction gaps; parking S32 on the ground only works while the player is grounded, which is why the module cancels the park in the air. Tenacity's TimerModule references C0F only at import level in this corpus.
modules.variations: Tenacity 6.0 TimerModule.java imports C0FPacketConfirmTransaction; Rise 6.1.30 Timer not present in corpus, 6.2.4 Timer is the representative.

modules.name: NoVoid / AntiVoid
modules.purpose: Cancel C0F (and all non-movement packets) while falling into the void so the server never registers the fall.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 5.99 NoVoid cancels every packet except C03 and C0F while the player is falling below a threshold, keeping the movement stream alive but suppressing the confirmations and other state that would let the server finalize the death. Rise 6.2.4 BlinkAntiVoid/WatchdogAntiVoid buffer C0F with a blink component and release on ground contact.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketSendEvent (cancel non-C03/C0F); motion check for the fall window.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling packets while falling is a classic anti-void that flags on servers with fall-check timers; the packet blacklist (keep C03+C0F) is what keeps the connection alive long enough for the client to place a block or land.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4/6.1.30 BlinkAntiVoid and WatchdogAntiVoid implement the same idea with the blink queue instead of a whitelist.

modules.name: VelocityModule (GRIM / VULCAN transaction filter)
modules.purpose: Velocity cancel that keeps the transaction stream consistent: GRIM mode drops the S32 that follows a cancelled S12 and then cancels the matching outgoing C0F, so the server never sees the velocity transaction complete.
modules.how_it_works: On EventPacket.In, an S12 aimed at the player is cancelled (CANCEL, GRIM, VULCAN) or scaled (REDUCE, REVERSE); under GRIM the following S32PacketConfirmTransaction is cancelled too and its action number is queued. The EventPacket.Out handler then matches every outgoing C0F uid against that queue and cancels the echo when the uid was queued, so the transaction is consumed client-side. VULCAN mode instead cancels one C0F per velocity hit while the funny flag is set. WATCHDOG_SAFE cancels S12 and folds the vertical motion into motionY only while on the ground.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.In (S12 and S32), EventPacket.Out (C0F), EventUpdate (GRIM queue drain check).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The uid-matched C0F cancel is precise: only the transaction tied to the removed velocity is dropped, so the container state stays in sync, which is the difference from blanket C0F cancellation.
modules.variations: November's approach mirrors Rise 6.2.4 VulcanVelocity (alternating uid spoof) but cancels the echo outright; the GRIM mode's transactionQueue is unique to this client in the corpus.

modules.name: Disabler (transaction buffer)
modules.purpose: Watchdog-style disabler that parks outgoing C0F and C00 packets in queues, then flushes C0F in small randomized batches so the server's transaction clock lags without the connection dying.
modules.how_it_works: The PacketEvent handler intercepts every C0F not already queued: when the uid digit count is 3 and the disabler is not yet armed it arms (abc = true), clears the queue, and starts the flush cycle; once armed it counts uid digits and, when fewer than 10 transactions have been flushed but the uid grew past 3 digits, flushes the whole queue early. Flushes release 3 to 9 random packets per cycle (or the full queue when the delay is even or divisible by 3 and the queue exceeds 100 entries) through NetworkManager.sendPacket. C00 keepalives get their own queue and are released on a separate timer, and every 155 ticks a C14 tab-complete with a huge random number is fired as a keepalive substitute.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The uid-digit heuristic (3 digits arms, growth past 3 flushes early) is a fingerprint of this Watchdog bypass; the randomized batch size and the C14 spam are designed to make the gap pattern look like lag.
modules.variations: Unlike Memeware's forged-uid disabler and November's uid rewrite, LiquidSense's variant buffers real packets and replays them; the C00 and C0F dual queue mirrors the Rise PingSpoofComponent park pattern.

modules.name: PingSpoof (LiquidBounce)
modules.purpose: Inflate measured ping by parking C0F and C00 in a timestamped map and releasing them after a random delay.
modules.how_it_works: PacketEvent cancels any C0F or C00 while the player is alive and not already parked, storing release time = now + randomDelay(min, max). UpdateEvent with ignoreCondition (so it runs while the module is off) sweeps the map and re-queues entries whose timestamp passed via addToSendQueue. The min and max delay settings clamp each other on change.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Releasing C0F and C00 together keeps the two gap series consistent, the same trade-off documented for Rise's PingSpoofComponent; the random per-packet delay makes the offset look like jitter.
modules.variations: The LiquidBounce classic module predates the Rise component approach: a HashMap keyed by packet identity plus a random delay, versus Rise's timed queue; the ignoreCondition update handler is the LiquidBounce idiom for running while disabled.

modules.name: Tp / LastestHypixelFly (transaction sentinel)
modules.purpose: Forge a C0F(0, -1, false) echo on enable as the first step of the Hypixel teleport and flight rigs, desynchronizing the server's transaction expectation before the C04 teleport hops.
modules.how_it_works: Both modules queue new C0FPacketConfirmTransaction(0, (short)(-1), false) through addToSendQueue immediately on enable, right before the C13 ability declaration and the two C04 position hops at y+0.17 and y+0.06. The forged uid -1 cannot match any pending server action, so the echo is silently dropped by the vanilla handler while the movement packets that follow do the real work.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The uid -1 with accepted=false is a fingerprint shared by the AquaVit teleport family; it is harmless against vanilla (a wrong uid is ignored) and aimed at anti-cheat transaction tracking that expects a continuous echo stream.
modules.variations: Tp.java and LastestHypixelFly.java carry identical sentinels; TeleportCommand (the chat command twin) skips the C0F but spams C13 per path node instead, covered in the C13 writeup.

modules.name: MixinNetHandlerPlayClient (transaction echo)
modules.purpose: Overwrite the vanilla S32 handler so the C0F echo always runs on the client thread and goes through LiquidSense's modified send queue.
modules.how_it_works: The @Overwrite handleConfirmTransaction re-implements NetHandlerPlayClient's logic: resolve the container for window 0 or the open container, and when the server did not accept, queue C0F(windowId, actionNumber, true). Because the mixin replaces the vanilla method, the echo is emitted even when other event handlers cancel packets, keeping the inventory state machine alive. The same mixin forces the MC|Brand C17 on join and fires EntityMovementEvent from S14 handling, and its addToSendQueue injection raises PacketSenEvent for every outgoing packet.
modules.vanilla_hook: handleConfirmTransaction overwrite (S32PacketConfirmTransaction in), addToSendQueue injection (PacketSenEvent out).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: This is infrastructure, not an exploit: it guarantees transaction continuity so the disabler and ping-spoof entries above can park C0F without desyncing the inventory. The echo goes through addToSendQueue, so LiquidSense's PacketEvent sees it like any other send.
modules.variations: The @Overwrite approach differs from the eight classic clients, which leave the vanilla echo untouched and only hook the send event.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketSendEvent (cancel/mutate C0F), PacketReceiveEvent (S32 trigger), motion/tick events for release timing; Rise 6.x uses component-based parking (PingSpoofComponent, TransactionFixComponent).
implementation.client_variations: Classic clients cancel or mutate the live packet in the event (Memeware, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity). Rise 5.99 uses PacketUtil.sendPacketWithoutEvent to replay forged C0F. Rise 6.x routes through PacketUtil.send/sendNoEvent and its PingSpoofComponent/TimedPacket queue; TransactionFixComponent (6.2.4/6.1.30) repairs transaction state under ViaVersion. November Recode 2.0 cancels or mutates C0F on EventPacket.Out (VelocityModule GRIM and VULCAN, DisablerModule BLOCKS_MC uid rewrite). LiquidSense Dev parks C0F in queues on PacketEvent and flushes through NetworkManager.sendPacket or addToSendQueue, forges sentinels in onEnable, and its MixinNetHandlerPlayClient overwrite re-emits the vanilla echo through the modified send path.

anticheat.overview: The transaction confirmation packet is the client's acknowledgement of a server transaction, and it gives anticheats a clean client-to-server round trip that is independent of the keepalive channel. That makes it the timing primitive for the timer and pingspoof check domains: Grim's Timer anchors the movement clock to the first confirmation after each movement, Frequency PingSpoofA compares the transaction ping against the keepalive ping, and classic timers (Azure, Negativity) use the same packet stream to discipline the movement rate.

checks.name: Timer (Grim)
checks.purpose: Ping-anchored timer check: the movement clock must never run ahead of the transaction round trip.
checks.how_it_works: A PrePredictionPacketReceiveListener. When a movement has been seen and the next WINDOW_CONFIRMATION (or PONG) arrives, it updates the known player clock from the movement clock. Each tick packet adds 50 ms to a real-time balance; when the balance overtakes System.nanoTime() the client is running faster than real time, the check flags, cancels the packet, and executes a setback. A clock-drift floor keeps the balance from falling behind the player's ping.
checks.detects: Timer cheats from about 1.01x upward, including clients that fake movement rate while keeping the transaction channel honest.
checks.variations: Grim's TickTimer, NegativeTimer and TimerLimit cover sub-1.0 and multi-account cases on the same transaction anchor; the comment block documents the transaction-gap proof behind the check.

checks.name: PingSpoofA (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Transaction-vs-keepalive ping comparison: a pingspoofer inflates the transaction ping, not the keepalive ping.
checks.how_it_works: On each flying packet it reads the transaction ping (measured from the transaction packets) and the keepalive ping. If the player has been online for more than 10 ticks and is not exempt (lagging, teleporting, TPS, chunk), a transaction ping that exceeds the keepalive ping by more than 50 ms fails the check.
checks.detects: Ping spoofers that hold transaction responses to fake a high ping for timer/velocity bypasses.
checks.variations: PingSpoofB in the same package and azure's PingSpoof check use the same two-channel comparison; Hydro's PingSpoof and Negativity's PingSpoofProtocol port it to their own ping trackers.

checks.name: Timer (Azure)
checks.purpose: Classic 1.8 flying-delay timer: the interval between movement packets must stay near 50 ms.
checks.how_it_works: On every PacketPlayInFlying it measures the delay from the previous packet. Intervals below 47 ms accumulate a threshold and compute the timer speed as 50 divided by the actual delay; after 7 consecutive fast intervals it raises a violation with the speed percentage. Intervals above 70 ms decay the threshold by 3, and a teleport resets it to -10.
checks.detects: Timer cheats that send movement packets faster than 20 per second, including timer variants in the 1.0-1.5x range.
checks.variations: TimerB in the same package adds a second timing axis; Frequency TimerA runs the deviation-and-allowance variant of the same idea on the flying stream.

checks.name: TimerProtocol (Negativity)
checks.purpose: Packet-budget timer: the number of movement packets per second must not exceed the server tick rate.
checks.how_it_works: On each packet-clear cycle it counts flying, position, look and position-look packets into a rolling per-second list, keeping the last 5 seconds. The mean and median of the counts are compared against the tick budget (20, or 40 in creative, plus a configured variation). An overflow of both mean and median alerts with a confidence derived from the player ping.
checks.detects: Timer cheats that exceed the movement packet budget per second, and packet-spam variants that inflate the movement stream.
checks.variations: CheaterDeleter's TimerCheck and PacketCountModuleManager enforce the same per-second budget on the Fabric packet stream; NCP's FlyingFrequency check is the classic ancestor.

wiki_notes: PLAY 0x0F: byte windowId plus short action number plus accepted as a byte-boolean echo of S32.
Vanilla only re-enables crafting on a matching window and uid; missing or wrong echoes cause no kick.
Window 0 inventory traffic is frequent, so its timing doubles as a latency and timer reference.

MCP 1.8.9 C0FPacketConfirmTransaction implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processConfirmTransaction; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readShort.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerPlayClient.handleConfirmTransaction sends new C0FPacketConfirmTransaction (line 1191): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/network/NetHandlerPlayClient.java

packets.name: Creative Inventory Action
packets.desc: Player sets the contents of a slot in creative mode. Used to spawn items or modify inventory contents directly.

fields.name: slotId
fields.desc: Slot index (-1 for cursor, 0-44 for inventory, 100-104 for armor)

packets.notes: Only processed by the server if the player is in creative mode (gamemode=1). Ignored silently in survival. Can set ANY slot including armor (100-104) and offhand slots. No known hacked client modules directly target this packet — it's used by vanilla creative mode mechanics. Gugustus has a CreativeGive command that constructs C10 via addToSendQueue.

writeup.p: C10 is the creative-mode inventory writer: a short slot id plus an ItemStack. Slot -1 addresses the cursor stack, slots 1 through 44 the survival inventory grid. The server only enters the handler when the player's gamemode is creative, and inside it applies its own bounds check: flag1 is true only for slots 1 to 44 inclusive, so slot 0, armor slots and the cursor path all fall through to a different branch. In vanilla it is emitted by PlayerControllerMP whenever the creative inventory GUI places or drops an item.

processCreativeInventoryAction first, and before any slot validation, inspects the incoming stack's NBT: if it carries a BlockEntityTag with x/y/z keys, the server reads the tile entity at that position and rewrites the tag from the live tile entity NBT. Only then does it validate: flag1 (slot bounds), flag2 (item id non-null), flag3 (metadata >= 0, stackSize 1..64). Valid inventory slots go through putStackInSlot; the cursor branch (slotId < 0) drops the item as an EntityItem with creative despawn age and increments itemDropThreshold by 20, capped at 200. Everything is skipped entirely for non-creative players.

None of the original 8 clients ships an inventory-scripting or ItemSpoof module that drives C10 directly; LiquidSense Dev's InventoryUtils.updateInventory does: it re-sends the full 44-slot main inventory as creative actions to force the server's copy back in sync. The remaining corpus hits are infrastructure. Rise 5.99 Crasher uses it in Window mode to inject a book with a deeply nested JSON page into slot 0. Rise 5.99 Freecam allow-lists C10 so creative actions keep working with a detached camera, and Tenacity 6.0's PacketUtil.isClientPacket whitelists it for the silent send helpers. That is the entire module surface.

The handler's ordering is the interesting part: BlockEntityTag processing runs before slot bounds, so a crafted stack forces a tile entity lookup even when the slot is invalid. Slot 0 and the cursor branch bypass putStackInSlot entirely, which means a creative client can push arbitrary NBT-bearing items at the server without them landing in inventory. Anti-cheats with creative checks (NCP's inventory heuristics, custom gamemode guards) flag C10 sent while the server-side gamemode is not creative; the packet is a silent no-op there, so the main abuse channel is the NBT payload itself.

implementation.overview: The creative-only inventory writer. No ItemSpoof-style module exists in the original 8 clients; LiquidSense Dev's InventoryUtils re-sends the whole inventory through C10, and elsewhere C10 appears as a crash payload carrier (Rise 5.99 Crasher Window mode), a freecam whitelist entry, and a silent-send whitelist entry in Tenacity.
implementation.server_handling: processCreativeInventoryAction: gamemode gate, BlockEntityTag sync, then flag1/flag2/flag3 validation. Slots 1..44 go through putStackInSlot, slot -1 drops the item as a creative-despawn EntityItem (itemDropThreshold +20 per drop, max 200), everything else is ignored. ItemStacks are not re-serialized against an item registry beyond getItem() != null, so crafted NBT survives to any plugin that reads the slot.
implementation.protocol_notes: short slotId (signed) + Slot-encoded ItemStack (short item id, byte count, short damage, optional NBT). Sent in PLAY state only. The client never sends it in survival: PlayerControllerMP.windowClick paths to C0EPacketClickWindow instead, so a survival server receiving C10 is already anomalous.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats that mirror the server gamemode flag C10 from a survival player as an inventory exploit attempt. Creative-gamemode servers rarely monitor it, which is exactly why crash payloads ride this packet: the handler still parses and processes NBT before the gamemode logic can matter to plugins.

modules.name: Crasher (Window)
modules.purpose: Inject a writable book carrying a deeply nested JSON page into slot 0 via C10 to crash servers whose chat/JSON parser chokes on the recursion.
modules.how_it_works: On PreMotionEvent, Window mode builds an NBTTagList whose single string is ~830 stacked {extra:[{...}} tokens, attaches it to a writable book, and sends C10 with slot 0. Runs every tick while enabled.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Only effective on creative-gamemode servers; on survival the handler is a no-op. The nested JSON targets server-side text/chat parsing, so the flag surface is the payload content, not the packet rate.
modules.variations: The same module's Click, Window, BEdit and One Packet modes push equivalent book NBT through C0EPacketClickWindow and C17PacketCustomPayload (MC|BEdit).

modules.name: Freecam (whitelist)
modules.purpose: Allow C10 through while freecam is active so creative inventory actions still reach the server from the detached camera.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketSend cancels every serverbound packet not in an explicit allow list; C10 (with C12, C0E, C16, C02 and a few others) is in the list. Everything else, including C03 movement, is suppressed so the server keeps the player frozen.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Not a C10-specific exploit; the whitelist is the module's general anti-desync mechanism. No anti-cheat measures freecam whitelists directly, movement suppression is what gets flagged.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus has a comparable whitelist for C10.

modules.name: PacketUtil (silent whitelist)
modules.purpose: Classify C10 as a legitimate client packet so Tenacity's packet helpers route it through the send path.
modules.how_it_works: isClientPacket returns true for every play-state serverbound packet including C10. The helper exists because Tenacity's packet send event historically let serverbound and clientbound packets through; the whitelist gates which ones the event system treats as client traffic.
modules.vanilla_hook: Packet send helper, no event hook.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No detection relevance; purely an internal routing gate.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99's PacketUtil has no equivalent whitelist; the same file in Tenacity also covers C11 through C19, which is why it reappears across several of these impl pages.

modules.name: InventoryUtils (creative inventory sync)
modules.purpose: Force the server's creative inventory copy back in sync by re-sending every main-inventory slot as a C10 creative action.
modules.how_it_works: updateInventory() loops slots 0..43 (offset 36 for the first nine to map the hotbar, 0 for the rest), and for each adds C10PacketCreativeInventoryAction(index + offset, mainInventory[index]) to the send queue. The rest of the class is armor and weapon scoring used by the AquaVit module set.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Only works in creative gamemode; the server drops C10 from survival players, so the resync is a no-op there. The slots map to the survival grid 1..44, which is exactly the flag1-valid range.
modules.variations: AquaVit modules call updateInventory after local inventory edits; the LiquidBounce core has no equivalent resync helper.

implementation.general_hooks: No client hooks C10 in a dedicated module; it is reached through generic PacketSendEvent interception (Rise 5.99) or helper whitelists (Tenacity). LiquidSense Dev drives C10 through a direct addToSendQueue call in a static utility, not through an event hook.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 constructs the packet directly with a forged ItemStack; Tenacity only classifies it. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and both Rise 6.x builds touch C10 solely through the vanilla PlayerControllerMP path. November Recode 2.0 registers C10 in its LuaEventPacket scripting id map (0x10) but has no module that constructs it.

anticheat.overview: Server-side anticheats treat the creative-inventory packet as the creative-mode inventory mutation stream. The corpus is thin: Grim keeps a simulated inventory in sync by applying the slot writes, and LightAntiCheat flags the packet when a non-creative player sends it. Most other corpus hits are gamemode-flag reads inside movement checks, not listeners for this packet.

checks.name: CreativeInventoryAction tracking (Grim)
checks.purpose: Keep the simulated inventory in sync with creative slot writes so item-dependent checks see the items the client claims to hold.
checks.how_it_works: Listens for CREATIVE_INVENTORY_ACTION and returns unless the player is in creative mode. The slot is validated against the 1.8 boundary (slots 1-44 on 1.8, 1-45 after) before the stack is written into the compensated inventory and the slot is marked as client-claimed.
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It is the feed that keeps enchantment and held-item state accurate in creative mode, and out-of-range slot values are dropped instead of crashing the simulation.
checks.variations: Artemis ships only the GPacketPlayClientSetCreativeSlot wrapper, and Negativity registers SET_CREATIVE_SLOT in its PacketType table, but neither runs a check on this packet.

checks.name: BadPacketsD (LightAntiCheat)
checks.purpose: Flag creative-slot packets sent by players who are not in creative mode.
checks.how_it_works: On SET_CREATIVE_SLOT, the check skips when the player is already creative or changed gamemode less than 500 ms ago, so a fresh switch to creative does not false-flag. It re-checks the condition one tick later to ride out lag, then flags.
checks.detects: Clients that send creative inventory packets in survival, which is the primitive behind item-spoof and creative-give exploits.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus runs this check; the rest of the C10 corpus is wrapper and gamemode plumbing.

wiki_notes: Picking up an item from the creative listings sends no packet until it is placed somewhere; picking an item up deletes it from the server while placing or dropping it tells the server to create it from scratch, which can be verified by disconnecting mid-drag. The destroy-item slot is a client-side detail meaning the item is simply not recreated.

MCP 1.8.9 C10PacketCreativeInventoryAction implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processCreativeInventoryAction; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readItemStackFromBuffer, readShort.

1.8.9 callers: PlayerControllerMP.sendSlotPacket sends new C10PacketCreativeInventoryAction (line 561): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/multiplayer/PlayerControllerMP.java

packets.name: Enchant Item
packets.desc: Player selects an enchantment option in the enchanting table window. Carries window ID and button (0=top, 1=middle, 2=bottom).
packets.notes: The server responds with S2FPacketSetSlot (enchanted item). The server validates the lapis lazuli count and XP level before applying. No major client module specifically targets this packet in the 6+ client codebases examined — enchantment is handled through vanilla GUI mechanics.

writeup.p: C11 selects an enchantment option in an open enchanting table: a byte window id and a byte button (0 top, 1 middle, 2 bottom). It is the only serverbound packet whose sole effect is triggering Container.enchantItem, and it is sent from the vanilla GUI through PlayerControllerMP.enchantItem. The server replies with S2FPacketSetSlot carrying the enchanted result plus XP and lapis deltas.

processEnchantItem gates on three conditions: the packet's window id must equal the player's openContainer.windowId, the container must report canCraft, and the player must not be a spectator. Only then does it call enchantItem(playerEntity, button), which re-derives the enchantment from the table's seed, validates the lapis and level cost against the real player state, applies the enchantment and calls detectAndSendChanges. Every cost check is server-side; the packet carries nothing but the two bytes.

There is no AutoEnchant module in the corpus; the hits are all plumbing. Rise 6.1.30 and Rise 6.2.4 expose sendEnchantItem in the script PacketAPI, Tenacity 6.0 lists C11 in PacketUtil.isClientPacket, and November Recode 2.0 maps C11PacketEnchantItem to wire id 0x11 in LuaEventPacket so its Lua scripting API can identify the packet by id instead of by class. Enchanting in all of these clients goes through the vanilla GUI, so the packet is never intercepted for spoofing.

The server re-validates everything, so the packet itself cannot grant free enchants; the historical abuse is ordering, not content. A client that clicks an enchant and a C0E window action in the same tick can race the slot sync, which is the dupe-era vector. Because the button byte indexes the table's three server-side options, sending a button with no matching cost is harmless: enchantItem simply fails the level check. Anti-cheats ignore C11 entirely.

implementation.overview: The enchanting-table selection packet. Zero modules in the corpus drive it; the hits are the Rise 6.x script PacketAPI enchant bridge, Tenacity's silent-send whitelist and November Recode 2.0's Lua packet-id map.
implementation.server_handling: processEnchantItem: window id match, canCraft check, spectator rejection, then Container.enchantItem which re-validates lapis and XP server-side. detectAndSendChanges pushes S2FPacketSetSlot with the enchanted stack. No rate limit beyond the container state machine.
implementation.protocol_notes: byte windowId + byte button on the wire. Valid only while an EnchantmentTable container is open; any other container makes the window id check fail. The button maps to the table's three server-side options, which are deterministic from the world seed and player position.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures C11; the packet is fully server-validated and carries no movement or timing signal. The only server-side observable is the ordering relative to C0E transactions during rapid enchanting.

modules.name: PacketAPI (script bridge)
modules.purpose: Expose C11 construction to the scripting layer so scripts can select enchantments programmatically.
modules.how_it_works: sendEnchantItem(windowId, enchantment) and sendEnchantItem(enchantment) build the packet and send it via PacketUtil.send; the overload without a window id reads thePlayer.openContainer.windowId at call time.
modules.vanilla_hook: No event hook; direct PacketUtil.send from script code.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. The server re-validates the selection, so scripts gain convenience, not an exploit.
modules.variations: Identical PacketAPI.java exists in Rise 6.1.30 with the same method bodies.

modules.name: PacketUtil (silent whitelist)
modules.purpose: Classify C11 as a legitimate client packet for Tenacity's packet routing helpers.
modules.how_it_works: isClientPacket includes C11PacketEnchantItem in the full play-state whitelist.
modules.vanilla_hook: Packet send helper, no event hook.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None.
modules.variations: Same whitelist pattern as C10; the file covers every serverbound play packet.

modules.name: LuaEventPacket (script bridge)
modules.purpose: Expose the serverbound packet id space to the Lua scripting API: scripts receive a numeric packet id instead of the raw class.
modules.how_it_works: A static block maps every serverbound play packet class to its 1.8.9 wire id, C11PacketEnchantItem to 0x11. The constructor resolves the id from the EventPacket payload via getOrDefault (falling back to -1) and stamps a direction string ('out' for EventPacket.Out, 'in' otherwise); Lua event wrappers then pass the id and direction to scripts. The source comment explains the map exists because runtime obfuscation would break reflection-based lookups.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.In/Out bus events translated into the Lua wrapper; no packet is constructed or sent here.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the wrapper only reads the packet class. Scripts that want to drive C11 still go through vanilla methods; the map is visibility, not control.
modules.variations: Parallel to Rise 6.x's PacketAPI sendEnchantItem bridge, but November Recode 2.0 only identifies packets; it does not expose a send helper for enchanting.

implementation.general_hooks: No module hooks C11 in the corpus; scripting access goes through PacketAPI (Rise 6.x) or the LuaEventPacket wrapper (November Recode 2.0), not packet events.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.x exposes it in the script API; Tenacity classifies it in a helper; November Recode 2.0 maps it in the Lua wrapper. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy, Rise 5.99 and Tenacity all send it only via the vanilla PlayerControllerMP.enchantItem path.

anticheat.overview: No anticheat in the 50-repo corpus implements a check on the enchant-item packet. The corpus hits are enchantment-attribute reads (depth strider, soul speed, efficiency, knockback) used by movement, fight and block-break checks, plus packet-type registrations in Negativity and Artemis wrappers. Server-side anticheats do not watch the enchantment-table interaction, so this packet is invisible to them.

wiki_notes: Two bytes: windowId plus button 0 top, 1 middle, 2 bottom; PLAY serverbound 0x11.
Accepted only when the id matches the open container and it can craft; spectators are rejected.
Server re-derives cost from seed, lapis and XP, so a bare button cannot grant free enchants.
MCP 1.8.9 C11PacketEnchantItem implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processEnchantItem; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte.

1.8.9 callers: PlayerControllerMP.sendEnchantPacket sends new C11PacketEnchantItem (line 551): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/multiplayer/PlayerControllerMP.java

packets.name: Update Sign
packets.desc: Player finishes editing a sign. Sends the block position and four lines of text as IChatComponents.

fields.name: lines
fields.desc: 4 lines of sign text as JSON ChatComponents

packets.notes: Jigsaw 0.26 OPSign module cancels and resends C12 twice to crash the server's sign data structure on vanilla 1.8-1.8.5 servers (exploit patched in 1.8.8+).

writeup.p: C12 commits sign text: a BlockPos plus four IChatComponent lines. GuiEditSign sends it on close, and the server writes the lines into the tile entity. It is one of the few serverbound packets that carries structured chat components rather than plain strings, which makes it a favorite vector for chat-parser and logging exploits.

processUpdateSign loads the block and requires the tile entity to be a TileEntitySign, then checks isEditable and that the editing player matches; a failed check logs a warning and returns. Each line is re-wrapped as new ChatComponentText with formatting codes stripped (EnumChatFormatting.getTextWithoutFormattingCodes), so the server discards JSON structure and colors before storing. No length cap is applied at this layer in the bundled 1.8.9 sources.

Three corpus hits. Rise 5.99's Crasher Sign mode injects the Log4Shell string as a sign line at BlockPos.ORIGIN, and Freecam allow-lists C12 so sign edits survive a freecam session. November Recode 2.0 maps C12PacketUpdateSign to wire id 0x12 in its LuaEventPacket wrapper so Lua scripts can recognize the packet by id. No client ships a SignSpoof or colored-sign module; the packet is otherwise vanilla-only across the corpus.

The interesting detail is where the payload lands: sign text is persisted to the world and re-broadcast, so a crafted line reaches every chunk viewer and any plugin that logs or formats tile entity data. The 1.8.x sign-crash (resending C12 twice against a vanilla bug) predates these clients and is not present in the corpus. Because the tile entity and ownership checks happen before any text processing, anonymous positions like BlockPos.ORIGIN are silently ignored unless a sign actually sits there.

implementation.overview: The sign-text commit packet. No SignSpoof or color-sign module exists in the corpus; C12 shows up only as Rise 5.99's Log4Shell crash carrier, a freecam whitelist entry and November Recode 2.0's Lua packet-id map.
implementation.server_handling: processUpdateSign: block loaded check, TileEntitySign cast, isEditable and owner match, then per-line sanitization into plain ChatComponentText with formatting codes stripped, markDirty and markBlockForUpdate. A non-matching owner logs 'just tried to change non-editable sign' and drops the packet.
implementation.protocol_notes: BlockPos (long-encoded) followed by four length-prefixed chat component JSON strings. Valid only while the client is in a sign-editing GUI, though the server never verifies that state, only the tile entity's editable flag. The four lines are not length-capped in 1.8.9 server code.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures C12; it carries no movement signal. Server-side plugins that sanitize or log sign text are the only watchers, and they operate on content. Spamming C12 at arbitrary positions costs one tile entity lookup per packet and is the only measurable abuse.

modules.name: Crasher (Sign)
modules.purpose: Send a sign update carrying the Log4Shell lookup string to servers whose logging pipeline formats packet content through log4j.
modules.how_it_works: On PreMotionEvent, Sign mode builds a 4-line IChatComponent array where line 0 is the string ${jndi:rmi://localhost:3000} and sends it at BlockPos.ORIGIN. Disables itself after one shot when using the Log4J chat variant.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Needs a vulnerable server; on patched servers the string is stored as literal sign text. The packet rate is one per tick, low enough to evade rate-based logging guards.
modules.variations: The same module carries the identical string in the Log4J mode through C01PacketChatMessage and in Book mode through C0EPacketClickWindow.

modules.name: Freecam (whitelist)
modules.purpose: Pass C12 through the freecam packet whitelist so sign edits still reach the server while the camera is detached.
modules.how_it_works: The onPacketSend allow list includes C12 alongside C10, C0E, C16 and C02; all other serverbound packets are cancelled during the freecam session.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No detection relevance beyond the movement suppression the whitelist is part of.
modules.variations: No comparable whitelist in the other 7 clients.

modules.name: LuaEventPacket (script bridge)
modules.purpose: Expose the serverbound packet id space to the Lua scripting API: C12 resolves to id 0x12 so scripts can recognize sign commits by id.
modules.how_it_works: A static block maps every serverbound play packet class to its 1.8.9 wire id, C12PacketUpdateSign to 0x12. The constructor resolves the id from the EventPacket payload via getOrDefault (falling back to -1) and stamps a direction string ('out' for EventPacket.Out, 'in' otherwise); Lua event wrappers then pass the id and direction to scripts. The map exists because runtime obfuscation would break reflection-based lookups.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.In/Out bus events translated into the Lua wrapper; no packet is constructed or sent here.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the wrapper only reads the packet class. The id map gives scripts awareness of sign commits, not the ability to forge them.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 is the only client with active C12 module logic (Crasher, Freecam); November Recode 2.0's hit is passive plumbing.

implementation.general_hooks: C12 is reached through generic PacketSendEvent handling in Rise 5.99; November Recode 2.0 sees it only through the LuaEventPacket wrapper.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 is the only client with module-level C12 references. All other clients emit C12 exclusively from the vanilla GuiEditSign close path; November Recode 2.0 additionally maps it in the Lua wrapper.

anticheat.overview: The sign-update packet is a thin but real anticheat surface. NoCheatPlus runs its AutoSign blockplace check on sign edits, timing the edit against the placement and the line content, and Intave kicks players whose sign lines exceed a length limit, which is the crash-exploit angle of this packet.

checks.name: AutoSign (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Catch instant sign-text macros that fill all four lines faster than a human can type.
checks.how_it_works: After a sign is placed, the blockplace listener stores a block hash and the open time. On the sign edit, the check compares the block hash, then estimates the minimum human edit time from the line count and the distinct characters (150 ms base, 50 ms per extra line, 50 ms per character). An edit faster than the estimate flags, with the violation level scaled by the time deficit.
checks.detects: Auto-sign macros, instant sign spam, and sign edits sent against a different block than the one placed.
checks.variations: Intave's ItemCrashTracker instead validates sign content length (see next entry); Vrekt-Arc-v2 and Artemis only ship UpdateSign wrappers.

checks.name: ItemCrashTracker sign limit (Intave)
checks.purpose: Block the sign-update crash exploit that sends oversized line components.
checks.how_it_works: Subscribes to the UPDATE_SIGN packet, reads the four chat components, and if any JSON serialization exceeds 500 characters it cancels the packet and kicks the player. The same module also carries Intave's window-click crash fix.
checks.detects: Sign update packets with oversized or malformed line components, which crash vanilla sign handling on 1.8 servers.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus validates sign content; the rest ignore the packet entirely.

wiki_notes: BlockPos coded as one 8-byte long followed by 4 chat-component JSON strings capped at 384 chars each.
Server requires a loaded TileEntitySign that is editable by that player, else logs and drops it.
Stored lines are flattened to plain text with formatting codes stripped before markDirty and update.

MCP 1.8.9 C12PacketUpdateSign implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.processUpdateSign; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBlockPos, readStringFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: GuiEditSign.onGuiClosed sends new C12PacketUpdateSign (line 59): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/gui/inventory/GuiEditSign.java

packets.name: Player Abilities
packets.desc: Player toggles flying state. Only sent for the flying flag change — the server controls all other ability flags via S39PacketPlayerAbilities.

fields.name: isFlying
fields.desc: True if the player is currently flying

fields.name: allowFlying
fields.desc: Whether player is allowed to fly

packets.notes: The client only sends this when the flying state changes (pressing space twice in creative mode). The server ignores all flags except isFlying for non-creative players. Even if you set allowFlying=true, the server won't let you fly unless it sent S39 with allowFlying=true first.

writeup.p: C13 announces ability state changes: a 4-bit flag byte (invulnerable, flying, allowFlying, creative) plus fly and walk speed floats. Vanilla sends it only when the flying flag flips, from EntityPlayerSP.sendPlayerAbilities. Despite the full struct, the 1.8.9 server reads exactly one bit: it writes isFlying into the player's capabilities and discards everything else.

processPlayerAbilities is a single line: capabilities.isFlying = packetIn.isFlying() && capabilities.allowFlying. The server's own allowFlying flag, set exclusively via S39PacketPlayerAbilities, ANDs out any client claim of flight, which is the core reason ability spoofing is a dead end against vanilla. The float fields are not stored at all in 1.8.9, so a forged flySpeed or walkSpeed never reaches server math.

The 8 clients show four families. (1) Disabler modes: Memeware Watchdog sends C13 with NaN flySpeed on Hypixel, Rise 5.99's hypixelSlime and c13 modes send allowFlying/isFlying true, Spicy's Disabler sends creative flags. (2) Rise 6.x AbilitiesDisabler spams C13 every 5 ticks. (3) Flight movement: Spicy LongJump, Fly and BackupFly forge full PlayerCapabilities with random flySpeed. (4) Utility: Rise 6.x Nuker syncs the flying flag before teleport-nuking, and the script PacketAPI exposes sendAbilities. The two new research clients add two more. November Recode 2.0 only maps C13 to id 0x13 for its Lua scripting API, with no dedicated module. LiquidSense Dev declares isFlying on enable in LastestHypixelFly and Tp, and TeleportCommand spams absurd flySpeed and walkSpeed floats (1.0E8F and 1.0E8F minus 1) along its C04 teleport path.

Because the server ANDs against its own allowFlying, the packet is the safest spoof in the protocol: a forged isFlying claim is dropped silently on any non-creative player, which is why disablers spam it freely. The NaN flySpeed in Memeware targets proxy and anti-cheat parsers that copy the float before the handler drops it. The real signal anti-cheats measure is not C13 but the motion that follows: clients that declare flying then move at fly speed without S39 authorization flag on movement checks, not on the packet itself.

implementation.overview: The ability-flag packet. The server keeps exactly one bit (isFlying, ANDed against server-side allowFlying); the 8 clients abuse it as a safe desync probe in disablers and as a client-side flight declaration in movement modules.
implementation.server_handling: processPlayerAbilities writes capabilities.isFlying = packetIn.isFlying() && capabilities.allowFlying and nothing else. The invulnerable, allowFlying, creativeMode, flySpeed and walkSpeed fields are parsed from the wire and discarded. S39PacketPlayerAbilities is the only way the server-side allowFlying changes.
implementation.protocol_notes: Flag byte (0x01 invulnerable, 0x02 flying, 0x04 allowFlying, 0x08 creative) + two floats. Vanilla clients emit it on double-tap-space in creative; modules emit it on ticks, strafe events or module enable. The wire format accepts any float, including NaN and values far outside the 0..1 range.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats treat C13 as a weak signal because vanilla discards most of it. NCP and Verus correlate declared flying with actual vertical motion; a client that spams isFlying=true but moves like a walker is suspicious, and one that moves like a flier without S39 authorization flags on motion. The NaN flySpeed trick only works against layers that deserialize the float before the vanilla handler.

modules.name: Disabler (abilities spoof)
modules.purpose: Send forged C13 payloads as part of anti-cheat disabler mode suites, usually alongside C0F and C00 manipulation.
modules.how_it_works: Memeware's Watchdog mode sends C13 with isFlying=true and NaN flySpeed every 30 ticks on Hypixel. Rise 5.99's hypixelSlime mode sends isFlying=true when the server allows flying; its c13 mode sends a bare C13 with allowFlying and flying set. Spicy's Disabler sends creative-flag capabilities from its own mode logic.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Low risk against vanilla because the handler ANDs the bit away; the NaN float is the only payload that can poison a parsing layer. Motion checks remain the actual flag surface.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 uses PacketUtil.sendPacket/sendPacketWithoutEvent; Spicy uses sendPacketNoEvent on the network manager; Memeware uses sendPacketSilent.

modules.name: AbilitiesDisabler
modules.purpose: Spam C13 with a fresh isFlying=true capabilities object to desynchronize anti-cheat ability tracking.
modules.how_it_works: On StrafeEvent, every 5 ticks, builds a PlayerCapabilities (isFlying=true, allowFlying left false) and sends it through PacketUtil.send. Gated on the parent Disabler's deprecated setting.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The default-constructed capabilities leave allowFlying false, so vanilla drops the flying bit; the spam targets packet-level fingerprinting only.
modules.variations: Byte-identical AbilitiesDisabler exists in Rise 6.1.30.

modules.name: Nuker
modules.purpose: Sync the server-side flying flag before teleport-nuking so airborne path movement is not treated as un-authorized flight.
modules.how_it_works: In Teleport mode, when the player can fly but is not flagged flying, the module mutates the shared capabilities and sends C13 with isFlying=true via sendNoEvent, then path-teleports with C04 packets.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Only meaningful when the server already granted allowFlying (creative or S39); otherwise the bit is ANDed out and the C04 teleports carry the flag risk.
modules.variations: Same code in Rise 6.1.30.

modules.name: Fly / LongJump / BackupFly (ability spoof)
modules.purpose: Declare flight abilities client-side and mirror the declaration to the server as part of Hypixel-targeted flight modules.
modules.how_it_works: LongJump's onEnable forges PlayerCapabilities with isFlying, allowFlying, isCreativeMode and a random flySpeed 0.1..9.0 and sends via sendPacketNoEvent. Fly and BackupFly repeat the same construct at fixed points in their damage-fly sequences.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The server ignores the forged allowFlying, so these modules still rely on the damage-fly trick for actual flight; C13 is a state declaration that keeps the client's own capabilities and the packet stream consistent.
