packets.name: Resource Pack Status
packets.desc: Client reports the resource pack load status to the server. Sent after S48PacketResourcePackSend.

fields.name: hash
fields.desc: SHA-1 hash of the resource pack (from S48)

packets.notes: The server can force a resource pack. If the client declines, the server may kick the player.

writeup.p: C19 is the client's reply to S48PacketResourcePackSend: a hash String plus an Action enum (SUCCESSFULLY_LOADED, DECLINED, FAILED_DOWNLOAD, ACCEPTED). Vanilla sends ACCEPTED when the user confirms the download prompt, then SUCCESSFULLY_LOADED or FAILED_DOWNLOAD after the download resolves. Servers that require a pack gate features or membership on the ACCEPTED reply.

The bundled 1.8.9 server handler, handleResourcePackStatus, is an empty method; decline kicks and pack-required logic are plugin territory. Client-side, NetHandlerPlayClient.handleResourcePackSend downloads the pack and reports the outcome through C19, and the download itself is a URL fetch with no scheme validation in vanilla, which is the hole the security modules patch.

Two families. (1) Security: Rise 6.x ResourcePackCheck (a SecurityFeature) and Tenacity's AntiExploit module and Enhancements utility intercept S48, validate the URL scheme, block level:// traversal and non-http hosts, and answer C19 with FAILED_DOWNLOAD so the server's state machine stays consistent. (2) Disabler: Rise 5.99's c19 mode sends C19 with an empty hash and ACCEPTED to unlock pack-gated features without downloading. LiquidSense Dev adds a third family: a mixin on NetHandlerPlayClient's handleResourcePack performs the same scheme guard as family (1), answering C19 with FAILED_DOWNLOAD and the real hash. November Recode 2.0 only registers C19 in its Lua scripting id map (0x19).

The level:// protocol reads files from the server's save directory; a malicious pack URL with path traversal is a server-to-client file disclosure vector, which is exactly what both security implementations check for. The empty-hash ACCEPTED spoof exploits plugins that match the hash against the last S48; a strict plugin sees the mismatch, a sloppy one unlocks the feature. Because the vanilla server handler is empty, declined packs never kick in vanilla; the whole battlefield is plugin-side.

implementation.overview: The resource-pack handshake reply. Security layers in Rise 6.x and Tenacity block malicious pack URLs and answer FAILED_DOWNLOAD, while Rise 5.99's Disabler spoofs ACCEPTED with an empty hash to unlock pack-gated features without downloading anything. LiquidSense Dev ships the same scheme guard as a mixin on the vanilla handler.
implementation.server_handling: handleResourcePackStatus is an empty no-op in the bundled 1.8.9 sources; pack-required kicks and feature gating live in plugins that read the Action. The client handler performs an unvalidated URL fetch, making S48 the disclosure vector and C19 the acknowledgment channel.
implementation.protocol_notes: String hash + VarInt enum action. The hash must echo the one from the triggering S48 for strict plugins. The enum order on the wire is SUCCESSFULLY_LOADED=0, DECLINED=1, FAILED_DOWNLOAD=2, ACCEPTED=3. C19 is only meaningful after an S48; a serverbound C19 with a hash the server never sent is the spoof signature.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures C19. Anti-exploit plugins validate pack URLs server-side and match C19 hashes against their own S48 log; an empty-hash ACCEPTED or a FAILED_DOWNLOAD for a pack the server never sent is the detectable pattern. The security modules' FAILED_DOWNLOAD replies are indistinguishable from a genuine failed download, which is what makes them stealthy.

modules.name: ResourcePackCheck
modules.purpose: Block malicious level:// resource packs and reply FAILED_DOWNLOAD to keep the server state machine consistent.
modules.how_it_works: As a SecurityFeature it intercepts S48, validates scheme and path (no traversal, must end in /resources.zip), and on violation sends C19 FAILED_DOWNLOAD via sendNoEvent and cancels the pack.
modules.vanilla_hook: SecurityFeature packet handle, no module toggle.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The FAILED_DOWNLOAD reply matches what a genuine failed download looks like, so pack-gated servers see a normal failure rather than a refusal.
modules.variations: Identical SecurityFeature in Rise 6.1.30. LiquidSense Dev implements the same scheme guard as a mixin on NetHandlerPlayClient (see the resource pack guard entry).

modules.name: AntiExploit
modules.purpose: Block malicious resource packs (and other exploit packets) at the receive layer, answering C19 FAILED_DOWNLOAD for blocked packs.
modules.how_it_works: The PacketReceiveEvent handler rejects non-http/https/level schemes and level:// URLs with traversal or a missing /resources.zip suffix, cancels the S48 and replies C19 with the pack's real hash.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Uses the real S48 hash in the reply, which makes the FAILED_DOWNLOAD fully consistent with the last pack the server sent; undetectable as a block.
modules.variations: Tenacity's Enhancements utility performs the same scheme check and C19 reply globally, outside any module toggle.

modules.name: Disabler (pack accept spoof)
modules.purpose: Spoof a resource-pack acceptance with an empty hash to unlock pack-gated server features.
modules.how_it_works: The c19 disabler mode sends C19 with an empty hash string and ACCEPTED via sendPacketWithoutEvent.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: A strict server matches the hash against its own S48 log and sees the empty hash; a sloppy one unlocks the gated features. No anti-cheat involvement.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus spoofs ACCEPTED; the other implementations block instead of accept.

modules.name: Enhancements (protocol guard)
modules.purpose: Globally reject non-http/https/level pack URLs and answer FAILED_DOWNLOAD outside any module.
modules.how_it_works: The static utility validates the S48 URL scheme, sends C19 FAILED_DOWNLOAD with the real hash for bad schemes and throws URISyntaxException to abort the vanilla download.
modules.vanilla_hook: S48 receive interception via the utility's integration point.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Same stealth profile as AntiExploit: the reply is a consistent FAILED_DOWNLOAD with the correct hash.
modules.variations: AntiExploit is the user-facing module; Enhancements is the always-on guard.

modules.name: MixinNetHandlerPlayClient (resource pack guard)
modules.purpose: Block malicious level:// resource packs at the vanilla handler and reply C19 FAILED_DOWNLOAD to keep the server state machine consistent.
modules.how_it_works: @Inject on handleResourcePack HEAD, cancellable: parse the S48 URL scheme, require http/https/level, and for level:// reject traversal (..) or a path not ending in /resources.zip. On URISyntaxException it logs, sends C19(hash, FAILED_DOWNLOAD) through netManager, and cancels the vanilla handler so the download never starts.
modules.vanilla_hook: @Inject on NetHandlerPlayClient.handleResourcePack; netManager.sendPacket for the reply.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The FAILED_DOWNLOAD carries the real S48 hash, indistinguishable from a genuine download failure; same stealth profile as the Rise 6.x SecurityFeature.
modules.variations: The same mixin class also overwrites handleConfirmTransaction and fires EntityMovementEvent, which is why it appears in the S32 and S14 impl pages.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on S48PacketResourcePackSend (Tenacity), SecurityFeature handle (Rise 6.x), direct send for the spoof (Rise 5.99).
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.x answers via PacketUtil.sendNoEvent; Tenacity via mc.getNetHandler().addToSendQueue or networkManager.sendPacket; Rise 5.99 via sendPacketWithoutEvent. PingSpoofComponent also holds C19 in its blink tuple in both Rise 6.x builds. November Recode 2.0 registers C19 in its LuaEventPacket scripting id map (0x19) but ships no pack-handling module.

anticheat.overview: Artemis is the only anticheat with real logic on the resource-pack-status packet. Its PingSpoofProtocol uses the packet as a cheap keepalive on 1.8 servers to detect ping spoofing, and ResourcePackTickHandler turns it into a tick-confirmation channel. Other corpus hits are packet-type registrations and FlopAC wrappers.

checks.name: PingSpoofProtocol (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Detect ping spoofing using resource-pack responses as keepalives.
checks.how_it_works: On 1.9 and older servers, the check pushes a fake resource pack whose URL encodes a numeric id, then expects the client's ResourcePackStatus response with FAILED_DOWNLOAD and a matching id, followed by the next keepalive. Missing, out-of-order, or non-numeric responses log violations. On 1.10+ it switches to fake teleports because the resource-pack hash was removed.
checks.detects: Ping spoofers that suppress or reorder keepalive packets, and clients that answer resource-pack requests they were never sent.
checks.variations: ResourcePackTickHandler in the same repo reuses the mechanism as a tick-confirmation channel on 1.8; FlopAC and Negativity only register the packet type.

checks.name: ResourcePackTickHandler (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Turn resource-pack status into a tick counter for the connection.
checks.how_it_works: On 1.8 servers, pushes a level:// resource pack whose hash encodes a numeric id, and accepts only FAILED_DOWNLOAD responses whose URL is numeric and contains the player name. The parsed id is stored as the player's resourcePackTick.
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It feeds the tick-confirmation infrastructure that other Artemis checks use to measure connection state.
checks.variations: PingSpoofProtocol is the same mechanism used for keepalive verification; the tick handler is the non-checking consumer of it.

wiki_notes: Hash string max 40 chars echoing the S48 hash (ctor truncates past 40) plus VarInt action 0-3.
Action order is 0 loaded, 1 declined, 2 failed download, 3 accepted; PLAY serverbound 0x19.
Vanilla 1.8.9 server handler is an empty no-op; required-pack kicks and gating live in plugins.

MCP 1.8.9 C19PacketResourcePackStatus implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayServer> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayServer.handleResourcePackStatus; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readEnumValue, readStringFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerPlayClient.handleResourcePack sends new C19PacketResourcePackStatus (line 1714): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/client/network/NetHandlerPlayClient.java

packets.name: Login Disconnect
packets.desc: Kicks the client during the login phase with a JSON chat component reason message (e.g. 'You are banned', 'Server is full').

fields.name: reason
fields.desc: The disconnect reason message displayed to the player

encoding: Serialized as JSON chat component string

writeup.p: S00PacketDisconnect is the LOGIN-state kick: the server sends it with a JSON IChatComponent reason whenever the handshake fails before the player exists. NetHandlerHandshakeTCP uses it for protocol version mismatches, NetHandlerLoginServer for banned, full, whitelisted or unverified players, and any plugin that rejects a join during login. The client's NetHandlerLoginClient.handleDisconnect closes the channel with the reason, which surfaces as the GuiDisconnected screen. Its PLAY-state sibling is S40PacketDisconnect, used for kicks after the world loads.

NetHandlerLoginClient.handleDisconnect calls field_147393_d.closeChannel(packetIn.func_149603_c()), which tears down the NetworkManager and shows the disconnect screen with the JSON reason rendered. The server side has no symmetric handler because this packet is server-to-client only; the server closes the connection after sending it. Because the client handler runs on the login thread path, a module hooking PacketReceiveEvent sees the packet before the channel close, which is the window the 10 clients use to clean up state.

Three families in the 10 clients use this packet as a state-hygiene signal. Rise 5.99 Speed (line 1917) and Timer (line 81) reset their balance accumulators on S00PacketDisconnect so the MMC timer-balance state starts clean on the next join attempt. Spicy Disabler clears its C0FPacketConfirmTransaction buffer on the packet so stale transactions are never flushed into a fresh connection. LiquidSense Dev's PingSpoof imports S00PacketDisconnect but never references it again: its buffered keepalive/transaction map is exactly the structure that needs flushing on kick, so the disconnect flush was planned and left unwired. No true AutoReconnect module hooks it in this corpus: the auto-rejoin features of these clients key off the play-state disconnect path or onDisconnect, not the login kick, which is why the packet sees no reconnect logic.

Cancelling the packet would suppress the kick screen, but the channel close is driven by the server's own side, so the client gains nothing. The useful behavior is the reverse: treat the packet as a reliable 'connection died' notification. Clearing buffered transactions on disconnect matters because a stale C0FPacketConfirmTransaction replayed after relog desyncs the new window/uid sequence and can trip transaction-based anti-cheats. Timer's balance reset is defensive in the same spirit: a leftover negative balance would gate timerSpeed to 1 on the next join for no reason.

implementation.overview: The LOGIN-state kick carrying the JSON reason. No module cancels it, because the server closes the channel anyway; Rise 5.99 Speed/Timer and Spicy's Disabler instead use it as a reliable connection-death signal to reset timer balance and flush buffered transactions before the next join; LiquidSense Dev's PingSpoof carries only a dead import of it.
implementation.server_handling: Sent by NetHandlerHandshakeTCP for protocol mismatch (lines 35/39), by NetHandlerLoginServer for banned/full/whitelist and auth failures (line 79), and by plugins during login. The server closes the connection after sending; the client's handleDisconnect closes the channel with the reason, showing GuiDisconnected.
implementation.protocol_notes: LOGIN state, id 0x00, one IChatComponent serialized as a JSON string with a VarInt length prefix. Clientbound only. Distinguished from the PLAY-state S40PacketDisconnect by connection state; the two share a name but are different classes. Because it arrives before the world exists, module event buses that only fire post-join never see it, which is why only receive-side state cleanup hooks it.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not an anti-cheat surface: the packet is server-initiated and carries no client-controlled data. Its relevance to anti-cheats is indirect, in what clients do in response: flushing buffered C0F transactions on disconnect keeps the exploit state machine clean, and a client that fails to do so can carry stale transaction state into the next session, which transaction-tracking anti-cheats (Verus-style) would flag.

modules.name: Speed / Timer (balance reset)
modules.purpose: Reset the timer-balance accumulator when the server kills a login, so the MMC timer exploit restarts from zero on the next join attempt.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent handler checks instanceof S00PacketDisconnect. Timer.java zeroes balance, sentMessage and lastPreMotion; Speed.java zeroes balance at line 1917. Timer's MMC mode otherwise maintains a balance of 50ms per game tick minus real elapsed time, and only allows timerSpeed above 1 when the balance drops below -1000, so a stale balance would silently disable the exploit after a failed join.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the reset only changes client-side state and never touches the wire. The server sees a normal S00 then connection close.
modules.variations: Speed.java (dev/rise/module/impl/movement/Speed.java) performs the same balance reset at line 1917 in its packet handler, alongside its S08PacketPlayerPosLook flag logic. Both are Rise 5.99; Rise 6.x drops the pattern in favor of its component-based timer.

modules.name: Disabler (buffer flush on kick)
modules.purpose: Drop the buffered C0FPacketConfirmTransaction queue when the connection dies, so no stale transaction is replayed into the next session.
modules.how_it_works: EventPacket pre handler checks instanceof S00PacketDisconnect and clears C0FPackets. The same queue is cleared on C00Handshake (new connection) and otherwise drained at 500-1250ms intervals via sendPacketNoEvent while the disabler is active. The module also flushes the remainder on disable.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Replaying a buffered C0F after relog would desync the fresh connection's transaction sequence and trip transaction checks; the flush-on-disconnect is what keeps the exploit state machine consistent across joins.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus clears state on S00PacketDisconnect. Tenacity 6.0's AdvancedDisablerModule and Sigma's Disabler do not reference this packet in their mined files.

modules.name: PingSpoof (import-only)
modules.purpose: Import-only reference: LiquidSense Dev's PingSpoof imports S00PacketDisconnect but never constructs or reads it in the shipped body, so the touchpoint is dead code from a planned disconnect flush.
modules.how_it_works: The live logic cancels C0FPacketConfirmTransaction and C00PacketKeepAlive on PacketEvent and re-sends them from onUpdate after a random delay in [minDelay, maxDelay] ms. The S00PacketDisconnect import at line 18 has no call site; the buffered keepalive/transaction map is exactly the structure that needs clearing on kick, so a Spicy-style flush was evidently planned and left unwired.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None from the import itself. The live delay logic is the standard ping-spoof surface; the missing disconnect flush means a buffered C0F can survive into the next connection if the player is kicked mid-spoof, the hazard Spicy's Disabler guards against by clearing its queue on S00.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99's Speed/Timer reset timer balance on S00 and Spicy's Disabler clears its C0F buffer; LiquidSense Dev is the only client whose S00 reference is a bare import with no handler.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent (Rise 5.99), EventPacket receive (Spicy) and PacketEvent/UpdateEvent (LiquidSense Dev PingSpoof). All fire before the vanilla handleDisconnect closes the channel; LiquidSense Dev's reference is a dead import with no handler.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 uses per-module onPacketReceive overrides; Spicy uses a central onEvent dispatcher with instanceof casts. LiquidSense Dev's PingSpoof imports the class without shipping a handler. None of the clients' auto-reconnect logic references this packet, so the hook is purely state cleanup.

anticheat.overview: The anticheat corpus treats the disconnect packet as a punishment transport rather than a check surface: Grim and BetterAnticheat construct WrapperPlayServerDisconnect packets to kick flagged players, Artemis wraps PacketPlayOutKickDisconnect in its packet library, and a long tail of Bukkit-era anticheats (Negativity, NoCheatPlus, ThotPatrol, Daedalus, AutoEye, AntiCheatReloaded, AntiCheatPlus) react to kicks through PlayerKickEvent instead of the wire packet. No anticheat inspects the login-state kick itself, because the server initiates it and it carries no client-controlled data.

checks.name: Kick disconnect wrapper (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Wraps PacketPlayOutKickDisconnect in Artemis's packet library so the anticheat can read the kick packet on the wire instead of relying on Bukkit events.
checks.how_it_works: GPacketPlayServerKickDisconnect is a GPacket annotated with @PacketLink to the PacketPlayServerKickDisconnect interface and implements ReadableBuffer. It is registered in PacketRepository at SERVER_PLAY + 39 and loaded by PacketExecutor and ProtocolGeneratorDirect, which keeps the play-state packet stream fully typed.
checks.detects: No detection logic. The wrapper lets Artemis observe every kick the server sends; punishment decisions live elsewhere.
checks.variations: Grim's PacketPluginMessage and BetterAnticheat's PunishmentManager build WrapperPlayServerDisconnect packets directly to perform kicks; Intave's cloud protocol sends a ClientboundDisconnect message instead of a Minecraft packet.

checks.name: Proxy-detection disconnect (PacketPluginMessage)
checks.purpose: Kicks players who route through a ViaVersion proxy, using the disconnect packet as the punishment transport.
checks.how_it_works: Watches the PLUGIN_MESSAGE channel for vv:proxy_details. When a player reports proxy details, Grim logs a warning, and if KICK_ON_VIA_PROXY is enabled it sends a WrapperPlayServerDisconnect with the configured disconnect message and then closes the connection. The disconnect packet is the server-side mechanism, not the target.
checks.detects: Proxy and ViaVersion-on-proxy setups that are incompatible with Grim's simulation, detected through the client's own plugin-message traffic.
checks.variations: BetterAnticheat's PunishmentManager sends WrapperPlayServerDisconnect for command-driven punishments and its ConfirmationTracker for timeouts; Shard's ShardPlayer builds the same wrapper for its admin disconnect command. All of them use the packet as the kick mechanism.

wiki_notes: LOGIN state id 0x00 with a single JSON chat field; client closes channel and shows GuiDisconnected after handling.
Distinct from PLAY-state S40 disconnect; modules use it only as a connection-death signal to flush C0F buffers and timer state.
MCP 1.8.9 S00PacketDisconnect implements Packet<INetHandlerLoginClient> dispatching to INetHandlerLoginClient.handleDisconnect; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readChatComponent.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerHandshakeTCP.processHandshake sends new S00PacketDisconnect (line 38) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/network/NetHandlerHandshakeTCP.java

packets.name: Keep Alive (Request)
packets.desc: Server sends a keep-alive ID that the client must echo back in C00PacketKeepAlive.

fields.name: id
fields.desc: Random keep-alive ID to echo back

writeup.p: S00PacketKeepAlive is the clientbound half of the play-state liveness probe. NetHandlerPlayServer sends it roughly once per second from its update loop with a server-chosen int key (field_147378_h), and the vanilla client echoes it back as C00PacketKeepAlive with the same key. NetHandlerPlayServer.processKeepAlive compares the echoed key and folds the round-trip into the player's ping EMA: ping = (ping * 3 + delta) / 4. Because it is the only timing-only packet in the play state, it is the reference clock that ping spoofers, disablers and timing-based velocity exploits all anchor on.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleKeepAlive echoes immediately: addToSendQueue(new C00PacketKeepAlive(packetIn.func_149134_c())). Server side, processKeepAlive is a pure timing check: a matching key updates the ping EMA, a wrong key is silently ignored. There is no per-connection timeout in the vanilla 1.8.9 server for a missing echo; timeouts are enforced by the network layer read timeout or by anti-cheat plugins. That asymmetry, an immediate client echo versus a server that never punishes a missing one, is what every keepalive-timing exploit depends on.

Four distinct uses in the 8 clients. (1) Debugger in Rise 5.99, 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 prints incoming keepalive ids to chat so the user can watch server cadence while tuning other modules. (2) Rise 6.2.4 WatchdogVelocity and WatchdogPredictionVelocity cancel the keepalive while a velocity spoof is armed, silencing the server's timing reference during the spoof window. (3) Sigma 4.11 Disabler Erisium mode captures the key on receive and replays a stale C00 every 1500ms, freezing the measured ping. (4) Rise 6.x NetworkAPI registers the class so JavaScript scripts can hook its receive. Note the corpus has no PingSpoof hit for S00: the spoofers in these clients intercept the C00 echo side instead.

Because the vanilla echo is immediate, any delay, cancellation or replay shows up as a ping shift or a stalled keepalive stream. The Watchdog velocity modules cancel S00 while holding S12/S32 packets so the server cannot correlate a latency spike with the velocity cancel; WatchdogPredictionVelocity re-injects the buffered keepalive on the strafe trigger to restore sequencing. Sigma's Erisium mode cancels C00 echoes and re-sends the last captured key on a timer, which keeps the server's key comparison failing silently so the ping EMA never updates. The trade-off is structural: cancellation is invisible to the packet stream but leaves the connection dead on servers that do track keepalive gaps.

implementation.overview: The clientbound keepalive, echoed instantly by vanilla and used by clients as the timing reference for ping, disabler and velocity-spoof logic. Corpus hits: Debugger (Rise 5.99/6.x), WatchdogVelocity and WatchdogPredictionVelocity (Rise 6.2.4), Sigma's Erisium disabler mode, and the Rise 6.x script NetworkAPI registry.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerPlayServer sends S00PacketKeepAlive(field_147378_h) roughly every second from its tick loop. processKeepAlive: if the echoed key matches field_147378_h, ping = (ping * 3 + (now - lastPingTime)) / 4; wrong or missing keys are silently dropped with no penalty. There is no vanilla timeout for a dead keepalive; connection liveness is the network layer's job.
implementation.protocol_notes: PLAY state, id 0x00, one VarInt int key (server-tick counter in vanilla). Clientbound; the serverbound echo is C00PacketKeepAlive with the same id value but a different class in the opposite direction. The key is opaque to the client: modules that mutate or replay it rely on the server never validating beyond equality with the last sent key. Because it arrives constantly, it is also the cheapest packet for modules to use as a timing beacon.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: NCP and AAC track keepalive timing to separate real latency from timer abuse; a frozen or wildly inflated ping is a classic timer/fly tell. Verus-era checks correlate keepalive gaps with C0F transaction gaps, which is why the Rise 6.2.4 Watchdog modes cancel S00 and S32 together, and why Sigma's Erisium mode replays keys instead of cancelling outright: pure cancellation is strong but lethal on servers with keepalive timeouts. Debugger and NetworkAPI are observation-only and never flag.

modules.name: Debugger
modules.purpose: Print incoming keepalive ids to chat so the user can observe the server's keepalive cadence while developing or tuning timing-based modules.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent handler checks instanceof S00PacketKeepAlive and prints 'KeepAlive | id: <key>' via Rise.addChatMessage; it prints S32PacketConfirmTransaction ids the same way. Rise 6.x gates the branch behind a keepAlive BooleanValue and formats through ChatUtil.display.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: observation only, no wire mutation, so the vanilla echo still fires and nothing is flagged.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 Debugger.java (lines 113-114) add the keepAlive BooleanValue toggle and switch to ChatUtil.display; both still read func_149134_c() for the id.

modules.name: WatchdogVelocity / WatchdogPredictionVelocity (keepalive cancel)
modules.purpose: Cancel incoming keepalives while a velocity spoof is armed, so the server's timing probes stay silent during the window where the client holds velocity and transaction packets.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent switch: while active, S12PacketEntityVelocity and S32PacketConfirmTransaction are buffered and cancelled, and the S00PacketKeepAlive case either cancels outright (WatchdogVelocity, gated by a spoof BooleanValue) or buffers it on every third tick (WatchdogPredictionVelocity). On the strafe/boost trigger the buffer is replayed through PacketUtil.receive, restoring the keepalive and transaction sequence.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Suppressing keepalive echoes during a knockback spoof prevents the server from measuring a latency spike that correlates with the velocity cancel. Cancelling S00 and S32 together keeps the two timing references consistent, which matters because Verus-style checks correlate keepalive gaps with transaction gaps.
modules.variations: WatchdogVelocity.java (line 125) cancels the keepalive without buffering it, gated by its own spoof BooleanValue and paired with S16/S15/S17 entity-look buffering; WatchdogPredictionVelocity adds the 3-tick buffering and yaw-based release logic.

modules.name: Disabler (Erisium keepalive replay)
modules.purpose: Freeze the server's ping measurement by cancelling C00 echoes and re-sending a stale captured key on a fixed 1500ms cadence.
modules.how_it_works: The EventPacket receive handler intercepts S00PacketKeepAlive, stores func_149134_c() as lastKey, and arms the erisium flag. In EventUpdate, when erisium is set and the timer hits 1500ms, the module sends C00PacketKeepAlive(lastKey) via sendPacketNoEvent. The send-side branch cancels real C00 echoes in Faithful, Erisium, SagePvP and ColdNetwork modes.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The stale key makes processKeepAlive drop the update silently, freezing ping with no packet-level anomaly. The periodic replay keeps the connection alive on servers that do track keepalive gaps, which pure cancellation cannot claim. The mode pairs with the transaction cancels in the same module (SagePvP/ColdNetwork) for servers that correlate the two.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus implements the capture-and-replay pattern on this packet; Rise 6.x and Memeware implement the same idea on the C00 send side instead.

modules.name: NetworkAPI (script registry)
modules.purpose: Expose S00PacketKeepAlive to the JavaScript scripting API so user scripts can hook its receive event.
modules.how_it_works: A static Class array named clientbound lists S00PacketKeepAlive.class alongside every other play-state server packet; the script engine maps the registered classes to receive events for script handlers. The corresponding serverbound array lists C00PacketKeepAlive.class for the send side.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: scripts run client-side and the registry itself never mutates packets; any flagging risk comes from what the script does with the event.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the identical registry at com/alan/clients/script/api/NetworkAPI.java. No other client exposes this packet to a scripting layer.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the universal hook for the clientbound S00. Rise 6.x uses @EventLink listeners; Sigma uses its RegisterEvent EventPacket bus; the script path routes through NetworkAPI's class registry.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 uses per-module onPacketReceive overrides; Rise 6.x uses component and @EventLink listener APIs with PacketUtil.receive/sendNoEvent for replay; Sigma mutates nothing on receive but stores the key for its send-side replay; Spicy, Memeware, Nekoware and Tenacity have no module-level reference in this corpus.

anticheat.overview: S00 is the server's keep-alive probe: the client must echo the id back in C00. Anticheats use the round trip as their latency clock: the server records when it sent each id and when the matching reply arrives, which yields the player's ping and exposes ping-spoof, timer and connection-manipulation cheats. The corpus shows the same echo-tracking pattern at every scale, from the four-line ConnectionManager in Frequency to NCP's keepalive-frequency check with kick actions and Grim's validation that the replied id was actually sent.

checks.name: BadPacketsO (Grim)
checks.purpose: Flags keep-alive replies whose id was never sent by the server, the signature of a spoofed or replayed keep-alive stream.
checks.how_it_works: Tracks every OUT keep-alive id in a queue. On the IN keep-alive reply, searches the queue for the id: a match removes the id (pruning the queue) and passes, while a reply with an unknown id flags and cancels the packet.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof clients that fabricate keep-alive replies, and lag-switch or timer tools that replay stale ids.
checks.variations: Hydro's KeepAliveTracker and Frequency's ConnectionManager implement the same echo matching; only Grim validates and cancels the reply.

checks.name: KeepAliveAdapter + KeepAliveFrequency (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Limits keep-alive reply frequency and records last keep-alive timing for the god-mode and moving checks.
checks.how_it_works: ProtocolLib adapter on both keep-alive directions: the receiving side always updates lastKeepAliveTime (even when the check is disabled, because fight.godmode depends on it) and runs the KeepAliveFrequency check, which cancels the reply when the frequency exceeds the configured limits; the sending side records the outgoing id so the expected-reply model stays consistent.
checks.detects: Keep-alive spam, timer manipulation that shows up as impossible reply frequency, and the desync that ping-spoofing produces.
checks.variations: Frequency's ConnectionManager keeps the same last-sent-time map but only computes ping; NCP adds frequency limits and actions.

checks.name: KeepAliveTracker (Hydro)
checks.purpose: Tracks the keep-alive round trip as the player's latency clock, feeding ping data to every other check.
checks.how_it_works: On the OUT keep-alive, stores the id with a send timestamp in an expected map. On the IN reply, looks up the id, removes it and computes keepAlivePing as the receive timestamp minus the send timestamp, setting the acceptedKeepAlive flag. The ping value is displayed in the /hydro debug command and feeds the ping-based exclusions.
checks.detects: Ping spoofing is exposed because the computed ping diverges from the transport-level expectation; the tracker itself is data, not a flagger.
checks.variations: Frequency and Tecnio's ConnectionTracker use the identical map-and-measure pattern; Hydro exposes the value to its GUI and checks.

checks.name: ConnectionManager (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Converts keep-alive and transaction echoes into a measured ping that every check reads for latency exemptions.
checks.how_it_works: TickManager sends the OUT keep-alive and stores the id with a timestamp; the incoming processor calls onKeepAlive when the reply arrives. ConnectionManager looks up the recorded send time for that id and stores the difference as keepAlivePing. PingSpoofA/B and the lag exemptions then compare this keep-alive ping against the transaction ping.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof and timer cheats: a keep-alive ping that disagrees with the transaction ping is the flag condition in PingSpoofA.
checks.variations: Hydro's KeepAliveTracker is the same pattern; Frequency pairs it with the transaction clock, which Hydro handles in a separate tracker.

wiki_notes: The server kicks the client if it does not respond to a keep-alive within 15 seconds, and the client disconnects with a timeout if the server sends none for 20 seconds.
The vanilla server generates the keep-alive ID from a system-dependent time in milliseconds.
MCP 1.8.9 S00PacketKeepAlive implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleKeepAlive; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerPlayServer.update sends new S00PacketKeepAlive (line 152): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/network/NetHandlerPlayServer.java

packets.name: Server Status
packets.desc: Responds to C00PacketServerQuery with the server's status as a JSON string (MOTD, players, version, favicon, mod info).

fields.name: jsonResponse
fields.desc: JSON-encoded ServerStatusResponse with version, players, description, favicon

packets.notes: The JSON response includes: version (name + protocol number), players (max + online + optional sample list), description (MOTD ChatComponent), and optionally favicon (base64-encoded PNG with 'data:image/png;base64,' prefix). For modded servers, may include Forge mod info.

writeup.p: The STATUS-state reply to C00PacketServerQuery. NetHandlerStatusServer.processServerQuery answers with `sendPacket(new S00PacketServerInfo(this.server.getServerStatusResponse()))`; the payload is one String holding the full ServerStatusResponse JSON: version name and protocol number, online/max player counts with an optional sample list, the MOTD as a serialized ChatComponent, an optional base64 favicon data URI, and the Forge mod list on modded servers. It is the only clientbound STATUS packet that carries data; S01PacketPong carries only a timestamp echo.

NetHandlerStatusClient.handleServerInfo is reached through the anonymous INetHandlerStatusClient that OldServerPinger installs per ping. It stores the parsed ServerStatusResponse into the ServerData entry (serverMOTD, gameVersion, playerList), records the current system time, and immediately sends C01PacketPing with that timestamp. The connection is then driven toward close: S01PacketPong returns, the latency is computed, and the channel closes with "Finished". RealmsServerStatusPinger uses the same handler shape for the Realms list.

None of the 8 reference clients touches it. Every corpus hit for S00PacketServerInfo is a net/minecraft vanilla file (OldServerPinger, EnumConnectionState registration, INetHandlerStatusClient, the packet class, RealmsServerStatusPinger, NetHandlerStatusServer). The reason is structural: the STATUS handshake runs before the module system exists, mc.thePlayer is null, and the 8 clients dispatch module events only in the PLAY state. Server detection in these clients (Hypixel checks, brand sniffing) happens later via ServerData after the list entry is filled by the vanilla handler, or in PLAY state via S02PacketChat.

There is no timing or state abuse available to a client here: the server builds the response, the client renders it. The interesting abuse runs the other direction. A malicious server can stuff the JSON with oversized favicon data (bandwidth cost per ping), hostile chat JSON, or a protocol number far from 47 to force the incompatibility screen. Vanilla 1.8.9 rate-limits nothing on processServerQuery, which is why proxy plugins and BungeeCord fronts exist to absorb ping floods. Anti-cheats have no stake in the STATUS state; the packet is invisible to movement checks.

implementation.overview: The STATUS-state server info reply. All 8 reference clients are byte-identical vanilla here: the corpus contains zero module files for this packet because the STATUS handshake runs before any module system loads. Server detection that these clients do perform happens later, in PLAY state.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerStatusServer.processServerQuery responds to every C00PacketServerQuery with `new S00PacketServerInfo(this.server.getServerStatusResponse())`. getServerStatusResponse caches the JSON string until the next tick; favicon and player-sample data are rebuilt on the server tick. There is no per-connection rate limit in the vanilla handler; a flood of queries simply gets a flood of responses, which is why ping-protection plugins and proxy fronts intercept the STATUS state.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: one String (VarInt length prefix + UTF-8) containing the JSON. The protocol number inside version.protocol must match the client's protocol (47 for 1.8.9) or the client shows an incompatibility screen before the MOTD renders. Ordering: the server sends S00 only in reply to the query; the client then sends C01PacketPing; S00 and S01 are not required to be adjacent, but vanilla always answers them in order. The favicon is a data URI ('data:image/png;base64,...') so the JSON length cap of 32767 bytes applies to the whole response.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: None. The STATUS state precedes encryption, authentication, and world state, so no anti-cheat measures this packet. The practical constraints are plugin-side: ping limits (per-IP query caps), MOTD/favicon validation, and protocol-version gating. A client module gains nothing by intercepting this packet, and none of the 8 clients does.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients ship the stock 1.8.9 handler tree unchanged: identical OldServerPinger anonymous handler, identical EnumConnectionState registration at clientbound id 0, identical RealmsServerStatusPinger. No client has forked any of these files.

anticheat.overview: The STATUS-state server info reply is invisible to server-side anticheats: it predates encryption and world state, and the corpus shows only registration and wrapper plumbing. Artemis maps the packet in its repository and wraps PacketStatusOutServerInfo for its packet library, Negativity lists SERVER_INFO in its packet type registry, and NoCheatPlus keeps deprecated protect-clients MOTD config constants that never became checks. Nothing client-controlled flows through the response, so there is no detection surface.

checks.name: Status packet registration and wrapper (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Registers PacketStatusServerInfo in Artemis's packet repository and wraps the raw status response so the library can read the packet stream.
checks.how_it_works: PacketRepository maps SERVER_STATUS + 1 to PacketStatusServerInfo.class and HardcodeMap binds the NMS name PacketStatusOutServerInfo to that interface. The wrapper class PacketStatusServerInfoServer extends GPacket and implements ReadableBuffer, giving the status packet a typed slot in the library.
checks.detects: No detection logic. The wrapper exists so STATUS-state traffic is fully typed; no Artemis check subscribes to it.
checks.variations: Negativity's PacketType lists SERVER_INFO ("OutServerInfo") alongside its proxy-side ServerInfo model, and NoCheatPlus carries deprecated PROTECT_CLIENTS_MOTD_ACTIVE and PROTECT_CLIENTS_MOTD_ALLOWALL constants in ConfPaths. Neither inspects the response.

wiki_notes: The JSON response has the shape version {name, protocol}, players {max, online, sample [{name, id}]}, description text component, and favicon data URI; players, description and favicon are all optional, and an omitted players object displays as ??? in the server list.
The favicon must be a 64x64 PNG encoded as base64 with a data:image/png;base64, prefix or the client will not render it, and sample player names are shown in the hover tooltip in order.
If the client receives a malformed response with a missing or wrongly typed field it closes the socket and falls back to attempting a legacy pre-1.7 ping.

packets.name: Encryption Request
packets.desc: Requests the client to enable encryption by sending the server's RSA public key, a verify token (random challenge), and server ID for Mojang session auth.

fields.name: serverId
fields.desc: Server ID for Mojang session auth (empty string in 1.8.9)

fields.name: publicKey
fields.desc: Server's RSA public key for encrypting the shared secret

fields.name: verifyToken
fields.desc: Random challenge bytes the client must encrypt and return

encoding: Length of DER-encoded RSA public key
Server's RSA public key in DER format
packets.notes: After receiving this, the client generates a random AES shared secret, encrypts it + the verify token with the server's public key, and sends them back in C01PacketEncryptionResponse. Also authenticates with Mojang's session server using the serverId hash.

writeup.p: The LOGIN-state RSA challenge. NetHandlerLoginServer sends it once the client has identified itself with C00PacketLoginStart: `new S01PacketEncryptionRequest(this.serverId, this.server.getKeyPair().getPublic(), this.field_147330_e)`. It carries the server's DER-encoded RSA public key, a random 4-byte verify token, and a server id that is empty in 1.8.9 because authentication hashes the key material itself. Receiving it is the client's first proof that the server runs online mode; offline-mode servers skip encryption and go straight to S02PacketLoginSuccess.

NetHandlerLoginClient.handleEncryptionRequest generates a fresh AES secret (`CryptManager.createNewSharedKey()`), computes the server-hash `sha1(serverId + DER key + secret)` as a hex BigInteger, and calls the session service's joinServer with the profile, token, and hash. On success it replies with C01PacketEncryptionResponse(secret, key, token) and, via the packet's GenericFutureListener, calls `networkManager.enableEncryption(secret)` so the stream switches to AES/CFB8 on flush. Failure paths close the channel with disconnect.loginFailedInfo variants.

No module in the original 8 clients references it; their full corpus for S01PacketEncryptionRequest is vanilla login plumbing: NetHandlerLoginClient, EnumConnectionState registration, INetHandlerLoginClient, the packet class, and NetHandlerLoginServer. LiquidSense Dev breaks that: MixinNetHandlerLoginClient intercepts handleEncryptionRequest and, when an MCLeaks alt session is active, replaces the Mojang session-server join with the mcleaks.net join-server API, then completes the handshake through ClientUtils.sendEncryption. November Recode 2.0 ships the stock handler with no corpus hit, consistent with a vanilla login path.

The crypto handshake is where session security lives, and it is unauthenticated: 1.8.9 validates neither the certificate chain nor key size, so a MITM proxy that terminates TLS and re-encrypts with its own key can read and rewrite everything, including harvesting the joinServer call. The verify token exists to prove the server holds the private key matching the public key it sent; a proxy must replay it. Server-side, a malicious server can only force a client to do a session-server round trip per join. No client-side abuse is present in the corpus. No client-side abuse is present in the original 8 clients; LiquidSense Dev's MCLeaks integration is the one client-side alteration, substituting the mcleaks.net auth endpoint for the Mojang session server on alt sessions.

implementation.overview: The LOGIN-state encryption challenge. Zero module hits in the original 8 clients; LiquidSense Dev instruments the handshake for MCLeaks alt accounts (MixinNetHandlerLoginClient plus ClientUtils.sendEncryption), and November Recode 2.0 has no corpus hit. Online-mode detection in the other clients is implicit (the packet simply never arrives on cracked servers) and happens in the vanilla handler, not in module code.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerLoginServer.func_147326_c runs the handshake: if the server is online-mode and the connection is not already local, it stores the verify token and sends S01PacketEncryptionRequest. The login state has a timeout; a client that never answers with C01PacketEncryptionResponse is dropped by the network read timeout. After processing the response, the server decrypts with its private key, verifies the token, joins the session server with the hashed server id, and only then proceeds to compression and S02PacketLoginSuccess.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire layout: String serverId, then VarInt length + RSA public key bytes (X.509 DER), then VarInt length + verify token bytes (4 random bytes). The client's reply C01PacketEncryptionResponse carries the same key and token encrypted with the server's public key plus the AES secret encrypted the same way. Encryption starts after the response flushes, so the first encrypted frame is the next packet after C01. Compression, when enabled, is negotiated separately in login state via S03PacketEnableCompression.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: None. This packet predates world state and is identical for every legitimate client; the only players here are the session server and the Mojang account backend. For cracked servers the whole exchange disappears. The realistic threat model is impersonation of the server (unvalidated public key), which is a network-level problem, not a module-level one.

modules.name: MixinNetHandlerLoginClient (MCLeaks login)
modules.purpose: Authenticate MCLeaks alt sessions during the login handshake by substituting the mcleaks.net join-server API for the Mojang session server.
modules.how_it_works: @Inject on handleEncryptionRequest HEAD, cancellable, active only when MCLeaks.isAltActive(): generate a fresh AES secret, compute the server hash from serverId + public key + secret, POST {session, mcname, serverhash, server} to https://auth.mcleaks.net/v1/joinserver, close the channel on any failure, and on success call ClientUtils.sendEncryption and cancel the vanilla handler.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Server-side this looks like a normal online-mode login because the S01/C01 exchange still happens; only the auth backend differs. Cracked servers never see it because they skip encryption entirely.
modules.variations: Part of the MCLeaks (mcleaks.net) integration; the sendEncryption step is factored into ClientUtils.

modules.name: ClientUtils (sendEncryption helper)
modules.purpose: Send the C01PacketEncryptionResponse and enable AES stream encryption after the S01 challenge is handled.
modules.how_it_works: sendEncryption(networkManager, secretKey, publicKey, encryptionRequest) builds C01PacketEncryptionResponse(secretKey, publicKey, encryptionRequest.getVerifyToken()) and sends it with a GenericFutureListener that calls networkManager.enableEncryption(secretKey) on completion, mirroring the vanilla handler's flow.
modules.vanilla_hook: Called from MixinNetHandlerLoginClient; networkManager.sendPacket plus GenericFutureListener.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None; this is the vanilla-compatible encryption continuation. It exists so the mixin path and any future callers share one code path.
modules.variations: ClientUtils also hosts the logger, fast-render toggle and chat helpers used across LiquidBounce.

implementation.client_variations: The original 8 clients ship the stock 1.8.9 NetHandlerLoginClient unchanged, and so does November Recode 2.0 per its corpus. LiquidSense Dev replaces the join flow only for MCLeaks alt sessions, keeping the vanilla path for real accounts. Rise 6.x renames the fields (verifyToken instead of field_147330_e) but the behavior is identical: same shared-secret generation, same joinServer call, same enableEncryption-on-flush listener.

anticheat.overview: The login encryption challenge is the least instrumented packet in this set: exactly one anticheat references it, and only as packet-library plumbing. Artemis maps SERVER_LOGIN + 2 to PacketLoginOutEncryptionBegin so login-state traffic is typed; no anticheat validates the RSA handshake, because the exchange is identical for every legitimate client and predates world state.

Client answers with C01 carrying AES secret plus token encrypted under server key, then enables AES/CFB8 stream on flush.

packets.name: Join Game
packets.desc: Welcomes the player into the world. Sends entity ID, gamemode, dimension, difficulty, max players, world type, and reduced debug info.

fields.name: maxPlayers
fields.desc: Max players (used to draw tab player list)

fields.name: reducedDebugInfo
fields.desc: Whether to hide coordinates in F3 debug screen

encoding: Player's own entity ID on the server
If true, hides coords from F3
packets.notes: This is the VERY FIRST PLAY-state packet the client receives after login. It creates the WorldClient and EntityPlayerSP. All modules that depend on mc.theWorld or mc.thePlayer being non-null must wait for this packet. It's the universal 'onWorldLoad' trigger.

writeup.p: The first PLAY-state packet and the world-join trigger. ServerConfigurationManager sends it as the final step of player placement: `new S01PacketJoinGame(entityId, gameType, hardcore, dimension, difficulty, maxPlayers, worldType, reducedDebugInfo)`. The client handler is where the world is born: NetHandlerPlayClient.handleJoinGame creates the PlayerControllerMP and WorldClient from the packet's world type and dimension, calls loadWorld, sets the player's entity id and dimension, shows GuiDownloadTerrain, and replies with the MC|Brand custom payload. Everything that needs mc.theWorld or mc.thePlayer non-null waits on this packet.

handleJoinGame first runs PacketThreadUtil.checkThreadAndEnqueue, which in the Rise 6.x and Tenacity trees special-cases S01PacketJoinGame in clientPreProcessPacket so the world creation is guaranteed on the main thread. Then: `this.gameController.playerController = new PlayerControllerMP(...)`, `this.clientWorldController = new WorldClient(this, new WorldSettings(...), ...)`, `loadWorld`, dimension and entity id assignment, currentServerMaxPlayers, reduced-debug flag, game type set, settings re-sent, and the C17PacketCustomPayload MC|Brand reply. After that the server streams chunks and the respawn/spawn chain.

Three non-vanilla references exist in the corpus. NetworkAPI (script api) lists S01PacketJoinGame.class at index 1 of its clientbound packet table, so JavaScript scripts can construct and inject it and can key script logic off world join. VulcanSpeed (movement/speed) imports the class but never uses it: the reference is a dead import. LiquidSense Dev's MixinNetHandlerPlayClient injects at handleJoinGame HEAD, cancellable, and re-runs the whole world-creation sequence itself when AntiForge blockFML is enabled, so the stock (Forge-aware) handler never executes. The clients that need join-time resets (Rise 5.99's WorldChangedEvent, Sigma's event system) fire their own world-change events from elsewhere rather than hooking this packet.

S01PacketJoinGame carries no movement data, so anti-cheats ignore it; its value is state. A module that misorders its join handling can inherit stale state: old entity id, wrong dimension, or a game type that contradicts the client's PlayerControllerMP. The vanilla handler is also the moment the client reveals its brand via MC|Brand, which server plugins use for client detection. Script-injected S01 packets (NetworkAPI receivePacket) let a script replay a join outside the normal flow, which desynchronizes client and server state; none of the 8 clients ships a module that does this.

implementation.overview: The world-join packet: vanilla handleJoinGame constructs the entire client world from its fields. Module interest is minimal in the corpus: Rise 6.x exposes it to scripts via NetworkAPI, one Rise 6.2.4 speed mode carries a dead import, and LiquidSense Dev re-implements the handler in a cancellable mixin for AntiForge blockFML. World-change events in the other clients fire from their own infrastructure.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager.initializeConnectionToPlayer builds the S01 payload from the player's game type, hardcore flag, the world provider's dimension id, difficulty, server max players, terrain type, and the reducedDebugInfo gamerule, then sends it as the first packet of the PLAY stream. The server then follows with S41PacketServerDifficulty, spawn position, and the chunk bulk. The client's MC|Brand reply arrives as C17PacketCustomPayload and is how vanilla records the client mod name.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire layout: int entityId, unsigned byte gamemode, byte dimension (signed: -1 nether, 0 overworld, 1 end), unsigned byte difficulty, unsigned byte maxPlayers, String worldType, boolean reducedDebugInfo. Ordering constraint: S01 is the very first PLAY-state packet; the client transitions the connection into PLAY on login success and expects S01 before any world-bearing packet. Re-sent on dimension change only via the respawn path, never as a plain re-join.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures this packet; it precedes position tracking. The security-relevant detail is the MC|Brand exchange immediately after it: brand-based client detection is a server plugin reading the C17 reply, and clients that want to hide their brand forge that packet, not this one. State-reset discipline after S01 matters for movement modules (fresh timer baselines), which is the reason Rise 6.x scripts hook it.

modules.name: NetworkAPI (script api)
modules.purpose: Expose S01PacketJoinGame to JavaScript scripts: scripts can detect world join and inject or read the packet through the Network API object.
modules.how_it_works: NetworkAPI keeps two Class arrays indexed by packet id (serverbound and clientbound). S01PacketJoinGame sits at clientbound index 1. instantiatePacket picks the constructor matching the argument count and either sends the packet through addToSendQueue or injects it into the receive queue via addToReceiveQueue; scripts call Network.receivePacket(1, params) to synthesize a join packet client-side.
modules.vanilla_hook: No event hook; a direct script API. Scripts register packet listeners through the same Network object and receive S01PacketJoinGame instances as typed objects.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Read-side use is invisible to the server. Injecting a synthetic S01 via receivePacket desynchronizes client world state from the server and would cascade into movement flags, but no shipped script does this.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the identical file at com/alan/clients/script/api/NetworkAPI.java; the clientbound table (and S01's index 1) matches 6.2.4 exactly.

modules.name: VulcanSpeed
modules.purpose: A Vulcan-server speed mode; its only link to this packet is an unused import.
modules.how_it_works: The corpus hit is line 28, `import net.minecraft.network.play.server.S01PacketJoinGame;`, and a grep of the whole file confirms no other occurrence: the import is dead. The mode itself implements a Vulcan bypass via block-placement tricks (C08PacketPlayerBlockPlacement against BlockAir checks) and never reads join state.
modules.vanilla_hook: None. The reference is an import only; the mode runs on motion events.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The dead import has no detection relevance. It suggests the author once planned a join-triggered state reset (common for speed modes that must survive world changes) and dropped it.
modules.variations: No other client references S01PacketJoinGame from a module; all remaining corpus hits are vanilla.

modules.name: MixinNetHandlerPlayClient (AntiForge)
modules.purpose: Re-implement NetHandlerPlayClient.handleJoinGame at the mixin level so LiquidBounce joins without the stock handler, backing the AntiForge blockFML mode.
modules.how_it_works: handleJoinGameWithAntiForge injects at handleJoinGame HEAD, cancellable. When AntiForge.enabled and blockFML are on (and the world is not singleplayer) it runs the entire vanilla world-creation sequence itself: new PlayerControllerMP, new WorldClient from packetIn's dimension/difficulty/world type, loadWorld, entity id and dimension assignment, max players, reduced-debug flag, game type, settings re-sent, then the MC|Brand C17PacketCustomPayload reply, and cancels the vanilla method so the default handler never runs.
modules.vanilla_hook: @Inject on NetHandlerPlayClient.handleJoinGame (HEAD, cancellable); the same mixin also overwrites handleConfirmTransaction and injects addToSendQueue and entity-movement events.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat surface: S01 precedes position tracking. The detection-relevant detail is the MC|Brand payload the mixin sends with the client's mod name, which server plugins read for client identification; blockFML targets Forge mod checks, not anti-cheats.
modules.variations: Rise 6.x reaches S01 only through its script API (NetworkAPI clientbound table index 1) plus a dead VulcanSpeed import; Memeware, Nekoware, Rise 5.99, Sigma 4.11, Spicy, Tenacity 6.0 and November Recode 2.0 have no module-level join-game hook.

implementation.general_hooks: Rise 6.x scripts access the packet through the NetworkAPI object; LiquidSense Dev replaces the vanilla handler with a cancellable @Inject mixin (AntiForge blockFML); the other 7 clients have no module-level hook for this packet and rely on their own world-change events.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 both ship NetworkAPI and the vanilla handler with PacketThreadUtil special-casing S01PacketJoinGame; Tenacity 6.0 also carries the PacketThreadUtil special case; Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy use the stock handler without module involvement. LiquidSense Dev is the only client that intercepts handleJoinGame itself, cancelling the vanilla handler in favor of its own world-creation sequence.

anticheat.overview: Server-side anticheats treat the join-game packet as the state anchor of a play session. It carries no movement or combat data, so no check flags it; instead the packet re-reads the player model (entity id, gamemode, dimension, world name) in modern simulation anticheats, while classic anticheats watch the login events that surround the join. The security-relevant detail is what the packet resets: any anticheat that keeps per-player state must re-arm it here or every later check inherits stale data.

checks.name: Join-game state reset (Grim)
checks.purpose: Re-sync the simulated player model to the join-game payload: entity id, gamemode, dimension, world name and the death-screen flag.
checks.how_it_works: PacketPlayerRespawn listens on PacketSendEvent with HIGH priority. The JOIN_GAME branch wraps the packet as WrapperPlayServerJoinGame, copies entityId, gamemode, dimensionType and worldName into the GrimPlayer, sets showsDeathScreen from isRespawnScreenEnabled on 1.15+ clients, and re-arms the compensated world dimension on 1.17+ servers. The same listener owns the respawn and update-health branches, so this file is the single state-reset point for the whole session lifecycle.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: it prevents desync between the server's world state and the movement simulation, which is the precondition for every later check. A player model that never received its join payload would false-flag reach, fly and velocity checks.
checks.variations: Shard's PacketListener routes JOIN_GAME into handleJoinGame, which stores the entity id and gamemode and clears the compensated entity list. Artemis registers GPacketPlayServerLogin in its packet repository (SERVER_PLAY + 40) and fires LoginCallback on login success. Daedalus starts a 60-tick lastLogin timer used to exempt movement checks after join.

checks.name: Join-game handling (Shard)
checks.purpose: Initialize the per-player packet state when the play session starts: entity id, gamemode and a clean compensated entity list.
checks.how_it_works: PacketListener.onPacketSend switches on Play.Server packet types. JOIN_GAME is wrapped as WrapperPlayServerJoinGame and passed to handleJoinGame, which stores the entity id and gamemode on the ShardPlayer and clears compensatedEntities. The same dispatch routes RESPAWN, the SPAWN_* family and DESTROY_ENTITIES, so the join handler is one branch of the packet-state machine that all simulation checks consume.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself. It guarantees the entity id used by the client-side self entity matches the server's, which every movement and combat check assumes.
checks.variations: Grim does the same job inside PacketPlayerRespawn; Hydro resets state from the login-success packet instead (PacketEventsJoinQuitListener). Shard also records login timestamps into its violation database (recordLogin) for session analytics.

checks.name: Logins (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Rate-limit simultaneous logins to blunt login-flood spam bots that join and disconnect repeatedly.
checks.how_it_works: A CHAT_LOGINS check driven by ChatListener.onPlayerLogin. It buckets login timestamps into a six-slot ActionFrequency ring per world (or globally when per-world counting is off), scores the bucket sum against cc.loginsLimit and cancels the login when the rate exceeds it. The join-game packet itself is never parsed; the check keys off the Bukkit PlayerLoginEvent that fires around the join handshake, which is how 1.8-generation anticheats watch the join domain without touching packet code.
checks.detects: Login spam and mass-bot joins; the paired Relog check adds per-player relog throttling with a configurable deny list.
checks.variations: Negativity and BetterAnticheat (Velocity) do the same on PostLoginEvent; Artemis runs LoginCallback after login success; Daedalus and NCP both keep a per-player login timestamp used by movement exemptions, which is the other common join-domain pattern.

packets.name: Pong
packets.desc: Echoes back the exact client timestamp from C01PacketPing. The client calculates round-trip latency from the difference.

fields.name: clientTime
fields.desc: The exact same timestamp the client sent in C01PacketPing

encoding: Echoed back from C01PacketPing — same System.currentTimeMillis() value
packets.notes: The final packet in the STATUS handshake. After receiving this, OldServerPinger closes the connection and stores the computed latency (pingToServer = currentTime - echoedTime).

writeup.p: The final packet of the STATUS handshake. NetHandlerStatusServer.processPing answers C01PacketPing with `new S01PacketPong(packetIn.getClientTime())`, echoing the client's timestamp untouched. OldServerPinger's anonymous handler computes the server-list latency as `pingToServer = Minecraft.getSystemTime() - echoedTime` and closes the channel with a "Finished" ChatComponentText. The packet carries no other data, so the entire exploit surface is the timing relation between send and echo.

The handler is the anonymous INetHandlerStatusClient that OldServerPinger installs per destination. handleServerInfo stores the response and sends C01PacketPing; handlePong then measures the round trip and closes. RealmsServerStatusPinger mirrors the same two-handler shape for the Realms list. Server side, processPing is stateless: any C01PacketPing in STATUS state gets its timestamp echoed verbatim, with no correlation or deduplication.

The corpus has exactly one non-vanilla reference: Rise 5.99 StaffAlert imports S01PacketPong at line 22, and the import is unused (the module's logic only touches S02PacketChat and the Hypixel API). Every other hit across the 8 clients is vanilla. The practical conclusion is that no module in the corpus touches STATUS ping at all: server-list latency display stays fully vanilla, and the PingSpoof-style modules in these clients all operate on the PLAY-state keepalive (S00PacketKeepAlive/C00PacketKeepAlive) instead.

Delaying or dropping S01PacketPong would only corrupt the local server list entry (frozen or stale ping), with no server-visible effect and no anti-cheat consequence; none of the 8 clients bothers. The server-side surface is the echo itself: processPing is unauthenticated and unthrottled, so a proxy or plugin that wants to fingerprint clients can measure ping intervals, and a flood of C01PacketPing generates an equal flood of S01 replies. For clients, the packet is a dead end.

implementation.overview: The STATUS latency echo. Pure vanilla in 7 of 8 clients; the only module hit is an unused S01PacketPong import in Rise 5.99 StaffAlert. Ping spoofing in these clients targets the PLAY-state keepalive, not the server list.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerStatusServer.processPing echoes the clientTime long verbatim via S01PacketPong. No validation, no rate limit, no connection state tracking: the handler is a pure reflector. The client closes the connection immediately after the echo, so the server never sees a follow-up packet in the STATUS state.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire layout: a single long (8 bytes), the client's System.currentTimeMillis() captured at C01PacketPing send time. The client computes latency locally as now minus echoed value; clock skew is irrelevant because both timestamps are client-side. STATUS state runs before encryption, so the timestamp is readable by any on-path observer, which is how proxies estimate client-server distance.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: None. STATUS ping is outside play state and no anti-cheat samples it. The measurement only feeds the server-list GUI. A client faking its list ping would fool nobody but its own user, which is presumably why the 8 clients never implemented it.

The module's actual logic listens for S02PacketChat (captures the Hypixel API key from chat), sends /api new until the key is set, then polls api.hypixel.net/punishmentstats on a timer thread and notifies on staff-ban deltas. The S01PacketPong, S02PacketLoginSuccess, C00Handshake and S40PacketDisconnect imports are all dead.

modules.anti_cheat_notes: Irrelevant here: the import is never exercised. The dead import is likely a leftover from an earlier design that detected staff via status pings.
modules.variations: No other client has any module reference to S01PacketPong; Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity and both Rise 6.x builds are vanilla-only for this packet.

implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients ship the stock OldServerPinger/RealmsServerStatusPinger/NetHandlerStatusServer. Rise 5.99 alone adds the dead import in StaffAlert; Rise 6.x and Tenacity rename handler params to final but keep behavior identical.

anticheat.overview: The STATUS pong has an empty corpus: zero of the 50 anticheats reference S01PacketPong or PacketStatusOutPong. The echo runs before encryption and world state, carries a single client timestamp, and feeds only the server-list latency display, so there is nothing for a server-side anticheat to measure or flag. Ping spoofing that anticheats do care about targets the play-state keepalive, not this packet.

wiki_notes: STATUS id 0x01: single long echoing the exact C01 ping timestamp; client computes list ping as now minus echoed value.
Stateless reflector with no validation; feeds only the server-list latency display, never play-state checks.
MCP 1.8.9 S01PacketPong implements Packet<INetHandlerStatusClient> dispatching to INetHandlerStatusClient.handlePong; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readLong.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerStatusServer.processPing sends new S01PacketPong (line 48): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/network/NetHandlerStatusServer.java

packets.name: Chat Message
packets.desc: Server sends a chat message or command response to the client.

fields.name: chatComponent
fields.desc: The chat message or command response

fields.name: type
fields.desc: 0 = chat box, 1 = system message (singleplayer), 2 = above hotbar

packets.notes: Position 0 shows in chat box. Position 2 shows above the hotbar (action bar).

writeup.p: The single channel for every server-to-client message in the PLAY state: player chat, command output, kill feed, actionbar text, plugin announcements, and anti-cheat notices. The payload is a JSON ChatComponent plus a byte position (0 chat box, 1 system message, 2 actionbar above the hotbar). Vanilla routing is trivial: NetHandlerPlayClient.handleChat sends type 2 to the ingame GUI overlay and everything else to GuiNewChat.printChatMessage. Because every server plugin funnels text through it, it is the most-intercepted clientbound packet in the corpus: 25 non-vanilla file hits across 6 of the 8 clients.

handleChat runs PacketThreadUtil.checkThreadAndEnqueue, then branches on the position byte: `if (packetIn.func_179841_c() == 2) this.gameController.ingameGUI.func_175188_a(component, false); else this.gameController.ingameGUI.getChatGUI().printChatMessage(component)`. The component is parsed leniently from JSON; malformed components degrade to plain text rather than disconnecting. Server-side, S02PacketChat is the delivery vehicle: ServerConfigurationManager.sendChatMsgImpl broadcasts it, EntityPlayerMP.addChatMessage sends it per player, and kick/actionbar paths construct it directly.

Six families in the corpus. Game-end and lobby automation: Sigma AutoGG, Rise 5.99 AutoHypixel, Rise 6.x AutoPlay (parse the kill feed and the /play click actions in the component's siblings). Staff and identity: Rise 5.99 StaffAlert (captures the Hypixel API key line), Sigma StreamerMode, Spicy HideName, Rise 5.99 Denicker, Rise 6.x Streamer (rewrite or cancel messages that contain the player's name). Kill-feed banter: Memeware DeathInsult, Spicy KillSults. Request automation: Sigma AutoTPA, Rise 5.99 FightBot and BedwarsTP, Tenacity TPKiller, Rise 6.x WatchdogAutoPhase. Auth: Rise 5.99 AutoAuthme reacts to auth-me prompt text. The rest of the field is heterogeneous: Rise Nuker, PlayerHacks, Phase, Disabler, Translator and Ranking, Rise 6.x APIKeyComponent, IRCInfoComponent, AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent (uses S02 as a frame-rate hint), LoggerRCECheck, and the Spicy meme modules. Nekoware v1 is the only client with zero module hits.

The JSON component is attacker-controlled server text, and the Log4Shell era made that concrete: Rise 6.x ships LoggerRCECheck, a SecurityFeature that pattern-matches `${...}` in the unformatted and formatted text of every S02PacketChat (and in S29 sound names) and blocks the packet before it reaches the logger. Beyond RCE, the component's click events carry runCommand actions, which AutoPlay extracts programmatically instead of waiting for a user click. Cancel-and-rerender name protection (StreamerMode) hides the player's name from the local log while the original packet never renders. DeathInsult appends a random hex suffix so message-spam filters cannot match the repeated insult string. Position matters: modules that must react to actionbar text (AutoPlay skips non-chat via isChat()) filter on the type byte.

implementation.overview: The chat/actionbar delivery packet and the most-intercepted clientbound packet in the corpus. Six module families parse it: game-end automation, staff detection and name protection, kill-feed banter, request automation, auth-me login, and a long tail of utility and security components. Nekoware v1 alone has zero module hits.
implementation.server_handling: Server emission points: ServerConfigurationManager.sendChatMsgImpl builds S02PacketChat and broadcasts to all players; EntityPlayerMP.addChatMessage sends to one player; NetHandlerPlayServer wraps kick reasons and actionbar messages. Nothing validates the component server-side because the server is the author of it. The client parses it leniently; the only client-side failure mode is a giant JSON string approaching the 32767-byte String cap, which degrades to a truncated render.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire layout: ChatComponent serialized as JSON (String, VarInt length + UTF-8), then a byte position (0 chat, 1 system/singleplayer, 2 actionbar). Components are trees: getFormattedText() includes color codes, getUnformattedText() strips them, getSiblings() exposes the child components where click actions (runCommand/suggestCommand) and hover events live. AutoPlay reads /play commands by splitting a sibling's toString() on quotes. Position 2 messages bypass the chat history and render above the hotbar; isChat() (type == 0) is the standard filter before pattern matching.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures chat content or rate, but anti-cheat messages themselves are data for modules: Tenacity TPKiller and Rise 6.x WatchdogAutoPhase and Nuker read server notices from this packet to trigger or reset their behavior. Server-side, the same channel is the delivery path for ban/kick notices, so watchdog-style anti-cheats both emit through it and are blind to its client-side consumption. The only hard security boundary is injection: LoggerRCECheck exists because a ${...} payload inside a chat component could reach the logging pipeline; the pattern match on both text forms is the mitigation.

modules.name: AutoGG / AutoPlay / AutoHypixel
modules.purpose: Detect game-end or lobby prompts in chat and react automatically: send gg, queue the next game, or rejoin.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent listener instanceof-checks S02PacketChat, filters on position, and pattern-matches the component text. Rise 6.x AutoPlay skips non-chat positions via chat.isChat(), looks for a 'play again?' prompt, iterates getSiblings(), and extracts the /play command embedded in a click action by splitting the sibling's toString() on quotes, then sends it via ChatUtil.send. Sigma 4.11 AutoGG matches kill-feed lines and calls ChatUtil to send gg.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Sending a /play command within milliseconds of the game-end prompt is the only tell, and server-side it is indistinguishable from a fast human click. No anti-cheat flags chat automation.
modules.variations: Sigma 4.11 AutoGG matches '1st Killer -' / 'Winner:' style lines and sends gg; Rise 5.99 AutoHypixel reacts to lobby prompts; Rise 6.x AutoPlay extracts the exact /play string from the component's click action, which is more robust than pattern tables. November Recode 2.0's AutoPlayModule matches the exact 'You won! Want to play again? Click here!' and 'You died! Want to play again? Click here!' lines, walks getSiblings() for a RUN_COMMAND ClickEvent, stores the command, and sends it via addToSendQueueSilent after a configurable delay; a BLOCKS_MC mode swaps to a paper item instead of a chat command.

modules.name: StaffAlert
modules.purpose: Track Hypixel staff bans by capturing the API key from chat and polling the punishment stats endpoint.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketReceive scans every S02PacketChat: if the unformatted text starts with 'Your new API key is ', the key is stored and a chat message confirms it. Until the key is set, onUpdate sends /api new every 10 ticks on Hypixel. Once set, a timer thread polls https://api.hypixel.net/punishmentstats?key=... and fires notifications when staff_total increases.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (S02PacketChat), UpdateEvent (polling and /api new), PacketUtil.sendPacket for the chat command.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Sending /api new every 10 ticks until the key arrives is chat-rate behavior only; Hypixel does not flag it. The HTTP polling happens off the game thread, so no tick overhead.
modules.variations: Rise 6.x moves API key capture into APIKeyComponent, a separate component that parses the same chat line, leaving StaffAlert-style polling out of the module tree.

modules.name: StreamerMode / HideName / Denicker / Streamer
modules.purpose: Keep the player's name out of chat rendering: rewrite the component locally or cancel the packet entirely.
modules.how_it_works: Sigma 4.11 StreamerMode: on incoming S02PacketChat with NAMEPROTECT enabled, if the unformatted text contains the player's name, it re-renders the message with the name replaced by a colored 'You' via ChatUtil.printChat and cancels the original; otherwise it cancels any message containing a word from a join/leave/death blacklist. Spicy HideName cancels chat packets that contain the player's name; Rise 5.99 Denicker and Rise 6.x Streamer do the same with their own component access.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket with isIncoming() and EventUpdate (Sigma); Spicy uses its packetEvent inside Module onEnable/onDisable; Rise hooks PacketReceiveEvent.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling a chat packet is invisible to the server: the message was already delivered, the client just declines to render it. The risk is user-facing, not detection: legit messages get eaten by the blacklist.
modules.variations: Spicy HideName cancels only name-bearing packets; Rise 5.99 Denicker replaces the name with a generic string in the component before letting it render; Rise 6.x Streamer gates on a name toggle and casts the packet the same way.

modules.name: KillSults / DeathInsult
modules.purpose: Reply to the kill feed with an insult when the player scores a kill.
