modules.how_it_works: Memeware DeathInsult matches seven kill-feed patterns on the unformatted text (killed by / slain by / void while escaping / magic while fighting / couldn't fly / fell to their death while escaping / Hypixel reward lines, plus a Spanish 'asesino ha' variant), then sends a random insult from a static table appended with a 12-character hex suffix via mc.thePlayer.sendChatMessage. Spicy KillSults runs the same idea on its own event bus with its own phrase table.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketInEvent (Memeware's LWJEB event bus); Spicy uses its packetEvent handler.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The send rate is one message per kill, far below spam thresholds. The hex suffix exists to beat chat filters, not anti-cheats; nothing movement-related is involved.
modules.variations: Spicy KillSults lives in modules/memes with DougDimmadome, FloofyFoxes and Furries, which import S02PacketChat for the same receive-hook pattern; Spicy's Account.java also parses S02PacketChat for login handling.

modules.name: AutoTPA / FightBot / BedwarsTP / TPKiller / WatchdogAutoPhase
modules.purpose: Trigger a game action from a specific chat line: accept teleport and party requests, respond to kill messages, or react to anti-cheat checks.
modules.how_it_works: Sigma AutoTPA matches 'has requested to teleport to you', 'has requested that you teleport to them', and party-invite lines on the formatted text, verifies the requester is in FriendManager.friendsList (name or alias), and sends /tpaccept or /party accept via ChatUtil.sendChat_NoFilter. Rise 5.99 FightBot and BedwarsTP parse kill/bed lines; Tenacity TPKiller reacts to anti-cheat or kill notices; Rise 6.x WatchdogAutoPhase watches for watchdog check messages to time a phase reset.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket with isIncoming() (Sigma RegisterEvent); the other clients use their PacketReceiveEvent equivalents.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Auto-accepting a friend's TPA looks like an instant manual click; no anti-cheat measures it. The friend-list gate is the anti-abuse control: strangers cannot bait the module into sending commands.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 FightBot (combat) and BedwarsTP (movement) parse their own pattern sets; Tenacity 6.0 TPKiller (exploit) reads kill/check messages; Rise 6.x WatchdogAutoPhase reads watchdog chat notices to reset phase timing. All share the instanceof + component-text read.

modules.name: AutoAuthme
modules.purpose: Automate registration and login on auth-me servers by reacting to the server's prompt messages.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketReceive scans S02PacketChat: if the unformatted text contains '/register' the module registers, if it contains '/login' it logs in. Register generates a random 8-char password, sends /register via sendChatMessage, schedules /login one second later on a static scheduled executor, and persists the per-server credentials to authmelogins.txt. The companion onPacketSend cancels the player's own /register and /login C01PacketChatMessage packets so nothing double-fires. State resets on WorldChangedEvent and GUI transitions.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (S02PacketChat prompts), PacketSendEvent (C01 cancellation), WorldChangedEvent and OpenGUIEvent (state reset).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Auth-me servers enforce no rate limit on login packets, so the one-second-delayed /login is indistinguishable from typing. The cancelled C01 packets never reach the server, so the server never sees the double-send.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus implements auth automation on S02PacketChat; Rise 6.x drops the module entirely.

modules.name: Phase (cage phase)
modules.purpose: Gate the cage-phase exploit on S02 chat signals: enable phasing when the server announces the cage countdown, disable when the fight starts.
modules.how_it_works: The EventPacket.In listener checks S02PacketChat; on BLOCKS_MC, unformatted text containing 'Cages open in: 2 seconds!' sets canPhase true, and 'Cages opened! FIGHT!' calls setState(false). The rest of the module removes the glass block under the player while cagePhasing and restores it on disable.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The chat gate makes the exploit self-timing: phasing only starts after the server's own announcement, so the window matches the server's expected transition rather than a fixed timer.
modules.variations: Tenacity TPKiller and Rise 6.x WatchdogAutoPhase are the other chat-triggered exploit modules, but November's is the only one tied to a cage-open announcement.

modules.name: AntiBot (HytBedwars)
modules.purpose: Extract real player names from S02 kill-feed and chat lines on the Hyt (Chinese) BedWars server, so KillAura skips anti-cheat bots.
modules.how_it_works: The HytBedwars branch of onPacket matches two regexes against the unformatted text: '杀死了 (.*?)\(' for kill feed and '> (.*?)\(' for chat names. Each captured name goes into the static playerName list for 6 seconds (a background thread removes it), and the entity check later exempts entities whose names are in the list.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketEvent (S02PacketChat), UpdateEvent, and entity checks on S14PacketEntity.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The kill-feed names are server-authored, so a bot list built from them inherits server trust; the 6-second expiry keeps the list from going stale mid-game.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus mines S02 for bot whitelisting; the regexes are hardcoded for the Chinese server's kill-feed format.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent / EventPacket(isIncoming) is universal across all 6 clients with hits. Components in Rise 6.x (APIKeyComponent, IRCInfoComponent, AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent, LoggerRCECheck) subscribe to the same receive pipeline as non-module listeners. November Recode 2.0 parses S02 in EventPacket.In (AutoPlayModule, PhaseModule); LiquidSense Dev parses it in PacketEvent (AntiBot).
implementation.client_variations: Sigma reads the component via func_148915_c() (getChatComponent) and routes replies through ChatUtil.sendChat_NoFilter. Memeware and Spicy use their own LWJEB packet events and mutate nothing. Rise 5.99 reads chatComponent directly and uses event.setCancelled. Rise 6.x wraps S02PacketChat and uses isChat() plus getSiblings() for structured extraction. November Recode 2.0 reads the component via getUnformattedText() and sends replies with addToSendQueueSilent; LiquidSense Dev matches Chinese kill-feed patterns with Pattern/Matcher and maintains a timed static name list.

anticheat.overview: S02 is the outbound chat packet: anticheats send their own alerts through it, but they cannot see what the client renders, so none of them validate the packet's payload on the server side. The chat checks that exist in the corpus run on the INBOUND chat packet or Bukkit chat events and then talk back through S02: Grim flags blank tab-complete and impossible chat, NCP gates chat behind a captcha, Photon flags chat while sprinting or with an open inventory, and BetterAnticheat flags chat while chat is set to hidden. From the anticheat's point of view S02 is the delivery channel, not the input.

checks.name: ChatA (Grim)
checks.purpose: Flags blank or slash-only tab-complete packets, an exploit probe that accompanies chat-related client abuse.
checks.how_it_works: Pre-Via listener on the inbound tab-complete packet: if the text is exactly a slash or trims to empty, the check flags and cancels the packet. This is the chat-domain check in Grim's corpus for S02 because the outbound chat packet is the visible counterpart; the detection itself happens on the client-to-server side.
checks.detects: Tab-complete spam and blank tab-complete exploitation attempts that usually target chat or command pipelines.
checks.variations: Grim has no outbound-chat check at all; like every anticheat it only emits through S02.

checks.name: Captcha (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Gates chat behind a generated captcha: players must answer correctly before chat is accepted, with kick actions on repeated failure.
checks.how_it_works: On the inbound chat listener, a player flagged by other chat checks is sent a captcha question through the outbound chat channel (S02). The captcha check compares the player's next message to the generated code, increments tries and violation level on mismatch, re-sends the question, and executes the configured actions (up to kicking) once tries exceed the threshold.
checks.detects: Spam bots, chat flooders and automated chat abuse that cannot solve a text captcha.
checks.variations: Grim and Photon detect impossible chat states instead of gating; NCP is the only corpus anticheat that actively gates the chat channel.

checks.name: ImpossibleChat (Photon AntiCheatAddition)
checks.purpose: Flags chat messages that a vanilla client could not physically send, because the player is sprinting, sneaking, blocking, dead or had an inventory open.
checks.how_it_works: Listens to Bukkit's async chat event rather than the packet. If the user is sprinting, sneaking, blocking, dead, or has had an inventory open for over a second, the chat is impossible and the module flags with 25 violation points, cancelling the event at the configured violation level.
checks.detects: Chat-spoofing clients and macro bots that send chat while the real player state says chat is impossible.
checks.variations: BetterAnticheat HiddenChatCheck targets the HIDDEN chat-visibility setting instead of body state; both are impossible-chat detectors.

checks.name: HiddenChatCheck (BetterAnticheat)
checks.purpose: Flags chat messages sent while the player's client settings declare chat visibility as hidden.
checks.how_it_works: Tracks the chat-visibility value from inbound client settings (FULL, SYSTEM or HIDDEN). When a chat message arrives and the tracked visibility is HIDDEN, the check fails; the first occurrence is used as an initial-flag grace so settings that arrive late do not cause false positives.
checks.detects: Clients that send chat while the client settings say chat is disabled, which is impossible for a vanilla client.
checks.variations: Photon ImpossibleChat checks body state; BetterAnticheat checks the declared chat mode, the two complementary reads of the same impossibility.

wiki_notes: Position 2 (above the hotbar action bar) is the overlay-style message, while position 0 goes to the chat box.
MCP 1.8.9 S02PacketChat implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleChat; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readChatComponent.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.displayGUIChest sends new S02PacketChat (line 780) +2 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Login Success
packets.desc: Confirms successful authentication. Contains the player's UUID and username. Transitions the connection state from LOGIN to PLAY.
packets.notes: After receiving this, the client connection state transitions to PLAY. The client creates the EntityPlayerSP (local player entity) with the received UUID and username. Compression may be enabled next via S03PacketEnableCompression.

writeup.p: The LOGIN-state success packet. NetHandlerLoginServer sends it after encryption and session validation complete: `new S02PacketLoginSuccess(this.loginGameProfile)`, carrying the confirmed UUID and username as two Strings. Vanilla client handling is the state transition itself: NetHandlerLoginClient.handleLoginSuccess stores the GameProfile, calls `setConnectionState(EnumConnectionState.PLAY)`, and installs the NetHandlerPlayClient over the same connection. From this instant the module system's world exists conceptually, but the world itself only materializes on S01PacketJoinGame.

handleLoginSuccess is three lines in the 1.8.9 sources: `this.field_175091_e = packetIn.func_179730_a(); this.field_147393_d.setConnectionState(EnumConnectionState.PLAY); this.field_147393_d.setNetHandler(new NetHandlerPlayClient(this.field_147394_b, this.field_147395_c, this.field_147393_d, this.field_175091_e));`. The gameProfile field is the canonical UUID/name the client uses for the whole session; the session service may return a name different from the one sent in C00PacketLoginStart, and this packet is where the correction lands.

The corpus has exactly one non-vanilla reference: Rise 5.99 StaffAlert imports S02PacketLoginSuccess at line 18, and the import is unused (the module's logic touches only S02PacketChat and the Hypixel API). No module in the 8 clients reads the UUID or name from this packet. The structural reason: the packet is consumed by the login handler before any module event bus is live, and clients that need their own UUID or username read them from mc.getSession() or their GameProfile, not from the network. Session-stealing or alt-login features that would care about this packet are absent from the corpus.

The profile data is server-asserted. An offline-mode server can send any UUID and username it likes, which is the entire basis of name-based alt accounts and cracked-server identity; clients that display 'authenticated' state off this packet would be trivially spoofed. On online-mode servers the values are Mojang-confirmed, so the packet is the client's first trusted identity. No timing or state abuse exists here: the transition to PLAY is instantaneous and any delay would only stall the loading screen.

implementation.overview: The LOGIN-state success packet that hands the client its confirmed UUID and username and flips the connection to PLAY. Pure vanilla in 7 of 8 clients; the only module hit is an unused import in Rise 5.99 StaffAlert. Nothing in the corpus reads the profile from this packet.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerLoginServer sends S02PacketLoginSuccess after the encryption response validates: the server decrypts the shared secret, verifies the token, joins the session server, then sets its own state to PLAY and sends the packet, optionally preceded by S03PacketEnableCompression when compression is configured. After the send, the server installs its NetHandlerPlayServer. The client treats the packet as authoritative for the session profile.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire layout: String UUID (36 chars with dashes), then String username (max 16). Compression, when enabled, is negotiated in LOGIN state before this packet, so the first PLAY packet may already be compressed. Ordering: S02PacketLoginSuccess is the last LOGIN-state packet; the connection then expects S01PacketJoinGame as the first PLAY-state packet. The username here can differ from the login-start name when Mojang renames or corrects it.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: None. The packet precedes world state and carries only identity; anti-cheats are irrelevant to it. The security-relevant property is authentication strength: on online-mode servers the UUID is Mojang-signed, on offline servers it is arbitrary, and plugins that trust UUIDs for permissions inherit that trust boundary. No client module in the corpus touches it.

modules.name: StaffAlert
modules.purpose: Hypixel staff-ban tracker. Its reference to this packet is an import only; the module does not use S02PacketLoginSuccess.
modules.how_it_works: The corpus hit is line 18, `import net.minecraft.network.login.server.S02PacketLoginSuccess;`. The module's actual logic captures the Hypixel API key from S02PacketChat, sends /api new until the key is set, and polls api.hypixel.net/punishmentstats on a timer thread. The login-success import, like the S01PacketPong, C00Handshake and S40PacketDisconnect imports, is dead.
modules.vanilla_hook: None for this packet; the module hooks PacketReceiveEvent for S02PacketChat and UpdateEvent for polling.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Irrelevant here: the import is never exercised. A login-success hook would have let the module reset its timer at session start; the author left the import but never wired it.
modules.variations: No other client has any module reference to S02PacketLoginSuccess; the remaining corpus hits across all 8 clients are vanilla login plumbing.

implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients ship the stock handleLoginSuccess. Rise 6.x and Tenacity rename handler parameters to final; Spicy and Tenacity keep the same three-line body. None of the clients forks the login handler to emit module events.

anticheat.overview: The login success packet is another near-empty corpus: only Artemis references it, as packet-library plumbing. PacketRepository maps SERVER_LOGIN + 4 to PacketLoginOutSuccess and GPacketLoginServerSuccess wraps the wire format so login traffic is typed. No anticheat reads the UUID or username, because the packet carries only server-asserted identity and arrives before any check-relevant state exists.

checks.name: Login success wrapper (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Wraps PacketLoginOutSuccess so Artemis's packet library can read the login-success UUID and username from the wire.
checks.how_it_works: GPacketLoginServerSuccess is linked to the PacketLoginOutSuccess interface and implements ReadableBuffer. Its read method handles both layouts: pre-1.16 reads a 36-char UUID string plus a 16-char name, and 1.16+ reads four ints that are reassembled into a UUID plus the name. The result is stored as a GameProfile.
checks.detects: None. This is a typed read of server-asserted identity, not a check. No Artemis check subscribes to the packet.
checks.variations: The other 49 anticheats never reference the packet. Its only role in the corpus is keeping Artemis's login-state stream typed.

wiki_notes: The username returned here is authoritative and can differ from the name sent in Login Start when accounts are renamed or corrected, so clients should adopt this profile for the session.

MCP 1.8.9 S02PacketLoginSuccess implements Packet<INetHandlerLoginClient> dispatching to INetHandlerLoginClient.handleLoginSuccess; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readStringFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerLoginServer.operationComplete sends new S02PacketLoginSuccess (line 128): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/network/NetHandlerLoginServer.java

packets.name: Enable Compression
packets.desc: Enables zlib compression for all subsequent packets. Sets the compression threshold — packets >= this size are compressed.

fields.name: compressionThreshold
fields.desc: Minimum packet size in bytes before compression is applied. -1 disables compression.

packets.notes: After this packet, all future packets start with a VarInt prefix indicating the uncompressed length. If length=0, the data is uncompressed (smaller than threshold). If length>0, the remaining data is zlib-compressed and must be inflated.

writeup.p: The only compression control in the 1.8 protocol, sent in the LOGIN state before the play state begins. NetHandlerLoginServer emits it with the server's configured compression threshold (vanilla 256) immediately after the login sequence accepts the player, and defers the login-to-play state flip until the write lands via a ChannelFutureListener. From that point every packet on the connection is framed with a VarInt uncompressed-length prefix: 0 means the payload is raw (below threshold), any other value means the remaining bytes are zlib data the receiver must inflate. A threshold of -1 disables compression entirely.

The client handler NetHandlerLoginClient.handleEnableCompression (func_180464_a in the MCP-named builds) does exactly one thing: networkManager.setCompressionTreshold(threshold), which swaps a compressor/decompressor codec into the Netty pipeline. The packet is processed on the Netty thread during the login phase, before the module event bus is wired to any gameplay traffic. None of the 8 clients modifies this handler: the corpus shows the vanilla file verbatim in Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity, and the Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 copies repackaged under Client-release2/Client/src/main/java with identical logic.

The corpus contains zero non-vanilla references for this packet across all 8 clients. Intercepting it is structurally pointless: the server decides compression unilaterally and compresses anything at or past its threshold, so a client that cancels the packet desynchronizes framing and dies on the next oversized packet instead of gaining anything. The only lever would be injecting a raw ChannelHandler ahead of the codec to observe decompressed traffic earlier, which none of the 8 clients does. Modules are also simply not active during login: the connection has no world, no player and no module state.

None exercised in the corpus. The packet arrives before any gameplay traffic, so anti-cheats never evaluate it and there is nothing to flag. The only failure mode is protocol-level: a client that ignores the threshold breaks framing once the first oversized packet crosses the wire, which shows up as a connection drop, not an exploit. Compression here is a bandwidth optimization, not a security boundary.

implementation.overview: Login-state one-shot that announces the server's compression threshold (vanilla 256) and flips both directions of the connection onto the zlib codec before play begins. No module in any of the 8 clients references it: login handlers sit outside the module event bus and the server frames compressed packets unilaterally, so there is nothing to intercept and nothing to gain.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerLoginServer sends S03PacketEnableCompression(this.server.getNetworkCompressionTreshold()) right after the login sequence accepts the player and before the connection state flips to PLAY. The write is paired with a ChannelFutureListener so the state transition only happens once the packet is flushed. After this point the server-side pipeline compresses any outgoing packet whose encoded size reaches the threshold, and expects the client to do the same in the reverse direction. The threshold is server configuration, typically 256 in vanilla; -1 disables compression.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format is a single VarInt threshold (readVarIntFromBuffer / writeVarIntToBuffer in MCP). The length-prefix framing applies to every subsequent packet in both directions: a zero prefix marks a raw payload, a nonzero prefix gives the uncompressed length of the zlib data that follows. The switch is asymmetric in time: the S03 packet itself travels uncompressed, then both directions switch together. Ordering is preserved because the pipeline mutation is deferred until the packet write completes, so no packet can slip across the boundary mis-framed.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats never see this packet: it is exchanged before the play state and before any gameplay event they track. The only party that could abuse compression framing is a MITM or proxy, and that is a transport-layer concern outside the packet itself. For cheat development the practical consequence is that packet-level inspection and injection sit above the codec in every one of the 8 clients, so compression is transparent to module code.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients ship the vanilla login handler. The corpus deltas are cosmetic: MCP-named func_180464_a in Memeware, Nekoware and Sigma versus handleEnableCompression in Rise, Spicy and Tenacity, plus the Rise 6.x repackaging under Client-release2/Client/src/main/java. No client registers a packet event for login-state traffic at all.

anticheat.overview: S03PacketEnableCompression is exchanged in the LOGIN state, before the anticheat pipeline exists, and the 50-anticheat corpus contains exactly one anticheat: Artemis, with two files that are packet-type plumbing, not checks. PacketRepository maps SERVER_LOGIN + 3 to PacketLoginOutSetCompression, and the packet interface itself is declared in the wrapper API. No anticheat hooks login-state traffic, and the server decides the compression threshold unilaterally, so there is nothing to validate, cancel or flag. The checks list is empty by corpus fact, not by omission.

wiki_notes: The packet is entirely optional: if compression is disabled the vanilla server simply never sends it rather than sending a disable value.
When present it must be sent before Login Success, and everything after it uses the compressed packet format with a VarInt uncompressed-length prefix per packet.

MCP 1.8.9 S03PacketEnableCompression implements Packet<INetHandlerLoginClient> dispatching to INetHandlerLoginClient.handleEnableCompression; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerLoginServer.tryAcceptPlayer sends new S03PacketEnableCompression (line 119): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/network/NetHandlerLoginServer.java

packets.name: Time Update
packets.desc: Synchronizes the world time (total world age and day/night cycle time). Sent every few seconds or when time accelerates (sleeping).

fields.name: totalWorldTime
fields.desc: Total ticks since world creation (monotonically increasing)

fields.name: worldTime
fields.desc: Current day/night time (0-24000). worldTime % 24000 for time-of-day.

packets.notes: Time values: 0=dawn, 6000=noon, 12000=sunset, 18000=midnight. When all players sleep, time jumps to 0 (dawn). S03 is used by modules to calculate server TPS (ticks per second) by measuring the time between S03 updates.

writeup.p: Two longs, totalWorldTime and worldTime, broadcast by MinecraftServer to every player in a dimension once per second (tickCounter % 20 == 0, line ~701 in the MCP builds) and re-sent on player join by ServerConfigurationManager (line ~787). worldTime is the day/night counter the client renders modulo 24000: 0 dawn, 6000 noon, 12000 sunset, 18000 midnight. The constructor folds the doDaylightCycle gamerule into the wire format by negation: when the rule is off the server transmits -worldTime, so the sign bit is the freeze flag and the boolean never exists as a packet field.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleTimeUpdate runs on the main thread via PacketThreadUtil and performs two writes: theWorld.setTotalWorldTime(packet.func_149366_c()) and theWorld.setWorldTime(packet.func_149365_d()). Between corrections the client advances time-of-day itself in its tick loop, so the packet is a periodic correction, not the clock source. That is the property the Ambiance family exploits: cancel the correction and the locally pinned time holds until the next one would have arrived.

The Ambiance family spans Memeware 7.3, Rise 5.99, Rise 6.1.30, Rise 6.2.4 and LiquidSense Dev (the AquaVit fork), and Tenacity 6.0 ships the same idea as AlwaysNight. All six cancel S03 on the receive event and overwrite world time on a per-frame hook: Memeware writes 0 or 20000 depending on a Morning/Night mode, Rise 5.99 writes time + elapsed * timeSpeed, Rise 6.x adds weather forcing, LiquidSense Dev offers Daytime/Night/DIY/DayWithNight with a cycling counter, Tenacity writes a configurable value defaulting to 12000. Notably absent is Fullbright: it is a gamma/lighting override that never touches this packet, and no TPS estimator in the corpus derives server lag from S03 deltas even though the two longs are a natural clock.

Cosmetic only and invisible to the server, because the client never reports displayed time back. Observers see the desync side effects: a pinned clock shows a frozen sky on the client's own screen, and when all players sleep and the server jumps time to 0 the module visibly fights the correction. No anti-cheat measures this packet. The only hazard is a module that writes worldTime unclamped, which can push the negative freeze encoding into the local renderer and break the sky shader path.

implementation.overview: Once-per-second world-clock correction (two longs, doDaylightCycle encoded as a sign bit). Six modules across the 10 clients cancel it and pin the client clock locally, all with the same two-step shape: cancel on receive, rewrite on frame. Pure client-side cosmetics with zero server visibility.
implementation.server_handling: MinecraftServer broadcasts S03PacketTimeUpdate(totalWorldTime, worldTime, doDaylightCycle) to all players in the dimension every 20 ticks (line ~701), and ServerConfigurationManager sends a fresh copy on player join (line ~787). When doDaylightCycle is false the server negates worldTime before sending; the constructor also maps a negated 0 to -1 so the freeze flag survives the zero case. The server never validates or rates the packet stream because it is the sole author.
implementation.protocol_notes: Two raw longs on the wire; the third constructor argument (doDaylightCycle) is encoded by negation, so worldTime < 0 means the day/night cycle is frozen server-side and the client should display abs(worldTime) without local advancement. Clients that only read the longs (all 5 module implementations here) are unaffected by the sign trick. The packet is sent in the PLAY state and is dimension-scoped, so it stops at the dimension boundary and a fresh one arrives on respawn.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat flags time manipulation: the client clock is cosmetic, server-authoritative only in the sense that the server periodically corrects it, and nothing gameplay-relevant derives from it. The modules are undetectable from the wire because cancellation happens before the packet reaches the vanilla handler and no corresponding serverbound traffic exists.

modules.name: Ambiance / Ambience
modules.purpose: Pin the client's day/night clock to a fixed value by cancelling server time corrections.
modules.how_it_works: A receive-side packet event cancels every S03PacketTimeUpdate, then a per-frame hook rewrites the world clock: Memeware 7.3 sets 0 (Morning) or 20000 (Night) on UpdateEvent; Rise 5.99 computes time + elapsedMillis * timeSpeed on Render3D; Rise 6.x does the same and additionally forces weather by cancelling S2BPacketChangeGameState states 1 and 2. The cancel prevents the server value from ever landing, so the local write is the only clock.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No detection surface: the packet is receive-only, the server never learns the client's displayed time, and the cancelled packets are invisible on the wire. The only tell is a frozen or wrong sky on the client's own screen.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 cancels on PacketReceiveEvent and writes time + elapsed * timeSpeed on Render3DEvent. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 (renamed Ambience) add a weather mode that also cancels S2BPacketChangeGameState rain/thunder states, a snow color override and a temperature hook for particle rendering. Rise 6.x additionally whitelists S03 in the script API (com/alan/clients/script/api/NetworkAPI.java) so JS scripts can observe it.

modules.name: AlwaysNight
modules.purpose: Hold the client's world time at a configurable value (default 12000, midnight) by cancelling server time updates.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent handler cancels S03PacketTimeUpdate; onEnable and a render-tick listener write the configured value into the world, and onDisable restores time 0. The number setting accepts any value in 0..24000 in 1000-step increments, so the module is a general time pin despite the AlwaysNight name.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Identical to the Ambiance family: receive-side cancellation is unobservable by the server, and no gameplay state depends on the client clock.
modules.variations: Tenacity is the only one of the 8 clients that ships this as a World-category module with a user-configurable value; the other four hardcode or speed-adjust the time in the render category.

modules.name: Ambience (LiquidSense Dev)
modules.purpose: Pin the client's day/night clock by cancelling every S03PacketTimeUpdate, with four time modes, in the AquaVit LiquidSense fork (LiquidBounce base).
modules.how_it_works: onPacket cancels any PacketEvent whose packet is an S03PacketTimeUpdate. onUpdate advances a private counter a by the DayWithNight step on an MSTimer and rewrites the world clock per mode: Daytime 1000, Night 16000, DIY the configured value (default 13000), DayWithNight the cycled counter wrapped at 24000.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketEvent (receive, @EventTarget) to cancel; UpdateEvent to rewrite.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Identical to the Ambiance family: receive-side cancellation is unobservable by the server and no gameplay state depends on the client clock, so there is no flag surface.
modules.variations: The AquaVit fork is the LiquidSense Dev representative; the CCBlueX LiquidBounce Dev tree itself has no S03 module hit in the corpus. Memeware/Rise pin two hardcoded values, Tenacity's AlwaysNight is configurable with no cycle, and this fork adds a DayWithNight cycling mode driven by an MSTimer.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent (PacketInEvent on Memeware, PacketEvent on LiquidSense Dev) to cancel, plus a per-frame hook (UpdateEvent, Render3DEvent or render tick) to rewrite world time.
implementation.client_variations: Memeware uses the lwjeb-style PacketInEvent with event.cancel(); Rise 5.99 and 6.x use PacketReceiveEvent with setCancelled and write on Render3D; Tenacity uses its IEventListener<PacketReceiveEvent> and cancels via event.cancel(). All six share the same two-step shape: cancel the correction, then own the clock. LiquidSense Dev (AquaVit fork) cancels via @EventTarget PacketEvent and rewrites on UpdateEvent driven by an MSTimer, adding the only cycling (DayWithNight) mode in the corpus.

anticheat.overview: The time update packet is a server-authoritative clock correction: two longs broadcast once per second, with the doDaylightCycle gamerule folded into the sign of worldTime. Server-side anticheats never reference it. The corpus sweep for the packet names S03PacketTimeUpdate and PacketPlayOutTimeUpdate returns zero hits, and the keyword pass over 'Time' only surfaces timer utilities, TimeUtil classes and tick-delta heuristics, none of which read this packet. The client never reports its displayed time back, so the cancel-and-pin time modules are invisible on the wire and no check in any cloned anticheat targets them.

wiki_notes: Time runs at 20 ticks per second with 24000 ticks per day, and time of day is the world time modulo 24000.
The default server increments world time by 20 every second.
MCP 1.8.9 S03PacketTimeUpdate implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleTimeUpdate; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readLong.

1.8.9 callers: MinecraftServer.updateTimeLightAndEntities sends new S03PacketTimeUpdate (line 762) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/MinecraftServer.java

packets.name: Entity Equipment
packets.desc: Updates an entity's equipped item in a specific slot (main hand, armor slots).

writeup.p: Per-slot equipment sync for tracked entities. EntityTrackerEntry pushes it when a tracked entity's equipment changes (line ~399 in the bundled sources) and EntityLivingBase broadcasts it on item or armor updates (line ~1644). The payload is the entity id, a short slot 0-4 (0 held item, 1-4 boots/legs/chest/helmet) and a Slot-encoded ItemStack that may be null to clear. The initial burst arrives at entity spawn so the client can render held items and armor before other entity data matters.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityEquipment resolves the entity and calls setCurrentItemOrArmor(slot, item), which writes into the EntityLivingBase equipment array that the render layers read every frame. The local player is exempt: the client's own equipment never arrives as S04, it is driven by inventory and held-item packets, so this channel is strictly about other entities.

The corpus yields two non-vanilla references, both dead imports: Rise 5.99 Aura.java imports S04 at line 43 and never uses it in the body, and Sigma 4.11 InventoryManager.java imports it at line 30 while actually processing S09PacketHeldItemChange and S1CPacketEntityMetadata. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 expose it only through the script API whitelist (NetworkAPI.java line 50). No ESP, tracer, nametag or AntiBot module hooks it, because those features read the equipment array the vanilla handler already updated: intercepting the packet would duplicate state the client already owns.

None in the corpus. The packet is server-authored and the client has no serverbound equipment channel to abuse. The theoretical value is weapon-switch intelligence: slot-0 S04 deltas reveal exactly when a tracked opponent swaps tools, which is timing data a combat module could use, but none of the 8 clients implements it. Anti-cheats do not police the packet because the client cannot influence it.

implementation.overview: Equipment sync for tracked entities that the vanilla handler commits straight into EntityLivingBase, which is why every armor-aware feature in the 8 clients reads the fields instead of the packet. The only non-vanilla references are two dead imports (Rise 5.99 Aura, Sigma 4.11 InventoryManager) and the Rise 6.x script whitelist; no module processes it, so the module list is empty by corpus fact, not by omission.
implementation.server_handling: The server-side senders are EntityTrackerEntry (on tracked-equipment change, line ~399) and EntityLivingBase (on item/armor updates, line ~1644). There is no serverbound counterpart: the client reports inventory changes through C09PacketHeldItemChange and C0EPacketClickWindow, and the server echoes the resulting equipment state to other trackers as S04. Nothing in the server validates the packet because it never receives it.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields in order: VarInt entity id, short slot, then a Slot-encoded ItemStack (short item id + count + damage + optional NBT, with id -1 encoding null). One packet per slot, so a full armor change is five packets; the client applies them independently and a late packet can overwrite a newer value if ordering slips, which is a known quirk of the 1.8 entity-equipment path.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures this packet: it is clientbound, server-authored and carries no timing or movement signal. The only consumer-side risk would be a module that uses slot-0 deltas to time attacks, which would inherit whatever the target's anti-cheat flags for reaction-time consistency; nothing in the corpus does this.
implementation.client_variations: The only client-side deltas are the dead imports (Rise 5.99 Aura, Sigma 4.11 InventoryManager) and the Rise 6.x script API entry; everything else in all 8 clients is the untouched vanilla handler.

anticheat.overview: Server-side anticheats see S04 only on send, and the real consumers split into two groups. State mirrors keep the simulated entity copy honest: Grim reads the packet in PacketEntityReplication and applies it through CompensatedEntities on the transaction clock. Countermeasure modules rewrite the outgoing payload so other clients cannot scout gear: Photon's information hiders and Intave's EquipmentFilter. The rest of the corpus is keyword noise: Rammelkast, NCP UseItemAdapter and LightAntiCheat hit on org.bukkit.inventory.EquipmentSlot armor reads inside movement checks, Artemis and Negativity contribute wrappers and registrations, and the Peyang and MinecraftAntiCheat NPC bait code sends the packet to fake entities, which is a send-side use, not a check.

checks.name: Entity equipment replication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Keeps the compensated entity copy's equipment mirror in sync with the server so checks that depend on other players' gear (elytra gliding, attack range, horse saddle state) evaluate the right items at the right tick.
checks.how_it_works: PacketEntityReplication reads WrapperPlayServerEntityEquipment on the ENTITY_EQUIPMENT send and schedules updateEntityEquipment as a real-time task on the transaction clock (lastTransactionSent), so the equipment change lands exactly when the client would have processed it. CompensatedEntities guards on the trackEntityEquipment flag, then folds each Equipment entry into the packet entity through setItemBySlot. PacketEntityHorse and PacketEntityNautilus enable tracking because saddle state is movement-relevant, and PacketEntityHappyGhast tracks its body slot.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: this is state replication. It removes equipment desync as a variable from checks that reason about what a tracked entity holds or rides.
checks.variations: The packet read lives in Grim PacketEntityReplication lines 161-162, the same transaction sandwich used for the metadata and player-info branches. No other anticheat mirrors other entities' equipment into a simulation.

checks.name: Information hider (Photon)
checks.purpose: Anti-ESP countermeasure: rewrite outgoing S04 payloads so other clients cannot infer a player's gear from durability, enchantments, lore or item counts.
checks.how_it_works: InformationHiderModule registers a HIGH-priority send listener on ENTITY_EQUIPMENT, parses the wrapper, skips the player's own entity, and hands every equipped item to the abstract hideInformation hook. DurabilityHider, EnchantmentHider and ItemCountHider subclass it, and PacketInformationHider routes the ENTITY_EQUIPMENT case by entity id for the visibility system. The server still sees the real items; only the forwarded copies are stripped.
checks.detects: Nothing: this is a protection module, not a violation check. It defeats client-side gear scouting such as enchantment and durability ESP that a server-side anticheat cannot observe directly.
checks.variations: Photon's LegacyPlayerEquipmentHider and ModernPlayerEquipmentHider replace the equipment list with empty stacks for hidden players. No other anticheat rewrites S04 payloads.

checks.name: Equipment filter (Intave)
checks.purpose: The same countermeasure family as Photon: strip enchantments, display names, lore and book contents from outgoing equipment packets so clients cannot scout items.
checks.how_it_works: EquipmentFilter subscribes to the ENTITY_EQUIPMENT outbound packet and rewrites the payload in place: amounts are set to 1, enchantments are removed and replaced with a single THORNS marker, book title and pages are cleared, firework effects are emptied, and display name and lore are blanked. It handles both the legacy single-item layout (1.8-1.15) and the slot-pair list layout (1.16+). The clone ships with enabled() returning false, so the filter is compiled but inactive by default.
checks.detects: Nothing: a defensive filter. It prevents other players' clients from reading real equipment data off the wire.
checks.variations: Intave's FakePlayer equipment actions (EquipmentArmorAction, EquipmentHeldItemAction) send S04 to bait NPCs instead of filtering it. Peyang and network-dev MinecraftAntiCheat NPC code also send S04 with armor stacks to fake entities; those are bait sends, not checks.

wiki_notes: PLAY id 0x04: VarInt entityId, short slot 0 held and 1-4 boots/legs/chest/helmet, then Slot ItemStack.
Empty slot encodes as item id -1; one packet per slot so a full armor change is up to five packets.

MCP 1.8.9 S04PacketEntityEquipment implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityEquipment; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readItemStackFromBuffer, readShort, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityLivingBase.onUpdate sends new S04PacketEntityEquipment (line 1814) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityLivingBase.java

packets.name: Spawn Position
packets.desc: Sets the player's spawn position (where compass points and respawn occurs).

writeup.p: Carries the world spawn as a packed BlockPos. ServerConfigurationManager sends it on player join (lines ~164 and ~476 in the bundled sources) and CommandSetDefaultSpawnpoint broadcasts it to all players when /setworldspawn runs (line ~45). The value drives the compass needle, the debug-screen spawn readout and the fallback respawn point; it is world metadata, not player state.

handleSpawnPosition runs on the main thread and performs two writes: thePlayer.setSpawnPoint(pos, true) (func_180473_a in MCP) for the personal bed spawn, and world.getWorldInfo().setSpawn(pos) for the world spawn. The packet never moves the player and touches no entity state, which is why nothing in the client reacts to it beyond the two field writes.

Zero module hits across all 8 clients; the only non-vanilla references are the Rise 6.x script whitelist entries (NetworkAPI.java line 51). Compass and waypoint features read mc.theWorld.getSpawnPoint() on render because the vanilla handler has already committed the value before any event bus runs, so intercepting S05 would only let a module lie to itself. There is no state transition in the packet for a module to key off.

None. A client-side mutation alters only the local compass and respawn UI, and the server re-sends the authoritative spawn on every join and respawn, so the change does not persist and cannot affect gameplay. No anti-cheat measures the packet.

implementation.overview: A one-field world-metadata write (BlockPos spawn) that the vanilla handler commits before any module event runs. Zero module hits in the 8-client corpus, so the module list is empty; compass and waypoint features read the committed value directly and have no reason to intercept the packet.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager sends S05PacketSpawnPosition on player join (line ~164 for the join sequence and line ~476 on respawn), and CommandSetDefaultSpawnpoint broadcasts it to all players when the spawn point changes. The BlockPos is packed as a single long on the wire. The server holds the authoritative copy and re-sends it at every world boundary, so a client-side alteration is always corrected within one join or respawn.
implementation.protocol_notes: Single BlockPos field encoded as one long (x << 38 | z << 12 | y in the 1.8 packing). Sent in the PLAY state, usually immediately after S01PacketJoinGame and before or alongside the initial chunk stream. Because the value feeds both the world info and the player's personal spawn, receiving it twice (join plus respawn) is normal and idempotent.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing to flag: the packet carries no timing, position or input signal, and the client cannot send a serverbound equivalent. Its only downstream effect, the compass direction, has no anti-cheat relevance.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients ship the vanilla handler unchanged; Rise 6.x additionally whitelists the packet for the script API. Rise 5.99 has no corpus entry for this packet at all.

anticheat.overview: S05 is a one-field world-metadata write (the spawn BlockPos) with no serverbound counterpart and no timing, position or input signal, so no anticheat consumes it. The corpus is two registrations: Negativity's PacketType SPAWN_POSITION constant and Artemis PacketRepository's SERVER_PLAY + 71 mapping to PacketPlayServerSpawnPosition, plus the Artemis packet interface itself. checks: [] reflects the corpus: nothing in any of the 50 anticheats reads the spawn position from this packet, and its only downstream effect (the compass) has no anti-cheat relevance.

wiki_notes: Before receiving this packet the client uses the default spawn of 8, 64, 8, and the packet also updates what compasses point to.
It can be sent at any time to update the compass target, not only at login.
MCP 1.8.9 S05PacketSpawnPosition implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleSpawnPosition; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBlockPos.

1.8.9 callers: CommandSetDefaultSpawnpoint.processCommand sends new S05PacketSpawnPosition (line 60) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/command/server/CommandSetDefaultSpawnpoint.java

packets.name: Update Health
packets.desc: Updates the player's health, food level, and saturation. Sent ~20 times per second during combat.
packets.notes: When health ≤ 0, the client shows the death screen overlay and sends C16PacketClientStatus(PERFORM_RESPAWN) on respawn button click.

writeup.p: The player's authoritative health, food and saturation sync. EntityPlayerMP sends it on join and on every health, food or saturation change (line ~382), which in combat means roughly once per damage tick. The wire carries a float health (0-20, 0.0 means dead), a VarInt food level and a float saturation. The client treats it as truth: it drives the hearts, the hunger bar and the death screen, and there is no serverbound health packet, so the client cannot push health back.

handleUpdateHealth writes the three values into EntityPlayerSP (setPlayerSPHealth, foodStats) and, when health is at or below 0, arms the death-screen state. Respawn itself is a separate round trip: the button click sends C16PacketClientStatus with PERFORM_RESPAWN and the server answers with S07PacketRespawn. Because S06 is receive-only, every client-side health read is a mirror of the last packet.

The corpus shows two live integrations and one dead one. Sigma 4.11 Ranking treats S06 as a damage-confirmation clock: a health drop triggers a scan of loaded players for a swing animation within the last 70 ms and 9 blocks, which is how its hidden telemetry attributes deaths. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 StaffDetector carries an S06 branch that is fully commented out, and Sigma 4.11 HitIndicator imports the packet but leaves its packet branch empty. The classic Regen/AutoPot/AutoSoup family that keys off S06 thresholds in other client generations does not appear here; in these 8 clients those modules poll local health on UpdateEvent instead.

The classic abuse is receive-side cancellation: a module that swallows S06 never learns it died, so the death screen never shows while the server keeps sending damage updates and eventually kicks the dead player. No module in the corpus does this. Anti-cheats flag nothing on S06 because the client cannot influence it; the only measurable cost is bandwidth during high-tick combat.

implementation.overview: The client's only authoritative health source, sent on join and on every damage, food or saturation change. The corpus uses it as a damage-confirmation clock (Sigma Ranking telemetry) and as abandoned scaffolding (Rise StaffDetector, Sigma HitIndicator); the Regen/AutoPot threshold pattern is absent from these 8 clients, which poll local health on ticks instead.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP pushes S06PacketUpdateHealth(health, foodLevel, saturation) whenever the player's stats change (line ~382 in the MCP builds), which covers join, damage, regeneration, hunger and saturation drift. The server never validates the packet stream because it is the sole author; the values are copied verbatim from the player's own stats. The death path is two-sided: the client arms the death screen from S06 health <= 0, and the respawn is driven by the client's C16 PERFORM_RESPAWN.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields in order: float health, VarInt food, float saturation. There is no serverbound health packet, so any module that wants to fake health must do it by suppressing the clientbound packet (cosmetic only) or by manipulating the server's damage logic through other packets. S06 arrives on the main thread and its writes are unconditional, so a cancelling module must intercept before the vanilla handler.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats treat S06 as render-state sync and measure nothing on it; the client cannot spoof health serverbound, so there is no flag surface. The practical detection risk belongs to modules that act on S06 (Sigma Ranking's HTTP telemetry, Rise's commented staff heuristic), which are privacy/ToS concerns rather than movement or combat flags.

modules.name: Ranking
modules.purpose: Hidden combat telemetry that uses S06 health drops to attribute deaths and prosecutions to specific players.
modules.how_it_works: On EventPacket, when S06 reports health at or below the client's current health, Ranking scans the loaded entity list for players that are not the local player, have a swing animation (S0BPacketAnimation) timestamp within the last 70 ms and sit within 9 blocks; each match becomes a prosecutor entity. health <= 0 calls onDeath, which resolves outstanding kill/death records and ships them through sendStat. The S06 packet is the timing anchor: the 70 ms window is measured from animation timestamp to damage confirmation.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket, registered alongside EventAttack and EventUpdate.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Unobservable: the module only reads clientbound state. The telemetry itself (HTTP stats reporting) is a privacy/ToS concern, not an anti-cheat one.
modules.variations: Sigma 4.11 HitIndicator imports S06 but its EventPacket branch is empty, so the import is dead. No other client in the corpus uses S06 for telemetry.

modules.name: StaffDetector
modules.purpose: Detect staff players from team and tab-list names and auto-run /hub; the S06 reference is commented-out scaffolding, not live logic.
modules.how_it_works: The packet listener matches names from S3EPacketTeams and S38PacketPlayerListItem against a hardcoded staff table (one comma-separated string of roughly 150 names) and triggers after 6 matches, sending /hub via C01 when autoLeave is on. The S06PacketUpdateHealth block exists only inside a comment, an abandoned idea that never shipped in either build.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (plus PreMotionEvent to decay the match counter).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the module consumes clientbound packets and sends ordinary chat. The hardcoded staff list is a maintenance liability, not a flag.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the same file with the same commented S06 block; the 6.2.4 copy is identical in the relevant region. Neither build ever enabled the health branch.

implementation.general_hooks: Sigma uses EventPacket with instanceof dispatch; Rise uses PacketReceiveEvent listeners. Both only read S06; no serverbound traffic is generated by S06 handling in either module.
implementation.client_variations: Sigma's event model is a single registered onEvent switch over EventAttack/EventPacket/EventUpdate; Rise uses per-listener @EventLink fields. Both treat S06 as pure input, which keeps the cross-client story simple.

anticheat.overview: The update-health packet is server-authored, so anticheats cannot see a client-spoofed health value; what they can see is the server's own health bookkeeping around it. Modern anticheats parse WrapperPlayServerUpdateHealth on the send side to track death and food state (Grim, BetterAnticheat), while regen and god-mode checks watch EntityRegainHealthEvent and damage events to catch fast-heal and damage suppression (Negativity, Arc, NoCheatPlus, Daedalus, ThotPatrol, MIU). The packet itself is never flagged; it is the reference clock for health-related checks.

checks.name: UpdateHealth death tracking (BetterAnticheat)
checks.purpose: Track the client-visible death state from the update-health payload and the client's own respawn acknowledgement.
checks.how_it_works: PlayerStatusTracker.handlePacketPlaySend wraps UPDATE_HEALTH as WrapperPlayServerUpdateHealth and, inside a confirmation transaction, pushes isDead = (health == 0) into a ten-slot BooleanManyState that flushes only after the client confirms the packet. The receive side mirrors it: a CLIENT_STATUS PERFORM_RESPAWN pushes isDead = false and flushes four slots at once, deliberately wiping stale death states to defeat disablers that delay selected responses.
checks.detects: Death-state desync: a client that selectively delays packet responses to hide its own death or respawn timing from the anticheat.
checks.variations: Grim does the same tracking in PacketPlayerRespawn: it stores lastHealth, lastFood and lastSaturation, marks the simulated self entity dead when health reaches zero and feeds BadPacketsM.onDeath; Artemis mirrors health into its emulator through BntityPlayerSP.setPlayerSPHealth.

checks.name: Regen (Negativity)
checks.purpose: Flag fast regeneration: health regaining faster than the version's natural regen interval allows.
checks.how_it_works: RegenProtocol.onRegen listens to EntityRegainHealthEvent for players. It skips players with active regen-affecting potions, records the time between regains and flags when the gap is below the version's timeBetweenTwoRegen plus ping (per-version table in Version). A gap under 50 ms plus ping is a hard violation, and the event is cancelled when setbacks are enabled. The protocol also tags the player's flying reason on golden-apple interactions so movement checks can discount regen-based vertical motion.
checks.detects: Auto-regen modules and fast-heal packets that produce health regains faster than the per-version interval tables permit.
checks.variations: Arc-v2 Regeneration compares the last health event against a configurable regen-time (3400 ms default); Daedalus Regen and ThotPatrol BadPacketsA use the same SATIATED-reason timing pattern; MIU FastHealA computes the expected interval from the player's health level and regen potion stage.

checks.name: Regeneration (Arc v2)
checks.purpose: Classic satiated-regen rate check: health must not regenerate faster than the configured interval.
checks.how_it_works: FightListener.onRegen records the SATIATED regain timestamp into FightData when the check can run; Regeneration.check computes now minus lastHealthEvent and fails when the gap is below the regen-time value read from the check config (3400 ms default). It is one of the smallest checks in the corpus: a timestamp, a subtraction and a threshold.
checks.detects: Fast-regen modules that exploit the satiated regeneration mechanic.
checks.variations: Negativity RegenProtocol adds per-version tables and potion exemptions; Daedalus Regen and ThotPatrol BadPacketsA count packets between regains; NoCheatPlus tracks regainHealthTime in FightData and feeds it into GodMode's expectation model.

checks.name: GodMode (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Detect players that ignore inflicted damage or keep an impossible health ceiling across regen and damage events.
checks.how_it_works: GodMode.check runs on damage events against FightData bookkeeping: regainHealthTime is stamped by FightListener.onEntityRegainHealth, godModeHealth tracks the highest health the player has held, and the check flags when current health stays above the expected post-damage value or when no damage lands despite a hit. The regain-tracking variant is what the corpus shows; the original 2012-era sensitivity path is marked as likely obsolete in the source.
checks.detects: God-mode exploits, damage suppression and health-ceiling manipulation around combat.
checks.variations: Kauri HealthSpoof is the modern replacement pattern; MIU AntiDamageA compares post-damage health against the expected drop; Daedalus Regen watches only the regain rate.

wiki_notes: Food saturation acts as a food overcharge so food values do not decrease while saturation is above zero.
New or respawning players automatically get a saturation of 5.0, and eating food raises saturation as well as the food bar.

MCP 1.8.9 S06PacketUpdateHealth implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleUpdateHealth; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readFloat, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.onUpdateEntity sends new S06PacketUpdateHealth (line 403): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Respawn
packets.desc: Sends respawn or dimension change request. The client must reload the world (clear chunks, entities) and re-sync position.
packets.notes: After receiving this, the client resets chunk loading, clears all entities, sends C00PacketKeepAlive to re-sync, and sends a C03/C06 position packet. The packet is used both for death respawn (same dimension) and portal dimension changes (dimension changes).

writeup.p: The respawn and dimension-change control. The server sends it on death respawn (ServerConfigurationManager line ~496), on portal dimension transfer (NetHandlerPlayServer line ~587, ServerConfigurationManager line ~473) and on gamemode changes; the payload is dimension id, difficulty, terrain type and gamemode. The client must treat it as a world-reload command: clear entities, rebuild chunk state, re-arm keepalive and re-sync position.

handleRespawn branches on the dimension: an equal dimension is a soft reset that rebuilds the player entity in place, a different dimension triggers a full world load with chunks unloaded, entities cleared and the player respawned. PacketThreadUtil special-cases S07 so the reload runs on the main thread and pre-processes the world transition before ordinary packet handling resumes. Every module that buffers per-world state (blink queues, transaction lists, teleport buffers, freecam position) must flush on this packet or carry stale state across the boundary.

The corpus reaction surface is exactly the flush pattern, and it lives in the disabler machinery. Rise 6.1.30 WatchdogDisabler clears its position, transaction and blink queues plus both stopwatches on S07; Rise 6.2.4 keeps only the import. UniversoCraftDisabler (both builds) uses S07 to arm a respawn-window transaction corruption. Tenacity 6.0 AdvancedDisablerModule carries a commented-out S07 import, evidence the reset was planned and disabled. No Freecam, AutoTool or inventory module hooks S07 in this corpus even though world reload visibly resets their state; those clients rely on vanilla world-load callbacks instead of the packet. LiquidSense Dev's MixinNetworkManager promotes S07 to a first-class EventRespawn: readpacket fires it right before the vanilla handler runs, giving every module a hookable world-reload signal.

The respawn window is the attack surface: after S07 the server re-arms the player's transaction stream, so replaying C0F uids from the previous world desynchronizes the server's bookkeeping. UniversoCraftDisabler weaponizes the window by overwriting C0F uids with Short.MIN_VALUE or Short.MAX_VALUE for the first 350 ticks after respawn, alternating on tick parity. Anti-cheats that key transaction continuity off confirm/transaction pairs are the target. S07 itself is server-authored and not client-spoofable in the vanilla protocol, so the client side is purely defensive: flush old state, then corrupt the new window.

implementation.overview: The world-reload command: death respawn, portal transfer and gamemode change all arrive as S07, and the client tears down and rebuilds world state in response. In this corpus the packet is consumed by disabler state machines (Rise WatchdogDisabler flush, UniversoCraftDisabler corruption window) and was planned-but-disabled in Tenacity's AdvancedDisablerModule. LiquidSense Dev turns the packet into a dedicated EventRespawn fired from its NetworkManager mixin.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager sends S07 on death respawn (line ~496) and on dimension transfer (line ~473), NetHandlerPlayServer sends it on its own dimension-change path (line ~587 in MCP builds), always with the player's current dimension, difficulty, terrain type and gamemode. After sending, the server waits for the client's position re-sync (C03/C06) before resuming normal tracking. The client never sends S07; the closest serverbound step is C16 PERFORM_RESPAWN from the death screen.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields in order: int dimension, unsigned byte difficulty, unsigned byte gamemode, String level type. PacketThreadUtil pre-processes S07 in Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 and Tenacity (lines ~31 and ~40 respectively), forcing the world transition onto the main thread ahead of queued packets. The dimension field is the branch key: equal dimension means soft reset, different dimension means full reload, and modules keying state resets on S07 catch both cases in one hook.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Transaction-continuity anti-cheats (Watchdog, Verus) reset their per-player counters on respawn, which is why stale C0F uids replayed across the boundary flag. The UniversoCraft corruption window targets exactly this reset: uid values of Short.MIN_VALUE and Short.MAX_VALUE alternating on tick parity are chosen to break the server's expectation of monotonic actions without a visible cancel pattern. The flush side (WatchdogDisabler) is the defensive mirror and is invisible; the corruption side is the detectable one if the server validates uids.

modules.name: WatchdogDisabler
modules.purpose: Hypixel Watchdog disabler mode that uses S07 as the hard reset point for its buffered packet state.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, S07 clears positionQueue, transactionQueue, blinkQueue and actionNumbers, resets pingStopwatch and transactionStopwatch and sets disabled=false. This is the defensive flush: after respawn or dimension change the old world's transaction stream is dead, so stale C0F uids and queued positions would desync the new world. The ping-spoof branch then restarts collecting negative-action S32 transactions, shuffling and replaying them a second later.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (S07 flush, S32 collection), PreMotionEvent (replay), PacketSendEvent (inventory spoof).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The S07 flush itself is invisible; the flag risk is the replay behavior it protects. Without the flush, a queued C0F from before the respawn arrives after the server reset its transaction counter and registers as an unknown action, a classic Watchdog flag.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4 drops the S07 receive handler entirely (import only at line 42), leaving the queue flush to the module's own lifecycle. The 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 files otherwise share the same structure.

modules.name: UniversoCraftDisabler
modules.purpose: UniversoCraft disabler mode that arms a respawn-window transaction corruption from the S07 packet.
modules.how_it_works: On the packet send listener, S07 sets disabling=true; C02PacketUseEntity clears it; C03PacketPlayer within the first 10 ticks sets it; and while disabling with ticksExisted below 350, every C0FPacketConfirmTransaction gets its uid overwritten with Short.MIN_VALUE or Short.MAX_VALUE alternating on tick parity. The S07 branch is redundant in practice because the C03-within-10-ticks branch arms the same flag, and its usefulness depends on the client's event wiring delivering clientbound packets to this listener.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Transaction uid corruption is the detectable surface: servers that validate C0F uids drop mismatches and can flag the alternating pattern. The respawn window matters because the server resets its transaction bookkeeping on S07, so corrupting uids during the first 350 ticks hits the anti-cheat before its counters warm up.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the identical file; the S07 branch and the C03 branch coexist in both builds.

modules.name: MixinNetworkManager (respawn event)
modules.purpose: Fire a dedicated EventRespawn on the LiquidBounce event bus whenever S07PacketRespawn arrives, giving every module a hookable world-reload signal at the exact boundary.
modules.how_it_works: readpacket injects into NetworkManager.channelRead0 right before Packet.processPacket runs: it posts EventPacketReceive and, when the packet is an S07PacketRespawn, also posts EventRespawn before the vanilla handler executes, then cancels the read if the event was cancelled.
modules.vanilla_hook: @Inject on NetworkManager.channelRead0 (HEAD and INVOKE processPacket, shift BEFORE); @Inject on sendPacket (HEAD).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the mixin only observes S07 and re-dispatches events. The cancel path is the generic LiquidBounce packet-cancel mechanism used by any listener, not a respawn-specific manipulation.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30's WatchdogDisabler consumes S07 as its flush point inside module code; LiquidSense Dev is the only client that promotes the packet to a first-class event on the bus.

implementation.general_hooks: Both disabler modes consume S07 to manage a state machine: WatchdogDisabler flushes on PacketReceiveEvent, UniversoCraftDisabler arms a flag on its send-side listener. The packet is never modified, only observed. LiquidSense Dev fires EventRespawn from a MixinNetworkManager channelRead0 injection when the packet is an S07, before the vanilla handler runs.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.x event model: @EventLink listener fields on Mode classes under the Disabler module. The 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 trees are structurally identical (com/alan/clients/...) with the 6.2.4 copy under Client-release2/Client/src/main/java. LiquidSense Dev observes S07 at the NetworkManager mixin level and re-dispatches it as a first-class EventRespawn; the Rise 6.x modes consume the packet inside module listeners.

anticheat.overview: The respawn packet is a state-reset command: the world reloads, so every anticheat that keeps per-player state must re-arm it on respawn. Simulation anticheats parse WrapperPlayServerRespawn on the send side and rebuild their player model (Grim, Shard, Artemis), while classic anticheats zero grace timers on PlayerRespawnEvent so freshly respawned players are not flagged by movement and combat checks. The packet itself is never flagged; it is the boundary that makes the checks after it trustworthy.

checks.name: PacketPlayerRespawn (Grim)
checks.purpose: Reset the entire simulated player model on respawn and dimension change: positions, ground flags, attributes, entity list and the death-screen state.
checks.how_it_works: The RESPAWN branch wraps the packet as WrapperPlayServerRespawn, invalidates the setback teleport (hasAcceptedSpawnTeleport = false), clears server entity positions on world change, and schedules a real-time task that resets onGround, pose, sprinting, food, known input, the self PacketEntity and the BadPacketsE/G/M/F state. KEEP_TRACKED_DATA and KEEP_ATTRIBUTES flags decide what survives on 1.20.2+; isWorldChange compares world name or dimension type to detect cross-dimension teleports that wipe chunks and entities.
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It prevents stale movement state (old ground flags, old velocity, old entity ids) from leaking across the respawn boundary, which would poison every downstream check.
checks.variations: Shard's handleRespawn clears compensatedEntities only; Artemis stamps lastRespawn in MiscellaneousPreProcessor and sets respawnTicks (150) in EmulatorPreProcessor; Kauri resets its lastRespawn TickTimer in PacketHandler; NCP re-inits moving data through dataOnJoin with the joinOrRespawn flag.

checks.name: Respawn pre-processing (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Stamp the respawn moment and clear inventory and vehicle state so every check can exempt the respawn window.
checks.how_it_works: fastHandle runs on the packet thread: GPacketPlayServerRespawn schedules a transaction-confirmed action that calls setLastRespawn(packet.getTimestamp()), closes the inventory state and drops the predicted vehicle. ExemptType.RESPAWN then exempts checks while lastRespawn is under three seconds or respawnTicks is positive, and MovementPreProcessor decrements respawnTicks each tick. The same timestamp is also set from the client's C16 PERFORM_RESPAWN command.
checks.detects: Nothing on its own; the mechanism is exemption bookkeeping. The dedicated DisablerRespawn check uses the respawn domain to catch clients that abuse the respawn window, while AimIdentical and BadPacketsN read respawnTicks to skip false positives.
checks.variations: Grim and Shard reset state on the packet directly; SalmonAC and FlopAC keep tick counters instead of wall-clock stamps; Kauri uses a TickTimer reset from WrapperPlayServerRespawn in its PacketHandler.

checks.name: Respawn-tick exemption (SalmonAC)
checks.purpose: Zero the per-player respawnTick on respawn so every movement and combat check skips the respawn window.
checks.how_it_works: PlayerEventListener.onRespawn (PlayerRespawnEvent) sets salmonPlayer.respawnTick = 0, and the counter increments in SalmonPlayer. Checks then bail early while the tick is under their threshold, from 20 ticks (ReachA, CriticalA, SpeedCode) to 60 ticks (TimerC, Invalid0A, JesusC). The same listener registers players on PlayerJoinEvent and zeroes respawnTick on join too.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: it is an exemption counter, and the corpus hits are the getRespawnTick() guards inside roughly 40 checks.
checks.variations: FlopAC guards with a respawnTimer.hasNotPassed(20) inside BadPacketsC, SpeedA/B and SprintA/B; LightAntiCheat keeps cache.lastRespawn in milliseconds and skips checks within 500 ms of respawn; ThotPatrol and Daedalus reset latency data on PlayerRespawnEvent.

checks.name: Respawn-window exemption (FlopAC)
checks.purpose: Skip the bad-packets teleport check while the player is still inside the respawn grace window.
checks.how_it_works: BadPacketsC watches the flying packet family and flags an invalid teleport when the client's horizontal delta exceeds the server-position speed. The exemption list includes getRespawnTimer().hasNotPassed(20), so a respawned player's first 20 ticks are never evaluated. The timer is armed from the respawn path in the action processor; the tinyprotocol WrappedOutRespawnPacket wrapper is the packet-side representation.
checks.detects: Nothing on its own; the guard prevents false flags for players that legitimately teleport into the world after respawn.
checks.variations: SalmonAC's respawnTick and LightAntiCheat's lastRespawn cache are the same grace-window idea; Grim instead resets the whole simulation and keeps checks active, trusting the reset rather than an exemption window.

wiki_notes: For a dimension change the server sends respawn followed by chunks for the new dimension and then a position and look packet, and the client unloads old chunks automatically.
Avoid respawning a player into the same dimension they are already in unless they are dead, since it causes glitches such as being unable to attack.

MCP 1.8.9 S07PacketRespawn implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleRespawn; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readInt, readStringFromBuffer, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerPlayServer.handleSpectate sends new S07PacketRespawn (line 674) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/network/NetHandlerPlayServer.java

packets.name: Player Position & Look
packets.desc: Forces the player to a specific position and rotation. The client must respond with a C04/05/06.
packets.notes: The client must send a movement confirm (C04/C05/C06) back. The Y coordinate in this packet is the head Y, not feet Y.

writeup.p: S08 is the server's authoritative position and rotation correction: three doubles, two floats and a byte bitmask of relative flags (0x01 X, 0x02 Y, 0x04 Z, 0x08 Y_ROT, 0x10 X_ROT). It fires on join, dimension change, /tp-style teleports and anti-cheat lag-backs, and the client must answer with a C06PacketPlayerPosLook confirm or the server keeps its own position and re-sends. It is the most-intercepted clientbound packet in the corpus: every movement exploit family reads it, and several non-movement modules use it as a state signal (spawned, flagged, respawned).

NetHandlerPlayClient.handlePlayerPosLook (Memeware copy, line 601) checks PacketThreadUtil, adds each absolute field to the current value when the matching relative flag is set, calls setPosition, then immediately replies C06PacketPlayerPosLook using the bounding-box minY as the feet position. The motion zeroing lines are commented out in the Memeware and Nekoware copies, a decompile artifact of the 1.5.2-era base. The first S08 flips doneLoadingTerrain, which is the spawned signal Memeware's Stealer waits for to clear its chest state.

Five families. Flight modes cancel S08 to avoid being snapped back and re-send a confirm that matches the spoofed position (Rise MineLandFlight, CreativeFlight; Sigma Fly; Spicy Fly and BackupFly; Tenacity FlightModule). Speed modules treat S08 as a flag and auto-disable or cancel per-mode (Memeware and Nekoware Flag Check, Rise 5.99 Speed Zonecraft and Vulcan2). Rotation strippers rewrite yaw and pitch before the vanilla handler runs (Rise 5.99 NoRot and Freelook, Sigma NoRotate). Phase and Blink count or suppress teleports (Rise VulcanPhase, Sigma Phase and Blink, Spicy Phase). AntiVoid and Disabler suites use S08 as a timing trigger (Spicy AntiVoid, Rise VerusCustomDisabler and WatchdogDisabler, Sigma Disabler, Tenacity DisablerModule, Memeware Disabler Sloth mode). Sigma AntiVelocity even rewrites S08 rotations in AACFlag mode while hurtResistantTime is active. The two new clients fit the same landscape: November's PhaseModule reads S08 as its setback timer, LiquidSense's LagBack auto-disables movement modules on S08, and Tp and TeleportCommand use the teleport as their arm signal.

The anti-cheat's blunt instrument is the rubberband: any server-side position desync ends in an S08. Clients fight it three ways: cancel the packet and re-send a spoofed C06 (keeps the client position, desyncs the server), accept the position but strip rotations (NoRotate), or ignore S08 only while a module state machine is armed (VulcanPhase counts teleports and then stands down after four). Rise 6.x TeleportCheck sits on the same packet to detect teleport exploits aimed at its own users. Every anti-cheat measures the C06 echo: the confirm must match the teleported coordinates, which is why cancel-and-spoof is only viable when the module replays the exact S08 position and why repeated cancels read as teleport-spam flags.

implementation.overview: The server's authoritative position correction: doubles plus floats plus a relative-flag bitmask, answered by a mandatory C06 confirm. The most-modded clientbound packet in the corpus: Flight cancels it, Speed treats it as a flag, NoRotate strips rotation, Phase counts it, AntiVoid uses it to time its rescue, and the disabler suites use it to re-arm ping-spoof and blink state.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerPlayServer.setPlayerLocation (Spicy and Tenacity copies, line 448) computes the absolute target, adds the relative offsets when flags are set, zeroes the player's motion and sends S08. processPlayer validates incoming C0x movement against the last sent position and re-sends S08 when the client drifts beyond tolerance, which is the rubberband. Vanilla 1.8.9 has no teleport-id counter, so the server trusts the next C06-style confirm and re-sends S08 only when subsequent movement disagrees; that gap is exactly what cancel-and-confirm spoofing exploits.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire order: x, y, z doubles, yaw, pitch floats, then one flags byte read via readUnsignedByte. Flagged fields are deltas added to the current client value, so the server can nudge a player with a partial teleport; the join S08 is absolute (empty flag set). The client replies with C06PacketPlayerPosLook (absolute position, bounding-box minY, current rotations, onGround flag) regardless of which fields were relative. Because the reply uses the client's post-processing position, any module that mutates the packet before the handler runs changes what the server records.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: S08 is where lag-back lands: speed, phase, ground and fly checks all terminate in one. Cancelling S08 without echoing the position forces the server into a re-send loop that is itself visible as teleport spam.
