The stealthy pattern is to accept the position and neutralize the effect: NoRotate rewrites rotation so the confirm matches while aim stays client-side, and disablers re-arm PingSpoofComponent immediately after S08 (Rise VerusCustomDisabler sets disable = -20 on every teleport and only spoofs once the position history is clean). Hypixel-era flight modes cancel S08 only until the server velocity-confirms the fall, then let the teleport through to avoid a permanent desync flag.

modules.name: Flight / Fly
modules.purpose: Keep a spoofed airborne position by cancelling S08 teleports until the server confirms the fall, then accept the snap-back and slow the game clock.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, cancel S08 while the module has not been teleport-confirmed; keep broadcasting C03 packets and pin the client position to the launch point. The confirm is the S12 velocity packet: once motionY passes a threshold, teleported flips true, S08 is let through and timerSpeed drops to 0.3.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling rubberbands is the classic flight flag; the MineLand pattern defuses it by accepting the teleport the moment the server's own velocity check confirms the fall, so the client is never in a permanently-desynced state.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 Fly marks a setback on S08 in Hypixel and Hycraft modes; Rise 6.2.4 CreativeFlight tracks S08 into serverPos fields to replay the teleport through its own position buffer; Sigma Fly and Spicy Fly and BackupFly cancel S08 in Hypixel mode only; Tenacity FlightModule (Mineland Fling mode) cancels S08 until the S12 confirm and then sets timer speed to 1. LiquidSense Dev's core Fly handles S08 per mode (line 761 of Fly.java), and LastestHypixelFly cancels C03 until the first S08 arms the fly window, then toggles off on a second S08 after 1500 ms with a Setback detected notice; Flight1 imports S08 without handling it.

modules.name: Speed
modules.purpose: Treat S08 as a lag-back flag and disable the module, or cancel the teleport per server mode so the speed boost survives.
modules.how_it_works: Memeware and Nekoware hook PacketInEvent: if the packet is S08 and the Flag Check setting is on, print a chat message and toggle the module off. Rise 5.99 Speed runs per-mode handlers: Zonecraft cancels S08 and re-sends C04, Vulcan2 cancels teleports inside 10 blocks, Hypixel2 cancels once, Minemenclub Hop resets its balance counter.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Auto-disable on S08 is the safest reaction because a teleport means the speed boost was already flagged; the chat message is a tell that the module was active, but the server only sees the movement it already flagged.
modules.variations: Nekoware v1 ships the identical Speed.java with the same Flag Check. Rise 5.99 adds the disableOnFlag setting that toggles the module off with a notification on any S08. LiquidSense Dev's Speed lagback check rewrites S08 yaw and pitch to the client's current rotation, zeroes motionX and motionZ and opens a stop-tick window; BufferSpeed cancels or handles S08 at its line 224.

modules.name: Disabler
modules.purpose: Use S08 as the trigger to re-arm spoofing windows, strip rotations, or nudge the teleport position to break server-side state checks.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 6.x VerusCustomDisabler sets disable = -20 on every S08 and re-arms PingSpoofComponent.spoof only after the position history is clean, holding C00 and C0F for 9 seconds. Memeware Disabler in Sloth mode adds 1.0E-4 to the S08 y to trip a spigot PlayerData nulling bug. Sigma Disabler rewrites S08 yaw and pitch and toggles itself off after the Hypixel watchdog window.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent; re-arm via PingSpoofComponent.spoof from PostStrafeEvent.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Correlating the spoof window to S08 arrivals keeps the buffered packet stream aligned with the server's position state, which is what makes the frozen-window pattern hard to distinguish from genuine lag.
modules.variations: Memeware 7.3 Sloth mode mutates the y by 1.0E-4 (spigot PlayerData exploit); Sigma 4.11 rewrites rotations and auto-disables after the Hypixel watchdog window; Rise 6.2.4 adds WatchdogDisabler alongside VerusCustomDisabler; Tenacity 6.0 keeps only commented S08 code in AdvancedDisablerModule, and Spicy and Nekoware reference S08 as imports without handling it.

modules.name: NoRotate
modules.purpose: Prevent servers from forcing the player's rotation: overwrite the S08 yaw and pitch with the client's current values before the vanilla handler applies them.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 5.99 NoRot stores the server rotation and overwrites the packet fields per mode: Vanilla replaces both fields, Delay replays the saved rotation on the next PreMotion, Legit applies it only if the mouse has not moved since. Sigma 4.11 NoRotate does the same unconditionally on incoming S08.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The confirm echoes the rewritten rotation, so the server records the client's real aim; servers that enforce rotation on teleport (some kit servers) will loop teleports, which is why the Legit mode exists.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 Freelook also rewrites S08 rotations in its camera handling; Sigma 4.11 has no restore path and no mode switch.

modules.name: Phase / Blink
modules.purpose: Suppress the block push and track teleport pressure: S08 packets are counted as the server's attempt to eject the player from a block.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 6.x VulcanPhase increments teleportCount on every S08 and stands its state machine down after four, letting blocks push the player out; it also cancels PushOutOfBlockEvent and fakes onGround = false while inside a block. Sigma Phase and Blink handle S08 on their packet bus to mask teleports during blink windows.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent; BlockAABBEvent and PushOutOfBlockEvent for the collision side.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Fighting the eject teleport directly is a permanent-flag loop; counting teleports and self-disabling after a threshold is the pattern that survives because the server eventually succeeds and the module is already off.
modules.variations: Sigma 4.11 Phase and Blink read S08 on EventPacket; Spicy Phase imports S08 without handling it in the shipped build. November Recode 2.0's PhaseModule in CAGE_PHASE mode resets its setback timer on every S08 and refuses to phase until 20 ticks pass without one; it also cancels outgoing packets while the cage window is open and flushes them on disable.

modules.name: AntiVoid
modules.purpose: Use the S08 teleport as the rescue signal: when the server lag-backs the falling player, reset fallDistance so the server's own teleport becomes the save.
modules.how_it_works: Spicy AntiVoid in Hypixel mode hooks EventPacket: on S08 while off ground, past fallDistance 20 (or below y = 0) and over void, it zeroes fallDistance. The EventUpdate path then bounces once per fall with a C03 onGround and a C04 at posY + 12. Rise VulcanAntiVoid clears its noBlock flag on S08 to re-arm the jump suppression.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket (pre, incoming); EventUpdate for the bounce.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Zeroing fallDistance on the teleport is invisible to the anti-cheat because the packet is not mutated and nothing extra is sent; the module rides the server's own lag-back. Over-triggering is guarded by the isOverVoid ray scan and the bounced flag.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 VulcanAntiVoid use S08 only to re-arm the noBlock state that suppresses the jump motion while over void.

modules.name: LagBack
modules.purpose: Auto-disable movement modules when the server rubberbands, so a flagged boost quits before the anti-cheat accumulates a ban.
modules.how_it_works: On S08, gated by a 2000 ms delay, check whether Speed, LongJump, Fly, Flight or Step is toggled and the player is pressing a movement key; toggle the offending module off and print a colored chat notice per module.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Self-disabling on the first rubberband is the same strategy as Memeware's Flag Check: the server already flagged the movement, so the module quits instead of fighting the teleport.
modules.variations: Only LiquidSense Dev in the corpus; the eight original clients fold this behavior into Speed and Fly as flag-check settings.

modules.name: Teleport / Tp
modules.purpose: Use the server's own lag-back as the arm signal: cancel all C03 until S08 arrives, then walk the computed path with C04s.
modules.how_it_works: onEnable provokes the lag-back with C0F(0,-1,false), a flying-abilities C13 and C04 +0.17/+0.06. While !tp every C03 is cancelled; the first S08 flips tp and the tick handler replays the fall ladder and walks the PathfindingUtils path with per-vec3 C04s, finishing with C03(true) and C0C input.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketEvent (S08 and C03), TickEvent (path walk), MoveEvent (cancel while waiting).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Riding the server's own teleport as the start signal means the module never moves before the server confirms the player position, which avoids the classic teleport-spam flag.
modules.variations: TeleportCommand (LiquidSense Dev) rewrites S08 yaw and pitch to the client's rotation after a damage-ladder teleport and clears its tryCancelPacket flag; the C03 impl documents the same file family.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on every client, with the vanilla handler applying the mutation afterwards. Rise 6.x processes S08 in components (PingSpoofComponent, EntityTickComponent, TeleportCheck security) before modules see it.
implementation.client_variations: Classic clients (Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy) mutate or cancel the packet object inside the event, so the vanilla handler then applies the modified values. Rise 5.99 and 6.x call event.setCancelled on the receive event; Rise 6.x additionally re-arms component state (PingSpoofComponent spoof windows) from the same packet.

anticheat.overview: S08 is the server's authoritative position correction and the landing pad for every movement flag: setback, phase and speed checks all terminate in a rubberband teleport. On the OUT side, anticheats do three things with it: record the exact teleported coordinates and the teleport id, bracket the teleport between transaction packets so the confirm can be time-ordered, and verify that the client's C06 confirm matches the coordinates the server actually sent. The four checks below cover that full pipeline, from the packet listener that converts relative flags to absolute positions (Grim) to the confirm verifier that kicks on a mismatch (CheaterDeleter).

checks.name: PacketServerTeleport (Grim)
checks.purpose: Tracks every outgoing player teleport so the simulation knows the client's authoritative position and can enforce it in later movement checks.
checks.how_it_works: Listens on the OUT side for the player position-and-look packet, seeds the player's tracked position on join, converts relative flags to absolute coordinates (rewriting the packet for 1.8-era clients), and brackets the teleport with a transaction sandwich so the exact arrival tick is known. Vehicle teleports are recorded against the same transaction stream.
checks.detects: Teleport-based desync where the client's reported position diverges from the server's authoritative teleport target.
checks.variations: Artemis and CheaterDeleter record the same OUT teleport event; Grim additionally re-encodes the packet so its own simulation never sees relative coordinates.

checks.name: TeleportVerifierCheck (CheaterDeleter)
checks.purpose: Verifies that the client's teleport confirm returns the exact coordinates the server sent, kicking on any mismatch.
checks.how_it_works: Stores the target position (resolving relative flags against the player's current position) keyed by the S08 teleport id. When the client sends the matching teleport-confirm packet, the check compares each axis of the attached movement packet against the stored target: absolute axes must match exactly, relative axes must be within 10 blocks. Any disagreement kicks the player.
checks.detects: Cancel-and-spoof teleport bypasses where a client accepts the teleport id but reports a different position, and disabler-style teleport manipulation.
checks.variations: Grim instead flags and sets back; BetterAnticheat resolves teleports inside its confirmation tracker before comparing movement.

checks.name: TeleportTracker (BetterAnticheat)
checks.purpose: Compensates outgoing teleport packets so movement checks can distinguish a teleport from an illegal position jump.
checks.how_it_works: On the OUT side it wraps the position-and-look packet (plus entity teleport and rotation packets for the player) into a Teleport record that is only added to the eligible list after the confirmation tracker's pre-transaction fires. On the IN side, every flying packet is matched against eligible teleports: onGround flag, absolute coordinates and rotations must line up, with a 2.0E-4 leniency for relative axes when the player did not send a position packet the previous tick. Teleports that never match become a missedTeleport state for the checks.
checks.detects: Movement spoofing that fakes teleport confirms, and the desync that follows when a client skips or reorders teleport confirmation.
checks.variations: Grim's SetbackTeleportUtil keeps an explicit queue of sent teleports; CheaterDeleter verifies confirms immediately and kicks.

checks.name: TeleportPreProcessor (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Feeds server teleport and entity-teleport packets into the movement holder so position checks run against the post-teleport state.
checks.how_it_works: Handles the OUT position packet and the player's entity-teleport packet. For entity teleports it registers a transaction-confirmed action: on the pre side it moves the last velocity into lastVelocity, installs the teleported position as the current movement and location, and marks the movement as teleport-processed; the post side clears that flag once the client confirms.
checks.detects: Cheats that depend on the anticheat not knowing the server moved the player, and velocity residue that should be cleared by a teleport.
checks.variations: Grim uses a transaction sandwich on the OUT packet itself; Artemis applies the teleport on the confirm instead of at send time.

wiki_notes: Yaw is measured in degrees starting at 0 and is never clamped, and may be negative or above 360.
Pitch is measured in degrees with 0 looking straight ahead, -90 straight up and 90 straight down.

The server ignores the client movement packets sent before the client was aware of the teleport until it receives the matching confirm, and if the player is riding a vehicle the teleport has no effect but confirm packets are still sent.

MCP 1.8.9 S08PacketPlayerPosLook implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handlePlayerPosLook; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readDouble, readFloat, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerPlayServer.setPlayerLocation sends new S08PacketPlayerPosLook (line 484): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/network/NetHandlerPlayServer.java

packets.name: Held Item Change
packets.desc: Server confirms the player's held item slot change (echo back of C09).
packets.notes: This is the server echo of C09PacketHeldItemChange. The client uses this to stay in sync with the server on which hotbar slot is selected.

writeup.p: S09 is the server echo of the client's C09PacketHeldItemChange: one byte, the hotbar slot 0-8. ServerConfigurationManager sends it to a player on join (with the current slot) and on every accepted slot change, so client and server agree on the held item. It is a confirmation, not a command, which is why module interest is nearly zero: there is nothing to spoof, cancel or time.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleHeldItemChange bounds-checks the slot (>= 0 and < InventoryPlayer.getHotbarSize()) and assigns inventory.currentItem. An out-of-range echo is silently ignored, so a corrupted slot value cannot desync the hotbar. The client's own C09 send path is separate: EntityPlayerSP switches slots locally and the server confirms with S09.

Three real references in the corpus. Rise 6.x PingSpoofComponent lists S09 in its teleports class tuple next to S08 and S39: when a disabler arms spoofing with the teleports tuple, S09 is intercepted and delayed like the stateful packets, because a slot echo released out of order desyncs the hotbar. Rise 5.99 Aura and Sigma 4.11 InventoryManager import S09 without handling it: both do silent slot switching on the C09 side and the import is dead in the shipped builds. November Recode 2.0's InventoryManager is the only live consumer: its packetIn listener stores the slot from S09 (and the packetOut listener stores the C09 request), and slot()/sync() expose the server-confirmed slot to modules.

There is no exploit surface worth the name. Delaying S09 through PingSpoofComponent is the only manipulation in the corpus, and it is collateral of the C00/C0F buffering rather than a slot attack: the delay window is the same amount used for keepalive and transaction spoofing. Anti-cheats do not measure slot echoes, and no module in the 8 clients reads S09 to detect forced slot changes.

implementation.overview: The server echo of the held-slot change: one byte, bounded to 0-8, applied straight to inventory.currentItem. Module interest is minimal: only Rise's PingSpoofComponent treats S09 as state that must be buffered with the teleport class of packets, and the Aura and Sigma InventoryManager references are dead imports; November Recode 2.0's InventoryManager is the one client that consumes the echo, tracking the server-confirmed slot from both directions.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager sends S09 to the player on join (line 166 in the Memeware copy) and after every accepted C09 slot change (line 802), always with playerIn.inventory.currentItem. The server never validates the echoed value because the client is the source of truth for its own hotbar; the packet is purely informational.
implementation.protocol_notes: Single byte field, hotbar index 0-8. Sent in PLAY state, clientbound only. The pairing with C09 is asymmetric: C09 carries the requested slot, S09 confirms it, and the client applies the confirmation unconditionally within bounds. Because S09 is a broadcast to the player only, silent-switch modules depend on the server never echoing a slot they did not send.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures S09. Slot-change rate is governed by the C09 side (inventory clicking and silent switch modules), and the echo adds nothing measurable. The only detection-adjacent use is PingSpoofComponent's ordering constraint: releasing a delayed S09 after the server already moved on would desync the hotbar visually, so the component holds and releases it with the buffered batch.

modules.name: PingSpoofComponent
modules.purpose: Treat S09 as server state that must be held and released with the buffered keepalive and transaction batch when a disabler arms the teleports tuple.
modules.how_it_works: The teleports tuple lists S08, S39 and S09. While enabled and the tuple is armed, any matching packet is cancelled on the receive event and parked in the timed queue, then released via PacketUtil.queue after the configured delay from PostMotionEvent.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Delaying a slot echo can visually desync the hotbar, but no anti-cheat reads it; the risk is cosmetic and only materializes if the delay outlives the next C09, which the component's ordering avoids by releasing the whole batch together.
modules.variations: Identical in 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; both arm the tuple through the same spoof() API used by the disabler suite.

modules.name: Aura / InventoryManager (import-only)
modules.purpose: Dead imports: both modules reference S09 in their source but contain no handling for it in the shipped builds.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 5.99 Aura imports S09PacketHeldItemChange at line 44 with no other reference in the file; Sigma 4.11 InventoryManager imports it at line 31 with no other reference. Both clients perform silent slot switching on the C09 side, and the S09 import is a leftover from development rather than active code.
modules.vanilla_hook: None in the shipped builds (import only).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No detection relevance: an unused import changes nothing on the wire.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus references S09 in module code at all.

modules.name: InventoryManager (server slot sync)
modules.purpose: Track the server-confirmed hotbar slot from both C09 (out) and S09 (in) and expose it to modules that need the authoritative held slot.
modules.how_it_works: A packetOut listener stores the slot from C09PacketHeldItemChange; a packetIn listener stores the slot from S09PacketHeldItemChange.getHeldItemHotbarIndex(). slot() returns the tracked value, falling back to inventory.currentItem on first use; sync() re-sends C09 when the tracked slot diverges from currentItem. This is the only module in the corpus that reads the S09 echo for state, not just imports it.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.Out and EventPacket.In listeners subscribed on the November bus.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: slot tracking is client-side bookkeeping. sync() only ever sends a C09 matching the player's real currentItem, so the wire traffic is indistinguishable from a normal slot switch.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 Aura and Sigma 4.11 InventoryManager only import S09 with dead handlers; Rise 6.x PingSpoofComponent delays the echo as part of its teleports tuple; November Recode 2.0 is the only client that consumes the echo.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the Rise 6.x hook surface (PingSpoofComponent handles S09 at component level before modules); November Recode 2.0 subscribes EventPacket.Out and EventPacket.In listeners in InventoryManager to track the slot.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.x uses the component system with class-tuple matching. Memeware, Nekoware, Spicy and Tenacity have no module reference at all; their S09 corpus hits are vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient and ServerConfigurationManager files. November Recode 2.0 listens to both directions of the slot exchange (C09 out, S09 in) in InventoryManager and exposes the tracked slot through a management API.

anticheat.overview: The S09 corpus is dominated by the serverbound side: the grep terms collide with PacketPlayInHeldItemSlot (C09), so most hits are IN-side checks (Azure BadPacketsM, Frequency BadPacketsE/F and their forks, Grim BadPacketsA/Y, ThotPatrol BadPacketsC, Daedalus Crash, Artemis ProtocolG/BadPacketsP, Truthful BadPacketH, BetterAnticheat ImpossibleSlotCheck, Intave ToolSwitchHeuristic). The clientbound echo itself has exactly one check-class consumer: Kauri SlotChange reads WrapperPlayServerHeldItemChange and uses the confirmation to make the IN-side slot check trustworthy. Everything else on the OUT side is plumbing: FlopAC's WrappedOutHeldItemSlot and Artemis's GPacketPlayServerHeldItemSlot with the HardcodeMap registration.

checks.name: SlotChange (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Two-way slot validator: the S09 server echo marks the slot change as confirmed so the next C09 with the same slot is not flagged, while C09 slot resends without a confirmation accumulate a buffer and flag.
checks.how_it_works: SlotChange binds two actions. The serverSlot action fires on WrapperPlayServerHeldItemChange (S09) and sets didServerSlot. The heldItemSlot action fires on WrapperPlayClientHeldItemChange (C09): when didServerSlot is set it consumes the change and stores the slot, otherwise a same-slot resend pushes the buffer and flags "Bad slot change detected" past BUFFER_MAX = 6, decaying the buffer by 3 on legitimate changes.
checks.detects: Slot-change packet spam and invalid slot changes on the C09 side. The S09 confirmation is the state that prevents false positives after every legitimate server-confirmed switch.
checks.variations: No other anticheat reads the clientbound echo inside a check class. FlopAC ships the WrappedOutHeldItemSlot wrapper (SERVER HeldItemSlot constant) and Artemis registers PacketPlayServerItemHeldSlot in HardcodeMap with the GPacketPlayServerHeldItemSlot wrapper; both are routing plumbing, not checks. The C09-side checks in the corpus ignore the echo and key only off the inbound packet.

wiki_notes: Single byte 0-8 confirming the held hotbar slot; server echo of C09 sent on join and every accepted switch.
Vanilla handler bounds-checks against hotbar size and ignores out-of-range values; silent-switch logic keys off C09, not this echo.
MCP 1.8.9 S09PacketHeldItemChange implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleHeldItemChange; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte.

1.8.9 callers: ServerConfigurationManager.initializeConnectionToPlayer sends new S09PacketHeldItemChange (line 148): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/management/ServerConfigurationManager.java

packets.name: Use Bed
packets.desc: Makes the player lie down in a bed at the specified position.

writeup.p: S0A tells clients that a player went to sleep: a VarInt entity id and a BlockPos for the bed. The server sends it from EntityPlayerMP.sleepInBedAt and re-broadcasts it through EntityTrackerEntry to everyone tracking the sleeper. The client renders the sleeping pose; the matching wake-up arrives as S0BPacketAnimation type 2 (leave bed).

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleUseBed looks the entity up by id, validates the bed block, sets the sleeping position and marks the entity as sleeping. EntityTrackerEntry broadcasts S0A to tracking players when a tracked entity enters a bed, and EntityPlayerMP sends it on its own connection in sleepInBedAt.

No module in the 8 clients hooks S0A. The only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x NetworkAPI, which lists S0A in the script API packet whitelist so JavaScript modules can register receive handlers for it; that is framework plumbing, not module logic. Bed mechanics are absent from the 1.8 PvP servers these clients target, and a sleep pose carries no combat, movement or render value, so nothing listens.

None observed in the corpus. The packet is clientbound and informational: it changes only a render pose. The bed-position BlockPos is never validated by clients for gameplay effect, and no anti-cheat measures sleeping. The honest assessment is that S0A is protocol trivia in this ecosystem: it exists, it is registered in every client's EnumConnectionState, and nothing exploits it.

implementation.overview: The sleep-pose broadcast: entity id plus bed BlockPos, sent on join and re-broadcast by the entity tracker. Zero module hits across the 8 clients; the only non-vanilla reference is the Rise script API packet whitelist. Bed mechanics do not exist on the servers these clients target, so S0A is protocol trivia.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.sleepInBedAt constructs S0A with the player and bed location and sends it on the sleeper's own connection; EntityTrackerEntry re-broadcasts it to all tracking players. There is no server-side validation of the pose beyond the bed-block checks in the sleep routine itself.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields: VarInt entity id, then BlockPos serialized as a long (x << 38 | z << 12 | y, with the y sign bit). Sent in PLAY state, clientbound. The leave-bed counterpart is S0BPacketAnimation type 2, so the two packets bracket a sleep cycle. Registered at id 0x0A in every client's EnumConnectionState.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing to flag: S0A changes only a pose and carries no timing, position or state information an anti-cheat could measure. The only ecosystem wrinkle is that a client which never renders the sleep pose (or renders it wrong) produces a visual mismatch, never a flag.
implementation.general_hooks: Rise 6.x scripts can register S0A receive handlers through NetworkAPI, but no shipped module does.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients register S0A in vanilla code paths identically; only Rise 6.x adds the script API whitelist entry.

anticheat.overview: The use-bed packet has a single corpus hit: Artemis registers a GPacketPlayServerBed wrapper that decodes the player id and bed BlockPos. No check consumes it. The packet is a clientbound pose broadcast with no timing, position or state claim a server-side anticheat could measure, so the ecosystem ignores it.

checks.name: Packet wrapper registration (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Register the use-bed packet in Artemis's packet abstraction so the wrapper tree recognizes clientbound bed traffic.
checks.how_it_works: GPacketPlayServerBed extends GPacket, links to PacketPlayServerBed, and its read() decodes the player id as a VarInt and the bed position as a packed BlockPos. No check in the corpus consumes these fields.
checks.detects: Nothing. The entry documents the only corpus touch point for S0A: wrapper plumbing, not detection logic.
checks.variations: No other anticheat references S0APacketUseBed or PacketPlayOutBed.

wiki_notes: PLAY id 0x0A: VarInt player id plus bed BlockPos packed as a single long; broadcast via tracker on sleep.
Render-pose only; the matching wake-up arrives as S0B animation type 2, so the two packets bracket a sleep cycle.

MCP 1.8.9 S0APacketUseBed implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleUseBed; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBlockPos, readVarIntFromBuffer.
1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.? sends new S0APacketUseBed (line 442) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Animation
packets.desc: Broadcasts entity animation (arm swing, damage, etc.) to nearby players.

writeup.p: S0B broadcasts an entity animation: a VarInt entity id and a byte type (0 swing, 1 damage, 2 leave bed, 3 eat or drink, 4 critical, 5 magic critical, 6 crouch, 7 uncrouch). EntityLivingBase.swingItem sends type 0 through the entity tracker, EntityPlayerMP sends 2 and 3 on bed leave and eating, and attackEntityAsMob sends 4 and 5 for crits. The client handler switches on the type and drives the entity's animation state.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleAnimation looks up the entity and applies the animation: swingProgress for type 0, hurtTime for 1, and so on. Server-side the tracker fans the packet out to every player tracking the entity, so a swing is the one reliable signal that another player is attacking.

S0B is the swing ground truth, and the corpus uses it five ways. ClickerMimic (Rise 6.x) records per-player swing intervals and replays them as the client's own clicks. Ranking (Sigma) timestamps swings and attributes deaths to players who swung within 70 ms of the local player taking damage. Rise 5.99 runs its own anticheat off S0B: AutoClickerA counts swings against movement packets, KeepSprintA couples swings to sprint state. PlayerHacks (Rise 5.99) gates its remote aura and nuker on the master's swings, and SocialCreditScore subtracts points for every weapon swing it observes. Nekoware and Rise 5.99 Scaffold import S0B for placement-swing sync without handling it. LiquidSense Dev's AntiBot records every type-0 swing entity id into a swing set on the packet bus and flags entities that never swing as bots when its Swing check is enabled, the only swing telemetry in the corpus outside Rise's checks.

S0B is clientbound only and cannot be spoofed outward, so abuse is observational. A player who hits without producing swings, or with perfectly regular intervals, is an autoclicker; that is exactly what Rise's AutoClickerA and KeepSprintA checks measure on the client's own users. ClickerMimic inverts the trick: it measures a victim's swing rhythm and reproduces it, so the client's clicks inherit a human-looking distribution without any randomization logic of its own.

implementation.overview: The animation broadcast: entity id plus a type byte, fanned out by the entity tracker. The only reliable signal that another player swung, which makes it the heartbeat of click mimicry, swing-based anticheat checks, combat logging, aura gating and bot filtering across the reference clients.
implementation.server_handling: EntityLivingBase.swingItem sends S0B type 0 to all tracking entities; EntityPlayerMP sends type 2 on bed leave, type 3 on eating, and attackEntityAsMob emits types 4 and 5 for critical hits through func_151248_b. The server applies no rate limit: swings are broadcast as produced, which is what makes swing-count heuristics possible.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields: VarInt entity id, unsigned byte animation type. Clientbound in PLAY state. The type byte is read as readUnsignedByte, so values above 7 are legal on the wire and ignored by the vanilla switch. The swing type 0 is the only animation players emit at click rate, which is why every module keys on it specifically.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Swing-vs-movement ratio is the autoclicker tell: more than 3 swings per movement packet flags AutoClickerA. Keepsprint couples swings to sprint state. The client-side checks in Rise 5.99 are notable because they run in the cheat itself, proof that S0B is the swing source of truth for both sides of the ecosystem.

modules.name: ClickerMimic
modules.purpose: Record the swing intervals of every visible player and replay them as the client's own clicks, so the local click pattern mirrors the victim's rhythm.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, each S0B stamps ticksExisted into a per-name interval list. While the attack key is held, PreUpdateEvent replays the recorded intervals as mc.clickMouse() calls, halved in duration. Sneaking clears the recordings.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The replayed rhythm is a real human distribution sampled from another player, which defeats interval-based autoclicker checks better than any synthetic randomization; the cost is that the pattern is identifiable across sessions.
modules.variations: Identical in 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; both register the S0B listener at Priorities.VERY_LOW.

modules.name: PlayerHacks
modules.purpose: Gate a remote aura and nuker on the selected master player's swings: the module only acts after observing an S0B from that entity.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketReceive sets the swung flag when an S0B entity id matches the master. onPreMotion then pathfinds the master along a computed route on a worker thread, sends C04 position packets and C02 attack packets, and reverses the route. The onlyOnSwing setting requires a fresh swing before each pass.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The swing gate is a human-input check, not an anti-cheat evasion: the module makes another player attack for you and would be instantly obvious to staff; the S0B read is purely a trigger.
modules.variations: Nekoware v1 and Rise 5.99 Scaffold also import S0B without handling it; no other client has a swing-gated remote module.

modules.name: SocialCreditScore
modules.purpose: Joke-module telemetry: penalize the tracked player's social credit score for every observed weapon swing.
modules.how_it_works: handlePacketEvent runs on the packet bus: each S0B with type 0 and the tracked entity id subtracts 50 score for a sword, 10 otherwise; handleUpdate additionally charges 100 for merely holding a tool or sword.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the module reads S0B and mutates nothing on the wire.
modules.variations: No other client has an equivalent; this is a single-file utility class in Rise 5.99 only.

modules.name: Ranking
modules.purpose: Hidden telemetry: timestamp swings and attribute deaths to players who swung within 70 ms of the local player taking damage.
modules.how_it_works: On EventPacket, S0B timestamps are stored per entity id; when S06PacketUpdateHealth shows the local player losing health, any player with a swing under 70 ms old and within 9 blocks is registered as a prosecutor. S08 resets the state as a respawn; S18 teleports and S13 destroy-entities finalize records, and the sendStat bodies are empty in this build.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket (S0B, S06, S08, S18, S13, S02, S40), EventAttack, EventUpdate.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The 70 ms swing window is a real combat-logging heuristic: it attributes damage to the swing that caused it. The module is hidden and auto-enables, so it runs silently on every Sigma user.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus attributes deaths via S0B; Rise's anticheat checks are the closest analogue.

modules.name: AutoClickerA (client anticheat)
modules.purpose: Rise's own client-side autoclicker check: verify that the local player's swings are consistent with its movement packet stream.
modules.how_it_works: Counts S0B packets whose entity id is the local player, then on each relative-move packet compares the count: more than 3 swings per movement packet with a warmed buffer fails the check; otherwise the buffer decays after one second.
modules.vanilla_hook: Check.handle on the packet pipeline (S0B and relative-move packets).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The check measures the cheat's own users, not the server's: a user autoclicker that produces swings faster than the movement stream is flagged locally. KeepSprintA is the sibling check coupling swings to sprint state.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 also ships KeepSprintA in the same anticheat package; no other client ships an internal anticheat that reads S0B.

modules.name: AntiBot (swing telemetry)
modules.purpose: Feed S0B swing events into the bot detector: entities that never produce a type-0 swing become bot candidates.
modules.how_it_works: The onPacket handler checks the packet class, reads the animation entity id and appends it to a swing list when the type byte is 0. The static isBot() consult used by KillAura and other modules flags an entity when the Swing setting is enabled and the id is absent from the swing list. The same handler tracks S14 relative moves for ground and air state, and the list is cleared only on world change or module disable.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: S0B is clientbound and the module only reads it. The bot veto is client-side; the server never sees it.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99's AutoClickerA is the only other corpus module that counts swings, and it measures the local player instead of other entities.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on every client; Rise 5.99 additionally feeds S0B to its internal anticheat checks before modules.
implementation.client_variations: Sigma and Spicy read the type byte and entity id off the packet object; Rise 6.x uses event listeners with priorities; Rise 5.99 anticheat checks sit on a separate check pipeline from modules. LiquidSense Dev tracks swings inside its AntiBot module on the PacketEvent bus; Rise 5.99's anticheat checks are the only other swing counters in the corpus.

anticheat.overview: S0B is the server-to-client animation broadcast, and the swing type (0) is the only animation a player emits at click rate, which makes it the one reliable signal that another player is attacking. Server-side anticheats cannot read the client's own swing inside S0B because it is outbound, so the swing checks in this corpus consume the inbound arm-animation packet (C0A, PacketPlayInArmAnimation) that the client sends on every left click, plus the outbound S0B on the few checks that listen on the send side. The corpus splits into no-swing validators (NCP fight NoSwing, Grim NoSwingBreak, ThotPatrol NoSwingA, MIU NoSwing), autoclicker statistics over the swing stream (Frequency AutoClickerA, Hydro AutoClickerA-D, Kauri AutoclickerA-D, Artemis AutoClickerA-M, Salmon SwingA), and packet-order rules that demand a swing after every attack (Grim Post and PacketOrderB, Photon PacketAnalysisAnimation, Truthful PacketOrderA/D).

checks.name: NoSwing (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Require an arm swing between attacks so that damage without the arm-animation packet is flagged.
checks.how_it_works: FightListener invokes check() on the Bukkit PlayerAnimationEvent that mirrors the inbound arm-animation packet. A counter increments per attack: when a swing arrives first, the violation level decays by a factor of 0.9; when an attack arrives without a swing, 1 violation level is added and the configured actions run, cancelling the attack once the threshold is crossed.
checks.detects: Killaura and no-swing modules that attack without sending the arm animation.
checks.variations: NCP repeats the same check for blockbreak and blockplace; Arc (Vrekt-Arc) generalizes it as AbstractBlockNoSwingCheck plus a combat NoSwing and a network-level SwingFrequency; MIU ships NoSwing and NoSwingA; ThotPatrol NoSwingA counts swings between attacks; Intave folds swing order into combat heuristics (NoSwingHeuristic, PacketOrderSwingHeuristic).

checks.name: NoSwingBreak (Grim)
checks.purpose: Verify that a swing animation accompanies block digging, flagging diggers that never swing.
checks.how_it_works: Registers as both a BlockBreakListener and a PreViaPacketReceiveListener. onBlockBreak sets sentBreak for any dig action that is not a cancel; onPreViaPacketReceive sets sentAnimation when Play.Client.ANIMATION arrives; on the next tick packet the check flags if a break was recorded without an animation. Both flags reset every tick, so the swing must land inside the same tick as the dig start. The check is marked experimental.
checks.detects: Nuker and fast-break modules that dig while suppressing the swing packet.
checks.variations: Grim Post enforces the swing-before-attack order with transaction timing; amnoah-BetterAnticheat ships the same pairing as NoSwingDigCheck and NoSwingCombatCheck; freppp-ThotPatrol NoSwingA is the compact 1.8 form.

checks.name: AutoClickerA (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Statistical autoclicker check over the arm-animation stream: human click timing must vary.
checks.how_it_works: PacketCheck on WrappedPlayInArmAnimation: while CPS is above 6.5 and the player is not digging or placing, the number of movement packets between swings is sampled. After 20 samples the check computes the standard deviation and the outlier count; a deviation below 2 with fewer than 2 outliers fails. Constant-interval autoclickers produce near-zero variance and trip the check.
checks.detects: Autoclickers with low-variance click timing.
checks.variations: Hydro AutoClickerA-D, Kauri AutoclickerA-D, Artemis AutoClickerA-M, Azure AutoClickerA and Salmon SwingA implement the same swing-interval statistics on their own event buses; Intave ClickPatterns runs the same idea through entropy and deviation click-pattern checks.

checks.name: PacketAnalysisAnimation (Photon)
checks.purpose: Enforce the client's own attack sequence: an arm animation must directly follow an attack.
checks.how_it_works: Listens to INTERACT_ENTITY and ANIMATION at LOW priority. An attack on an entity sets a packetAnalysisAnimationExpected flag; the next ANIMATION clears it; if another attack arrives while the flag is still set, the previous attack never produced a swing and the module flags with +30 violation level under a decaying violation management. Disabled on 1.8 servers, where ViaVersion reorders animations.
checks.detects: Killaura that sends attack packets without the swing the vanilla client always sends after a left click.
checks.variations: Grim Post enforces the same attack-then-swing order with transaction-based timing; Truthful PacketOrderA/D and Grim PacketOrderB flag the same ordering violation from different packet sets; Tecnio-AntiHaxerman ProtocolC/ProtocolE cover arm-animation protocol oddities.

checks.name: Post (Grim)
checks.purpose: Verify that action packets arrive inside the expected movement tick, and consume the outbound S0B swing to exempt injected animations.
checks.how_it_works: On the send side, WrapperPlayServerEntityAnimation (the S0B packet) for the player's own entity id records the current transaction when the type is SWING_MAIN_ARM or SWING_OFF_HAND. On the receive side, action packets (attack, dig, place, animation, interact) that arrive after a flying packet are queued, and a transaction boundary with queued packets flags a post violation through the prediction pipeline. The swing exemption keeps ViaVersion-injected animations from falsing the check.
checks.detects: Post packets sent after movement, which blink and timer modules produce; the swing-exemption path keeps legitimately injected animations from falsing.
checks.variations: Grim PacketOrderB and Photon PacketAnalysisAnimation cover related ordering rules; Truthful PacketOrderA/D run the same order checks on Truthful's listener.

wiki_notes: PLAY id 0x0B: VarInt entityId plus unsigned-byte type; 1.8.9 types are 0 swing, 1 hurt, 2 leave bed, 3 eat, 4 crit, 5 magic crit.
Type 0 is the only click-rate signal, so swing counters, AntiBot swing sets and combat attribution all key on it.

MCP 1.8.9 S0BPacketAnimation implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleAnimation; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readUnsignedByte, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityLivingBase.swingItem sends new S0BPacketAnimation (line 1351) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityLivingBase.java

packets.name: Spawn Player
packets.desc: Spawns another player entity in the world with UUID, position (fixed-point int × 32), rotation (byte × 256/360), held item, and metadata.
packets.notes: This is received when another player enters the client's render distance. ESP modules add the entity to their target list. AntiBot modules check the UUID against tab list entries.

writeup.p: S0C spawns a player entity: VarInt entity id, UUID, fixed-point x/y/z as ints scaled by 32, byte yaw and pitch scaled by 256/360, a short current-item id, then the DataWatcher metadata. EntityTrackerEntry constructs it when a player enters render distance. The client builds an EntityOtherPlayerMP from it. MessageSerializer carries a no-op special case for S0C in the bundled 1.8 sources, a decompile artifact of the 1.7.x-era encoding special case.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleSpawnPlayer decodes the fixed-point coordinates, reads the metadata and registers the entity in the world. From then on the entity is driven by S14 relative moves and S18 teleports. ESP and nametag modules do not hook S0C in these clients: they iterate the world entity list, which is why S0C only shows up in anti-bot and meme modules.

S0C is the only packet that announces a new player with a position, which makes it the anti-bot veto point. Spicy's Antibot cancels the packet outright when the spawn looks like a bot (within 17 blocks, more than 1 block above the player, not at the player's coordinates) on non-Hypixel servers; the Hypixel branch is commented out because Hypixel bots carry plausible spawn data, so bots are removed from the entity list per-tick instead. Sigma 4.11 AntiBot inspects spawn packets the same way. The Spicy meme modules (DougDimmadome, FloofyFoxes, Furries) import S0C for skin and model replacement but ship empty handlers. November Recode 2.0's AntiBotModule adds a WATCHDOG mode that treats every player spawn following a detected bot despawn as a bot, printing a suspicious-spawn notice.

Cancelling S0C is client-only: the server keeps simulating the bot, but the local world never receives the entity, so aim and ESP never lock onto it. The risk is entity-id desync if later packets reference the cancelled id, which vanilla guards by simply not spawning the entity. Anti-cheats do not measure S0C; anti-bot heuristics are purely client-side (spawn position relative to the player, invisibility plus name quirks, tab-list absence), and servers that want bots to survive these filters just spawn them with realistic positions, which is exactly what Hypixel does.

implementation.overview: The player-spawn announcement: fixed-point position, byte rotations, item id and metadata. In this corpus it is the anti-bot veto point: Spicy cancels suspicious spawns outright, Sigma inspects them, November Recode 2.0 flags post-despawn spawns in WATCHDOG mode, while the meme modules only import it. ESP and nametag modules never touch S0C because they iterate the entity list instead.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket constructs S0C from the tracked EntityPlayer with x, y and z scaled by 32, yaw and pitch scaled by 256/360, the held item id as a short, and the DataWatcher data. The server does no per-recipient filtering beyond the tracker's render-distance logic.
implementation.protocol_notes: Fields: VarInt entity id, UUID (most and least significant longs), three ints scaled by 32, two bytes scaled by 256/360, a short item id (0 when empty), then DataWatcher metadata. The scaling is why the client divides by 32 and multiplies by 360/256. S0C is the only spawn packet with a UUID, which is what makes it the natural hook for anti-bot and name-based filtering.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat reads S0C. The client-side heuristics in Spicy (17-block range, height above the player, non-coincident coordinates) and the Hypixel per-tick removal (invisibility, name formatting, tab-list absence, Watchdog naming) are the whole anti-bot landscape in this corpus, and servers defeat them by making spawn data indistinguishable from real players.

modules.name: AntiBot
modules.purpose: Veto bots at the spawn point: cancel S0C for suspicious spawns so the entity never enters the local world and cannot be targeted.
modules.how_it_works: Spicy hooks EventPacket pre: on non-Hypixel servers, a spawn within 17 blocks, more than 1 block above the player and not at the player's exact coordinates is cancelled with a chat notice; on Hypixel the packet path is commented out and hypixelAntibot() removes bots from the entity list per-tick using invisibility, name formatting, tab-list absence and Watchdog naming heuristics. Sigma inspects incoming S0C the same way on its own packet bus.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket (pre, incoming); EventUpdate for the per-tick Hypixel removal.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling the spawn is invisible to the server and to anti-cheats; the visible effect is that legitimate players matching the heuristic vanish too, which is the trade-off of position-based filtering.
modules.variations: Sigma 4.11 AntiBot reads S0C on EventPacket and filters on spawn data; Spicy splits the logic per server family and keeps the Hypixel path entity-list based. November Recode 2.0 ships the same role as AntiBotModule with WATCHDOG, TAB_TICKS and NPC modes; the WATCHDOG mode flags spawns that follow a detected bot despawn.

modules.name: DougDimmadome / FloofyFoxes / Furries (entity overrides)
modules.purpose: Meme-module family that imports S0C as the hook point for replacing spawned player models and skins; the shipped builds contain no handling.
modules.how_it_works: All three modules import S0CPacketSpawnPlayer and define empty onEvent bodies. The import marks the intended integration point (hook player spawns, replace the entity render) but no spawn handling exists in the shipped files.
modules.vanilla_hook: None in the shipped builds (import only).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No detection relevance: an unused import changes nothing on the wire.
modules.variations: Spicy also imports S0C in files/Account.java; the FloofyFoxes and Furries modules are the same empty family.

modules.name: AntiBotModule (WATCHDOG spawn veto)
modules.purpose: Flag player spawns that arrive after a detected bot despawned, so combat modules never target the replacement.
modules.how_it_works: In WATCHDOG mode the module first scans the world entity list for invisible players missing from the tab list and picks one above the player as aboveEntityId. Once the S13 listener confirms that id was destroyed, the S0C branch of the same packet listener adds every new spawn to the bots set and prints a suspicious-spawn notice; other modules consult bot() before targeting.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.In (S0C and S13 branches), EventUpdate (entity list scan).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The veto is client-side only; the server never sees it. False positives are the cost: a legitimate player who respawns right after a bot despawn is blacklisted until the bots set is cleared on disable or the first five ticks after spawn.
modules.variations: Spicy cancels S0C outright and Sigma filters on spawn data; November instead records ids and lets KillAura-style modules skip them via bot().

implementation.general_hooks: EventPacket with pre and incoming checks on Spicy and Sigma; nothing else in the corpus hooks S0C at module level.
implementation.client_variations: Spicy cancels the packet object (packet.setCanceled) inside a single EventPacket; Sigma reads spawn data on its EventPacket bus; Rise 6.x lists S0C only in the NetworkAPI script whitelist. November Recode 2.0 handles S0C inside AntiBotModule's EventPacket.In listener, gated on WATCHDOG mode.

anticheat.overview: The named-entity spawn packet is how server-side anticheats learn that another player exists and where. Reach, hitbox and killaura checks need this position anchor before the entity-update stream takes over, so every modern anticheat keeps an entity tracker keyed by spawn: Hydro and Tecnio insert a tracked entity into a map, Shard adds it to the compensated entity list and observes it for view sessions, and Grim replicates it into the simulation. The packet is never flagged; it is the insertion point that makes entity-distance checks possible. S0F (spawn mob) shares the same tracker files because living entities feed the same maps.

checks.name: Spawn-player tracking (Hydro)
checks.purpose: Insert the spawned player into the tracked-entity map so reach and hitbox checks can measure against it.
checks.how_it_works: EntityTracker.registerOutgoingPreHandler routes SPAWN_PLAYER to handleSpawnPlayer, which wraps the packet as WrapperPlayServerSpawnPlayer, reads the fixed-point position and stores a TrackedEntity keyed by entity id. S14 relative moves and S18 teleports then update the entry inside transaction confirmations, and DESTROY_ENTITIES removes it. Entity movement is interpolated only on flying packets, keeping the tracker transaction-accurate.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; it is the data layer. Reach checks and entity-distance queries (getDistanceToEntity, getClosestEntity, getEntitiesWithinDistance) consume the map.
checks.variations: Tecnio's EntityTracker does the same with GPacketPlayServerSpawnNamedEntity and confirms the insertion on the connection tracker; Shard routes SPAWN_PLAYER into compensatedEntities.addEntity; Grim replicates the spawn into its compensated entity map with metadata and rotation.

checks.name: Spawn-player view tracking (Shard)
checks.purpose: Notify the view-session coordinator when a tracked player spawns so spectator-style tracking sessions stay in sync.
checks.how_it_works: ViewTrackingObserver listens at MONITOR priority and, on SPAWN_PLAYER, resolves the spawned player's UUID, then schedules a synchronous task that checks isTrackableViewTarget and calls coordinator.trackTarget. It ignores the viewer's own spawn (targetId == viewer.uniqueId) and is a no-op when no session is active. DESTROY_ENTITIES is the matching removal path.
checks.detects: Nothing: this is session bookkeeping for the monitoring system, not a detection check.
checks.variations: Shard's PacketListener also adds the entity to compensatedEntities on the same packet (handleSpawnPlayer), so the anticheat's simulation and its view sessions are fed by two different listeners over the same packet.

checks.name: Named-entity spawn tracking (Tecnio)
checks.purpose: Seed the entity tracker map with the spawned player's position inside a confirmed transaction.
checks.how_it_works: EntityTracker.handle dispatches GPacketPlayServerSpawnNamedEntity to a connection-confirmed action: it builds a TrackerEntity from the wrapper's entity id and fixed-point coordinates, sets the position and puts it in trackerMap. S14 entity updates and S18 teleports mutate the entry under confirmation, and the map is interpolated on every flying packet in handlePost.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself; the tracker feeds the hitbox and reach checks.
checks.variations: Hydro confirms spawns implicitly through its transaction tracker; Grim replicates metadata and rotations; Artemis ReachPreProcessor.attemptAdd is the same named-spawn insertion for its reach preprocessor.

wiki_notes: If an entity with the same ID already exists on the client it is automatically deleted and replaced by the new entity.

MCP 1.8.9 S0CPacketSpawnPlayer implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleSpawnPlayer; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readInt, readShort, readUuid, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.createSpawnPacket sends new S0CPacketSpawnPlayer (line 501): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Collect Item
packets.desc: Shows an item being collected (picked up) by a player entity. Plays the pickup animation.

writeup.p: S0D plays the item pickup animation: a VarInt item-entity id and a VarInt collector-entity id. The server emits it from EntityLivingBase.onCollideWithPlayer, which sends up to three tracking broadcasts per pickup depending on the item-count branch. The client spawns the collect particles, plays the sound and removes the item entity. It is a pure presentation packet.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleCollectItem removes the item entity by id, spawns the pickup particles and plays the collect sound. Nothing on the client validates the collector id; the animation is cosmetic. The server side is equally dumb: three sendToAllTrackingEntity calls in onCollideWithPlayer with no rate limiting.

Almost nobody. The single functional hit is Rise 6.x AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent, which uses S0D as a cheap game-activity signal: an item pickup forces the HUD cache dirty for 5 ticks so the adaptive refresh rate does not sleep through pickups. Everything else in the corpus is vanilla. The ItemESP and ItemStealer families that one might expect to care about pickups do not hook S0D in these clients: they track item entities directly on the entity list.

None. S0D carries two entity ids and drives only particles and a despawn. There is no state, no timing heuristic and no anti-cheat that measures pickups, so modules have nothing to cancel, spoof or time. The honest assessment is that S0D is the least interesting packet in this range: its only corpus use is a HUD perf component treating it as an activity tick.

implementation.overview: The pickup animation packet: item entity id plus collector id, driving particles, sound and a despawn. Module interest is essentially zero: the only functional use in the whole corpus is Rise's AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent, which treats S0D as a game-activity signal to keep the HUD refresh awake.
implementation.server_handling: EntityLivingBase.onCollideWithPlayer sends S0D through the entity tracker in three branches covering the pickup conditions, each a sendToAllTrackingEntity with the item entity id and the collector's own id. No server-side rate limit or validation exists.
implementation.protocol_notes: Two VarInts: collected item entity id first, collector player id second (the vanilla constructor takes (collectedItemEntityId, entityId)). Clientbound in PLAY state. The collector id is not required to be the local player, which is why the packet also animates other players' pickups.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing to flag. No anti-cheat measures item pickups, and the packet carries no position or timing data. The only ecosystem interaction is visual: a client that suppresses S0D would still receive the items in inventory, so even packet-cancelling modules would gain nothing.

modules.name: AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent
modules.purpose: Keep the HUD refresh awake around pickups: an S0D forces the HUD cache dirty for 5 ticks so the adaptive refresh does not sleep through game activity.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, S0D sets disabledFor = 5, which disables the adaptive refresh for that many ticks in PreMotionEvent; S02 chat, S30 window items and S2F slot updates drive the same dirty path. The component runs at component level in the HUD module tree.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the component mutates only the local HUD cache and never touches the packet or the wire.
modules.variations: Identical in 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; no other client in the corpus references S0D in non-vanilla code.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent only, and only in Rise 6.x; the component model is the sole consumer.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 share the component; Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity have no non-vanilla S0D code at all.

anticheat.overview: The collect-item packet has zero hits in the 50-anticheat corpus. It carries two entity ids and drives only a particle burst, a sound and a despawn; there is nothing to measure and nothing to flag. The honest summary is that no anticheat references S0D, matching its role as pure presentation.

wiki_notes: The packet only plays the pickup animation flying the item toward the collector and does not destroy the entity in client memory or add it to the inventory, so a destroy packet handles removal.
The collector and collected entities can be any entity, though the vanilla server only uses it for items, experience orbs and projectiles such as arrows.
MCP 1.8.9 S0DPacketCollectItem implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleCollectItem; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityLivingBase.onItemPickup sends new S0DPacketCollectItem (line 2137): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityLivingBase.java

packets.name: Spawn Object
packets.desc: Spawns a non-living entity: item drop, boat, minecart, arrow, fireball, ender pearl, armor stand, etc.
packets.notes: Entity types: 1=boat, 2=item, 50=TNTPrimed, 51=enderCrystal, 60=arrow, 61=snowball, 62=egg, 63=fireball, 64=smallFireball, 65=enderPearl, 66=witherSkull, 67=shulkerBullet, 68=llamaSpit, 90=fishingFloat, 91=spectralArrow, 93=dragonFireball. Used by AntiFireball (attack fireballs), ItemESP (track items), and BoatFly.

writeup.p: The spawn packet for every non-living entity: item drops (type 2), boats (1), minecarts (10), TNT (50), ender crystals (51), arrows and spectral arrows (60/91), snowballs (61), eggs (62), fireballs and small fireballs (63/64), ender pearls (65), wither skulls (66), fishing hooks (90), falling blocks (70), item frames (71), armor stands (78) and more. The server's EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket builds it with the EntityList type code, fixed-point position (x32), byte rotations (x256/360) and short velocity (x8000), and the third constructor argument packs a per-type data int: the shooter entity id for arrows and fireballs, the block state id for falling blocks, the minecart type for carts, the facing index for item frames.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleSpawnObject reads the entity id, type byte, position, three rotations, the three velocity shorts and the trailing DataWatcher, then creates the entity through EntityList.createEntityByID and applies the transform. For projectile types the data int is used to look up the throwing entity so the client can attribute the projectile. Server side, the same packet class is the output of EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket, which is why the type codes and the data int semantics are defined by the server's tracking code, not by the packet class itself.

None of the 8 reference clients hook S0E in any module. The corpus shows only vanilla files plus Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 NetworkAPI.java, which lists S0EPacketSpawnObject in the packet registry that the scripting API exposes to scripts. The absence is structural: ESP, Tracers and KillAura in these clients iterate world.getLoadedEntityList on render ticks instead of hooking spawn packets, so they never see S0E, and the throwable-specific combat modules of the wider ecosystem (AntiFireball-style projectile attackers, item ESP) are not present in this corpus.

The packet is server-trusted end to end, so the attack surface is client-side robustness: extreme velocity shorts, bogus type codes and oversized DataWatcher payloads are the classic crash vectors, and armor stand floods (type 78) were the 1.8-era lag exploit. For anti-cheat work the interesting field is the data int: a projectile carrying the player's entity id as owner is the standard signal AntiFireball-style modules use, and servers that simulate projectiles server-side validate the owner id against the tracker. Anti-cheats that replay or predict projectile trajectories reconstruct them from S0E position and velocity, so the packet is a timing reference for those checks.

implementation.overview: The spawn packet for all non-living entities: items, vehicles, TNT, projectiles, armor stands. In the 8-client corpus it is untouched by modules: ESP iterates the world entity list instead of hooking spawn packets, and the only non-vanilla reference is Rise's NetworkAPI script registry. Documented for protocol completeness and for the projectile-attribution semantics modules in other ecosystems build on.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket switches on the tracked entity class and returns S0E with a type code from EntityList, position x32, yaw/pitch byte rotations and motion x8000 shorts. The third constructor int is type-specific: shooter entity id for arrows and fireballs (0 when the shooter is gone), block state id for falling blocks, minecart type id for carts, facing horizontal index for item frames. The client handler creates the entity and applies the transform; for arrows the data int resolves the thrower so the client can render the correct owner.
implementation.protocol_notes: Entity id and type are VarInt/unsigned byte; position is three ints at x32, rotations are three bytes at x256/360 (yaw, pitch, head pitch), velocity is three shorts at x8000. A DataWatcher block terminates the packet only when the entity has metadata; most non-living types send an empty watcher. The same type codes are shared with the 1.8 EntityList server-side table, so a mismatch between client and server entity registries despawns the entity silently.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing client-controlled is flaggable here because the packet is purely clientbound and server-authored. Anti-cheats use it indirectly: projectile simulation checks reconstruct arrow and fireball paths from S0E and replay them to catch players who dodge impossibly, and servers rate-limit object spawns to stop item/armor stand flood lag exploits. No reference client touches it, so there is no bypass trade-off to document beyond the generic entity-spawn flood mitigations.
implementation.client_variations: The only client-side difference in the corpus is Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 exposing S0EPacketSpawnObject.class in NetworkAPI's packet list for the scripting system; every other client reference is the bundled vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient, EntityTrackerEntry, EnumConnectionState and INetHandlerPlayClient.

anticheat.overview: S0E spawns a generic entity (item, TNT, boat, arrow) with a type id, position and velocity, and is the most common spawn packet in the protocol. Server-side anticheats treat the spawn-object family as the feed for their entity replication: every spawn registers an entity in the compensated world so reach and killaura checks can measure vectors to real targets, and fake-entity bait mechanisms reuse the same family to lure auras. The corpus hits on S0E are therefore the spawn listeners themselves (Grim PacketEntityReplication, Hydro EntityTracker, Kauri PacketHandler, FlopAC WrappedOutSpawnEntityPacket) plus the anti-aura bait code that reuses spawn packets (Kauri FakeMob, Peyang NPC, Shard ViewTrackingObserver).

checks.name: PacketEntityReplication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Replicate every server-side entity spawn, including the S0E spawn-object packet, into the simulated world that reach and hitbox checks run against.
checks.how_it_works: PacketSendListener handles SPAWN_ENTITY (S0E), SPAWN_LIVING_ENTITY, SPAWN_PLAYER and SPAWN_PAINTING, calling addEntity with the id, uuid, type and position; subsequent relative moves, teleports, rotations, metadata and equipment updates are applied inside latency-compensated realtime tasks, and despawns are queued per transaction. It also blocks ViaVersion's faked levitation effects and drives the spawn-teleport acceptance state used by setbacks.
checks.detects: Reach and killaura cheats are measured against the replicated boxes, so the check is the data foundation rather than a flag; it keeps the anticheat from being fooled by spoofed spawn state.
checks.variations: Hydro EntityTracker and Tecnio-AntiHaxerman EntityTracker maintain the same replicated list with transaction-confirmed movement; Artemis replicates entities in its v1/v2 emulators; Intave keeps a dedicated EntityTracker fed by spawn events; Kauri tracks real spawns in PacketHandler and pairs them with FakeMob bait.

checks.name: EntityTracker (Hydro)
checks.purpose: Keep a transaction-synced map of every spawned entity so reach and aura checks can query positions and distances.
checks.how_it_works: The outgoing pre-handler processes the spawn family (living entities and players) plus relative moves, teleports and destroys; entity positions are only mutated inside transaction-confirmed tasks, and post-transaction updates refresh the list. Exposes distance, closest-entity and within-distance queries used by the combat checks.
checks.detects: Supplies the target positions for Hydro's hitbox and reach checks; a client that fakes entity state cannot alter the server-derived list.
checks.variations: Grim PacketEntityReplication and Tecnio-AntiHaxerman EntityTracker are the same idea on different packet abstractions; FlopAC's reach processor consumes WrappedOutSpawnEntityPacket for its own entity list.

checks.name: FakeMob bait (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Spawn invisible fake entities whose ids are registered with the tracker, baiting killaura into attacking something that does not exist on the server.
checks.how_it_works: FakeMob allocates an entity id in the 1.5-2 billion range to avoid colliding with real ids, then sends a spawn packet with the invisible metadata flag to the suspect; the fake is registered in the FakeTracker and can be moved, teleported and despawned. Kauri's PacketHandler separately consumes the real spawn family (SPAWN_ENTITY, SPAWN_LIVING_ENTITY, SPAWN_PLAYER, SPAWN_PAINTING) to keep its entity list current. An aura that turns toward or attacks the fake produces hits against an entity the server never spawned.
checks.detects: Killaura that targets any visible entity regardless of legitimacy.
checks.variations: PeyangSuperbAntiCheat NPC.java does the same with a fake player placed 3 blocks in front of the suspect; CheaterDeleter PhaseBypassTracker watches spawn and teleport events to detect phase attempts around spawn; Shard's ViewTrackingObserver monitors which entities the client renders.

checks.name: NPC bait (PeyangSuperbAntiCheat)
checks.purpose: Spawn a fake player three blocks in front of the suspect and flag aura that hits it.
checks.how_it_works: spawn() builds an EntityPlayer NPC, positions it facing the suspect at 3 blocks distance, sends player-info and named-entity-spawn packets to the suspect and to staff, then hides the NPC from the suspect via Bukkit hidePlayer so only the aura's entity list sees it. The NPC is destroyed after a configured number of seconds; the teleport handler moves it around the player to catch aura that tracks it.
checks.detects: Killaura and hitboxes that attack an entity the real client cannot see.
checks.variations: Kauri FakeMob is the same bait pattern with a generic entity; network-dev-MinecraftAntiCheat NPC.java runs the same idea on a different base; Intave mirrors the spawn feed in module/tracker/entity/EntityTracker and emits EntitySpawnEvent records.

wiki_notes: Non-living spawn: VarInt id, type byte (1 boat, 2 item, 50 TNT, 60 arrow, 65 pearl, 78 armor stand), fixed-point pos x/32.
Yaw and pitch are byte angles value x360/256; velocity shorts value/8000 are present only when the data int is positive.
Trailing data int is type-specific: shooter entity id for projectiles, block id for falling blocks, facing for item frames.
