packets.name: Spawn Mob
packets.desc: Spawns a living entity (mob/animal/monster) with entity type, position, rotation, velocity, and metadata.
packets.notes: Entity types: 50=creeper, 51=skeleton, 52=spider, 53=giant, 54=zombie, 55=slime, 56=ghast, 57=zombiePigman, 58=enderman, 59=caveSpider, 60=silverfish, 61=blaze, 62=magmaCube, 63=enderDragon, 64=wither, 65=bats, 66=witch, 67=endermite, 68=guardian, 69=shulker, 90=pig, 91=sheep, 92=cow, 93=chicken, 94=squid, 95=wolf, 96=mooshroom, 97=snowman, 98=ocelot, 99=ironGolem, 100=horse, 101=rabbit, 120=villager.

writeup.p: The living-entity counterpart of S0E: mobs, animals and monsters spawn through S0F instead of S0E. EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket returns it for every EntityLivingBase; the payload carries the entity id, the EntityList type code (50=creeper up through 120=villager), fixed-point position (x32), yaw/pitch/head rotations (x256/360), velocity shorts (x8000) and a full DataWatcher block. The metadata is what renders health, potion effects and nametags without follow-up packets, which makes S0F one of the heaviest spawn packets on the wire.

handleSpawnMob creates the living entity through EntityList.createEntityByID, sets position and rotations, applies the velocity and reads the DataWatcher. Server side, EntityTrackerEntry deliberately suppresses the velocity-update packet on the spawn tick: the sendVelocityUpdates branch skips entities that just arrived via S0F because the spawn packet already carries the initial motion, avoiding a redundant S12 immediately after spawn.

No user-facing module in the 8 clients references S0F. Mob ESP, KillAura target lists and Tracers here iterate the loaded entity list each render frame rather than hooking spawn packets, so they consume the spawned EntityLivingBase objects after vanilla handling instead of the packet itself. The only non-vanilla client code is Rise's TranslationComponent (the PacketType enum's SPAWN_MOB entry decodes the fixed-point coordinates into the entity-position map used by the Translation bypass) and the NetworkAPI script registry listing the class.

The DataWatcher is the attack surface: a crafted metadata block can declare absurd health, invisible flags or armor values, and mob spawn floods are the classic lag vector. The type byte is unvalidated by the client, so a proxy-crafted id despawns the entity silently. For bypass engineering the interesting property is that S0F is the only clientbound packet that fully defines an entity's state at once, which is why the Translation component hooks it: rewriting the spawn position desyncs the client's rendering from the server's simulation without emitting a single movement packet.

implementation.overview: The spawn packet for every living mob, carrying a full DataWatcher. No module in the 8 clients hooks it: ESP and KillAura read the world entity list instead. The one piece of real client code is Rise's TranslationComponent, whose PacketType enum decodes S0F spawn coordinates into the position map that powers its spawn-repositioning bypass.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket returns new S0FPacketSpawnMob((EntityLivingBase) trackedEntity) for any tracked living entity, and the sendVelocityUpdates branch skips S12 on the same tick the mob spawns because the spawn packet already carries initial velocity. The packet constructor snapshots position, rotations, velocity and the full DataWatcher at tracking time. The client handler reverses this: create entity, set transform, apply motion, read metadata.
implementation.protocol_notes: Same fixed-point layout as S0E: VarInt entity id, unsigned byte type, three x32 ints, three rotation bytes, three x8000 velocity shorts, then the DataWatcher block which is mandatory for living entities and can run to dozens of bytes. Because the type id is the EntityList id and not the entity class, the client must have a matching entity registry or the spawn is dropped.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats use S0F as a state anchor: knockback checks know the mob's spawn velocity, and bot-detection heuristics on some servers correlate S0F rate with chunk activity. The Translation-style spawn repositioning is a rendering-layer desync, invisible to server-side movement checks but detectable by servers that verify client-reported entity positions. No reference client ships a module that abuses it; the corpus hit is purely the component infrastructure.

modules.name: PacketType / TranslationComponent (SPAWN_MOB)
modules.purpose: Decode S0F spawn coordinates and rotations into the entity-position map that the Translation bypass feeds on.
modules.how_it_works: PacketType is an enum registry consumed by TranslationComponent on every PacketReceiveEvent: the SPAWN_MOB entry casts to S0FPacketSpawnMob, converts x32 ints to doubles and x256/360 bytes to floats, and stores a Position in the entityPositions map keyed by entity id. Subsequent S14/S18 packets update the same map, and S13 removes entries.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent, consumed by the TranslationComponent in both Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Repositioning on spawn is a rendering desync, not a movement cheat: the server never sees it because no serverbound packet is involved. It only matters to servers that reconcile client-rendered entity positions, and it carries no flag risk for the player's own movement.
modules.variations: The PacketType enum is byte-identical in intent across 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; 6.2.4 also carries ENTITY_HEAD_LOOK. This is the only non-vanilla reference to S0F in the 8-client corpus.

implementation.general_hooks: No module-level hooks exist for S0F in the corpus; the only hook surface is Rise's TranslationComponent component consuming PacketReceiveEvent.
implementation.client_variations: All other clients touch S0F only through the bundled vanilla handler; Rise additionally exposes it in NetworkAPI's script packet list.

anticheat.overview: The living-entity spawn packet carries the full state of a mob: type, position, rotations, velocity and the DataWatcher. Anticheats consume it on the send side to learn entity ids and types before any reach or hitbox measurement: Photon caches the entity type per id, TruthfulAC snapshots the spawn box into its compensation history, and Grim replicates the entity into the simulation used by reach and knockback checks. The type byte matters because hitbox dimensions depend on it, and a spawn without a tracker entry would leave every later entity packet orphaned.

checks.name: Living-entity id lookup (Photon)
checks.purpose: Cache the entity type for every spawned living entity so later modules can resolve an entity id to its type without Bukkit lookups.
checks.how_it_works: LivingEntityIdLookup registers a PacketSendEvent listener for SPAWN_LIVING_ENTITY, wraps the packet as WrapperPlayServerSpawnLivingEntity and stores (entityId, entityType) in a Guava cache capped at one million entries with a five-second default expiry. A delayed task pre-warms the cache from all loaded worlds at startup, and getEntityType serves id-to-type lookups for modules that need hitbox or behavior data.
checks.detects: Nothing: it is a utility cache. Modules such as the DamageIndicator and information hider consume it.
checks.variations: Grim replicates the full entity with metadata and rotations; Artemis resolves spawn ids through its EntityType registry; intave keeps EntityTypeDataRegistry with per-type hitbox sizes.

checks.name: Spawn compensation (TruthfulAC)
checks.purpose: Snapshot every spawned entity's position and hitbox into the compensation history so reach checks can backtrack against it.
checks.how_it_works: TruthfulPacketListener routes SPAWN_ENTITY (the 1.19+ living spawn) into CompensationTracker.handleSpawn, which stores a CompensatedEntity keyed by id with a ring of up to 30 tick snapshots and a base reach taken from the entity type (3.0 for players, 1.5 boats, 4.5 shulkers). handleEntitySnapshot re-stamps live Bukkit entities each tick, and getEntityData serves the backtracking reach check with up to 8 ticks of history.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; it is the compensation data layer behind the reach and hitbox checks.
checks.variations: Grim replicates spawns into compensatedEntities; Hydro inserts a TrackedEntity; Tecnio and Artemis seed their reach trackers from the same packet family.

checks.name: Entity replication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Replicate every spawned entity, including mobs, into the compensated entity map so reach, hitbox and velocity checks see the client's view.
checks.how_it_works: PacketEntityReplication.onPacketSend wraps SPAWN_LIVING_ENTITY as WrapperPlayServerSpawnLivingEntity and calls addEntity with entity id, uuid, type, position, rotations and the full metadata. The replicated entity then receives S14 relative moves and S18 teleports exactly like the client's copy, and DESTROY_ENTITIES removes it after the transaction that delivers the packet. Spawn velocity from the packet feeds knockback compensation without a separate S12.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: it is the replication layer. Reach and velocity checks consume the map, and the firework-boost path even setbacks players who destroy a boosting firework entity early.
checks.variations: Shard adds living spawns to compensatedEntities; Hydro tracks them in its entityMap; Kauri routes SPAWN_LIVING_ENTITY through its PacketHandler into the world tracker.

wiki_notes: Living-entity spawn: VarInt id, unsigned-byte EntityList type (50 creeper through 120 villager), pos x/32, angles x360/256, vel /8000.
Carries a mandatory DataWatcher block rendering health, effects and nametags; tracker skips a duplicate S12 on the spawn tick.

packets.name: Spawn Painting
packets.desc: Spawns a painting entity with type, position, and facing direction.

writeup.p: The spawn packet for painting entities, and the only spawn packet that identifies its entity by a String art title instead of a numeric type code. The payload is entity id, the art name (Kebab, Alban, Aztec and friends), a BlockPos anchor and a direction byte (0=south, 1=west, 2=north, 3=east). EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket emits it for EntityPainting, and the client resolves the title through the EnumArt table, which fixes the artwork's pixel dimensions and therefore how much wall space the painting occupies.

handleSpawnPainting reads the title, position and direction, then constructs an EntityPainting at the anchor block with the facing applied. The client-side placement uses the EnumArt dimensions to compute the entity's bounding box against the wall; a title that does not map to a known art falls back to the default 16x16 Kebab art. Server side the packet is produced straight from the tracked EntityPainting.

None of the 8 reference clients reference S10 outside the bundled vanilla files and Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 NetworkAPI.java, which lists the class in the scripting registry. This is the honest, expected outcome: paintings are stationary cosmetic entities with no combat value, ESP implementations filter them from entity lists, and KillAura never targets them. In this corpus the packet is pure vanilla.

Minimal. The art-title String is a lookup key into a fixed EnumArt table, so a bogus title degrades to default art rather than crashing. The direction byte is used as an index into a facing array and is not range-checked by the vanilla handler, the only hardening gap of note. Realistically there is nothing here for either cheats or anti-cheats; the packet matters only for protocol completeness and for proxies that must re-serialize it verbatim.

implementation.overview: The spawn packet for paintings, identified by art title rather than type code. Zero module hits across the 8 clients: the only non-vanilla reference is Rise's NetworkAPI script registry. Documented honestly as a pure-vanilla packet whose only notable detail is the EnumArt dimension lookup and the unvalidated direction byte.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket returns new S10PacketSpawnPainting((EntityPainting) trackedEntity) when the tracked entity is a painting; the constructor snapshots the art title from the EntityPainting's EnumArt, the block position and the facing direction. The client handler creates the entity and places it against the wall using the EnumArt dimensions.
implementation.protocol_notes: VarInt entity id, then a length-prefixed String art title, then a BlockPos packed as a single long, then a direction byte. Direction semantics are reversed from the visual: 0 faces south, 1 west, 2 north, 3 east. The title string is not validated against EnumArt by the handler, so unknown art names silently fall back to the default painting.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing to flag: the packet is clientbound, cosmetic and server-authored. Anti-cheats and anti-exploit plugins ignore paintings entirely, and no reference client touches the packet. The only mitigation in the wider ecosystem is the generic entity-spawn rate cap that also covers painting floods used as a minor lag vector.
implementation.client_variations: Only Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 differ from vanilla, and only by listing S10PacketSpawnPainting.class in NetworkAPI's script packet registry; every other corpus reference is the bundled vanilla code.

anticheat.overview: The painting spawn packet has zero hits in the 50-anticheat corpus. Paintings are cosmetic stationary entities; the packet carries an art title, a BlockPos and a direction byte, and no anticheat references it. The only hardening gap of note, the unvalidated direction byte, is an exploit-surface footnote, not a detection surface.

wiki_notes: VarInt entityId, art-title string (Kebab, Alban, etc.), anchor BlockPos as long, direction byte 0 south 1 west 2 north 3 east.
Client resolves size from the EnumArt table; unknown titles fall back to default art instead of crashing.

packets.name: Spawn Experience Orb
packets.desc: Spawns an experience orb entity with position and XP value.

writeup.p: Spawns experience orbs: entity id, fixed-point position (x32) and a short XP value. The server splits orb value at 2000 when an XP source drops, so a large experience drop produces several S11 packets instead of one huge orb. EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket emits it for EntityXPOrb. The packet is frequent on farming servers and essentially free of state: no rotation, no velocity, no metadata.

handleSpawnExperienceOrb creates an EntityXPOrb, sets its position and assigns the xpValue. The client's XP bar is driven by pickup events and S06 health/xp updates, not by this packet, so S11 has no visible effect beyond the floating orb entity. Server side, orb value splitting happens at drop time, so the value in the packet is already the split value.

Exactly one module in the corpus references S11: Tenacity 6.0 AntiExploit, which rate-limits orb spawns as a crash-exploit guard (two S11 packets within 1 ms increments a violation counter that cancels the second packet). No AutoFarm or XP-tracker module exists in the 8 clients: XP collection modules iterate EntityXPOrb instances in the world entity list rather than hooking spawn packets, mirroring how ESP treats every other spawn packet.

The orb-flood: a hostile server or proxy streaming S11 at high rate creates hundreds of EntityXPOrb instances per second, each with its own render state, which is the classic XP-lag crash vector. Tenacity's 1 ms rate gate is the canonical mitigation. The xpValue short is unsigned server-side; values above 32767 wrap negative client-side, which makes the orb render but breaks pickup logic. Nothing here is flaggable by anti-cheats because the packet is clientbound and server-authored.

implementation.overview: Spawns experience orbs, one of the most frequent and least stateful clientbound packets. Only one corpus hit: Tenacity 6.0 AntiExploit rate-limits S11 as a crash-exploit guard. No XP tracker exists in the 8 clients because farming modules iterate EntityXPOrb instances in the world list instead of hooking spawn packets.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket returns new S11PacketSpawnExperienceOrb((EntityXPOrb) trackedEntity) for tracked XP orbs, snapshotting the orb's value. The server splits any XP drop exceeding 2000 into multiple orbs before they are tracked, so each S11 carries a value at or below the split cap. The client handler creates the orb and assigns the value with no validation.
implementation.protocol_notes: VarInt entity id, three x32 position ints, then a short XP value. No rotations, velocity or metadata fields. Because the value is a signed short, values in the 32768-65535 range arrive negative; the vanilla client does not guard against it. The packet is emitted in bursts when an XP source is destroyed, which is what makes it a flood-exploit vector.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats ignore S11 entirely: it is clientbound, cosmetic and cannot be influenced by the player. The relevant defense is client-side (Tenacity's rate gate) and server-side (spawn rate caps on XP sources). No bypass trade-off exists for this packet.

modules.name: AntiExploit
modules.purpose: Rate-limit XP orb spawns and other clientbound floods so a hostile server cannot lag or crash the client.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent handler tracks the timestamp of the last S11. If a new one arrives within 1 ms, invalidExperience increments and the packet is cancelled on the second violation with a chat warning; a gap longer than 1 ms resets the counter. The same handler sanitizes resource pack URIs, S43 camera teleports, S2A particle floods, S27 explosion strength and S18 teleport coordinates.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Client-side exploit hardening, not an anti-cheat bypass: cancelling S11 removes orbs from the renderer, which a server can observe as missing orb pickups only if it tracks them, which vanilla does not.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus touches S11. Tenacity's own PacketRate/anti-flood logic is folded into this single module.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the only hook surface in the corpus, used by Tenacity 6.0 AntiExploit.
implementation.client_variations: All clients except Tenacity 6.0 reference S11 only through bundled vanilla code; Rise additionally lists it in NetworkAPI's script packet registry.

anticheat.overview: The experience-orb spawn packet has zero hits in the 50-anticheat corpus: no anticheat references S11PacketSpawnExperienceOrb or its ProtocolLib name. The packet is clientbound, server-authored, and carries no player claim that a server-side check could validate. Anti-cheats ignore it entirely; the only defense that exists in the wider ecosystem is client-side rate limiting against server floods, which is outside the anticheat corpus.

wiki_notes: VarInt entityId, three fixed-point ints decoded x/32, then a short XP count; no rotation, velocity or metadata fields.
Server splits drops above 2000 XP into multiple orbs, so big rewards arrive as bursts; classic orb-flood lag vector.
