packets.name: Entity Velocity
packets.desc: Sets an entity's velocity (e.g., from knockback, explosion, piston push).
packets.notes: Velocities are encoded as (value * 8000). Real velocity = encoded / 8000.

writeup.p: The velocity/knockback packet: entity id plus three motion shorts at x8000. The server emits it in three situations: EntityTrackerEntry broadcasts when a tracked entity's motion changes beyond a threshold (sendVelocityUpdates with lastTrackedEntityMotionX/Y/Z), EntityPlayer.attackEntityFrom sends it to the damaged player with the knockback vector, and explosions apply their push through S27. handleEntityVelocity overwrites the target entity's motion directly, which makes this the single most important clientbound packet for anti-knockback work.

EntityTrackerEntry compares the tracked entity's current motion to the last tracked values each tick and sends S12 when the delta crosses the threshold; EntityPlayer.attackEntityFrom sends the knockback vector straight to the damaged player's connection. On the client, handleEntityVelocity sets motionX/Y/Z = value / 8000.0 with no interpolation and no validation, so the packet is a direct write into the physics state that every movement check in the tick loop reads.

The most-handled clientbound packet in the corpus after S08. Four families: (1) cancel-or-scale anti-knockback (Memeware, Nekoware, Spicy, Tenacity, Rise 5.99 Custom); (2) per-anticheat timing games that cancel selectively or replay the knockback the way the anticheat expects (Rise 5.99 Vulcan/Tick Cancel/Stack/Follow First Tick/Ground, Sigma AACPush/AACFlag, the Rise 6.x ten-mode Velocity suite); (3) movement modules that consume S12 as a boost trigger (Rise 6.x GrimFlight TNT, WatchdogLongJump, WatchdogFireball, MatrixFlight, MineLandFlight, WatchdogBowLongJump; Rise 5.99 Fly Minemenclub and LongJump Hycraft/Vulcan; Sigma Fly; Tenacity FlightModule); (4) infrastructure: Rise's PingSpoofComponent buffers S12 in the velocity class, EntityTickComponent and ItemDamageComponent observe it, and Timer/Breaker/HurtCamera cancel it as collateral. November Recode 2.0's VelocityModule adds REDUCE, REVERSE, CANCEL and the per-anticheat GRIM, VULCAN, WATCHDOG and WATCHDOG_SAFE modes, with GRIM buffering S32 transactions and VULCAN cancelling the C0F echo.

The server recomputes knockback from attack packets and expects the resulting motion to appear in the player's reported positions over the next ticks. Cancelling S12 desyncs those reports, which is exactly what velocity checks measure, so the arms race is about timing: Tick Cancel and Stack modes cancel the first N velocity packets and let one through to satisfy the check, Sigma's AACFlag injects a NaN position to blind the check, and WatchdogVelocity modes apply the knockback client-side exactly as the server computes it. The companion S27PacketExplosion carries its own knockback and must be handled separately, which is why every serious module pairs S12 and S27. Rise 5.99 even ships an anticheat-side velocity recorder in dev/rise/anticheat/data/PlayerData.java and a dcOnVeloCheck disconnect in AutoHypixel that reacts to velocity-based server checks.

implementation.overview: The knockback packet: three shorts at x8000 written directly into entity motion. The most-handled clientbound packet in the 8-client corpus, spanning cancel-or-scale anti-knockback (Memeware, Nekoware, Spicy, Tenacity, Rise 5.99), per-anticheat timing suites (Sigma AAC modes, Rise 5.99 modes, the Rise 6.x ten-mode Velocity module), movement modules that use S12 as a boost trigger (GrimFlight TNT, WatchdogLongJump, WatchdogFireball, Sigma Fly), and component infrastructure (PingSpoofComponent buffers it as the velocity class).
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry keeps lastTrackedEntityMotionX/Y/Z and sends S12 to tracked players when the entity's motion changes beyond a threshold (sendVelocityUpdates). EntityPlayer.attackEntityFrom sends S12 to the damaged player with the knockback vector from the attacker's motion. The client applies value / 8000.0 directly to motionX/Y/Z with no validation, so the packet is a trusted write into the physics state. Explosion knockback travels separately in S27 and is not covered by S12.
implementation.protocol_notes: VarInt entity id plus three shorts at x8000, no rotations, no metadata. Values are signed, so negative motion (pulled, pushed back) encodes naturally. The client divides by 8000.0 on apply; the short range limits motion to roughly -4.096 to 4.096 blocks/tick. Because the write is direct, packet order matters: an S12 arriving after the tick's movement code runs applies one tick late, which knockback-timing modules exploit.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Velocity checks reconcile the knockback vector with the player's reported position over the following ticks. Cancelling S12 is instantly measurable, so modern modes instead cancel selectively (first N packets, then pass one), reverse the vector (Sigma AACPush converts it into a strafe boost), or replay the exact server motion (WatchdogVelocity). Grim and Vulcan are sensitive to delayed application, which is why Rise 6.x splits the Velocity module into per-anticheat modes (GrimVelocity, VulcanVelocity, MMCVelocity, RedeskyVelocity, UniversoCraftVelocity, WatchdogPredictionVelocity) and why Rise 5.99's own anticheat records S12 in PlayerData.java for its checks.

modules.name: Velocity / AntiKnockback (cancel and scale)
modules.purpose: Remove or scale knockback by intercepting the S12 that targets the local player.
modules.how_it_works: A packet-receive handler checks the entity id; if it matches the player, the packet is cancelled outright (Memeware, Nekoware, Rise 5.99 at 0% settings) or its motion fields are scaled by horizontal/vertical percentages (Spicy, Tenacity). S27PacketExplosion is cancelled or scaled in the same handler because explosion knockback bypasses S12.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Outright cancellation is the fastest flag on any velocity-check anticheat; scaling to a nonzero percentage passes on servers that only check for complete absence of motion. Rise 5.99's Custom mode layers timer and attack-time scaling to blur the cancel.
modules.variations: Memeware and Nekoware are byte-for-byte the same cancel logic. Spicy scales via settings and cancels S27 always. Tenacity scales via NumberSettings and cancels both packets at 0%. Rise 5.99 adds modes (Reverse, Ground, Stack, Follow First Tick) on top of the same Custom scale. November Recode 2.0's VelocityModule is the same-role module with per-mode scaling (REDUCE, REVERSE) and anticheat-specific cancels (GRIM, VULCAN, WATCHDOG_SAFE).

modules.name: AntiVelocity (Sigma AAC modes)
modules.purpose: Defeat knockback with anticheat-specific tricks instead of a plain cancel.
modules.how_it_works: Basic mode scales or cancels S12 and cancels S27. AACPush samples the knockback vector, cancels the packet and turns the stored motion into a decaying strafe boost over 10 ticks. AACFlag cancels the packet and injects a C04 with NaN Y while the player is in hurt time, desyncing the anticheat's position model.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket (registerEvent with EventUpdate), pre stage for clientbound.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The AACFlag NaN-position injection is a hostile desync that several 1.8 anti-cheats mis-handle; it is also the most detectable pattern in the module when the server sanity-checks NaN coordinates. AACPush keeps motion nonzero, which defeats simple knockback-absence checks.
modules.variations: The module also guards Sigma's own BowFly: when Fly is in BowFly mode the S12 for the player is left intact so the bow-boost velocity is preserved.

modules.name: Velocity / Rise 6.x suite (per-anticheat modes)
modules.purpose: Per-anticheat anti-knockback: ten modes in the Velocity module, each tuned to a specific server anticheat.
modules.how_it_works: Each mode is a Mode subclass of the Velocity module handling PacketReceiveEvent: StandardVelocity scales/cancels and optionally copies the server's vertical motion into motionY; GrimVelocity, VulcanVelocity, MMCVelocity, RedeskyVelocity and UniversoCraftVelocity tune cancellation and replay timing per anticheat; WatchdogVelocity and WatchdogPredictionVelocity emulate the knockback the Watchdog check expects; BufferAbuseVelocity and LegitVelocity delay or minimize application. The onSwing gate skips handling unless the player is swinging, which hides the module's presence during combos.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent, PreMotionEvent, TeleportEvent; packet replaced via event.setPacket.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The suite's core trick is not cancelling but reshaping: rescale the packet and re-set it so the pipeline delivers a modified but present velocity, then let one tick of real knockback through. The commented-out Watchdog strafe logic in StandardVelocity shows the iteration history of the mode.
modules.variations: 6.2.4 adds WatchdogPredictionVelocity to the 6.1.30 lineup; the mode set otherwise matches (Grim, Legit, MMC, Redesky, Standard, UniversoCraft, Vulcan, Watchdog, BufferAbuse).

modules.name: Flight / LongJump (movement boost)
modules.purpose: Use the player's own S12 as a trigger or fuel for flight and longjump acceleration.
modules.how_it_works: Flight and longjump modes listen for S12 targeting the player and either flip a state flag that enables teleport-style flight (GrimFlight TNT), buffer the velocity for a follow-up boost (WatchdogLongJump, WatchdogFireball), or scale it into movement acceleration (Sigma Fly, Tenacity FlightModule). The packet is deliberately not cancelled, because the anti-cheat expects the knockback motion to exist.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: These modes are the flip side of anti-knockback: they need the S12 to arrive intact, so they must not conflict with the Velocity module, and they exploit the fact that the server cannot distinguish a knockback-boosted jump from a legitimate one when the packet was never tampered with.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 uses S12 in Fly Minemenclub and LongJump Hycraft/Vulcan; Rise 6.x spreads it across GrimFlight, MatrixFlight, MineLandFlight, WatchdogFlight, WatchdogJesus, WatchdogLongJump, WatchdogBowLongJump, WatchdogFireball, NCPSpeed and WatchdogSpeed; Sigma handles it inside Fly; Tenacity inside FlightModule.

modules.name: PingSpoofComponent (velocity buffer)
modules.purpose: Delay S12 alongside transactions and keepalives while ping spoofing, which delays knockback application as a side effect.
modules.how_it_works: The component classifies packets into tuples: S12 is grouped with S27 in the velocity tuple. While a spoof is active, matching packets are cancelled from the event stream and parked in a timestamped queue; onPostMotion flushes entries whose delay elapsed via PacketUtil.queue, which bypasses the event bus. The players tuple holds S13 and the S14/S18/S19/S20 entity stream so entity ordering survives the buffering.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Delayed S12 is safe against velocity checks that sample a single tick (the knockback still arrives), but dangerous against checks that measure the gap between the hit and the motion, which is why the component is paired with per-anticheat Velocity modes in the same client.
modules.variations: Identical component in 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; 6.2.4's PingSpoof and Timer modules both drive it via the static spoof() entry points.

modules.name: VelocityModule (per-anticheat modes)
modules.purpose: Per-mode anti-knockback: scale, reverse or cancel S12 for the local player, with anticheat-specific transaction handling for Grim and Vulcan.
modules.how_it_works: The packet listener ignores S12 whose entity id is not the local player, then switches on mode. REDUCE and REVERSE scale the motion fields in place with horizontal and vertical percentages and REVERSE negates the result; CANCEL, GRIM and VULCAN cancel the event; INTAVE and WATCHDOG are TODO stubs; WATCHDOG_SAFE cancels then re-applies only the vertical component to motionY while on the ground. GRIM mode additionally buffers S32 confirm-transaction actions and cancels the matching C0F echo on the send side; VULCAN cancels a single C0F echo after the first knockback.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: In-place scaling is the stealthiest path; outright cancel is the fastest flag on any velocity check. The GRIM transaction buffer exists because Grim correlates the S32/C0F gap with knockback, so the module hides both at once; the WATCHDOG_SAFE vertical re-apply keeps the server's expected motion curve while zeroing horizontal drift.
modules.variations: Memeware and Nekoware cancel with no modes; Rise 6.x splits per-anticheat handling across Mode subclasses of the Velocity module; November packs the modes into one class with transaction buffering built in.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is universal; the packet is re-set on the event in Rise (event.setPacket) and mutated or cancelled in place on classic event buses (Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy). Rise 6.x handles it through the component system and the Velocity module's Mode classes.
implementation.client_variations: Memeware/Nekoware cancel inside PacketInEvent; Spicy mutates the packet object and cancels the event; Tenacity cancels or scales via IEventListener; Rise 5.99 replaces the packet on the event; Rise 6.x re-sets it and additionally buffers it in PingSpoofComponent; Sigma mutates or cancels and injects C04 for the AACFlag mode. November Recode 2.0 cancels or mutates the packet inside EventPacket.In and additionally hooks C0F sends for the GRIM and VULCAN transaction games.

anticheat.overview: S12 is the server telling the client to apply a velocity vector, normally knockback, and every anticheat treats it as a promise: the client's next movement ticks must reflect the vector it was sent. The corpus splits into direct statistical checks (Azure VelocityA compares the vertical delta against the sent vector) and transaction-ordered simulation checks (Grim KnockbackHandler, Artemis VelocityPreProcessor, Frequency VelocityManager) that know exactly when the packet arrived at the client and require the knockback in the following prediction. This packet is the reason anti-knockback cheats cancel or alter S12 specifically.

checks.name: KnockbackHandler / AntiKB (Grim)
checks.purpose: Requires the client's simulated motion to include the exact knockback vector the server sent, flagging any reduction or delay.
checks.how_it_works: On the OUT side, wraps each entity-velocity packet for the player (or their vehicle) between two transaction packets, recording the vector with the first transaction id. As client transactions arrive, knockbacks move from a future queue into known-taken state; the prediction engine then compares the player's actual movement against the required knockback, accumulating a threshold-bounded buffer and triggering a setback above the immediate threshold.
checks.detects: Anti-knockback, velocity cancel and velocity reduction cheats, including selective cancels that take partial knockback.
checks.variations: Artemis VelocityPreProcessor applies the velocity in a transaction-confirmed pre action; Grim instead leaves it in a queue until the client's transactions prove arrival.

checks.name: VelocityA (Azure)
checks.purpose: Classic 1.8 statistical check: the reported upward move after a knockback packet must be at least 77 percent of the sent vertical velocity.
checks.how_it_works: Reads the OUT entity-velocity packet, keeps the vertical component (field c divided by 8000.0) when the entity id matches the player, and skips causes that do not produce knockback (starvation, fire, drowning, poison, wither, thorns, fall, lava). On the next upward move it compares deltaY to the recorded velocity and reports the taken percentage as a violation.
checks.detects: Anti-knockback that reduces or zeroes vertical velocity; the percentage reported makes the flag self-documenting.
checks.variations: Rammelkast VelocityCheck and MIU AntiVelocity use the same sent-vector-vs-delta comparison; Grim and Artemis add transaction ordering on top.

checks.name: VelocityManager feed (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Records every player-targeted S12 into a short-lived velocity window that all movement checks read for exemptions and baselines.
checks.how_it_works: The outgoing packet processor wraps each entity-velocity packet, and when the entity id is the player, pushes the vector into the VelocityManager. The manager keeps snapshots with horizontal and vertical magnitudes for two seconds, exposing max values that the speed and invalid checks add to their expected baselines, and the VELOCITY exemption type switches off checks while a recent velocity is active.
checks.detects: Anti-knockback cheats are detected by the speed and invalid checks because the expected velocity baseline is missing or reduced.
checks.variations: Azure VelocityA keeps a single vertical velocity scalar; Frequency keeps a time-windowed deque so exemptions decay naturally.

checks.name: VelocityPreProcessor (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Applies the S12 velocity to the movement holder only after the client confirms the packet, so prediction checks see it in the correct tick.
checks.how_it_works: Matches the OUT entity-velocity packet for the player's entity id, builds a Velocity object, and registers it in the connection's transaction confirmation. The pre action moves the current velocity into lastVelocity and installs the new vector as processed; the post action clears the processed flag when the transaction returns.
checks.detects: Velocity spoofing where a client applies knockback at the wrong time or not at all, which shows up as a prediction residual.
checks.variations: Grim queues knockbacks against transaction ids; Artemis installs them in a confirmation callback, which is the same ordering idea with different storage.

wiki_notes: PLAY id 0x12: VarInt entityId plus three signed shorts; real motion equals encoded value / 8000.0, clamped near +-3.9.
Handler writes motionX/Y/Z directly with no interpolation, so cancel-or-scale hooks are the standard anti-knockback point.

MCP 1.8.9 S12PacketEntityVelocity implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityVelocity; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readShort, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.? sends new S12PacketEntityVelocity (line 238) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Destroy Entities
packets.desc: Removes one or more entities from the client's render list.

fields.name: entityIDs
fields.desc: Array of entity IDs to destroy

packets.notes: This is how entities are removed when they die, despawn, or players disconnect.

writeup.p: The batch removal packet: a VarInt count followed by that many VarInt entity ids. The server flushes it from EntityPlayerMP.destroyEntitiesInWorld each tick with the accumulated destroy list, and sends the single-id form when a specific entity is removed (player disconnect, entity despawn). The client removes each id from the world's loaded entity list and clears the render manager's entry in handleDestroyEntities, which is how dead mobs, picked-up items and left players vanish.

EntityPlayerMP accumulates entity ids to destroy and sends one S13 per tick in destroyEntitiesInWorld; the single-id constructor is used by removeEntity and on player disconnects. NetHandlerPlayClient.handleDestroyEntities iterates the ids, removes each from world.loadedEntityList, clears the entity's render state and drops it from the client's entity lookup. Because removal is id-based and immediate, any client cache keyed by entity id must prune itself on S13 or it will hold stale entries.

Cleanup is the theme. Sigma 4.11 Ranking removes hit and prosecutor records for destroyed ids so a kill stat cannot fire after the target despawns. Rise's TranslationComponent maps S13 through the DESTROY_ENTITY entry of its PacketType enum, deleting the entity's position from the bypass map. Rise's PingSpoofComponent buffers S13 inside the players tuple so destruction stays ordered relative to held entity updates. KillAura and ESP target lists in these clients hold entity objects from the world list, so the vanilla removal handles them with no packet hook. November Recode 2.0's AntiBotModule watches S13 in WATCHDOG mode: when the destroyed ids include the bot it detected above the player, it prints a staff-removal notice and re-arms the spawn veto.

S13 is a pure removal vector: the server despawns arbitrary ids, and the client has no say in it. The abuse angle is timing: entities destroyed on the server remain attackable client-side only if the client delays the packet, which is exactly what buffering S13 in PingSpoofComponent does, keeping ghost entities alive for the spoof window. Anti-cheats watch for players attacking ids that were destroyed server-side (attack-after-desync), the signature of ghost-entity kill aura; a client that buffers S13 must also stop targeting those ids when the flush lands.

implementation.overview: The batch entity-removal packet. In the reference corpus its handlers are all cache pruning: Sigma's Ranking drops hit/prosecutor records, Rise's TranslationComponent removes map entries through DESTROY_ENTITY, and Rise's PingSpoofComponent buffers it with the entity stream so destruction stays ordered while ping spoofing. KillAura and ESP need no hook because their target lists are world-entity objects.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.destroyEntitiesInWorld collects pending entity ids and sends a single S13 per tick; the single-id form is sent by removeEntity and on player disconnects. The client handler iterates the ids, removes each entity from world.loadedEntityList, clears its render state and drops it from the entity lookup. No validation is applied to the id list, so ids that do not exist are ignored.
implementation.protocol_notes: VarInt count, then count VarInt entity ids. The count field makes the packet self-describing; 1.8 clients accept any count including 0. Entity ids are server-assigned and unique per world session, which is why id-keyed caches (Sigma's hit maps, Rise's translation map) can prune by id without ambiguity. The packet is emitted every tick the destroy list is non-empty, so it arrives in bursts.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: The packet itself is never flagged; its timing is. Attack-after-desync detection compares the ids a client attacks with the ids the server destroyed, so any buffering or replay of S13 that outlives the destroy is the detectable pattern. Ping-spoof buffering of S13 is safe only while the flush stays inside the anticheat's entity-desync tolerance, which is why Rise pairs the component with per-anticheat velocity and teleport handling.

modules.name: Ranking
modules.purpose: Track kills and deaths against named players and report stats, pruning records when targets despawn.
modules.how_it_works: Hidden module that records attacked players in hitEntities and suspects in prosecutorEntities via EventAttack, correlates S0B animation with S06 health drops and S02 chat messages to attribute kills, and on S13 iterates the destroyed ids through onEntityRemoved so a removed player's record cannot later fire a kill stat. S18 teleport and S08 respawn share the cleanup paths.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Stat tracking is invisible to anti-cheats. The S13 handling matters for correctness, not stealth: without it, a killed player's record would fire a duplicate kill when the death message arrives after the destroy packet.
modules.variations: Only Sigma 4.11 ships a module of this shape in the corpus; the sendStat() body is stubbed, so the tracking exists but the telemetry sink is disabled in this build.

modules.name: PingSpoofComponent (players buffer)
modules.purpose: Hold S13 in the entity-stream buffer while ping spoofing so destruction stays ordered relative to buffered entity updates.
modules.how_it_works: S13 is listed in the players tuple of the component's packet classification. While a spoof is active, matching packets are cancelled from the event stream and parked in a timestamped queue; onPostMotion flushes entries whose delay elapsed. Holding S13 alongside S14/S16/S15/S17/S18/S19/S20 keeps replay order coherent so a flushed destroy cannot land before the entity updates that precede it.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Buffered destruction keeps ghost entities alive client-side for the spoof window; modules that target entities must respect the flush or they attack ids the server already destroyed, which is the attack-after-desync flag.
modules.variations: Identical component in 6.1.30 and 6.2.4, driven by PingSpoof and Timer through the static spoof() entry points.

modules.name: PacketType / TranslationComponent (DESTROY_ENTITY)
modules.purpose: Remove destroyed entity ids from the entity-position map the Translation bypass maintains.
modules.how_it_works: The DESTROY_ENTITY entry of the PacketType enum casts to S13PacketDestroyEntities, iterates getEntityIDs() and removes each from the entityPositions map. The map is the single source of truth for the Translation component's entity tracking, so a missed removal would let the bypass interpolate a despawned entity.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent, consumed by TranslationComponent in both Rise versions.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Pure cache hygiene: without the removal the translation map leaks positions for despawned entities, which only corrupts the bypass's own rendering. No anti-cheat interaction beyond the general desync surface of the Translation feature.
modules.variations: Same enum in 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; the 6.2.4 build also carries ENTITY_HEAD_LOOK. This is the only non-vanilla entity-cache reference to S13 besides PingSpoofComponent in the corpus.

modules.name: AntiBotModule (WATCHDOG despawn watch)
modules.purpose: Confirm that a detected bot was destroyed server-side, so the module can re-arm the S0C spawn veto and warn that staff removed the entity.
modules.how_it_works: In WATCHDOG mode the packet listener iterates the destroyed entity ids of every S13. If one equals aboveEntityId (the bot the module detected above the player), it prints a removed-from-world notice and resets the tracker to -1, which re-arms the S0C branch of the same listener to flag the next spawn as a bot.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Pure read: the module never touches the packet. The desync risk of buffered S13 (Rise's PingSpoofComponent) does not apply here because November never delays the destroy.
modules.variations: Sigma's Ranking and Rise's TranslationComponent prune id-keyed caches on S13; November uses it as a state machine trigger instead of a cache cleanup.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on every corpus hit; the module-level hook appears in Sigma's Ranking (EventPacket) and November Recode 2.0's AntiBotModule (EventPacket.In), while Rise processes S13 through components (PingSpoofComponent, TranslationComponent).
implementation.client_variations: Sigma cancels nothing and only reads ids. Rise does not read the ids at all in PingSpoofComponent (the packet is buffered by class) and reads them only in TranslationComponent. Memeware, Nekoware, Spicy and Tenacity touch S13 solely through bundled vanilla code. November Recode 2.0 reads the destroyed ids inside AntiBotModule and uses them as a state trigger for its WATCHDOG bot logic.

anticheat.overview: The destroy packet removes entity ids from the client's world, and server-side anticheats mirror that removal in their entity trackers. Because reach and hitbox checks must never measure against an entity the client no longer sees, destroy handling is data hygiene: Kauri removes fake-mob state on the confirming keepalive, intave decodes the destroy payload across three protocol layouts, and Hydro deletes the tracked entity on the send side. The packet is never flagged; keeping the tracker in sync with it is what keeps entity checks honest.

checks.name: Destroy handling (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Remove fake-mob state for destroyed entities on the keepalive that confirms the destroy packet reached the client.
checks.how_it_works: PacketHandler routes DESTROY_ENTITIES (both modern and legacy wrappers) to EntityTrackHandler.onEntityDestroy, which schedules a keepalive action: for each destroyed id it calls removeFakeMob, despawning any fake mobs the anticheat placed next to the tracked entity and clearing the client-has-entity flag. Fake mobs are the anti-hitbox probes Kauri spawns around combat entities, so their lifecycle must mirror real despawns exactly or reach checks would measure against ghosts.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; the removal prevents ghost-entity false flags in the hitbox-based reach checks that use fake mobs.
checks.variations: Grim schedules entity removal on the destroy transaction and also clears serverPositionsMap and dashable and firework state; Tecnio and Hydro just remove the ids from their tracker maps; Artemis ReachPreProcessor drops the entity from reach tracking on the same packet.

checks.name: Destroy reader (intave)
checks.purpose: Decode the destroy payload across all protocol layouts and feed each entity id to the entity tracker.
checks.how_it_works: EntityDestroyReader implements EntityIterable over the destroy packet. It branches on protocol era: an int list on 1.17.1+, a single int on 1.17.0, and an int array on 1.16 and below, exposing both forEach and a substitution iterator so the tracker can read or rewrite ids. PacketReaders registers it under ENTITY_DESTROY, and EntityTracker.receiveEntityDestroy processes each id, dismounting riders and marking destroyed entities so AttackRaytrace can ignore them.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; the reader is the decode layer. The tracker's destroyed-entity marker (Entity.Destroyed) is what lets hitbox checks ignore dead entities.
checks.variations: Grim and Hydro wrap WrapperPlayServerDestroyEntities directly; FlopAC's WrappedOutEntityDestroy is the same idea on its tinyprotocol reflection layer.

checks.name: Destroy tracking (Hydro)
checks.purpose: Remove destroyed entities from the tracked-entity map so reach and entity queries never see despawned ids.
checks.how_it_works: EntityTracker.registerOutgoingPreHandler routes DESTROY_ENTITIES to handleDestroyEntities, which wraps WrapperPlayServerDestroyEntities and removes each id from the concurrent entityMap. Because insertion happens on spawn and removal on destroy, the map always mirrors the client's visible entity set; getDistanceToEntity and getClosestEntity simply cannot return a destroyed entity.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; it is the cleanup half of the tracker. Without it, reach checks would measure against entities the client no longer renders, producing false flags.
checks.variations: Tecnio removes ids from trackerMap on GPacketPlayServerEntityDestroy; Shard ejects riders before removing ids; Kauri defers cleanup to the confirming keepalive; TruthfulAC marks the entity destroyed with a grace window instead of deleting it outright.

wiki_notes: VarInt count followed by that many VarInt entity ids; server flushes the destroy list once per tick.
Id-keyed caches must prune on it; delaying it keeps ghost entities attackable, the attack-after-destroy flag pattern.

MCP 1.8.9 S13PacketDestroyEntities implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleDestroyEntities; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.onUpdate sends new S13PacketDestroyEntities (line 303): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Entity
packets.desc: Base class for entity relative movement and rotation updates. Subclasses S15 (rel move), S16 (look), S17 (move+look).

subclasses.name: S17PacketEntityLookMove
subclasses.desc: Both relative move and rotation update.

packets.notes: S14 is the abstract base — the actual packet IDs are 0x15 (S15), 0x16 (S16), 0x17 (S17). All share the same class hierarchy. The client adds the relative deltas to the entity's current server position to get the new position.

writeup.p: S14PacketEntity is the abstract base for the three relative entity-movement packets. The wire IDs are S15PacketEntityRelMove (0x15), S16PacketEntityLook (0x16) and S17PacketEntityLookMove (0x17); the base class itself is never registered as a sendable ID and EnumConnectionState registers only the subclasses. Every variant carries a VarInt entityId and an onGround flag, plus byte deltas (x 32) and/or rotation bytes (x 256/360). The client accumulates the deltas onto the entity's last server position, so a position error in one tick carries into every later tick until the server sends an absolute S18.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityMovement (Memeware 7.3 bundle, line 551) is shared by all three subclasses: it adds the packet's posX/posY/posZ to entity.serverPosX/Y/Z, recomputes the position as serverPos / 32.0, keeps the current yaw/pitch unless the packet carries rotation (S16/S17), then calls setPositionAndRotation2 with interpolation factor 3 and teleport flag false, and finally writes packetIn.onGround into entity.onGround. Server-side, EntityTrackerEntry picks the variant by motion magnitude: look-move when both position and rotation changed, rel-move when only position changed, look when only rotation changed (corpus lines 213-217, 265).

The 8-client corpus shows three consumer families, none of them ESP. Rise 6.x combat: LegitReach accumulates a server-truth realPosition from S14 deltas for its ping-spoof reach, and WatchdogVelocity buffers the S15/S16/S17 subclasses and replays them for its Watchdog Backtrack mode. Rise 6.x infrastructure: the translation component's PacketType enum maps ENTITY_REL_MOVE, ENTITY_LOOK_MOVE and ENTITY_LOOK into a per-entity position cache, and PingSpoofComponent classifies all S14 subclasses in its players tuple. Rise 5.99 anticheat: PlayerData re-derives position, deltas and onGround from S15/S17 and feeds KeepSprintA, SpeedA, EagleA and GroundSpoofA/B. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity reference the packet only through the vanilla handler. LiquidSense Dev consumes the stream for bot detection: AntiBot records per-entity ground/air/invaildGround flags from the S14 onGround bit, and its MixinNetHandlerPlayClient fires an EntityMovementEvent from handleEntityMovement for modules that react to entity movement. November Recode 2.0 has no S14 corpus hit; it processes the packet through the vanilla handler only.

Relative deltas are trusted per packet and corrected only by S18, which makes the S14 stream the raw material of every position-based client-side simulation: reach modules reconstruct the opponent's true position, anticheats reconstruct it to verify onGround transitions and speed. The onGround bit is authoritative for the tick it arrives in, which is exactly what GroundSpoofA/B and EagleA test. Reach exploits work through latency: LegitReach delays all player-class packets so the server keeps a stale player position while the client attacks from a closer interpolated one. Dropping or reordering S14 packets is invisible to the server because they are clientbound state announcements with no acknowledgement.

implementation.overview: The relative movement family (S15/S16/S17 under the S14 base) is the highest-frequency entity state in the play state. In the 8 clients it feeds three things: Rise 6.x reach and backtrack modules that rebuild a server-truth position, Rise 6.x packet-classification components, and the Rise 5.99 built-in anticheat that replays server-side style checks against the reconstructed position stream. LiquidSense Dev's AntiBot reads the same stream to classify bots by onGround transitions.
implementation.server_handling: The server never processes S14 on receive; it is purely clientbound. The client handler accumulates: entity.serverPosX += posX (and Y/Z), position = serverPos / 32.0, rotation kept unless S16/S17 carry bytes, then setPositionAndRotation2(..., 3, false) and entity.onGround = packet onGround. Because the accumulation never resets, any dropped packet permanently shifts the entity by its delta until an S18 arrives. EntityTrackerEntry emits S15/S16/S17 at the tracking update rate (every 2 ticks for players, more often for fast entities) and switches to S18 once the one-tick displacement exceeds the 4-block threshold.
implementation.protocol_notes: Deltas are signed bytes x 32, so a single packet moves an entity at most 3.97 blocks per axis; rotation bytes decode as yaw * 360 / 256. The onGround flag is present on the base class and therefore on all three subclasses. S16 (look) and S17 (look-move) are the only places the body yaw/pitch of a tracked entity changes; S19PacketEntityHeadLook separately updates only the head yaw. There is no ordering guarantee between S14 and S18 for the same entity; a teleport supersedes any pending deltas because it overwrites serverPosX/Y/Z.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Client-side anticheats (Rise 5.99) and server anticheats both treat the S14 stream as ground truth for movement verification. Ground-spoof detection keys on the onGround flag combined with block probes; eagle detection on the sneak flag in the S1C metadata stream timed against S14 ticks; keepsprint on the speed delta around S0B animations. For cheat clients, the S14 stream is what makes ping-spoof reach and backtrack possible: buffering it has zero server cost, and the server cannot distinguish a delayed entity stream from lag. The trade-off is visual, not statistical: held entity packets produce stutter and frozen-head artifacts that staff can spot.

modules.name: LegitReach
modules.purpose: Extend effective attack range by ping-spoofing the server's view of the player while the opponent's real position is tracked from the S14/S18 stream.
modules.how_it_works: On PostMotionEvent it picks the nearest target (TargetComponent.getTargets(9)). realPosition is seeded from the entity's client position and then maintained on PacketReceiveEvent: S14 deltas are added via getPosX() / 32D, S18 snaps it to absolute coordinates. When realDistance exceeds clientDistance and lands inside 2.3-5.9 blocks, it calls PingSpoofComponent.spoof(maxPingSpoof, true, true, true, true) so all incoming player-class packets are parked for up to the configured milliseconds; otherwise it disables and dispatches the component. Render3DEvent draws the real-location bounding box with eased animation.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The server never sees the S14 packets (clientbound), so the exploit is purely about the server's measured player position going stale. Servers that timestamp hits against the latest player position defeat it; Watchdog-style anticheats that confirm position before damage registration flag the hit timing.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the identical module (same package and class); the only difference is the corpus path (com/alan/clients/... without the Client-release2 prefix).

modules.name: WatchdogVelocity
modules.purpose: Velocity cancel combined with an entity backtrack: the S14 subclasses are held and replayed to keep the client and server entity timelines deliberately divergent.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, S12 velocity for self is cancelled (with a stacking option), C0F/C00 are held while active, and with Watchdog Backtrack enabled the three S14 subclasses plus S19PacketEntityHeadLook and S18PacketEntityTeleport are cancelled and queued. The queue is replayed through PacketUtil.receive after 100-250 ms, when the distance to the tracked realPosition crosses the 4.5/2.5 thresholds, when the player takes damage (hurtTime == 9), or during the first 100 ticks of a world. realPosition is accumulated from S14 and re-anchored by S18.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent, JumpEvent, PreUpdateEvent, StrafeEvent, PostStrafeEvent, Render3DEvent.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Buffering clientbound packets is invisible to the server, so the backtrack itself never flags. The velocity-cancel half is the detectable part: a missing motionY after a confirmed hurt status is the classic flag, which is why the module gates cancellation on offGroundTicks, water and scaffold state.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 does not reference the S14 subclasses in its WatchdogVelocity (the corpus hit is 6.2.4 only).

modules.name: KeepSprintA / GroundSpoofA (Rise anticheat)
modules.purpose: Client-side reproductions of server anticheat checks; the S14 stream is their movement clock and position source.
modules.how_it_works: PlayerData.handle converts S15/S17 deltas into per-tick position, deltas and onGround (block probes at y - 0.43 and y - 0.99). KeepSprintA times S0B arm swings against S14 ticks, samples horizontal speed into attackingSamples vs beforeAttackingSamples and fails when the attack-period average exceeds the baseline by more than 0.15 while on ground. GroundSpoofA/B and SpeedA consume the same reconstructed state. EagleA is documented under S1CPacketEntityMetadata because it needs the sneak flag from the metadata stream.
modules.vanilla_hook: Raw packet stream via PlayerData.handle (no event bus); S14, S18, S12, S0B.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: This is Rise's own anticheat for serverside-style protection of its users; the S14-derived position is rebuilt exactly as a server would, so the checks inherit the server's blind spots (they only see what the server sent, which is all the server knows).
modules.variations: SpeedA, EagleA and GroundSpoofA/B are separate checks over the same PlayerData; PacketUtil.isRelMove / isLookMove in dev/rise/anticheat/util/PacketUtil classify the subclasses.

modules.name: PacketType (translation component)
modules.purpose: Maintain a per-entity position cache that mirrors server state independently of the vanilla interpolation, fed by the S14 subclasses, S18, S19 and spawn packets.
modules.how_it_works: An enum of packet classes with a BiFunction per entry: ENTITY_REL_MOVE adds deltas to the cached Position, ENTITY_LOOK_MOVE and ENTITY_LOOK replace yaw/pitch (returning null when no entry exists), ENTITY_TELEPORT sets the entry to absolute coordinates, DESTROY_ENTITY removes it, and ENTITY_HEAD_LOOK writes the decoded head yaw into the yaw slot. Decoding is / 32.0 for position and * 360 / 256 for angles.
modules.vanilla_hook: Invoked from the translation component's packet receive path.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Pure client-side bookkeeping with no server interaction. The look-only handlers returning null for unknown entities means the cache silently drops rotations until a spawn packet seeds it, a quirk downstream aim code must tolerate.
modules.variations: Identical in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; the corpus path differs only by the Client-release2/Client/src/main/java prefix.

modules.name: AntiBot (movement tracking)
modules.purpose: Classify anti-cheat bots by their S14 movement stream: which entities ever touch ground, fly in air, or move while reporting onGround.
modules.how_it_works: onPacket fires for every S14PacketEntity: if the entity is a player, record the entity id in the ground/air lists by the onGround bit, and count in invaildGround every onGround packet where prevPosY != posY (halved on air packets). isBot() consumes the lists: groundValue flags entities never seen on ground, airValue flags never-seen-in-air, invaildGroundValue flags a count >= 10, plus the usual name/tab/derp checks.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketEvent (receive), UpdateEvent for the removal loop, AttackEvent for hit tracking.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The bot checks feed isBot(), which per the module description KillAura consults before targeting; the movement-derived heuristics (never grounded, invalid ground) are signature based and only as good as the S14 stream the server sends.
modules.variations: The invaildGround counter treats onGround with a y change as suspicious, a heuristic aimed at teleporting bots; no other corpus client derives bot state from S14.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent in Rise 6.x for modules; the Rise 5.99 anticheat receives every packet through PlayerData.handle instead of an event bus. LiquidSense Dev re-dispatches S14 as an EntityMovementEvent from its handleEntityMovement mixin on NetHandlerPlayClient; its AntiBot reads the raw packet on the client PacketEvent.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 anticheat decodes S14 via MCP-style accessors (func_149062_c, func_149060_h); Rise 6.x uses getPosX/getYaw accessors, and WatchdogVelocity switches on the packet class with Java 17 pattern matching while LegitReach and PacketType use instanceof chains. Deltas are consistently divided by 32.0 and angles multiplied by 360/256 across every client. November Recode 2.0 has no S14 corpus hit. LiquidSense Dev reads S14 in AntiBot and re-dispatches it as EntityMovementEvent from the NetHandlerPlayClient mixin.

anticheat.overview: Server-side anticheats never see S14 on the wire: it is a clientbound announcement of entity relative movement, rotation and ground state. What they do see is the same stream on the send side, and the richest anticheats use it to keep a lag-compensated copy of every tracked entity's position so reach, phase and velocity checks compare the player against where the server actually believes entities are. The corpus splits into position-replication trackers (Hydro, Kauri, AntiHaxerman), wrappers that classify the S14 subclasses into a packet pipeline (Frequency, Artemis, FlopAC), and reach checks that either consume the replicated positions or, in ThotPatrol's case, admit that rel-move plus AABB would beat their own Bukkit-based math.

checks.name: TrackedEntity (entity position replication)
checks.purpose: Rebuild other entities' positions from the S14 relative-move stream so reach and aim checks can query server-truth entity locations instead of trusting the player's rendered view.
checks.how_it_works: handleMovement(deltaX, deltaY, deltaZ) wraps the S14 byte deltas into an EntityMovement of type RELATIVE, marks the entity as awaiting confirmation, and applies the deltas to every TrackedPosition in the queue. handlePostFlying advances the queue when the player's next flying packet confirms the tick, and handlePostTransaction removes positions that the confirmed state has passed. Confirmed and pending positions are exposed separately (getX/getY/getZ versus getPendingPosition), so checks can evaluate both the server-known location and the one the client has just been told about.
checks.detects: Position desync between the server's entity stream and the client's render state, and provides the entity location used to verify reach against delayed or interpolated entity positions.
checks.variations: Hydro's EntityTracker drives this class from PacketSendEvent, applying the deltas inside the transaction tracker's confirm window. AntiHaxerman's EntityTracker accumulates the same deltas into serverPosX/Y/Z and divides by 32.0 on connection confirm; Kauri's EntityTrackHandler adds the deltas into an interpolating EntityLocation with transaction-anchored application.

checks.name: EntityTrackHandler (entity move tracking)
checks.purpose: Keep a server-side copy of every tracked entity's interpolated location from the S14 stream, and spawn fake mobs around a target to verify that the client's own entity tracking and aim match the server's.
checks.how_it_works: onRelPosition looks up the entity in the world tracker, skips non-allowed types, then adds the packet's x, y, z, yaw and pitch to the entity's new EntityLocation and sets the interpolation increment to 3. onFlying advances interpolation for every tracked entity whenever the player sends a flying packet. runAction delays the state change until a transaction confirms, or uses an instant action for the current combat target, timestamping entity updates against the player's connection. For a teleporting target it spawns three magma-cube fake mobs around the entity plus a slime on the player's aim ray, then moves them with the entity, so the client's hitbox testing can be verified server-side.
checks.detects: Killaura that attacks where the server holds no entity, hitbox spoofing, and clients whose entity tracking diverges from the sent stream.
checks.variations: The same handler applies S18 teleports through onTeleportSent and S20 attributes through updateAttributes; WPacketPlayOutEntity is Kauri's internal wrapper for the S14 subclasses. Hydro and AntiHaxerman cover the same tracking duty with simpler, non-interpolating position queues.

checks.name: ReachD (reach against player positions)
checks.purpose: Classic 1.8 reach check; the corpus hit is the author's own TODO comment stating that tracking PacketPlayOutRelEntityMove and testing the AABB would be far more accurate than the Bukkit-position math the check actually uses.
checks.how_it_works: On PacketAttackEvent the check measures the distance between attacker and victim eye locations, subtracts the vertical difference and a fixed 0.32 hitbox accommodation, and compares the result against maxReach. The threshold is inflated by ground state, yaw difference, recent horizontal speed (tracked on PlayerMoveEvent), the average ping of both players, TPS and the attacker's speed potion level. Three consecutive exceedances log a cheat.
checks.detects: Blatant reach abuse against players, with tolerance for lag, elevation and speed.
checks.variations: The commented TODO names the S14-based approach (accumulating rel-move deltas and testing the entity AABB) as the accurate alternative; the modern trackers in this corpus (Hydro TrackedEntity, Kauri EntityTrackHandler, AntiHaxerman EntityTracker) implement exactly that approach and feed it into their own reach checks.

checks.name: NetworkFilter (entity packet admission control)
checks.purpose: Whitelist the packet classes AntiHaxerman's trackers may consume, including the three S14 subclasses, so entity replication only runs for state that actually reaches the client.
checks.how_it_works: The constructor registers GPacketPlayServerEntity and its Look, RelEntityMove and RelEntityMoveLook inner classes, plus entity teleport, spawn, destroy, velocity, attributes and the movement/transaction set. isAllowed is the gate every later pipeline stage checks before processing a packet.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; it is admission control for the tracker pipeline that feeds reach, velocity and position checks.
checks.variations: Artemis reaches the same packet family through GPacketPlayServerEntity, Frequency through WrappedPacketPlayOutEntity, and FlopAC through its tinyprotocol NMSObject/Packet layer; all three appear in the corpus for the same reason.

checks.name: WrappedPacketPlayOutEntity (S14 wrapper)
checks.purpose: Minimal 1.8 wrapper exposing the S14 base packet to Frequency's outgoing packet pipeline.
checks.how_it_works: The class extends PacketWrapper over PacketPlayOutEntity, giving the processor layer a typed handle for entity move packets. The identical file ships in the FrequencyPlus fork and in Degrade, which is a Frequency derivative.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; infrastructure for the processor pipeline that classifies entity packets.
checks.variations: FrequencyPlus (MinecraftUserHAN1110) and Degrade (splatboydev) carry byte-identical copies of the file. AutoEye's PacketPlayOutEntity wrapper and FlopAC's tinyprotocol layer serve the same role on their own bases.

wiki_notes: Yaw and pitch in the rotation updates are new absolute angles, not deltas, and for entities with separately rotating heads the yaw sets body rotation while head facing uses the head rotation packet.

MCP 1.8.9 S14PacketEntity implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityMovement; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBoolean, readByte, readVarIntFromBuffer.
1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.? sends new S14PacketEntity (line 205): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Entity Teleport
packets.desc: Teleports an entity to an absolute position (fixed-point int × 32) and rotation.

fields.name: onGround
fields.desc: Whether the entity is on ground

packets.notes: Unlike S14 (Entity Relative Move), S18 sets ABSOLUTE position — the entity moves to this exact location regardless of where it was. Used when players teleport (ender pearls, chorus fruit), mobs teleport (endermen), or when S14 cumulative errors need correction.

writeup.p: S18PacketEntityTeleport carries an absolute fixed-point position (ints x 32), rotation bytes and an onGround flag for one entity. It is the only entity-position packet with full coordinates, so it is both the correction mechanism for accumulated S14 error and the transport for genuine jumps: ender pearls, endermen, dimension changes and anything that moves more than 4 blocks in one tick. EntityTrackerEntry constructs it when the tracked entity's one-tick displacement exceeds the relative-move threshold (corpus line 222), and NetHandlerPlayServer sends it to a player on teleport (line 259).

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityTeleport (Memeware 7.3 bundle, line 511) overwrites serverPosX/Y/Z with the absolute values, computes position as serverPos / 32.0 with y + 0.015625 (half a block in fixed point, the eye-height accommodation), decodes yaw/pitch as * 360 / 256, and calls setPositionAndRotation2 with interpolation 3 and the teleport flag. If the entity is already within 0.03125 blocks (x/z) and 0.015625 (y) of the target it keeps the current position and applies only rotation, which prevents micro-jitter on repeated teleports.

Five distinct consumers in the corpus. Rise 6.x: LegitReach snaps its realPosition to the absolute coordinates, WatchdogVelocity includes S18 in its spoof packet set and re-anchors on it, and PingSpoofComponent classifies it in the players tuple so teleports are delayed with the rest of the entity stream. Rise 5.99: PlayerData re-anchors serverPosX/Y/Z and zeroes ticksSinceLastTeleport so checks skip the teleport tick. Sigma 4.11: Ranking treats S18 as an entity-removal signal that finalizes kill/death records. Tenacity 6.0: AntiExploit cancels S18 with any coordinate beyond 30,000,000. Spicy: NoClip and Phase import the class but never branch on it, a leftover from their Sigma 2 lineage.

S18 is clientbound and absolute, so the abuse direction is server to client: a malicious server can emit fixed-point coordinates that corrupt client-side position bookkeeping or trigger bounds bugs, which is exactly what Tenacity's AntiExploit threshold mitigates. For cheats, S18 is the epoch boundary of every position-based state machine: accumulated S14 error resets here, so reach and backtrack modules must re-anchor their reconstructed positions on it. The S08PacketPlayerPosLook + S18 pair is the server's complete teleport vocabulary, and disablers and reach modules watch both because a missed teleport poisons every later delta.

implementation.overview: The absolute teleport packet is the reset point of entity position state. Cheat clients re-anchor their reconstructed position caches on it (LegitReach, WatchdogVelocity, Rise 5.99 anticheat), Sigma uses it as an entity-left signal, Tenacity hardens against server-side coordinate abuse, and Spicy's movement modules carry it as a dead import.
implementation.server_handling: The server side only emits S18, never validates it on receive. EntityTrackerEntry chooses it when the tracked entity moved 4+ blocks in a tick, and NetHandlerPlayServer sends it to a player being teleported. The client handler overwrites the entity's serverPosX/Y/Z, applies the +0.015625 y offset, keeps the current position when the entity is already within a 32nd of a block (rotation-only update), then interpolates with the teleport flag set. Because the client trusts the coordinates, a server can move an entity anywhere in the fixed-point range, which is the abuse AntiExploit guards against.
implementation.protocol_notes: Three ints (x 32), two bytes (x 256/360) and a boolean follow the VarInt entityId. The y offset of 0.015625 (0.5 / 32) is applied only on the client and is not part of the wire value. S18 supersedes any pending S14 deltas for the same entity because it overwrites the accumulated serverPosX/Y/Z. The packet is also sent to a player on respawn and dimension change, which is why Ranking's S08 + S18 combination distinguishes death from mere teleport.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Server anticheats emit S18 as a correction and watch whether the client's later C03 positions rejoin the corrected location; a client that ignores the teleport or desyncs after it flags as position desync. The S08+S18 pair is the standard disabler/reach watch point: modules that delay clientbound traffic must flush on it or their position cache goes permanently stale. The client-side mirror (Rise 5.99 PlayerData) uses ticksSinceLastTeleport to suppress checks for a tick, an acknowledgment that even legitimate teleports produce movement anomalies.

modules.name: LegitReach
modules.purpose: Re-anchor the tracked target's server-truth position on the absolute teleport so the ping-spoof reach window keeps measuring the real distance.
modules.how_it_works: In the same PacketReceiveEvent handler that accumulates S14 deltas, an S18 for the tracked target replaces realPosition with new Vec3(getX() / 32D, getY() / 32D, getZ() / 32D). Without this branch, a teleported target would leave the accumulated position permanently wrong and the reach window would either never open or stay open against a ghost position.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Re-anchoring is a correctness requirement, not an exploit: a stale realPosition makes the module either inert or visibly wrong. The reach abuse itself lives in the ping-spoof half, not in the S18 handling.
modules.variations: Identical module in Rise 6.1.30 (path without the Client-release2 prefix).

modules.name: Ranking
modules.purpose: Track kills and deaths for the client's stats system; an S18 teleport for a tracked player finalizes the pending record because a teleporting opponent is out of reach context.
modules.how_it_works: A hidden, always-on module registered for EventAttack, EventPacket and EventUpdate. On EventAttack it records HitEntity entries per player; S0B animations timestamp attacker candidates; on S18 it calls onEntityRemoved(entityId), which flips the HitEntity to removed and reports killed() or prosecuted() if a chat message already matched the name in the last 3 seconds. S08PacketPlayerPosLook resets all prosecutor records (death/respawn), S13 destroys remove entities, S40 with 'ban' in the text reports a ban stat.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Passive telemetry collection; the S18 branch is just an entity-lifetime heuristic. No packet is mutated or replayed, so there is no detection surface.
modules.variations: The sendStat methods are stubs in the shipped source; the kill/death reporting path is a framework for a stats backend that was never filled in.

modules.name: NoClip / Phase
modules.purpose: Corpus hit is an import only: both movement modules import S18PacketEntityTeleport but never branch on it.
modules.how_it_works: NoClip's onEvent sends C03PacketPlayer.C04PacketPlayerPosition through sendPacketNoEvent when collided horizontally, then teleports the local player by 3 blocks up to break free; Phase cancels block hitboxes (EventGetBlockHitbox) and nudges the player position in a 3-stage loop while sending C03PacketPlayer(true). NoClip's header comment credits Sigma 2's Phase as the source, which explains the vestigial S18 import in both files.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The movement abuse is in the C03 stream, which is what anti-cheats flag (vertical motion while inside blocks). The unused S18 import has no effect on detection.
modules.variations: Phase.java (Spicy) carries the same dead import and additionally imports EventSendPacket; its hitbox-cancel approach is the more aggressive variant.

modules.name: AntiExploit
modules.purpose: Harden the client against server-side crash and grief exploits; the S18 branch blocks teleport coordinates beyond the world border.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, an S18 with any |getX()/getY()/getZ()| above 30,000,000 is cancelled and logged as 'Blocked Exploit: Teleport'. The same handler validates S48 resource pack URIs (http/https/level only, no path traversal), blocks S43 camera outside spectator, rejects particle floods, rate-limits S27 explosions and S11 experience orbs to 1 per millisecond, and caps total incoming packets at 100/second.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling clientbound packets is invisible to the server and cannot be flagged. The 30,000,000 bound matches the vanilla world border at which the server itself clamps movement.
modules.variations: Tenacity 6.0 is the only one of the 8 clients with a crash-exploit hardening module touching S18.

modules.name: WatchdogVelocity
modules.purpose: Include the teleport in the backtrack packet set and use it to re-anchor the tracked target's realPosition.
modules.how_it_works: isSpoof2Packet returns true for S18PacketEntityTeleport, so it is cancelled and queued with the S14 subclasses and S19 head look while the backtrack is active, and replayed through PacketUtil.receive on the flush conditions. Separately, an S18 for the target re-anchors realPosition to the absolute coordinates, keeping the distance gating (4.5/2.5 block thresholds) honest across teleports.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Holding a teleport client-side only delays the visual snap; the server state is unaffected. Flushing on hurtTime == 9 keeps the replay aligned with the player's damage timeline.
modules.variations: Not present in Rise 6.1.30's WatchdogVelocity corpus hit.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent across all consumers; the Rise 5.99 anticheat consumes S18 inside PlayerData.handle.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.x uses getX()/getY()/getZ() double accessors and divides by 32.0; Rise 5.99 and Sigma use the MCP-style func_149449_d/func_149451_c accessors; Tenacity reads getX() directly on the fixed-point ints (no /32), which is fine for the magnitude check. Only Rise 5.99 tracks ticksSinceLastTeleport as state.

anticheat.overview: S18 is the clientbound absolute-position correction for one entity, and server anticheats consume it on the send side as the reset point of entity state. Trackers re-anchor their replicated entity positions on it (Hydro, AntiHaxerman), teleport processors re-sync the player's own movement state when the teleport targets the checked player (Artemis, Frequency, BetterAnticheat), and the same packet is what makes reach verification and phase checks trust the server's entity locations. Because the packet is clientbound, no anticheat validates its contents; they only timestamp and consume it.

checks.name: EntityTracker (teleport re-anchoring)
checks.purpose: Re-anchor the replicated position of a tracked entity when the server sends its absolute teleport, so reach checks keep measuring against the corrected location.
checks.how_it_works: handleEntityTeleport wraps the ENTITY_TELEPORT packet in WrapperPlayServerEntityTeleport, looks up the entity, and applies handleTeleport(x, y, z) inside the transaction tracker's confirm-pre window, with confirm-post advancing all entity queues. The same tracker handles spawn, relative moves and destroy packets, so the entity map mirrors the full server-side entity stream.
checks.detects: Entity position desync after teleports; provides the corrected entity location used by Hydro's reach and combat checks.
checks.variations: AntiHaxerman's EntityTracker sets the absolute coordinates the same way but keeps the vanilla epsilon check (0.03125 for x/z, 0.015625 for y) so micro-teleports keep the old position. Kauri's EntityTrackHandler interpolates the new absolute location with increment 3 instead of snapping.

checks.name: TeleportPreProcessor (self entity teleport)
checks.purpose: Treat an S18 targeting the checked player as a movement reset: rebuild the player's movement, location and rotation from the teleport coordinates on transaction confirm.
checks.how_it_works: The processor matches GPacketPlayServerEntityTeleport, ignores it unless the entity id equals the player's own id, then schedules a transaction-confirmed action. The pre phase stores the last entity teleport, copies the current velocity into lastVelocity, rebuilds PlayerMovement and PlayerRotation from the teleport values, and sets processedEntityTeleport true; the post phase clears the flag.
checks.detects: Position desync caused by the server teleporting the player; the processedEntityTeleport flag lets downstream checks skip the teleport tick.
checks.variations: Frequency's OutgoingPacketProcessor calls the action manager's onTeleport() for a self S18 without rebuilding movement state; BetterAnticheat's TeleportTracker queues the teleport and matches it against the player's next flying packet, flagging missed teleports.

checks.name: OutgoingPacketProcessor (self teleport action)
checks.purpose: Detect when the server teleports the checked player and reset the action manager state so movement checks exempt the teleport tick.
checks.how_it_works: On PacketPlayOutEntityTeleport the processor wraps the packet, and when the entity id matches the player it calls playerData.getActionManager().onTeleport(). The same processor feeds S12 velocity into the velocity manager for the self entity, and treats PacketPlayOutPosition as a teleport too.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself; it feeds the action manager that movement checks consult to exempt legitimate teleports.
checks.variations: Identical copies ship in FrequencyPlus and Degrade. Artemis rebuilds full movement state for the same event; Frequency only resets the action flag.

checks.name: EntityTracker (absolute teleport snap)
checks.purpose: Snap a tracked entity's replicated position to the S18 absolute coordinates so reach and hitbox checks use the corrected server location.
checks.how_it_works: On GPacketPlayServerEntityTeleport the tracker overwrites serverPosX/Y/Z with the absolute fixed-point values and computes the new position by dividing by 32.0, but only if at least one axis differs by more than the vanilla epsilon (0.03125 for x/z, 0.015625 for y); otherwise the current position is kept. The update runs inside a connection-confirm action, so it applies at the player's confirmed tick.
checks.detects: Entity position desync after teleports; the epsilon branch mirrors the vanilla client's micro-jitter suppression on repeated teleports.
checks.variations: Hydro's EntityTracker snaps unconditionally; Kauri interpolates to the new location over three ticks. Both share the transaction-anchored application model.

checks.name: TeleportTracker (teleport confirmation)
checks.purpose: Queue every teleport sent to the player, including S18 self teleports, and verify that the player's next flying packet rejoins the teleported position, rotation and ground state.
checks.how_it_works: handlePacketPlaySend wraps ENTITY_TELEPORT for the player's own entity id into a Teleport record (position, rotation, relative flags, onGround) and adds it to eligibleTeleports when the confirmation begins. On each flying packet, match() compares onGround, then the absolute or relative position coordinate by coordinate, then rotation; a teleport still eligible at tick end sets missedTeleport. The strictness depends on whether the player sent a position in the previous tick (2.0E-4 leniency when not).
checks.detects: Teleport desync, clients that ignore or delay server teleports, and position spoofing that fails to rejoin the teleported location.
checks.variations: Artemis and Frequency reset movement state on self teleports without verifying the rejoining position; BetterAnticheat's ArtificialPositionCheck consumes the missedTeleport signal to flag impossible position jumps.

wiki_notes: The server sends this absolute-position correction when an entity moves far enough that relative deltas cannot represent it, documented in the current protocol as moves of more than 8 blocks.

MCP 1.8.9 S18PacketEntityTeleport implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityTeleport; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBoolean, readByte, readInt, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.? sends new S18PacketEntityTeleport (line 221) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Entity Head Look
packets.desc: Updates an entity's head yaw rotation independently of body rotation.
packets.notes: Head yaw is separate from body yaw — entities can look in a different direction than they're moving. Used by Backtrack modules to track the full entity rotation, and by ESP modules for accurate head-position aim prediction.

writeup.p: S19PacketEntityHeadLook updates only the head yaw of an entity, independent of the body yaw carried by S16/S17. The wire format is a VarInt entityId plus one byte decoded as yaw * 360 / 256. The server sends it whenever the head rotation changes: EntityTrackerEntry broadcasts it to tracked players (corpus line 236, sendPacketToTrackedPlayers(new S19PacketEntityHeadLook(trackedEntity, (byte) l))) while body rotation travels in the S14 family. It is the only rotation packet keyed to the head rather than the body.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityHeadLook (Memeware 7.3 bundle, line 573) resolves the entity and calls setRotationYawHead(yaw * 360 / 256.0F). Only yaw is transmitted; the head pitch is derived from the body pitch at render time, and the model's head mesh rotates around the neck joint using this value. The body rotation is untouched, which is why a player can look sideways while running straight.

None of the 8 clients has an ESP, Tracers or KillAura module that reads S19. The corpus consumers are all Rise 6.x infrastructure and one velocity module: WatchdogVelocity includes S19 in the spoof packet set so a held head-look update completes the backtrack illusion, PingSpoofComponent classifies it in the players tuple (delayed with the S14 family and S18), the translation PacketType maps ENTITY_HEAD_LOOK into the position cache, and NetworkAPI whitelists it for scripts in both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4. Renderers skip it because aim indicators are derived from body yaw/pitch in S16/S17; head yaw only affects the model mesh.

The packet is cosmetic clientbound state with no serverbound counterpart and no server-side validation, so there is no direct abuse. The interesting quirk is in the translation cache: ENTITY_HEAD_LOOK writes the decoded head yaw into the Position.yaw slot while keeping pitch, so the cached orientation becomes the head yaw until the next S16/S17 overwrites it. Any aim or rotation math fed from that cache inherits the error. Backtrack modules that hold S19 along with the movement set produce the visible frozen-head artifact, which is a staff-visible tell rather than a detection risk.

implementation.overview: The head-look packet is the least-touched entity packet in the corpus: no renderer or aim module in the 8 clients reads it. It survives only in Rise 6.x packet-classification components (PingSpoofComponent, translation PacketType) and WatchdogVelocity's backtrack set, plus the script API whitelist.
implementation.server_handling: Clientbound only. The server emits it from EntityTrackerEntry when the tracked entity's head yaw changes, and the client applies it as setRotationYawHead with the * 360 / 256 decode. There is no rate limit or validation; a server can spam it harmlessly. The client-side consequence is limited to the model's head rotation and any module that consumes rotation state.
implementation.protocol_notes: Single byte angle, decode yaw * 360 / 256.0F. Body yaw lives in S16/S17; head yaw lives here; the two can differ by up to 180 degrees for a player looking over the shoulder. S19 arrives at the same tracking cadence as the S14 family and typically interleaves with it. The translation cache's ENTITY_HEAD_LOOK handler overwrites the yaw slot, so cached positions diverge from vanilla rotation semantics until the next look packet.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No server anticheat consumes head yaw; killaura rotation-sync detection works on the serverbound C05/C06 look packets, not on this clientbound announcement. For cheat clients the only relevance is fidelity: backtrack and reach modules that reconstruct entity state must either include S19 in the held set (WatchdogVelocity) or accept that the reconstructed orientation drifts. There is no flag surface, only visual artifacts.

modules.name: WatchdogVelocity
modules.purpose: Hold S19PacketEntityHeadLook with the S14 movement subclasses and S18 so the backtracked target's full state, including head rotation, replays coherently.
modules.how_it_works: isSpoof2Packet returns true for S19PacketEntityHeadLook, so while the backtrack is active the packet is cancelled in PacketReceiveEvent and queued, then replayed through PacketUtil.receive on the flush conditions (elapsed 100-250 ms, distance threshold crossing, hurtTime == 9, world age under 100 ticks).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Clientbound buffering is invisible server-side. The delayed head-look replay is exactly what produces the frozen-head visual when the target's head snaps late.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 has no WatchdogVelocity hit for S19; the packet reaches 6.1.30 only through the components and NetworkAPI.

modules.name: PingSpoofComponent
modules.purpose: Classify S19PacketEntityHeadLook as player traffic so it is parked with the rest of the entity stream while ping spoofing is active.
modules.how_it_works: The players tuple lists S19PacketEntityHeadLook next to the S14 subclasses, S18PacketEntityTeleport, S20PacketEntityProperties and S13PacketDestroyEntities. While the component is enabled, every packet whose class matches an enabled tuple is cancelled on send/receive and parked as a TimedPacket, then flushed via PacketUtil.queue on PostMotion when the delay elapses or on world change.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Delaying clientbound state is not detectable from the packet stream. The side effect is the same stutter that any ping spoof produces on the entity render.
modules.variations: Identical tuple in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; the 6.2.4 corpus path carries the Client-release2 prefix.

modules.name: PacketType (translation component)
modules.purpose: Write the decoded head yaw into the per-entity position cache used by the translation system.
modules.how_it_works: ENTITY_HEAD_LOOK decodes headYaw as getYaw() * 360 / 256.0F, looks up the entity's cached Position and stores new Position(posX, posY, posZ, headYaw, currentPitch). It returns null when no entry exists, so head-look updates for entities that never spawned through the cache (no S0F/S0C seen) are silently dropped.
modules.vanilla_hook: Invoked from the translation component's packet receive path.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No server interaction. The yaw-slot overwrite is a fidelity bug relative to vanilla (head yaw and body yaw are separate there), and downstream consumers inherit it until the next look packet.
modules.variations: Identical in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent in Rise 6.x; no other client in the corpus registers any hook for S19PacketEntityHeadLook.
implementation.client_variations: The packet appears in Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity only via the vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient handler; the entire non-vanilla surface is Rise 6.x components and the script API NetworkAPI whitelist.

anticheat.overview: No server anticheat consumes the head-look packet: it carries only the head yaw byte, which plays no role in movement or combat verification. The corpus shows exactly two kinds of references: Artemis's packet-abstraction layer wraps the packet for its pipeline, and the NPC test rigs (PeyangSuperbAntiCheat, MinecraftAntiCheat) emit head rotations for fake players used to bait killaura. The packet is cosmetic clientbound state with no flag surface.

checks.name: GPacketPlayServerEntityHeadRotation (packet wrapper)
checks.purpose: Register the head-rotation packet in Artemis's packet abstraction layer so the pipeline can classify it; the read buffer is empty.
checks.how_it_works: The class is annotated with @PacketLink(PacketPlayServerEntityHeadRotation.class) and extends GPacket, binding the wrapper to the packet name; read() does nothing because no Artemis stage consumes the fields.
checks.detects: Nothing; structural registration only.
checks.variations: The same pattern appears for every play-state server packet in Artemis (entity, entity teleport, entity status, entity metadata).

checks.name: NPC head rotation (killaura test rig)
checks.purpose: Emit head-rotation packets for fake players so NPC bait looks alive while testing whether a player's aim tracks them.
checks.how_it_works: PeyangSuperbAntiCheat's NPCTeleport drives a fake EntityPlayer in a circle around the suspect (aura bot mode) or a panic radius (aura panic mode), sending PacketPlayOutEntityTeleport every tick plus PacketPlayOutEntityHeadRotation with the head yaw derived from the player's own head rotation. MinecraftAntiCheat's NPC utility sends the head-rotation packet through rotateHead alongside a look packet for any staff-created fake player.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself; the head rotation is part of the NPC bait that killaura checks observe from the attack side.
checks.variations: MinecraftAntiCheat builds the packet with raw field reflection (fields a and b) and always pairs it with PacketPlayOutEntityLook; PSAC computes the head yaw from the suspect's own rotation to make the NPC look at the target.

wiki_notes: While the entity is stationary the body also rotates toward the head direction after a delay without changing the entity yaw value, and the body rotates back toward yaw once the entity starts moving.
While the entity is moving, head rotation is clamped to a maximum distance from body rotation, and for remote players the server keeps updating head rotation alongside body yaw.

packets.name: Entity Status
packets.desc: Sends a status event for an entity (death sound, hurt effect, taming, wolf shaking, etc.).
packets.notes: Status codes: 2=hurt, 3=death, 6=taming, 7=tamed, 8=shaking, 9=hearts, 10=wolfSmoke, 11=accept, 12=witherSpawn, 15=redstoneTorches, 16=ironGolem, 17=sheepEat, 18=trueGod, 19=endermanScream, 20=zombieVillagerCure, 21=guardianElder, 22=petWolf, 23=zombieVillagerReplacing, 24=arrowCount, 25=particles, 26=thorns, 27=snowParticles, 28=shulkerTeleport, 29=ironGolemGiveRose.

writeup.p: S19PacketEntityStatus carries a single opcode byte for one entity: the client-bound event channel for hurt (2), death (3), wolf taming, hearts, wither spawn and a dozen more codes. The server broadcasts it through WorldServer.setEntityState, which routes to the entity tracker (corpus line 880), and EntityPlayerMP sends code 9 to the player itself (line 893). For a cheat client the only actionable signal is the hurt/death transition of the local player, which is why the sole module consumer is a velocity module.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityStatus (Memeware 7.3 bundle, line 897) special-cases opcode 21 (guardian sound) and otherwise forwards the code to entity.handleHealthUpdate, which plays the hurt/death sounds, wolf effects, totem-like particles and so on.
