The handler is a pure dispatch table: no state is stored, no position is involved.

The corpus has exactly one module consumer: Rise 6.x GrimVelocity, in both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4, which uses opcode 2 (hurt) on the local player as the precondition for cancelling the following S12 velocity. Rise's NetworkAPI whitelists the packet for scripts in both versions. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity reference it only through the vanilla handler. The thinness is structural: the packet has no position or rotation data, so movement, render and combat modules have nothing to consume; only the hurt-to-knockback contract matters.

The S19(2) then S12 pairing is the knockback contract: the server announces damage, then the velocity that results from it. Cancelling S12 after seeing the hurt status is the classic velocity bypass, and GrimVelocity hardens it by sending a C07 dig packet at the player's own position on the next PreUpdate, so the server observes a legitimate block interaction on the damaged tick instead of a missing motion change. Anticheats that detect velocity cancel measure the absent motionY after a confirmed hurt status; the dig packet is the counter because it gives the server an acceptable action to attach the tick to.

implementation.overview: The status opcode channel is nearly invisible to the 8 clients: one module, GrimVelocity in Rise 6.x, uses opcode 2 as the trigger for a velocity bypass, and the script API whitelists it. Everything else in the corpus is the vanilla dispatch handler.
implementation.server_handling: Clientbound only. WorldServer.setEntityState broadcasts the opcode through the entity tracker to every tracking player; EntityPlayerMP sends code 9 (the eating effect) to the player directly. The client dispatch is entity.handleHealthUpdate with a special case for 21. There is no per-player state kept on either side; the packet is a one-shot event.
implementation.protocol_notes: VarInt entityId plus one unsigned byte opcode. The opcode set is defined by Entity.handleHealthUpdate: 2 = hurt, 3 = death, 6 = taming, 7 = tamed, 8 = wolf shaking, 9 = eating, 10 = wolf smoke, 11 = accept, 12 = wither spawn, 15 = redstone torches, 16 = iron golem, 17 = sheep eating, 19 = enderman scream, 20 = zombie villager cure, 21 = guardian elder, 22 = pet wolf, 24 = arrow count, 26 = thorns, 27 = snow particles, 28 = shulker teleport, 29 = iron golem rose. The opcode for the local player arrives on the same connection as the S12 that follows.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Velocity detection is the only anticheat interaction: the hurt status confirms damage, and the subsequent S12 must produce the expected motion change. Cancelling S12 without a substitute is the classic flag; GrimVelocity's substitute is the C07 dig at the player's own position, which the server processes as a normal block interaction. Server anticheats cannot see the client's S19 handling at all, so the entire exploit surface is the S12 side of the pairing.

modules.name: GrimVelocity
modules.purpose: Grim-targeted velocity bypass: cancel the knockback S12 after confirming the hurt status, then emit a benign C07 dig so the damaged tick still carries a legitimate server action.
modules.how_it_works: A VERY_LOW priority PacketReceiveEvent handler checks S19PacketEntityStatus first: when the entity is the local player and the opcode is 2, it sets realVelocity. The next S12PacketEntityVelocity for the local player is then cancelled, realVelocity clears and velocity is set. On the following PreUpdateEvent, if velocity is set, it sends C07PacketPlayerDigging (START_DESTROY_BLOCK while looking at a block and swinging, otherwise STOP_DESTROY_BLOCK) at the player's own position and clears the flag.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The hurt-status gate prevents cancelling velocities that never arrived. The C07 dig at the player's own feet is a no-op block action that still registers server-side, giving the anticheat a legitimate interaction instead of a bare missing knockback.
modules.variations: Identical in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 (same package com/alan/clients/module/impl/combat/velocity).

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent in Rise 6.x; no other hook exists in the corpus.
implementation.client_variations: Only Rise 6.x touches the packet outside vanilla. The 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 GrimVelocity files are identical apart from the corpus path prefix.

anticheat.overview: The status opcode channel has no server-side check surface: the only corpus references are Artemis's packet wrapper and MinecraftAntiCheat's NPC utility, which emits status packets to animate fake players. The opcode byte matters to clients (hurt, death, taming), but anticheats never branch on it. This is one of the thinnest packets in the entity family.

checks.name: GPacketPlayServerEntityStatus (packet wrapper)
checks.purpose: Wrap the entity status packet in Artemis's packet layer; the wrapper reads the entity id and the opcode byte.
checks.how_it_works: The class binds to PacketPlayServerEntityStatus via @PacketLink, reads entityId as an int and logicOpcode as a byte from the buffer, and stores them as fields for any consumer.
checks.detects: Nothing; the fields are exposed but no Artemis check reads them.
checks.variations: The wrapper mirrors the generic GPacket pattern; the head-rotation wrapper in the same package carries an empty read.

checks.name: NPC status emission (fake player lifecycle)
checks.purpose: Send entity status packets for fake players so they show hurt and death effects like real players during staff testing.
checks.how_it_works: setStatus(byte) builds a PacketPlayOutEntityStatus, sets the entity id and status fields by reflection, and sends it; the NPCStatus enum wraps the opcode ids. The packet is only ever emitted for NPCs created by the anticheat's staff tools.
checks.detects: Nothing; the emission exists so NPCs behave like players for testing killaura and reach checks.
checks.variations: PeyangSuperbAntiCheat does not send status packets for its NPCs; it animates them with teleport and head-rotation packets instead.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x19: int entityId plus one opcode byte handled by Entity.handleHealthUpdate.
Opcode 2 is hurt and 3 is death; others cover taming, wolves, wither spawn and particles.
One-shot event with no ack; hurt status arrives just before S12 velocity on damage.
MCP 1.8.9 S19PacketEntityStatus implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityStatus; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readInt.

1.8.9 callers: CommandGameRule.func_175773_a sends new S19PacketEntityStatus (line 83) +2 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/command/CommandGameRule.java

packets.name: Entity Attach
packets.desc: Attaches an entity to another (player on horse, animal on leash, leach knot).

fields.name: vehicleId
fields.desc: Entity ID of the vehicle (-1 for detach)

writeup.p: S1BPacketEntityAttach is the mount and leash state channel. Opcode 0 attaches an entity to a vehicle (vehicleId -1 detaches), opcode 1 manages leash knots. The corpus server senders: EntityTrackerEntry broadcasts (0, trackedEntity, ridingEntity) when a tracked entity enters range and on mount changes (lines 166, 387), EntityPlayerMP sends (0, self, ridingEntity) when the player mounts (line 630), and EntityLiving broadcasts (1, self, leashedToEntity) on leash attach and detach (lines 991, 1016). The wire format is three ints: leash code, entityId and vehicleId.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityAttach (Memeware 7.3 bundle, line 852) resolves both entities and branches on the code. For code 0 it clears the boat empty flag for the local player, shows the 'mount.onboard' sneak hint when the player mounts a vehicle, and calls mountEntity(vehicle). For code 1 it calls setLeashedToEntity or clearLeashed on the living entity. The handler is a pure state mirror: the client applies whatever the server announces.

Zero module hits in the 8-client corpus. The only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x NetworkAPI, the script packet whitelist, in both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4; no module in any client branches on S1B. The structural reason: attach state is fully client-rendered and server-authoritative, and the movement exploits that involve vehicles (boat fly, entity control) act on the serverbound side, on C03 positions sent while riding and on local rider physics, not on this clientbound announcement. There is nothing to gain by intercepting a state change the client must apply verbatim.

The packet is a clientbound state mirror with no acknowledgement, so the abuse direction is server to client: a malicious server can spam attach packets to desync mount state or flip the client's ridingEntity, which corrupts the movement code path (client movement while riding uses the vehicle's physics). Anti-cheats flag vehicle abuse on the serverbound side: impossible vertical C03 deltas while the player's ridingEntity is set server-side. No cheat in the corpus interacts with this packet, and none needs to.

implementation.overview: The mount/leash packet is the one clientbound entity packet with no module consumers in the 8 clients: the only non-vanilla reference is the Rise 6.x script API whitelist. Vehicle movement exploits live entirely on the serverbound C03 side, so this announcement is left to vanilla.
implementation.server_handling: Clientbound only. The server emits it from EntityTrackerEntry on tracking start and mount/leash changes, from EntityPlayerMP when the player mounts, and from EntityLiving on leash transitions. The client applies mountEntity or setLeashedToEntity/clearLeashed and shows the onboarding hint for the local player. No validation, no rate limit, no serverbound counterpart.
implementation.protocol_notes: Three ints: code (0 = riding, 1 = leash), entityId, vehicleId (-1 or null entity for detach/clear). The boat empty flag is a client-side convenience derived from the local player's mount state, not part of the wire format. The packet is sent once per state transition, not continuously; movement while riding travels through the S14/S18 stream of the vehicle entity.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anticheat inspects S1B because it is clientbound. Vehicle exploits are detected from the serverbound stream: boat fly produces C03 deltas inconsistent with the mounted entity's physics, and entity-control exploits abuse C09 slot changes. The packet matters to anti-cheat designers only as the trigger for the server-side riding state that those checks key on.
implementation.general_hooks: None in the corpus. Rise 6.x scripts can receive it via the NetworkAPI whitelist (com/alan/clients/script/api/NetworkAPI.java, both versions), but no shipped module registers a handler.
implementation.client_variations: Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity appear only through the vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient handler; Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 through the script API whitelist. The vanilla handler is identical across all eight bundles.

anticheat.overview: S1B is clientbound mount and leash state, and the corpus shows three real consumers: Grim converts the 1.8 attach into its 1.9+ mount format inside PacketEntityReplication, Artemis folds the player's attach into the prediction vehicle under a transaction confirmation, and Intave registers an AttachEntityReader plus an entity-tracker hook. The remaining hits are noise: NCP's attach terms are listener and block-attachment bookkeeping, Argus's CheckAttachedModules is its own client-module report channel, and Negativity, FlopAC and Artemis contribute constants and wrappers. The flagging side of vehicle exploits stays on the inbound C03 stream; these checks exist to keep the simulated vehicle state honest.

checks.name: Attach replication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Mirror the server's mount state into the compensated entity tracker so movement and vehicle checks know what the player and tracked entities are riding.
checks.how_it_works: PacketEntityReplication parses WrapperPlayServerAttachEntity on the ATTACH_ENTITY send, ignores it on 1.9+ servers (replaced by SET_PASSENGERS), and for non-leash attaches converts the 1.8 format into handleMountVehicle: vehicleId -1 dismounts using the stored legacyPointEightMountedUpon, otherwise the mount pair is recorded. An attach naming an untracked entity logs a warning because the client itself would ignore it. SetbackTeleportUtil sends the matching detach during teleport setbacks so a player cannot re-enter a vehicle to keep a cheat active.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: state replication. It removes mount-state desync as a variable when movement checks evaluate vehicle motion, and the setback-time detach closes the vehicle-reentry bypass during lag-backs.
checks.variations: Grim SetbackTeleportUtil (line 246) emits the detach itself on the 1.8 wire path during setbacks. No other anticheat mirrors attach state into a simulation.

checks.name: Vehicle prediction sync (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Apply the player's attach and detach to the prediction engine under a transaction confirmation so movement emulation knows when the player rides a vehicle.
checks.how_it_works: MiscellaneousPreProcessor matches GPacketPlayServerEntityAttach: when the attach targets the player's own entity id, it registers a confirmFunctionAndTick on the TRANSACTION confirmation; at pre() the prediction vehicle is set from the vehicle id through NMS, and a null vehicle triggers resetMotion so the emulator stops attributing vehicle physics to the player.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: state sync. It feeds EmulatorPreProcessor's vehicle-aware movement simulation, which is what keeps vehicle-related motion flags accurate.
checks.variations: Kauri PacketHandler (line 431) wraps the same packet on the send side. Intave tracks attach state through EntityTracker.sendAttachEntityPacket (line 120) in addition to its reader. FlopAC's WrappedOutAttachEntity and Artemis's own GPacketPlayServerEntityAttach are wrappers; Negativity's ATTACH_ENTITY constant is a registration.

checks.name: Attach reader (Intave)
checks.purpose: Expose the attach packet's two int fields (entity id, vehicle id) to the substitution pipeline so entity filters can rewrite or drop attach packets.
checks.how_it_works: AttachEntityReader extends AbstractPacketReader and implements EntityIterable: entityId() and vehicleId() read the two ints, and the SubstitutionIterator allows filters to write either field back into the packet (slot 1 rewrites the entity id, slot 2 the vehicle id). It is registered in PacketReaders as ATTACH_ENTITY.
checks.detects: Nothing directly: a packet reader. It is the intake point for Intave's entity substitution and filtering, which feed the entity tracker that movement checks consult.
checks.variations: Intave's EntityTracker also subscribes to the attach packet directly, and firework-rocket attach tracking in MovementMetadata is a separate 1.9+ mechanism. NCP's attach corpus hits are logger and listener bookkeeping, and Argus's CheckAttachedModules is its own client-module report channel; neither reads S1B.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x1B: int entityId, int vehicleEntityId, unsigned byte leash flag.
Leash byte 0 means riding and 1 means leash; vehicle -1 or null detaches.
Sent once per mount or leash change; movement while riding uses vehicle packets.

MCP 1.8.9 S1BPacketEntityAttach implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityAttach; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readInt, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: EntityLiving.clearLeashed sends new S1BPacketEntityAttach (line 1179) +2 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityLiving.java

packets.name: Entity Metadata
packets.desc: Updates an entity's DataWatcher metadata (health, skin, flags, name, etc.).
packets.notes: S1C carries changed or new DataWatcher entries for an entity. Metadata indexes: 0=flags (onFire/sneaking/riding/sprinting/flying), 1=airTicks, 2=nameTag, 3=nameVisible, 6=health (for living), 15/variant, 16/color (for horses), etc.

writeup.p: S1CPacketEntityMetadata carries DataWatcher updates for one entity: a list of WatchableObject entries, or the full watcher dump on spawn. EntityTrackerEntry sends the full watcher with the metadata flag true when a player enters tracking range (corpus line 360) and incremental changed entries otherwise (line 303). The client merges them into the entity's DataWatcher. Relevant indexes: 0 is the byte flags (sneaking, sprinting, invisible, riding), 2 the name tag, 3 name visibility, 6 health for living entities. The sneak flag (bit 1, byte value 2) is the one the corpus actually reads.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityMetadata (Memeware 7.3 bundle, line 468) resolves the entity, guards against a null list and calls entity.getDataWatcher().updateWatchedObjectsFromList(list). The DataWatcher then notifies the renderer and any systems watching specific indexes. The same list rides inside S0CPacketSpawnPlayer and S0FPacketSpawnMob for the initial state.

The canonical ESP/AntiInvis reads (invisibility flag, name-tag index) do not appear in the 8 clients; their renderers read entity fields after the vanilla handler applies S1C. The real hits: Rise 5.99 EagleA reads the sneak byte from the WatchableObjects, the only genuine module consumer; Sigma 4.11 AutoPot and InventoryManager import the class but never process it, polling isPotionActive and inventoryContainer on EventUpdate instead, so both imports are dead code; Rise 6.x PingSpoofComponent classifies S1C in its regular tuple, delayed with C0F and C00 during spoof, and NetworkAPI whitelists it for scripts.

Metadata is read-only intelligence: 1.8.9 has no serverbound metadata packet, so the stream is the only place the server's view of entity state leaks back to the client. That makes it the natural feed for anti-invis and name-tag modules, and its absence in these 8 clients is a design choice, not a protocol limitation. The sneak flag is the load-bearing bit for anticheats: eagle checks (Rise 5.99) read it against the S14 ground state, and any client that spoofs sneak serverbound via C0B must keep the server-visible flag consistent or the mismatch is a flag.

implementation.overview: The metadata stream is the server's mirror of entity state, but only one module in the corpus genuinely reads it: Rise 5.99's EagleA, which checks the sneak flag byte. Sigma's AutoPot and InventoryManager carry dead imports, and Rise 6.x classifies the packet for ping-spoof delay and scripts.
implementation.server_handling: Clientbound only. EntityTrackerEntry sends the full DataWatcher on tracking start and incremental entries on change; the client merges them via updateWatchedObjectsFromList. Index 0 byte flags encode sneaking (bit 1), sprinting (bit 3), invisible (bit 5) and riding (bit 6). No validation is applied to incoming values, so a malicious server can inject arbitrary metadata, which is why clients that care about server-side state reads (name tags, invisibility) consume it defensively.
implementation.protocol_notes: The packet carries a VarInt entityId followed by the DataWatcher serialization: repeated (index byte, type byte, value) triples terminated by 127, with an empty list meaning no changes. A full dump is flagged server-side by the boolean constructor argument (true on tracking start). Sneak is bit 1 of the flags byte, which decodes to exactly 2 when it is the only set bit, matching EagleA's equality check. Metadata changes do not touch position or rotation, so the packet interleaves freely with the S14/S18 stream.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: The sneak flag is the anticheat-relevant field: eagle and shift-tap checks correlate the flag with S14 ground transitions, and the Rise 5.99 EagleA check flags a sneak byte that appears within two ticks of walking off a ledge. Server anticheats compare the sneak flag against serverbound C0B sneak actions; a client whose metadata-visible sneak disagrees with its C0B stream leaks the discrepancy. Everything else in the packet (name tags, health) is cosmetic to anticheats.

modules.name: EagleA
modules.purpose: Detect eagle (auto-sneak at block edges) by reading the sneak flag byte out of the tracked player's metadata stream.
modules.how_it_works: On S14 relative moves it sets shouldEagle when the packet's onGround flag is true and the block below the reconstructed position is air, then counts ticks. On S1CPacketEntityMetadata for the tracked player it scans the WatchableObjects for a Byte whose value is exactly 2 (the sneak bit alone), and if shouldEagle is set with ticks <= 2 it increases the buffer and fails past 10; otherwise the buffer decays by 5.
modules.vanilla_hook: Raw packet stream via PlayerData.handle (S14 and S1C).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: This is Rise's own client-side anticheat check. The equality check (byte == 2) only fires when sneak is the sole flag set, which misses combos (sneak + invisible), a blind spot of the shipped check.
modules.variations: EagleA is the only check in the Rise 5.99 anticheat that consumes S1C; the S14 branch it shares with KeepSprintA, SpeedA and GroundSpoofA/B is documented under S14PacketEntity.

modules.name: AutoPot / InventoryManager
modules.purpose: Corpus hit is an import only: both modules import S1CPacketEntityMetadata but no shipped handler branches on it.
modules.how_it_works: AutoPot registers only EventUpdate and decides when to drink from mc.thePlayer.isPotionActive and getHealth, then pots by swapping, sending C05 look and C08 placement. InventoryManager likewise registers only EventUpdate and manages inventoryContainer slots. The metadata import is a development leftover from an earlier design that read potion or armor state from the watcher stream; the shipped logic polls local state instead, which is equivalent because the vanilla handler already applied S1C to the entity.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventUpdate only; the S1C import is unused.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Dead imports have no detection surface. The honest takeaway is that Sigma's potion logic trusts local entity state, which the server already keeps consistent via S1C.
modules.variations: InventoryManager (info/sigmaclient/module/impl/player/InventoryManager.java, 498 lines) carries the same dead import and the same EventUpdate-only design; AutoArmor in the same client shares the pattern.

implementation.general_hooks: Rise 5.99 anticheat consumes S1C through PlayerData.handle; Rise 6.x components hook it via the packet event system for classification.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 reads the WatchableObjects list via func_149376_c and iterates raw objects; Rise 6.x never reads fields, only classifies the packet class. Sigma's modules import the class without using it, which the corpus confirms by the absence of any EventPacket registration for S1C.

anticheat.overview: The metadata packet is the server's mirror of entity state, and anticheats read it for two reasons: to keep the player's own simulation state honest (sneak, gliding, pose, sleeping) and to hide or rewrite health information so clients cannot exploit it. The corpus splits into self-metadata listeners (Grim PacketSelfMetadataListener, intave MetadataTracker), a health rewrite check (Kauri HealthSpoof, disabled), Photon's damage-hiding module, and wrapper layers (FlopAC). The sneak and health indexes are the only fields any check actually touches.

checks.name: HealthSpoof (health metadata rewrite)
checks.purpose: Rewrite the health metadata entry (index 6, float) to 1.0 for other entities so clients cannot read real health values; the shipped check is disabled and the handler is commented out.
checks.how_it_works: The commented @Bind handler intercepts WrapperPlayServerEntityMetadata, skips the viewer's own entity, copies the metadata list, and replaces any float entry at index 6 with 1.0f, then sends the rewritten packet silently. With the block disabled the check registers nothing.
checks.detects: Would prevent health-reading and health-based combat modules that rely on the client-visible metadata health; in the shipped source it is dead code.
checks.variations: Photon's DamageIndicator implements the same idea live, rewriting health to 0.5 for entities other than the viewer, and additionally rewrites the generic.maxHealth attribute in S20. No other anticheat in the corpus rewrites metadata health.

checks.name: PacketSelfMetadataListener (self metadata into simulation)
checks.purpose: Read metadata sent to the checked player and fold flags, pose, gravity, frozen and use-item state into the prediction simulation, timestamped by transaction.
checks.how_it_works: On ENTITY_METADATA for the player's own entity id, the listener strips the pose entry on 1.14+ clients, reads the flags byte for gliding, swimming and sprinting bits, the gravity boolean, powder-snow frozen ticks, bed position and the use-item/riptide byte, and applies each via latencyUtils real-time tasks anchored to the last transaction. The strip of pose metadata keeps old clients from receiving state that would desync their movement model.
checks.detects: Pose and state desync that would otherwise poison movement prediction; also protects the simulation from metadata the client version cannot represent.
checks.variations: intave's MetadataTracker covers the same ground for bed position, gliding and pose with a packet-tick feedback wrapper; Grim's EntityMetadataPoseUtil resolves the pose metadata index per entity type.

checks.name: MetadataTracker (sleep, gliding, pose state)
checks.purpose: Extract sleeping bed position, gliding flag and pose from the self entity's metadata so the movement simulation knows the player's physical state.
checks.how_it_works: The tracker subscribes to the ENTITY_METADATA packet, reads the bed position entry, the gliding bit of the flags byte and the pose entry (1.14+), and applies them through user.packetTickFeedback. A bed position re-anchors the player's position to the bed coordinates, which is the only legitimate teleport-free position reset in the protocol.
checks.detects: Simulation divergence caused by stale sleep, gliding or pose state; the extracted state feeds the physics search that flags movement impossibilities.
checks.variations: Grim's PacketSelfMetadataListener applies the same fields with transaction-anchored tasks. The EntityMetadataReader class in the corpus is the reader this tracker drives.

checks.name: DamageIndicator (health metadata hiding)
checks.purpose: Spoof the health metadata of entities other than the viewer so clients cannot learn real health from the metadata stream.
checks.how_it_works: The module subscribes to ENTITY_METADATA and UPDATE_ATTRIBUTES. On metadata it rewrites any float entry at the version-specific health index to 0.5, skipping the viewer's own entity and dead entities; on attributes it rewrites generic.maxHealth to 1.0 and clears its modifiers. Entity types are filtered by config (players versus others), with ender dragon and wither exempt.
checks.detects: Prevents health-reading combat aids and health-based decision making in killaura modules.
checks.variations: Kauri's HealthSpoof is the same idea but disabled; the S20 half of this module (max-health rewrite) is noted under S20PacketEntityProperties.

checks.name: WrappedOutEntityMetadata (metadata wrapper)
checks.purpose: Tinyprotocol wrapper exposing the entity id and watchable-object list of the S1C packet to FlopAC's packet layer.
checks.how_it_works: The wrapper resolves the watchableObjects and entityid fields via reflection, copies the watchable list, and can rebuild the packet from an entity id and object list via setPacket. FlopAC's processors consume entity state through wrappers like this one.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; infrastructure.
checks.variations: Artemis and FlopAC both ship generic packet layers; Artemis additionally reads the metadata into its emulator through EmulatorPreProcessor.

wiki_notes: Any metadata properties not included in the packet are left unchanged on the client rather than reset.

MCP 1.8.9 S1CPacketEntityMetadata implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityMetadata; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.sendMetadataToAllAssociatedPlayers sends new S1CPacketEntityMetadata (line 314): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Entity Effect
packets.desc: Applies a status/potion effect to an entity.
packets.notes: Effect IDs: 1=speed, 2=slowness, 5=strength, 8=jump_boost, 11=absorption, 16=wither, etc.

writeup.p: S1DPacketEntityEffect applies one potion effect to one entity. The server has three send sites: EntityTrackerEntry broadcasts an entity's new effect to every player watching it, EntityPlayerMP.addPotionEffect and refreshActivePotionEffect send it to the affected player directly, and ServerConfigurationManager replays effects (beacon, team) on respawn and on player join. Wire layout is entityId VarInt, effectId byte, amplifier byte, duration VarInt in ticks, hideParticles boolean. In 1.8.9 the effect is a full state push: the client stores it in the entity's active potion map and the server never asks for confirmation.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityEffect runs on the client thread via PacketThreadUtil, resolves the entity with getEntityByID, and for EntityLivingBase targets builds a PotionEffect(effectId, duration, amplifier, false, hideParticles), calls setPotionDurationMax(duration), then addPotionEffect. From that point every renderer (armor, HUD, particles, the player's own effect tab) reads the entity's activePotionMap. Effects on non-living entities are silently dropped, and an unknown entityId does nothing.

The 8 reference clients leave S1D to vanilla; the only non-vanilla hit among them is Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 NetworkAPI.java, which registers S1DPacketEntityEffect in the clientbound class table (index 72) so scripts can build and inject it via receivePacket. Effect-aware features in those clients (effect HUD rows, potion ESP) poll the entity's active potion map after vanilla applies the packet, or render from EntityLivingBase state, so no packet interception is needed. November Recode 2.0 is the exception: AutoPotModule hooks S1D as the server's implicit confirmation that a thrown splash potion landed, resetting its potion sequence only when the effect packet for the local player arrives. The PotionHUD/AntiPotion entries in older packet docs come from Sigma 3.9, which is not part of the reference set; Sigma 4.11's corpus has no S1D hit.

Cancelling S1D in a receive event is a client-side potion bypass: the server keeps applying the effect and its movement math, the client simply never renders or stores it. That grants nothing for movement because speed, jump and health attributes are server-authoritative. Anti-cheats never measure this packet; it is one-directional cosmetic state. The only bandwidth note is that EntityTrackerEntry sends one S1D per effect per tracked entity on the tracking loop, so rapid effect churn is amplification surface for griefing plugins, not for cheat modules.

implementation.overview: Effect application is a pure server-to-client state push. The 8 reference clients have no module interest in it and every effect-aware feature reads the entity's potion map after vanilla applies the packet; the sole non-vanilla hit among them is Rise 6.x NetworkAPI registering the class for script injection. November Recode 2.0's AutoPotModule is the only module that hooks S1D, using it as the ack that a splash potion actually applied.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry line 418 sends S1D to each playerNetServerHandler in the watching list when a tracked entity gains an effect; EntityPlayerMP lines 922/927 send it to the affected player for addPotionEffect and refreshActivePotionEffect; ServerConfigurationManager lines 193/509 replay active effects on respawn and join. The server does no validation on the receiving side: there is no processX handler because the packet is clientbound only.
implementation.protocol_notes: The amplifier byte is the level minus one (0 means level I). Duration is in ticks on the wire; the client stores it as the effect duration and also as durationMax, so the potion icon countdown and the expiry timestamp both come from this single value. hideParticles maps to the PotionEffect showParticles flag; an S1D with the same effectId overwrites the previous entry in the active potion map rather than stacking.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat in the 1.8.9 ecosystem flags S1D handling. Movement-relevant effects (speed, jump boost, slowness) are validated from server-side attribute and motion math, so a client that drops the packet only sees wrong visuals. Servers that want to detect a modified client would have to query the client for its potion state, which vanilla 1.8.9 has no packet for.

modules.name: AutoPotModule (pot confirmation)
modules.purpose: Use the S1D effect packet for the local player as the server-side confirmation that a thrown splash potion landed, so the potion sequence only advances after the effect applies.
modules.how_it_works: The potion sequence is staged: C09 held-item change, C08 block placement for the throw, then the module sets waitingClientUpdate and waits. The S1D listener checks the packet's entity id against the local player; while waitingClientUpdate is set it resets the pot stage, restarts the delay timer and re-syncs the inventory, scheduling the next pot.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None: the module only reads S1D. The effect arrives for any potion the server applies, so the ack also fires when a server-side effect lands, which only makes the sequence more robust.
modules.variations: No other client in the reference corpus hooks S1D at module level; effect-aware features elsewhere poll the active potion map instead.

implementation.general_hooks: The only module in the reference corpus registering a packet receive handler for S1D is November Recode 2.0's AutoPotModule (EventPacket.In). Rise 6.x NetworkAPI exposes clientbound packets to JavaScript scripts by class-table index.
implementation.client_variations: Memeware 7.3, Nekoware v1 private, Sigma 4.11, Spicy and Tenacity 6.0 ship the vanilla handler byte-for-byte. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 additionally register the class in NetworkAPI (script/api/NetworkAPI.java). November Recode 2.0 is the only client that reads S1D in a module, inside AutoPotModule's EventPacket.In listener.

anticheat.overview: Server-side anticheats treat the entity-effect packet as state synchronization, not a cheat signal. The corpus splits into packet-driven potion trackers (Grim, Artemis, BetterAnticheat, Kauri, Intave) that decode S1D and mirror the effect onto their simulated player or entity, and Bukkit-polling checks (FlopAC, Hydro, Frequency) that read getActivePotionEffects and only see the effect after the server applies it. The trackers matter because movement checks must know the exact speed, jump and slowness multipliers the client has; a potion state mismatch causes false flags in speed and flight checks, so the apply packet is transaction-confirmed before the effect lands in the simulation.

checks.name: Effect state replication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Keep the compensated entity's potion state in sync with the server so movement predictions apply the same speed, jump and slowness multipliers the client sees.
checks.how_it_works: PacketEntityReplication listens on the packet-send side. For ENTITY_EFFECT it decodes the potion type and amplifier, cancels the packet when ViaVersion would fake an effect the client version does not support, forces a transaction when the effect targets the player, and schedules entity.addPotionEffect on the compensated entity at the transaction's real-time position. The remove branch in the same listener mirrors this with entity.removePotionEffect.
checks.detects: No cheat directly. It is state replication: speed, jump boost and levitation modifiers on the simulated entity must match the client's, or flight and speed checks misjudge legitimate motion.
checks.variations: Artemis (PotionPreProcessor, EmulatorPreProcessor) and BetterAnticheat (PotionTracker) use the same transaction-confirmed pattern; Kauri's PotionHandler adds the effect into a thread-safe list; Intave decodes the fields with EntityEffectReader.

checks.name: Potion preprocessor (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Maintain the user's active effect list from the entity-effect packet so checks and the emulator can read current potion modifiers.
checks.how_it_works: fastHandle matches GPacketPlayServerEntityEffect, builds a PotionEffect from the effect id, duration and amplifier, then queues the add behind a transaction confirmation: pre() inserts the effect and marks it processed, post() clears the marker. It also clears the using-item flag when the effect ends item use.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; it feeds checks that must distinguish potion-boosted motion from cheat motion.
checks.variations: The same anticheat's EmulatorPreProcessor applies the identical pattern to the emulated entity; Grim and BetterAnticheat use equivalent confirmations.

checks.name: Potion tracker (BetterAnticheat)
checks.purpose: Track each potion type's amplifier and duration as a lag-compensated many-state so checks read the effect that actually reached the client.
checks.how_it_works: PotionTracker subscribes to ENTITY_EFFECT on the send side, takes a confirmation handle, and stages the new Potion in an ObjectManyState: addNew on begin, flushOld plus an active-count after the client confirms. REMOVE_ENTITY_EFFECT stages an EMPTY_POTION the same way so an expired effect cannot linger.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself; getPotion() exposes the confirmed state to checks that need the speed or jump modifier.
checks.variations: Grim and Artemis use transaction confirmations rather than a confirmation tracker; FlopAC polls Bukkit's getActivePotionEffects instead of reading the packet.

checks.name: Potion handler (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Keep a thread-safe potion effect list on the player data so movement and velocity checks can query current modifiers.
checks.how_it_works: PotionHandler seeds the list from the Bukkit player's active effects at construction, then onPotionEffect(WrapperPlayServerEntityEffect) replaces the entry for the potion type under a write lock, storing the amplifier, duration and visibility flags. hasPotionEffect and getEffectByType expose the state to checks.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; the handler is the query surface for checks that must subtract potion-boosted motion from the allowed envelope.
checks.variations: Artemis and Grim decode the packet into their own effect model; Tecnio whitelists both effect packets in NetworkFilter and tracks potion levels in AttributeTracker.

checks.name: Entity effect reader (Intave)
checks.purpose: Extract effect type, amplifier and duration from the entity-effect packet across every supported protocol version.
checks.how_it_works: EntityEffectReader is registered for the ENTITY_EFFECT packet in PacketReaders. effectType() reads the potion-type field on 1.19+, the integer slot on 1.18.2, and the legacy byte below; effectAmplifier() and effectDuration() shift their field indexes at 1.21. Each accessor falls back to 0 on a missing field.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself; the reader feeds the effect tracker that movement characteristics consume.
checks.variations: Grim and Artemis read the same fields through PacketEvents and the cc.ghast wrapper tree instead of ProtocolLib.

wiki_notes: The client displays the effect level as amplifier plus one, so amplifier 0 means level 1.

MCP 1.8.9 S1DPacketEntityEffect implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityEffect; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.? sends new S1DPacketEntityEffect (line 452) +2 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Remove Entity Effect
packets.desc: Removes a potion effect from an entity.

writeup.p: S1EPacketRemoveEntityEffect clears one effect from one entity. The only server send site in the corpus is EntityPlayerMP.removePotionEffect, which fires when an effect expires naturally, is cured (milk), is overwritten by a higher-tier re-application, or is stripped on death/respawn. Wire layout is entityId VarInt plus effectId byte. It is the mirror image of S1D: where S1D pushes a full PotionEffect, S1E carries only the potion ID and the client derives everything else from its stored effect.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleRemoveEntityEffect resolves the entity and calls removePotionEffectClient(effectId) on EntityLivingBase. That deletes the map entry, re-applies the entity's attribute modifiers (an expired speed effect removes its movement bonus) and triggers the potion expiry render path. The HUD and effect icons update from the map, so removal needs no separate notification. Unknown entity IDs and unknown effect IDs are ignored without error.

No module in the 8 reference clients hooks S1E. The only non-vanilla corpus hit is the Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 NetworkAPI registration (clientbound index 73) for script use. Effect-removal timing is irrelevant to these clients: HUDs redraw from the entity's potion map, and nothing needs to know the exact tick an effect ended because the client never sends effect state back to the server.

Cancelling S1E in a receive event leaves the effect visible client-side while the server has already removed it. Because attributes are re-derived server-side, the client keeps stale visuals only: a cancelled speed-removal leaves the speed icon but not the speed, which is the classic tell of a sloppy client-side potion bypass. Anti-cheats ignore the packet entirely; the abuse surface is purely cosmetic and self-reporting.

implementation.overview: Effect removal is a two-field state push with zero module usage across the 8 reference clients. The only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x NetworkAPI registering the class for scripts; everything else is the vanilla handler.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP line 932 sends S1E to the affected player whenever removePotionEffect is called on the server-side entity. EntityTrackerEntry does not broadcast removals to watchers in 1.8.9: other players learn about the change through the next attribute or metadata update, which is why effect removal is a per-player packet. There is no server-side inbound handler, as the packet is clientbound.
implementation.protocol_notes: Two fields only: entityId VarInt and effectId byte, no duration, no amplifier, no flags. The client must have received the matching S1D earlier; an S1E for an effect never applied is a no-op. Ordering relative to S1D matters: a remove arriving before the apply is silently dropped, so the effect sticks until its natural expiry.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing flags S1E. Movement effects are enforced from server-side state, so a client that ignores removals can never outrun the server's speed model. Plugin-side detection would require a client state query that 1.8.9 does not define.
implementation.general_hooks: None of the 8 clients register a packet receive handler for S1E. Rise 6.x exposes the class through NetworkAPI's clientbound table for script injection only.
implementation.client_variations: Memeware 7.3, Nekoware v1 private, Sigma 4.11, Spicy and Tenacity 6.0 keep the vanilla handler. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 add the NetworkAPI registration; no other client code touches the packet.

anticheat.overview: The remove-effect packet is the mirror image of S1D: it deletes one potion from one entity. Anticheats that replicate effect state on the server (Grim, Artemis, BetterAnticheat) handle it in the same tracker as the apply packet, with the same transaction confirmation, because an effect that outlives its removal in the simulation keeps inflating the allowed speed and jump envelope. Tecnio whitelists both effect classes in its network filter so the pipeline can route them. No anticheat flags S1E directly: the packet carries only an entity id and an effect id, and the interesting state change happens on the entity, not in the packet.

checks.name: Remove-effect replication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Drop the potion from the compensated entity at the tick the client processes the removal, so the simulation stops crediting the effect's speed or jump bonus.
checks.how_it_works: The REMOVE_ENTITY_EFFECT branch of PacketEntityReplication decodes the entity id and potion type, forces a transaction when the removal targets the player, and schedules entity.removePotionEffect at the transaction's real-time position. The apply branch in the same listener mirrors the add.
checks.detects: No cheat directly. A removal that lands late in the simulation keeps the effect's multipliers active too long and desyncs flight and speed checks.
checks.variations: Artemis EmulatorPreProcessor and PotionPreProcessor remove the effect from the emulated entity and user list with the same transaction confirmation; BetterAnticheat stages an EMPTY_POTION in the many-state.

checks.name: Effect removal on emulated entity (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Remove the potion from the emulated entity so the prediction engine stops applying the effect's movement modifiers.
checks.how_it_works: EmulatorPreProcessor matches GPacketPlayServerEntityEffectRemove for the local player, then confirmFunctionAndTick queues data.entity.removePotionEffect(effectId) to run at the transaction-confirmed tick.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; it keeps the emulated entity's potion state identical to the client's so predictions of speed and jump stay valid.
checks.variations: Grim and BetterAnticheat implement the same removal with their own confirmation mechanisms; the sibling PotionPreProcessor tracks the user-level effect list instead of the emulated entity.

checks.name: Potion removal tracker (BetterAnticheat)
checks.purpose: Transition the potion state to empty on removal, under the same confirmation as the apply path.
checks.how_it_works: On REMOVE_ENTITY_EFFECT for the local player, PotionTracker stages EMPTY_POTION into the potion map on confirmation begin and flushes the old active state after confirm, so getPotion() returns an inactive state as soon as the client receives the removal.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself; checks reading the potion map stop applying the effect's modifiers after the removal confirms.
checks.variations: Grim removes the effect directly from the compensated entity; Artemis tracks the user effect list and the emulated entity in two processors.

checks.name: Effect packet filter (Tecnio)
checks.purpose: Whitelist both entity-effect packets in the network filter so the pipeline can route them to the attribute tracker.
checks.how_it_works: NetworkFilter's constructor adds GPacketPlayServerEntityEffect and GPacketPlayServerEntityEffectRemove to the allowed-class set. isAllowed gates packet processing, so these two clientbound classes pass into the tracker layer while unlisted packets are ignored.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; the filter is the routing table that lets potion state reach checks.
checks.variations: Other anticheats subscribe to the packets directly through their event systems and need no explicit whitelist.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x1E: VarInt entityId plus unsigned byte potion effect ID.
Mirror of S1D apply; client drops the stored effect and refreshes attributes and HUD.
Unknown entity or effect ID is ignored; remove before apply is a no-op.

MCP 1.8.9 S1EPacketRemoveEntityEffect implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleRemoveEntityEffect; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readUnsignedByte, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.onFinishedPotionEffect sends new S1EPacketRemoveEntityEffect (line 1061): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Set Experience
packets.desc: Updates the player's experience bar (level, total XP, progress).

writeup.p: S1FPacketSetExperience synchronizes the player's XP bar: experienceBar float (0.0-1.0 progress to next level), totalExperience VarInt, level VarInt. The server sends it from EntityPlayerMP when XP changes (line 401 in the corpus) and from ServerConfigurationManager on respawn/join (line 477). It is a pure display-state push: the client stores the three values and the HUD renders from them; the client never reports XP back, so the server's XP math is the only authoritative copy.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleSetExperience calls thePlayer.setXPStats(progress, totalXp, level), which writes the player's experience, experienceTotal and experienceLevel fields. GuiIngame draws the bar and the level number from those fields every frame. Unlike health (S06) there is no client-side regeneration model behind it: the packet is the entire state.

Exactly one module in the 8 clients references S1F: Rise 5.99 Disabler, whose Hypixel Slime mode cancels the packet in onPacketReceive. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 only register the class in NetworkAPI (clientbound index 74). The XPHUD/AutoEnchant entries from older packet docs have zero corpus hits in the reference clients: XP is read from the player object, not from the packet.

Cancelling S1F freezes the client-side XP bar while the server continues its own XP bookkeeping. Because the client never acknowledges XP, the divergence is invisible in the packet stream, and enchanting/anvil costs are computed server-side so nothing gameplay-relevant is gained. The Rise 5.99 usage is a state-freeze side effect of the Hypixel Slime disabler mode, which cancels the XP sync together with slime sound and particle packets so the client's stored minigame state stays static during the bypass window.

implementation.overview: A three-field display push for the XP bar with a single module hit in the reference set: Rise 5.99 Disabler's Hypixel Slime mode cancels it to freeze client state. Everything else is vanilla or the Rise 6.x script registry.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP sends S1F at line 401 whenever the player's XP fields change (addExperience, addExperienceLevel, onEnchant, the level-up path). ServerConfigurationManager sends it at line 477 when a player joins or respawns so the bar starts correct. There is no inbound validation because the packet is clientbound; the server trusts its own XP math entirely.
implementation.protocol_notes: Three fields in order: float progress (0.0-1.0), VarInt total XP, VarInt level. The float is written as a 32-bit IEEE value, so progress is exact to the wire format. The client stores all three as player fields; GuiIngame renders progress as the bar fill and level as the number. A cancelled S1F leaves the previous values in place, which is the freeze the Rise 5.99 mode relies on.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures S1F. XP is never echoed by the client, so a frozen bar cannot be distinguished from a laggy one by packet inspection alone. Servers that need XP for gameplay (enchanting, anvils, spawners) compute it server-side, which is why cancelling the packet is safe and why no bypass value exists beyond cosmetics or minigame state sync.

modules.name: Disabler
modules.purpose: The Hypixel Slime mode cancels S1FPacketSetExperience so the client's stored XP state stays frozen while the rest of the mode's state-freeze bypass runs.
modules.how_it_works: In onPacketReceive, when the hypixelSlime toggle is enabled, the handler rewrites S02PacketChat type-2 messages that contain 'UNAVAILABLE', cancels S29PacketSoundEffect with sound name 'mob.slime.big', cancels S2APacketParticles of type SLIME, and cancels S1FPacketSetExperience. The XP cancel keeps the minigame's XP sync from mutating client state mid-bypass.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (onPacketReceive); the module also uses PreMotionEvent, TeleportEvent, AttackEvent, StrafeEvent, PacketSendEvent and WorldChangedEvent.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Low risk: the server never sees a response to S1F and XP is never echoed, so the cancel is indistinguishable from packet loss. The visible side effect is a frozen XP bar in the HUD.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 ship their own exploit/Disabler.java but the corpus shows no S1F reference in it; those versions only touch S1F through NetworkAPI's script registration. No other reference client has any S1F module hit.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on Rise 5.99. The single real module hit for this packet is a cancel inside a multi-mode disabler, not a dedicated XP module.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 uses a boolean-toggle mode matrix inside one Disabler class. Rise 6.x replaces the module structure entirely (component system) and only lists the packet in NetworkAPI.

anticheat.overview: The experience packet has no detection story. The corpus shows one functional use: Intave writes S1F itself as a telemetry channel, packing ping and simulation data into the level field, and Artemis registers a PacketPlayServerExperience interface in its wrapper tree. The other hits are incidental: Negativity lists the packet in a type enum, NCP prints the player's exp in an admin inspect command, and the Photon hit is a keyword collision with SPAWN_EXPERIENCE_ORB (S11), not S1F. No anticheat reads S1F to detect anything.

checks.name: Experience telemetry channel (Intave)
checks.purpose: Reuse the experience packet as a covert data channel: Intave sends S1F with the level field packed with telemetry instead of real XP.
checks.how_it_works: sendPacketWithExperience builds an EXPERIENCE packet with progress 0 and total XP 0, writes the level field to a packed value, and sends it to the player. ConnectionMetadata encodes ping averages (ping times 1000 plus short ping) when LATENCY_PING_AS_XP_LEVEL is on; Physics.java sends the simulation rate limiter counter; StorageLoader replays a storage tag as a recurring level set.
checks.detects: Nothing. This is the only functional S1F usage in the corpus and it is outbound telemetry, not detection.
checks.variations: Artemis registers PacketPlayServerExperience as a wrapper interface (repository entry at SERVER_PLAY + 34); Negativity lists EXPERIENCE in its packet-type enum; NCP prints the player's exp in the admin inspect command; the Photon corpus hit is a keyword collision with SPAWN_EXPERIENCE_ORB, which is S11, not S1F.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x1F: float bar progress 0.0-1.0, VarInt level, VarInt total XP.
Pure display sync for HUD bar and level number; server keeps authoritative XP.
Sent on XP change, join and respawn; client never echoes XP back.

MCP 1.8.9 S1FPacketSetExperience implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleSetExperience; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readFloat, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.onUpdateEntity sends new S1FPacketSetExperience (line 422) +1 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Entity Properties
packets.desc: Updates an entity's generic attributes (movement speed, max health, knockback resistance, etc.).
packets.notes: Attribute keys: generic.movementSpeed, generic.maxHealth, generic.knockbackResistance, generic.followRange, horse.jumpStrength, zombie.spawnReinforcements, etc. Movement speed can be read to predict horse speeds or detect speed-modified players.

writeup.p: S20PacketEntityProperties is a full attribute snapshot for one entity: entityId VarInt, property count int, then per property a String key, double base value, modifier count, and per modifier a UUID, name, amount and operation byte. The server sends it from EntityTrackerEntry when an entity's attributes change (line 267/311 in the corpus) and to new watchers when they start tracking (line 329/374). This is the only channel by which the client learns other entities' movement speed, knockback resistance, max health and attack damage.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityProperties resolves the entity and throws IllegalStateException if it is not EntityLivingBase ('Server tried to update attributes of a non-living entity'). It then walks the snapshot list: unknown attribute keys are registered on the fly as RangedAttribute with the full double range, setBaseValue is applied, all modifiers are removed and re-added from the wire. EntityLivingBase reads these attributes for its own speed, health and knockback math, so the packet directly drives client-side entity physics.

Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 PingSpoofComponent include S20PacketEntityProperties in the 'players' class tuple: when a module enables players=true spoofing, incoming S20 packets are cancelled and released late. Rise 6.x NetworkAPI also registers the class (clientbound index 75). Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity carry only the vanilla handler; the AntiBot/TargetInfo attribute-reading modules from older docs have no corpus hits in the reference set.

The interesting abuse is buffering, not reading: PingSpoofComponent holds S20 for other entities so their attribute snapshots arrive after their position updates, keeping the client's view of entity speeds consistent with frozen positions during blink windows. Delaying entity-state packets does not touch the player's own server-authoritative motion, so no anti-cheat flags it. A client that reads S20 precisely could predict player speeds for aim/velocity math, but none of the 8 clients does.

implementation.overview: The client's only window into other entities' attributes. Rise 6.x PingSpoofComponent buffers S20 as part of its 'players' spoof category, and NetworkAPI registers it for scripts; the other six clients leave the vanilla handler untouched.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry sends the full attribute map on change (line 267/311) and on watcher start (line 329/374). The packet carries base values plus modifiers, so the client rebuilds the complete attribute state from scratch on every arrival; there is no delta encoding and no inbound handler. Server-side validation is absent by design: the packet is clientbound.
implementation.protocol_notes: The property count is a plain int, not a VarInt, unlike most 1.8.9 counts. Attribute keys are the unlocalized names ('generic.movementSpeed', 'generic.knockbackResistance', 'generic.maxHealth', 'generic.attackDamage', 'horse.jumpStrength', 'zombie.spawnReinforcements'). Modifier operation is a byte (0 add, 1 multiply, 2 multiply-base). The client registers unknown keys as RangedAttribute with near-infinite bounds, so a server can push arbitrary named attributes.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Entity attribute state is derived server-side, so anti-cheats never validate S20 traffic. The only observable effect of buffering it is delayed visual entity speed, which looks like normal lag. This is why PingSpoofComponent can park S20 for hundreds of milliseconds without risk.

modules.name: PingSpoofComponent
modules.purpose: Buffers S20PacketEntityProperties for other entities during a spoof/blink window so attribute snapshots arrive late and stay consistent with frozen entity positions.
modules.how_it_works: The 'players' Tuple lists S20PacketEntityProperties alongside S13PacketDestroyEntities, S14PacketEntity variants, S18PacketEntityTeleport and S19PacketEntityHeadLook. onPacketReceive cancels any listed class when its category flag is enabled and parks it as a TimedPacket; onPostMotion flushes entries whose time plus the spoof amount has elapsed, and dispatch() releases everything on world change or disable.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (cancel + park), PostMotionEvent (flush), WorldChangeEvent (dispatch), PacketSendEvent (serverbound park).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Low risk: only entity-state packets are delayed, never the player's own movement or transaction stream, so server-side motion checks see nothing unusual. Delayed entity attributes render as slightly stale entity speeds, which reads as latency.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4 carries an identical file under Client-release2/Client/src/main/java. Rise 6.0 (outside the reference set) has the same component; within the reference set only 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 count.

implementation.general_hooks: Rise 6.x component system: @EventLink listeners on PacketReceiveEvent, PacketSendEvent, PostMotionEvent and WorldChangeEvent. Modules request spoofing via PingSpoofComponent.spoof(amount, ...) and blink().
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 are the only reference clients with non-vanilla S20 code, both through the component plus NetworkAPI registration. Classic clients (Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity) ship the stock handler.

anticheat.overview: The attribute snapshot packet is the server's only channel for entity attribute state, and anticheats treat it as authoritative input for movement simulation. Trackers capture the movement-speed attribute and its modifiers (Hydro, AntiHaxerman, intave), Grim clamps attribute values to the wiki-defined client bounds and excludes the sprinting modifier from the base value, TruthfulAC records attribute snapshots from the Bukkit API that mirrors the S20 state, and Photon rewrites the max-health attribute. Knockback resistance is present in the packet but no check in the corpus consumes it.

checks.name: ValuedAttribute (attribute range validation)
checks.purpose: Model one server-sent attribute with wiki-defined min/max bounds and recompute its value from the S20 property, so the simulation never trusts an out-of-range base or modifier sum.
checks.how_it_works: with() recomputes the value as (base + addition sum) x (1 + multiply-base sum) x product of (1 + multiply-total) and clamps to [min, max]; the sprinting modifier is removed first because Grim tracks sprint separately in CompensatedEntities. requiredVersion gates value changes behind a client version, and setRewriter/getRewriter adapt the value per client and server version. The constructor rejects defaults outside the range.
checks.detects: Attribute abuse where the server sends values the client would clamp, and version-dependent attribute quirks that would otherwise desync the simulation.
checks.variations: CompensatedEntities.updateAttributes feeds the same property list into per-entity attribute maps, watching specifically for the movement-speed sprint modifier and horse jump strength; PlayerBaseTick consumes the resulting movement speed and scale during simulation.

checks.name: AttributeTracker (movement speed tracking)
checks.purpose: Capture the player's walk speed from the S20 update, combine it with speed and slowness potion effects, and expose the effective move speed the simulation checks use.
checks.how_it_works: handleAttributeUpdate matches generic.movementSpeed in the property list and stores the base value inside the transaction-confirm window. Entity-effect packets feed speed, slowness and jump boost levels, and getMoveSpeed(sprint) composes walk speed with the 0.3 sprint modifier and 0.2/-0.15 potion modifiers.
checks.detects: Speed-state desync between the server's attributes and the movement the player reports; feeds speed and flight simulation.
checks.variations: AntiHaxerman's AttributeTracker keeps a full snapshot list of the player's attributes on connection confirm; intave's AttributeTracker stores modifier sets and derives the sprint flag from the presence of the sprinting modifier.

checks.name: AttributeTracker (attribute snapshot)
checks.purpose: Keep the player's current attribute snapshot and potion levels, refreshed on connection confirm, so movement checks know the exact speed and effect state.
checks.how_it_works: The tracker handles GPacketPlayServerUpdateAttributes for the player's own entity id and stores the full Snapshot list inside a connection-confirm action; entity-effect packets update the potion map the same way. getPotionLevel and hasPotion expose the effect state.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; feeds speed, flight and velocity checks with the confirmed attribute state.
checks.variations: Hydro keeps only the movement-speed value plus potion levels; intave additionally derives the sprint state from the modifier set.

checks.name: AttributeTracker (sprint speed detection)
checks.purpose: Read the S20 attribute collection for the player, store the server's modifier set, and derive whether the player has the sprinting modifier active.
checks.how_it_works: sentAttributes reads the attribute collection modifier of the UPDATE_ATTRIBUTES packet for the player's own entity id, converts each WrappedAttribute into intave's Attribute model, clears the stored modifiers, then stores the server's modifier set and sets movement.hasSprintSpeed when the SPRINTING_MODIFIER is present. Base values update the ability metadata.
checks.detects: Speed-state desync where the client moves as if sprinting while the server attributes say otherwise.
checks.variations: Hydro and AntiHaxerman track the same attribute stream with simpler base-value snapshots; Grim goes further and recomputes the full value with range clamps.

checks.name: AttributeEngine (simulation attribute history)
checks.purpose: Record walk speed, gravity, jump strength, step height, movement efficiency and potion levels over a 1.5 second window so the simulation checks bound their physics assumptions.
checks.how_it_works: updateStateCache in PlayerData reads the Bukkit attribute API (generic.movementSpeed, generic.gravity, generic.jumpStrength, generic.stepHeight, generic.movementEfficiency, player.sneakingSpeed) and potion levels, then calls attributeEngine.record. The engine keeps a timestamped deque, exposes max walk speed, min gravity, max jump strength and step height, and hasAttributeTransition detects attribute changes within the window. The debug tags (ATTR_LOW_GRAVITY, ATTR_SPEED, ATTR_JUMP, ATTR_STEP) label the active conditions.
checks.detects: Physics assumptions violated by attribute changes; the recorded history lets the simulation checks tolerate legitimate speed and jump changes instead of flagging them.
checks.variations: The engine is fed from the Bukkit API rather than parsing S20 directly, but it mirrors the same server-side attribute state the packet announces. Grim and Hydro feed their simulations from the packet stream itself.

wiki_notes: Modifier operations apply in a fixed order: all addition modifiers first, then multiply-base percentage modifiers, then multiply-total modifiers.

MCP 1.8.9 S20PacketEntityProperties implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEntityProperties; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readDouble, readInt, readStringFromBuffer, readUuid, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityTrackerEntry.sendMetadataToAllAssociatedPlayers sends new S20PacketEntityProperties (line 324): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/EntityTrackerEntry.java

packets.name: Chunk Data
packets.desc: Sends a chunk section (16x16x16 blocks) with compressed block data, light values, and biome info.

fields.name: groundUpContinuous
fields.desc: True if this is a fresh chunk (sends biome + skylight)

fields.name: bitmask
fields.desc: Which 16-block sections are present (bit 0 = bottom section)

fields.name: data
fields.desc: Zlib-compressed chunk data (block IDs + block light + sky light + biomes)

packets.notes: Each section in the bitmask contains: 4096 block IDs (2 bytes each), 2048 block light (4 bits per block), 2048 sky light (4 bits per block). For groundUp=true: 256 biome bytes at end. Data is zlib-compressed. XRay modules intercept this to replace block IDs or prevent chunk updates.

writeup.p: S21PacketChunkData carries one chunk's block, light and biome data. Server send sites: PlayerManager sends a ground-up chunk on initial load (line 365 in the corpus) and section updates with a bitmask on the chunk update tick (line 447), EntityPlayerMP sends the player's spawn chunk with bitmask 65535, and S26PacketMapChunkBulk is the multi-chunk variant. Wire layout: chunkX int, chunkZ int, groundUpContinuous bool, bitmask unsigned short, dataLength VarInt, then zlib-compressed bytes holding per-section block IDs, block light, sky light and 256 biome bytes for ground-up chunks.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleChunkData first handles unloads: a ground-up packet with bitmask 0 calls doPreChunk(false). Otherwise it invalidates the block receive region, fetches the chunk (loading it if missing), applies the extracted sections through chunk.func_177439_a, marks the range for render update, and resets relight checks for non-surface dimensions. This is the heaviest decompression and block-write path in the play state, and it runs on the client thread.

None of the 8 reference clients hook S21 in a module. The only non-vanilla corpus hit is Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 NetworkAPI, which registers the class (clientbound index 76) so scripts can synthesize chunk packets. The XRay/Search/ChestESP entries from older docs reference Sigma 3.9, which is not in the reference set. Modules that want block data read the loaded Chunk object after vanilla applies it; rewriting chunk content would force them to decompress and re-encode the packed sections, which none of these clients does.

Cancelling S21 empties the client's view of the world while the player stays in the server world, the core of chunk-void behavior; the server never notices because there is no acknowledgement. The heavier abuse is bandwidth: PlayerManager caps per-tick chunk traffic server-side, but a plugin that floods S21 can stall a client's single-threaded handler. On the client side, Rise 6.x scripts can call receivePacket with a fabricated S21 to draw fake terrain locally, which is render-only and has no server effect.

implementation.overview: Chunk payload delivery with zero module usage in the 8 reference clients: block-aware features read the loaded world instead of hooking the packet, and the only non-vanilla reference is the Rise 6.x script registry entry.
implementation.server_handling: PlayerManager sends ground-up S21 (bitmask 0, line 365) when a player enters a chunk's watch range, and section updates (groundUp=false, line 447) on the per-chunk update tick, batching changed sections into the bitmask. EntityPlayerMP sends the spawn chunk with all 16 sections (65535). Chunk data is extracted and zlib-compressed at send time; there is no inbound handler because the packet is clientbound.
implementation.protocol_notes: Each section in the bitmask contributes 4096 block IDs at 2 bytes each plus 2048 block-light and 2048 sky-light nibbles; ground-up chunks append 256 biome bytes. The data field is zlib-compressed as a whole, so the client must inflate it before touching any block. A ground-up packet with bitmask 0 means chunk unload, not empty data. S26PacketMapChunkBulk reuses S21PacketChunkData.Extracted for the bulk variant.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats never measure S21; the server cannot tell what the client rendered. Chunk-based cheats (XRay, cave finder) are undetectable server-side in principle, which is why they are banned by staff rather than flagged. The client-side risk is stability: malformed or flooded chunk data crashes the vanilla handler, the basis of chunk-ban exploits that server plugins mitigate by validating senders.
implementation.general_hooks: No module in the 8 clients registers a receive handler for S21. Rise 6.x exposes the class to scripts via NetworkAPI; all other references are vanilla net/minecraft files.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients ship the vanilla handleChunkData. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 additionally list the class in NetworkAPI; Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity differ only in the bundled vanilla source revision.

anticheat.overview: S21 delivers a full chunk column to the client, and it is the transport that makes xray and world-downloader cheating possible. Server-side anticheats approach it from two directions: xray checks score ore-breaking behavior (BAC XRayCheck, AntiCheatPlus XRayListener, Negativity XRayProtocol), sentinel modules neutralize world downloaders at the plugin-message level (Photon WorldDownloaderSentinel), and simulation anticheats parse the chunk bytes into a compensated world so their movement and phase checks see the same blocks the client sees (Grim PacketWorldReaderEight, Hydro WorldTracker, Truthful CompensatedWorld, Kauri Chunk and World, Intave block caches). The corpus for S21 is dominated by the replication side, because every block-based check depends on it.

checks.name: XRayCheck (BasicAntiCheat)
checks.purpose: Ghost-block xray heuristic: spawn fake ore blocks in front of the player and flag anyone who breaks them.
checks.how_it_works: On BlockBreakEvent, when the player breaks an ore, the check walks up to 9 blocks in the player's facing direction and replaces a buried stone block with the same ore type, recording it as a ghost block with a proximity counter. On PlayerMoveEvent, ghost blocks that the player approaches too often and then breaks (5 or more close encounters) fail the check; sneaking while standing over a block also registers it. The check is marked as heavy beta in the config.
checks.detects: Xray users who path straight to ores through solid rock and break ghost blocks that were never visible.
checks.variations: AntiCheatPlus XRayListener and XRayTracker score ore ratios per player instead of ghost blocks; Negativity XRayProtocol runs a similar ore-ratio heuristic; Observer ChestESP is the render-side cousin of the same idea.

checks.name: XRayListener and XRayTracker (AntiCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Ore-ratio xray detection: players who mine far more ores per total blocks than the server average are flagged.
checks.how_it_works: BlockBreakEvent feeds per-ore counters (diamond, iron, gold, lapis, redstone) and a total block counter into XRayTracker for every checked player; creative players are skipped unless checkCreativeXRay is enabled. XRayStats snapshots the counts and the scheduled XRay checker compares ratios against the server baseline at the configured alert interval.
checks.detects: Xray users whose ore-to-block ratio is statistically above legitimate mining.
checks.variations: Negativity XRayProtocol uses the same ratio idea; BAC XRayCheck detects via ghost blocks instead; LightAntiCheat hooks unloaded-chunk movement (UnloadedChunkListener) to catch players walking through terrain that should not exist.

checks.name: PacketWorldReaderEight (Grim)
checks.purpose: Parse the raw S21 chunk data bytes into Grim's compensated world so simulation checks see the exact blocks the client received.
checks.how_it_works: BasePacketWorldReader dispatches the outbound chunk packets: handleMapChunk reads the chunk x/z, ground-up flag, section mask and size, decodes each 16-section column with the 1.8 endian-flipped palette reader, skips biome and light arrays, and merges the result into the compensated world cache with the transaction id. The 1.9+ and 1.18 readers are separate implementations; unloads are queued via removeChunkLater.
checks.detects: Feeds ground, collision and phase simulation; without it, ghost-block and phase cheats would read a stale world.
checks.variations: Hydro WorldTracker and Truthful CompensatedWorld keep the same compensated cache with chunk snapshots; Kauri World and Chunk classes store WrappedBlock arrays; Intave BlockCaches and ChunkAccessPatcher build the block cache for its physics simulator; Artemis CachedWorld does the same for its emulator.

checks.name: WorldDownloaderSentinel (Photon)
checks.purpose: Detect WorldDownloader mods and disable their chunk caching, entity saving and container saving over the wdl plugin-message channel.
checks.how_it_works: Registers the wdl/init and wdl/control plugin-message channels. When a client announces itself on wdl|INIT, the module answers on wdl|CONTROL with two packets that disable future functionality, general saving, chunk caching, entity and tile-entity saving and container saving per config, then runs the standard sentinel detection. Chunk data (S21 and S26) is the mod's raw material, so the module closes the hole at the channel handshake.
checks.detects: WorldDownloader clients that would otherwise persist every chunk the server sends.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus speaks the wdl channels; Negativity (WorldRegionBypass) and LightAntiCheat approximate the same protection with region bypass and unloaded-chunk checks.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x21: chunkX and chunkZ ints, groundUp bool, bitmask short, data byte array.
Each set bit adds one 16x16x16 section: 8192 block bytes plus 2048 blocklight and 2048 skylight.
Ground-up true appends 256 biome bytes; ground-up with bitmask 0 unloads the chunk.

MCP 1.8.9 S21PacketChunkData implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleChunkData; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBoolean, readByteArray, readInt, readShort.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.? sends new S21PacketChunkData (line 340) +2 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Multi Block Change
packets.desc: Updates multiple blocks within a single chunk. More efficient than sending many S23 packets.

fields.name: changedBlocks
fields.desc: Array of (block coordinate, new block state) pairs

encoding: Block position in chunk + new block state

writeup.p: S22PacketMultiBlockChange batches block updates for one chunk. PlayerManager's chunk update tick collects changed positions into a short[] and sends a single packet: chunkX int, chunkZ int, record count VarInt, then per record a short crammed position and a VarInt block state id. The crammed short packs y in the low 8 bits, x in bits 12-15 and z in bits 8-11 (y | x<<12 | z<<8). It is the batched sibling of S23PacketBlockChange and the only efficient way the server pushes many block edits in one tick.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleMultiBlockChange iterates the BlockUpdateData array and calls world.func_180503_b(position, state) for each record, a no-notify setBlockState. The chunk must already be loaded; the packet never triggers a chunk load. Render updates are not batched here, so rapid multi-block streams can cost a client more in re-renders than in parsing.

None of the 8 reference clients hook S22 in a module; the only non-vanilla hit is Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 NetworkAPI registering the class (clientbound index 77). FastBreak-style sync modules (which wait for the server's block-change echo to confirm a broken block) exist in other clients but have no corpus presence here. Block-scanning features re-scan the loaded world rather than parse per-packet records, so the packet stays vanilla.

Dropping or rewriting S22 records desyncs the client's block map from the server's. Scaffold and FastBreak flows depend on the S22 echo to re-sync ghost blocks; a client that ignores it keeps stale visuals and can misplace subsequent placements.
