The server never validates application, so the desync is invisible in the packet stream. The crammed short encoding is the one real parsing hazard for any module that does touch this packet.

implementation.overview: Batched block-change delivery with no module usage in the 8 reference clients. The only non-vanilla reference is the Rise 6.x NetworkAPI script registration; block-aware features re-scan the loaded world instead.
implementation.server_handling: PlayerManager line 460 (Memeware/Nekoware/Sigma corpus) sends S22 with the tick's accumulated numBlocksToUpdate and locationOfBlockChange array to every player watching the chunk. Records carry the block state id resolved from Block.BLOCK_STATE_IDS at construction. There is no inbound handler: the packet is clientbound and the server never learns whether the client applied the changes.
implementation.protocol_notes: Record count is a VarInt; each record is a short crammed as y | x<<12 | z<<8 (x and z 4 bits each, y 8 bits) followed by a VarInt block state id. The short encoding is why records are bounded to 4096 per chunk. Arrival order within the packet is the order the server collected the edits; the client applies them sequentially with no sorting.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures S22. Server-side block verification (NCP's 'block' checks) operates on the server's own world model and the player's dig/place packets, so client-side application of S22 is never audited. The practical detection surface is gameplay-based: a client that desyncs from S22 places ghost blocks that staff can see in replays.
implementation.general_hooks: No module in the 8 clients registers a receive handler for S22. The only non-vanilla reference is the NetworkAPI class table entry in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients keep the vanilla handler. Rise 6.x adds the NetworkAPI registration; Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity differ only by vanilla source revision.

anticheat.overview: S22 batches up to 4096 block changes into one chunk-section update, the form the server uses for explosions, pistons and large world edits. Server-side anticheats treat it as a compensated-world mutation: the changed blocks must be applied to the replicated cache before any movement or visibility check runs, otherwise phase, scaffold and ray-trace checks would judge the player against a stale world. The corpus for S22 is the block-change pipeline (Grim CompensatedWorld, NCP BlockChangeTracker and BlockChangeListener, Hydro WorldTracker, Kauri BlockUpdateHandler, Intave MultiBlockChangeReader), all feeding the same cache that xray and phase detection query.

checks.name: BlockChangeTracker and BlockChangeListener (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Compensated block cache: record every server block change, including S22 multi-block updates, with validity intervals so movement checks can tell whether a block existed at the time the player used it.
checks.how_it_works: BlockChangeListener registers Bukkit events (piston extend and retract, redstone, entity block change, block form, player interact) and forwards each change into BlockChangeTracker.addBlockChange with a change id, tick and direction. The tracker stores per-coordinate linked lists of BlockChangeEntry objects that expire by tick; movement checks (SurvivalFly, Passable, Visible) query getBlockChangeEntry and matchBlockChange with a BlockChangeReference to test whether the block was solid at the player's position at move time.
checks.detects: Feeds ground and passable decisions; prevents false flags when a block was legitimately changed by an explosion or piston between the client's view and the server's world.
checks.variations: Grim CompensatedWorld and Hydro WorldTracker are the same compensated cache in modern anticheats; Kauri BlockUpdateHandler applies S22 updates with a keepalive-action queue; Intave MultiBlockChangeReader decodes the packet into positions and block data for its BlockUpdateTracker.

checks.name: CompensatedWorld block changes (Grim)
checks.purpose: Apply S22 multi-block and S23 single-block changes to Grim's compensated world with transaction accuracy.
checks.how_it_works: Block changes from the server, including multi-block-change batches, are queued and applied inside runSafely and applyBlockChanges at the correct transaction point, so the async world matches the client's view when movement simulation reads it; updateBlock writes combined block ids and getBlock and getBlockStateId serve every check that needs a block. Piston and chunk events route into the same cache, and unloaded-chunk regions are tracked for setback logic.
checks.detects: Keeps phase, ground-spoof and scaffold checks honest by presenting the block state the client actually had instead of the server's current state.
checks.variations: NCP BlockChangeTracker is the classic equivalent; Hydro WorldTracker applies single and multi block changes with the same transaction confirmation; Truthful CompensatedWorld forwards updates to a global world cache.

checks.name: BlockUpdateHandler (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Maintain Kauri's per-player replicated world from server block updates, including the S22 multi-block-change packet.
checks.how_it_works: PacketHandler feeds WrapperPlayServerBlockChange and WrapperPlayServerMultiBlockChange into runUpdate, which applies each encoded block to the current World object inside a keepalive action so the update lands at the right server tick; chunk data and bulk chunk data go through the same path. The replicated world stores WrappedBlock values in 16x384x16 Chunk arrays, and getBlock and getRelative queries serve the reach, phase and interaction checks.
checks.detects: Supplies the block truth for Kauri's checks; clients cannot fake the world because the cache is server-derived.
checks.variations: Grim CompensatedWorld and Hydro WorldTracker apply the same updates with transaction timing; Intave BlockUpdateTracker combines its packet readers with an acknowledgeBlockChange sequence to keep the cache in lockstep with 1.19+ sequenced block changes.

checks.name: MultiBlockChangeReader (Intave)
checks.purpose: Decode the S22 packet into absolute block positions and block data for Intave's block update tracker.
checks.how_it_works: CompiledPacketReader that reads either the 1.16.2+ section-relative encoding (section position plus 12-bit relative coordinates) or the legacy MultiBlockChangeInfo array, and exposes blockPositions() and blockDataList() to the BlockUpdateTracker, which applies them to the block cache and acknowledges the sequence number.
checks.detects: Feeds the block cache that Intave's interaction ray-trace, phase and physics checks query; no direct flag.
checks.variations: Hydro WorldTracker handleMultiBlockChange and Kauri runUpdate(WrapperPlayServerMultiBlockChange) are the equivalent decode-and-apply paths; NCP BlockChangeListener converts the same updates into validity-timed entries.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x22: chunkX and chunkZ ints, VarInt record count, batched records.
Each record is a crammed short plus VarInt block state from Block.BLOCK_STATE_IDS.
Crammed short packs x in bits 12-15, z in bits 8-11 and y in low 8 bits.

MCP 1.8.9 S22PacketMultiBlockChange implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleMultiBlockChange; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readInt, readShort, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: PlayerManager.onUpdate sends new S22PacketMultiBlockChange (line 505): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/management/PlayerManager.java

packets.name: Block Change
packets.desc: Updates a single block in the world — position and new block state (combined ID+metadata).

writeup.p: S23 is the server's single-block state correction. The server sends it whenever one block in a loaded chunk changes and the change is cheap to express, with the alternative S21PacketChunkData / S22PacketMultiBlockChange reserved for bulk edits. The block state is encoded as a VarInt into the Block.BLOCK_STATE_IDS registry, not as the old blockId | (meta << 12) split; every block in 1.8.9 has a unique registry ID. NetHandlerPlayServer pushes it from the block-breaking path (line 481), the block-placement path (line 535), ItemInWorldManager.tryHarvestBlock (line 254) and PlayerManager's chunk watcher broadcast (line 436).

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleBlockChange calls PacketThreadUtil.func_180031_a for main-thread dispatch, then clientWorldController.func_180503_b(pos, state), which is WorldClient.setBlockState: it replaces the local block, updates the lightmap, and re-renders the region. That is the entire effect; there is no server round trip. Because the handler writes straight into the world, any module that reads world state after the event bus gets the correction for free, which is why so few clients intercept S23 directly.

Only one module in the 8-client corpus references S23PacketBlockChange: Rise 6.2.4's WatchdogJumpSprint, a Scaffold sprint mode. It treats every S23 as proof the server accepted a placed block: the PacketReceiveEvent handler sets start3 = true and increments a block counter, and the pre-motion handler then uses start3 to fire a spoofed C08PacketPlayerBlockPlacement with an ice ItemStack against the player's own position (line 116), which is the Watchdog anti-cheat block-placement trigger used to keep the player's on-ground state consistent while sprint-jumping. The counter also feeds previousBlockValue / previousTick logic that paces how often the exploit packet is sent.

S23 is clientbound and carries no player identity, so there is nothing to spoof server-side; the abuse is entirely on the receiving end. Ghost-block clients that locally predict block state must reconcile against S23 when the server disagrees, and scaffold / nuker modules can use the arrival timing of S23 as a cheap ping-free ack. Anti-cheats watch the reverse direction: they validate that a C08PacketPlayerBlockPlacement is followed by a matching S23 echo and check the placed block against the client's claimed reach, which is exactly the surface WatchdogJumpSprint's ice-placement trick plays on.

implementation.overview: The server's authoritative one-block correction. In this corpus it is used by exactly one module, Rise 6.2.4's WatchdogJumpSprint, which reads S23 arrivals as placement acknowledgements to pace a Watchdog-targeted ice-block C08 exploit. Everything else in the 8 clients lets the vanilla handler write the state into WorldClient and reads the world afterwards.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerPlayServer sends S23 on block break (processPlayerDigging, ~line 481), on placement and its neighbor update (~line 535), plus a second packet for the offset block when the placed block has a block-on-use neighbor. ItemInWorldManager sends it after a successful harvest, and PlayerManager.sendToAllPlayersWatchingChunk broadcasts to every player with the chunk loaded. In 1.8.9 there is no server-side validation of the client's C08 beyond reach and interval checks in the digging/placement handlers.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: BlockPos as a packed long (readBlockPos) followed by a VarInt block state registry ID. The state is resolved at construction time from the world, so the server always sends what it believes is current, and a stale S23 can overwrite a newer client-side prediction. In PLAY state only. Frequency is bounded by player block interactions, which is what makes it a usable ack channel.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: S23 itself is never flagged; it is server-originated truth. Anti-cheats use it to detect ghost blocks and reach abuse: a placed block whose S23 echo position lies outside the client's valid reach, or a C08 that gets no echo, feeds reach and scaffold checks. Clients that spoof block placement need the echo to keep their internal state honest, and the timing between C08 and S23 is a latency signal that modules like WatchdogJumpSprint fold into their pacing.

modules.name: WatchdogJumpSprint
modules.purpose: Use S23 block-change arrivals as placement acks to pace a Watchdog-targeted ice-block placement exploit inside Scaffold.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent listener checks for S23PacketBlockChange, sets start3 = true and increments the block counter. The PreMotionEvent handler then uses start3 to send a spoofed C08PacketPlayerBlockPlacement aimed at the player's own position with an ice ItemStack and randomized hit vectors, one-shotting start3 per ack so the exploit packet only fires after the server confirms a placement.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Reading S23 is passive and undetectable; the flag surface is the ice C08 itself, which is why the module only sends it after a genuine server ack and randomizes hitX/hitZ per send.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30's WatchdogJumpSprint does not reference S23 (only the script NetworkAPI does); the 6.2.4 variant is the only module in the corpus touching this packet.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on every client; the vanilla handler is the only consumer for most clients.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients ship the vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient.handleBlockChange untouched. The only divergence is Rise 6.2.4's scaffold mode intercepting the packet on its own event bus; Rise 6.x also exposes S23 to its scripting API (NetworkAPI.java).

anticheat.overview: S23 changes a single block and tells the client about it; it is the smallest world mutation in the protocol. For server-side anticheats it is still a compensated-world event: the cache must apply the change before checks judge the player, and scaffolding checks use the client-facing block state to validate placement supports. The corpus for S23 is the block-change pipeline again (Grim AirLiquidPlace and CompensatedWorld, NCP BlockChangeTracker and BlockChangeListener, Intave SingleBlockChangeReader, Kauri BlockUpdateHandler, FlopAC WrappedOutBlockChange), with the same world-cache pattern as S22 but per block.

checks.name: AirLiquidPlace (Grim)
checks.purpose: Flag block placements against air or liquid supports, which scaffolding and tower cheats produce.
checks.how_it_works: BlockPlaceListener reads the placement position and the compensated world's block state at the support location; it first checks blockHistory for recent START_DIGGING or netty-sync modifications at that position so instant-breaking plus placing in the same tick does not false. If the support is air or a no-place liquid, the check flags and resyncs the placed block. The file's comment documents years of false-positive archaeology around dig-then-place ordering.
checks.detects: Scaffold and tower modules that place against supports the client should not see as solid.
checks.variations: NCP blockplace fastplace and Grim's other scaffolding checks handle adjacent placement abuse; Kauri BlockD applies the same support validation against its replicated world.

checks.name: SingleBlockChangeReader (Intave)
checks.purpose: Decode the S23 packet into a single block position and block data for the block update tracker.
checks.how_it_works: AbstractPacketReader implementing BlockChanges: reads the BlockPosition field through a thread-local converter and returns the packet's block data as single-element lists, which the BlockUpdateTracker applies to the block cache and acknowledges.
checks.detects: Feeds the block cache for Intave's interaction ray-trace and physics checks; registered for BLOCK_CHANGE and BLOCK_BREAK in PacketReaders.
checks.variations: FlopAC WrappedOutBlockChange wraps the same packet for the reach processor; Hydro WorldTracker handleBlockChange and Kauri runUpdate(WrapperPlayServerBlockChange) are the equivalent apply paths.

checks.name: WrappedOutBlockChange (FlopAC)

checks.how_it_works: Resolves the NMS PacketPlayOutBlockChange class and its fields: legacy 1.7.10 x/y/z ints plus block and data fields, or the 1.8+ BlockPosition and IBlockData fields. process() populates a BaseBlockPosition from whichever layout the server version uses, and the constructor can build the packet from a Bukkit Block for server-side resync.
checks.detects: Feeds the compensated world and reach processor; a thin protocol layer rather than a flagging check.
checks.variations: Intave SingleBlockChangeReader and Kauri runUpdate(WrapperPlayServerBlockChange) do the same decode on different packet libraries.

checks.purpose: Ingest server block changes, including S23 single-block updates, into NCP's compensated BlockChangeTracker.

Single-block correction; bulk edits use S21 chunk data or S22 multi change.

packets.name: Block Action
packets.desc: Triggers a block action animation/event (chest open, piston extend, note block play, etc.).
packets.notes: Block actions: chest open/close, piston extend/retract, note block note, door open, dispenser click, etc.

writeup.p: S24 is a block-level event trigger: chest open/close, piston extend/retract, note block note, dispenser click, door open, beacon power. It carries a BlockPos, two action bytes (event ID and parameter) and the block type. The server broadcasts it from WorldServer's block-event queue (line 934 in the 1.8.9 corpus) to every player within 64 blocks of the position via sendToAllNear, which means it is a proximity event, not a per-player one.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleBlockAction calls PacketThreadUtil.func_180031_a then world.addBlockEvent(pos, blockType, data1, data2), which fans out to every IWorldAccess (render global, sound handler). The action bytes are interpreted per block: BlockChest uses data1 for open state, BlockNote uses data1 as the pitch index, BlockPiston uses data1 as the direction and data2 as extend/retract. The block type field is a cross-check; the client only plays the event if the local block matches.

Zero module hits in the 8-client corpus. The only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's script API (NetworkAPI.java), which registers the packet class so Lua scripts can listen, not a shipped module. The reason is structural: S24 describes transient animations, and every piece of information it carries (chest open state, piston position) is already derivable from the block state or from S23 block changes, so ESP and chest modules read the world instead of the packet stream.

S24 is entirely cosmetic and server-trusted, so there is no meaningful exploit surface. The 64-block broadcast radius is the only measurable property, and it is too coarse for tracking. A malicious server could spam S24 with garbage data bytes, but the vanilla handler bounds the damage to a single addBlockEvent call per packet, and the local-block cross-check drops mismatches, so there is no crash or desync primitive.

implementation.overview: A cosmetic block-event trigger (chests, pistons, note blocks) broadcast within 64 blocks. No module in the 8 clients consumes it; the only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's scripting API registration. Every fact it carries is derivable from block state, which is why clients ignore it.
implementation.server_handling: WorldServer keeps a BlockEventData queue; each tick it drains entries and sends S24 via mcServer.getConfigurationManager().sendToAllNear(x, y, z, 64.0D, dimensionId, packet). The 64.0 range is hardcoded in the server handler, matching the client's sound-render distance for block events. No rate limiting, no validation of the action bytes.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: BlockPos long, byte action ID, byte action parameter, VarInt block registry ID. The block type is read as a full Block object server-side via Block.getBlockById. The two bytes are raw event semantics decided by the block class, so the same byte values mean different things for a chest vs a piston.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not monitored. Block-action packets carry no player motion, timing or position claims, so anti-cheats ignore them entirely. The only conceivable use is a server-side sanity check that a piston event is accompanied by an actual piston block change, which no major anti-cheat implements for 1.8.9.
implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent exists on all clients but no module registers for S24 in the corpus.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients keep the vanilla handler. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 additionally expose S24 in their script NetworkAPI, which is a class-registration table, not module code.

anticheat.overview: The block-action packet (chest open, piston, note block) has a single corpus hit: Artemis registers a GPacketPlayServerBlockAction wrapper in its packet library so the abstraction layer can route the clientbound packet. The wrapper is a read-stub: its read() body is empty, and no Artemis check consumes the packet. No anticheat flags S24 or derives state from it, because it carries transient animation data with no movement, timing or position claim.

The read() method is empty, so the wrapper decodes no fields; it exists purely so the packet has a typed class in the cc.ghast.packet wrapper tree. No check in the corpus reads its payload.

checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus references S24PacketBlockAction or PacketPlayOutBlockAction.

Broadcast to players within 64 blocks; client ignores it if local block type mismatches.

packets.name: Block Break Animation
packets.desc: Shows block break progress (crack stages 0-9) on a block. Sent by all players, not just the miner.

fields.name: entityId
fields.desc: Entity breaking the block (-1 = stop animation)

writeup.p: S25 streams block-break progress: an entity ID (the breaker), a BlockPos, and a stage byte 0-9, with stage 10 (or entity ID -1) resetting the crack animation. WorldManager sends it to every player within 64 blocks of the broken block (corpus line 101), so other players see the crack overlay grow while someone mines. The client stores the per-position stage in WorldClient's damagedBlocks map and renders the crack texture at that stage.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleBlockBreakAnim dispatches through PacketThreadUtil and calls world.sendBlockBreakProgress(entityId, pos, stage), which updates the damagedBlocks map and re-renders the affected block faces. The animation is purely client-side state; the server never asks for an echo and never verifies the client saw it. A new S25 for the same position simply overwrites the previous stage.

Zero module hits in the 8-client corpus; only Rise 6.x's script NetworkAPI registers the class. XRay-style clients that suppress block rendering could in principle use S25 to hide crack overlays on ores, but none of the 8 clients do. The information is redundant for gameplay: the stage sequence is a faithful timing signal of another player's mining progress, yet no ESP or radar module in the corpus consumes it.

No meaningful surface. S25 is server-originated, unacknowledged, and its only effect is a texture overlay. The stage bytes are never validated by the client, but the worst a hostile server achieves is drawing a crack texture on a block. The one theoretical client-side value is latency inference: the rate of stage increments for a nearby miner is a coarse tick/ping signal, which is why the packet is occasionally mentioned in anticheat research, though no corpus module uses it.

implementation.overview: The break-progress animation stream (crack stages 0-9 per block). Zero modules in the 8 clients consume it; the only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's scripting API registration. Its data is redundant with block-change state and it carries no exploitable claim.
implementation.server_handling: WorldManager.func_180441_b (world-wide broadcast path) sends S25 to players within 64 blocks of the block being mined, keyed by the breaker's entity ID. The server emits a fresh packet per stage change as the player's digging progress advances, then a stage-10 reset when mining completes or is aborted. No validation of the breaker entity or the target block.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: VarInt entity ID (breaker), BlockPos long, byte stage. Stage 10 means reset/stop; the client also handles entity ID -1 as a reset. Because the handler overwrites damagedBlocks per position, out-of-order packets from a laggy server simply land on the latest stage, which is a self-healing property of the animation state.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not flagged. The packet exposes only animation state and cannot be spoofed client-side in a useful direction. Server-side, anti-cheats ignore it entirely; the only adjacent check is on the digging packets (C07) that precede it.
implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is available on all clients; none of the 8 register for S25.
implementation.client_variations: Vanilla handler in all 8 clients. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 add the class to their script NetworkAPI table only.

anticheat.overview: The block-break-animation packet has a single corpus hit: Artemis registers a GPacketPlayServerBlockBreakAnimation wrapper so its packet library recognizes the clientbound packet. No check reads it; the break stage sequence is redundant with the digging packets (C07) that anticheats actually monitor. The packet is unacknowledged, server-authored animation state, so no anticheat flags it.

Its read() decodes the packet into entityId, position and stage fields, but no check in the corpus consumes those fields. The wrapper is infrastructure, not a detection.

packets.name: Map Chunk Bulk
packets.desc: Sends multiple chunks at once. Used for initial world load and large area updates.

fields.name: chunks
fields.desc: Array of chunk data with X/Z/bitmask/compressed data

encoding: X, Z, bitmask, dataSize, compressed data
packets.notes: S26 is the bulk version of S21 — sends many chunks in a single packet. Used on world join and loading large areas. XRay modules also cancel S26 alongside S21 to prevent chunk updates.

writeup.p: S26 is the bulk chunk loader: one packet carrying many chunk columns with a shared sky-light flag. Each column is x/z ints, a 16-bit section bitmask, a VarInt data size, then the compressed section data. The server builds it in EntityPlayerMP when a player joins or moves between chunk groups (corpus line 330), batching all newly-loaded columns so the client can decode them in one pass. It is the load-bearing packet for world join and teleport.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleMapChunkBulk loops the columns, calls doPreChunk to mark each as loaded, invalidates the block receive region, then reads each chunk via the shared PacketUtil.readCompressed path and loads it into the world. Sky-light presence is decided once per packet by the boolean flag. The client then re-renders the whole batch; on 1.8.9 this is one of the few handlers that visibly blocks the render thread while decompressing.

Zero module hits in the 8-client corpus. The only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's script NetworkAPI class registration. The packet metadata for S26 mentions XRay cancelling bulk chunks, but in these 8 clients no XRay module references S26PacketMapChunkBulk at all (Tenacity's XRay touches S21PacketChunkData, not S26). The absence is practical: cancelling S26 on a join breaks the world wholesale, and the ores an XRay wants to hide are already filtered in the chunk-render path, not at the packet layer.

The real abuse surface is server-to-client: a malicious server can send an S26 with an enormous uncompressed payload or a huge column count to stall the client's decompression loop, a classic 1.8 lag-machine vector. Client-side there is nothing to exploit; the packet is inbound truth. Chunk-banning clients that want to blank specific regions do it by editing the column bitmask before the vanilla handler runs, which no module in this corpus implements for S26.

implementation.overview: The bulk chunk-load packet used on join and teleport. Zero modules in the 8 clients consume it; the only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's scripting API registration. Its payload is inbound world truth, and the exploitable direction is server to client.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP gathers pending ChunkCoordIntPair columns and constructs S26 when the load queue is flushed. The sky-light boolean is set once from the world's dimension provider. There is no per-packet size cap in vanilla; the server trusts its own chunk generation. A client can request chunks (C03 position movement) but cannot dictate the bulk layout.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: boolean skyLightSent, VarInt column count, then per column: int x, int z, short bitmask, VarInt data length, compressed byte[]. The bitmask is a 16-bit section selector; sections absent from the mask are inherited from the previous chunk state. The compressed payload is zlib via PacketUtil.readCompressed, with the data length prefix on the wire.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat inspects S26 content; it is inbound and unspoofable. The relevant protection is on the client: crash-patch modules that bound the column count or payload size. None of the 8 clients ship one for S26 specifically; Tenacity's AntiExploit covers explosion and particle floods instead.
implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on all clients; no module registers for S26 in the corpus.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients keep the vanilla handler. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 expose S26 in the script NetworkAPI table only. Tenacity's XRay/Search chunk filtering is done against S21PacketChunkData, not S26.

anticheat.overview: S26 is the bulk chunk variant of S21 used by 1.7 and 1.8 servers: one packet carries several chunk columns with a shared skylight flag. Anticheats treat it exactly like the single-chunk packet: the bytes are decoded into the compensated world (Grim PacketWorldReaderEight handleMapChunkBulk, Intave MapChunkBulkReader, Kauri World update via ChunkDataBulk, Truthful CompensatedWorld via the global chunk cache), and the same xray and world-downloader protections apply (Photon WorldDownloaderSentinel). The corpus for S26 is therefore the replication pipeline with bulk-specific readers.

checks.name: PacketWorldReaderEight map-chunk-bulk (Grim)
checks.purpose: Decode the S26 bulk packet into Grim's compensated world, column by column.
checks.how_it_works: handleMapChunkBulk reads the skylight boolean, column count, and per-column x/z and section masks, then for each column decodes the 16 sections with the 1.8 palette reader, skips the 256 biome bytes plus 2048 block-light (and 2048 sky-light when the flag is set) per section, and merges the column into the compensated world cache with the transaction id. The dispatch lives in BasePacketWorldReader, which routes chunk-data-bulk packets here.
checks.detects: Feeds the ground, collision and phase simulation the same way handleMapChunk does for S21; bulk loading cannot bypass the cache.
checks.variations: Intave MapChunkBulkReader reads only the per-column x/z coordinate arrays and hands them to the block cache; Kauri runUpdate(WrapperPlayServerChunkDataBulk) applies bulk columns inside keepalive actions; Hydro WorldTracker handleChunkBulk stores the sections in its chunk map.

checks.name: MapChunkBulkReader (Intave)
checks.purpose: Read the chunk coordinates of every column in the S26 bulk packet for Intave's chunk coordinate tracking.
checks.how_it_works: ChunkCoordinateReader implementation that clones the packet's x and z integer arrays, giving the block cache the coordinates of every column in the bulk; PacketReaders registers it as setup(MAP_CHUNK_BULK, MapChunkBulkReader::new). The coordinates feed the multi-chunk block cache that physics and interaction checks use.
checks.detects: Keeps the block cache's chunk grid in sync when whole regions load at once; no direct flag.
checks.variations: Grim handleMapChunkBulk and Kauri runUpdate(WrapperPlayServerChunkDataBulk) decode the full columns; ChunkCoordinateReader is Intave's shared interface with MapChunkReader for S21.

checks.name: WorldDownloaderSentinel (Photon)
checks.purpose: Detect WorldDownloader mods at the wdl channel handshake and disable their chunk caching and saving.
checks.how_it_works: Same module as the S21 entry: it answers wdl|INIT with wdl|CONTROL packets that disable general saving, chunk caching, entity, tile-entity and container saving per config, then runs the sentinel detection. Bulk chunk delivery (S26) is the mod's highest-bandwidth input, so the module closes the hole before the client can persist anything.
checks.detects: WorldDownloader clients on 1.7 and 1.8 servers, where the bulk packet makes whole-region capture trivial.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus speaks the wdl channels; Negativity and LightAntiCheat approximate the protection with region bypass and unloaded-chunk checks.

checks.name: Chunk column cache (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Store the 16x384x16 block grid of each replicated chunk so Kauri's checks can query block states.
checks.how_it_works: Chunk holds a synchronized WrappedBlock[16][384][16] array keyed by chunk x/z; updateBlock writes into it (with the negative-y offset for 1.18 worlds) and getBlockAt returns an Optional of the block, mapping coordinates into the local grid. World fills these chunks from chunk-data and chunk-data-bulk packets via runUpdate, and BlockUpdateHandler routes S22 and S23 updates into the same storage.
checks.detects: Supplies block truth for Kauri's phase, reach and interaction checks; the S26 corpus hit is the ChunkDataBulk consumption in BlockUpdateHandler that fills these grids.
checks.variations: Truthful CompensatedWorld delegates to a global world cache of ChunkSnapshot objects with a last-chunk access cache; Hydro WorldTracker stores PacketEvents BaseChunk arrays; Grim Column records hold BaseChunk[] plus the transaction id.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x26 bulk loader: skylight bool, VarInt column count, then per-column data.
Each column sends X and Z ints plus a 16-bit section bitmask and compressed payload.
Used for join and large loads; column layout reuses the S21 section encoding.

packets.name: Explosion
packets.desc: Server notifies the client of an explosion (TNT, creeper, bed in Nether/End, etc).

fields.name: motionX/Y/Z
fields.desc: Player knockback velocity from the explosion

packets.notes: Affected blocks are sent as byte triplets (x, y, z) relative to the explosion center. The client applies particle effects and knockback to the local player.

writeup.p: S27 is the server's explosion broadcast: center x/y/z floats, strength, a list of affected block positions encoded as byte triplets relative to the center, and a per-player knockback vector as three floats. WorldServer sends one S27 per affected player (corpus line 901), with the knockback floats computed per player from the explosion's player knockback map. The client both renders the destroyed blocks and applies the knockback vector to the local player, which is why it is the second half of every velocity module's packet filter alongside S12PacketEntityVelocity.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleExplosion builds an Explosion object from the center and strength, calls doExplosionB(true) to spawn particles and sounds, then adds the packet's motion floats straight into thePlayer.motionX/Y/Z. Critically, the knockback is applied unconditionally on the main thread; there is no entity-ID check because the packet is per-player. That makes S27 the standard fallback for anti-cheat velocity implementations: servers that hide S12 knockback in explosion packets still deliver S27, so clients must filter both.

S27 is the most-touched clientbound packet in this batch. Every velocity module in the corpus filters it: Memeware and Nekoware cancel it in a shared combat/Velocity pattern, Rise 5.99's Velocity scales or cancels it, Sigma's AntiVelocity handles it in basic mode, Spicy's AntiKnockback cancels it, and Tenacity's VelocityModule scales it by the same horizontal/vertical settings as S12. Rise 6.x splits this into a suite of per-server modes (Standard, Vulcan, Redesky, UniversoCraft, BufferAbuse), all of which touch S27. Movement modules also consume it: Rise 5.99's Fly (Minemenclub) and LongJump (Hycraft, Vulcan) cancel S27 to control knockback timing, and Sigma's Fly uses it for explosion-based boosting. LiquidSense Dev's PingSpoof imports S27PacketExplosion but never references it in the module body; the import is dead scaffolding from the upstream LiquidBounce PingSpoof.

The exploit surface is bidirectional. Client-side, scaling or cancelling the knockback floats is invisible to the server because S27 is one-way; anti-cheats can only infer from resulting motion, which is why velocity modules keep the S12 and S27 paths symmetric. Server-side, a hostile server can send S27 with huge motion floats (Rise's ExplosionCheck guards against motion >= Byte.MAX_VALUE) or enormous affected-block lists to stall the client's block-position loop, which is exactly the flood Tenacity's AntiExploit rate-limits. Rise's ItemDamageComponent also counts S27 as a damage source to resync the player's health model.

implementation.overview: The explosion broadcast that carries both destroyed-block positions and a per-player knockback vector. Every velocity module in the corpus filters it alongside S12PacketEntityVelocity; Rise 6.x dedicates five per-server modes to it, movement modules cancel it to shape knockback, and Tenacity's AntiExploit rate-limits it against crash floods. The packet is one-way, so all client abuse is invisible to the server.
implementation.server_handling: WorldServer.createExplosion computes the affected block list and a per-player knockback Vec3 from the blast, then sends a dedicated S27 to each EntityPlayerMP (corpus line 901). The knockback map is filled only for players the explosion actually hits, so players outside the blast receive an S27 with zero motion floats but still get the visual. No client acknowledgement and no rate limiting in vanilla.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: three floats (center), float strength, int record count, then count byte triplets as offsets from the center (each block position is center + signed byte), then three floats of player motion. The triplet encoding caps the block list extent at 127 blocks from the center, which is why ExplosionCheck thresholds at Byte.MAX_VALUE. PLAY state only.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats cannot see the mutation, so they infer velocity removal from motion deltas: after a flagged hit they compare the player's acceleration against the expected knockback curve. That is why legit-looking modes exist: Tenacity's horizontal/vertical percentages, Rise 6.x's per-server modes, and movement modules that cancel S27 only while airborne. The Rise 6.x BufferAbuse and PingSpoofComponent keep the S27 path consistent with transaction buffering, since a desynced knockback stream is a strong velocity flag on Vulcan and Watchdog.

modules.name: Velocity / AntiKnockback
modules.purpose: Cancel or scale explosion knockback so hits from TNT, creepers and beds apply reduced or zero motion.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent filter: if the packet is S27PacketExplosion, either cancel it outright or multiply motionX/Y/Z by horizontal/vertical percentage settings before the vanilla handler applies them. Tenacity scales in place; Memeware/Nekoware/Spicy cancel; Rise 5.99 and Sigma switch behavior per configured mode.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: In-place scaling is safer than cancel: the server still sees a packet pass and the client motion delta stays consistent with a legitimately weaker explosion. Full cancel flags on anti-cheats that measure knockback absence, which is why modes like Rise's Minemenclub variants only zero S27 while airborne.
modules.variations: Memeware and Nekoware cancel S27 in combat/Velocity. Rise 5.99 scales per mode (Cancel/Push/etc.). Sigma AntiVelocity handles S27 in basic mode only. Spicy AntiKnockback cancels it. All six clients pair the S27 filter with the S12PacketEntityVelocity filter in the same handler.

modules.name: StandardVelocity / VulcanVelocity / RedeskyVelocity / UniversoCraftVelocity / BufferAbuseVelocity
modules.purpose: Per-server velocity modes that each define their own S27 (and S12) handling, from full cancel to percentage scaling to transaction-buffered removal.
modules.how_it_works: Each mode is a Rise Mode<Velocity> subclass with an @EventLink PacketReceiveEvent listener. StandardVelocity scales or cancels S27 based on horizontal/vertical sliders and an Explosion Ignore boolean. VulcanVelocity, RedeskyVelocity and UniversoCraftVelocity cancel or mutate S27 to match each server's knockback checks. BufferAbuseVelocity folds S27 into the client's transaction-buffer manipulation so the knockback stream stays consistent while transactions are delayed.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The per-server split exists because each anti-cheat (Vulcan, Redesky, UniversoCraft, etc.) measures knockback differently. Percentage modes are low-risk; full-cancel modes only run when the server's velocity check is known to be weak, and BufferAbuse keeps S27 consistent with the buffered transaction stream so the two cannot be cross-correlated.
modules.variations: The same five modes exist in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 with near-identical bodies; 6.2.4 adds WatchdogPredictionVelocity and Grim-family modes that do not reference S27. PingSpoofComponent in both versions lists S27PacketExplosion in the velocity packet class set it buffers, and ItemDamageComponent counts S27 as a damage input.

modules.name: Fly / LongJump
modules.purpose: Cancel explosion knockback inside movement exploits so a mid-air boost or long jump is not interrupted by server-applied velocity.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 5.99's LongJump cancels S27 (and S12) in onPacketReceive when the Hycraft or Vulcan mode is active; its Fly cancels S27 in the Minemenclub mode. Sigma's Fly treats S27 as a velocity source for explosion-boost movement. The cancel keeps the server's knockback from perturbing the carefully staged motion values the module computes each tick.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling S27 mid-jump is one of the oldest velocity tells because the motion discontinuity is measurable. These modes rely on the server's knockback check being absent or on the jump's speed exceeding what the anti-cheat expects, which is why they are mode-gated to specific servers.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 Fly handles S27 in Minemenclub mode; Sigma Fly uses S27 as an explosion boost input in its packet handler; Sigma's InfiniteAura imports S27 (the corpus shows the import only, unused in the visible body).

modules.name: AntiExploit
modules.purpose: Block crash-exploit S27 floods from malicious servers by bounding explosion strength and arrival rate.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent handler: cancels S27 when abs(strength) > 1 or when two explosions arrive within 1 ms, printing a blocked-exploit chat message. The same handler covers resource-pack, camera, particle and teleport crash vectors with the same pattern, and a separate packet-count throttle kicks the client-side watchdog when inbound packet rate exceeds 100/sec.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Not a cheat at all, it is client-side self-defense against lag machines. Nothing flags it because it only cancels inbound packets. Its strength heuristic is coarser than Rise's ExplosionCheck, which thresholds the motion floats at Byte.MAX_VALUE instead of the strength float.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 ship the equivalent as a security feature, ExplosionCheck.java, which cancels S27 when any motion float exceeds Byte.MAX_VALUE (mirroring the wire format's signed-byte block offsets).

modules.name: Debugger
modules.purpose: Print explosion velocity values to chat as part of a packet-level debug overlay for development and bypass work.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent handler: when the Velocity toggle is on and the packet is S27PacketExplosion, prints DeltaX/DeltaY/DeltaZ from func_149149_c / func_149144_d / func_149147_e, the same motion floats velocity modules mutate. The debug output shows the exact knockback vector a server sends, letting a developer tune a velocity mode's scaling against real traffic.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Read-only; prints to chat only. It exists to make the velocity suite's tuning data visible, and it is the only module in the corpus that reads S27 without mutating or cancelling it.
modules.variations: Identical in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4. Rise 5.99 has a PacketDebugger module for the same role, but the corpus shows no S27 reference in it.

modules.name: PingSpoof (unused import)
modules.purpose: Documented for completeness: LiquidSense Dev's PingSpoof imports S27PacketExplosion but does not process the packet in this build.
modules.how_it_works: The module buffers C0FPacketConfirmTransaction and C00PacketKeepAlive on the send side and flushes them after a random delay on the update loop. S27PacketExplosion appears only in the import list (line 23) and is never referenced in the module body, so no explosion handling exists.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketEvent (onPacket) for C0F/C00 buffering; no S27 hook.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No detection relevance: an unused import changes nothing on the wire.
modules.variations: No other corpus client carries a dead S27 import in a ping-spoof module; Rise 6.x PingSpoofComponent genuinely buffers S27 in its velocity tuple.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the universal hook: every S27 consumer in the corpus registers on the receive path before the vanilla handler applies the knockback.
implementation.client_variations: Classic clients mutate or cancel the packet object inside the event. Rise 5.99/6.x call event.setPacket / event.setCancelled on their own event bus. Tenacity and Spicy use IEventListener-style lambda handlers. Rise 6.x additionally routes S27 through components (ItemDamageComponent, PingSpoofComponent) and a security layer (ExplosionCheck) in addition to modules. LiquidSense Dev touches S27 only through an unused import in PingSpoof.java; its velocity handling does not exist in this build.

anticheat.overview: S27 is the explosion packet: it carries the knockback vector the client must apply plus the destroyed block records. Anticheats read the velocity component on the OUT side and require it in the client's subsequent motion, exactly like entity knockback, and the block records give simulation anticheats the world mutation the explosion caused. The corpus shows two approaches: Grim brackets the explosion vector with transactions and flags when the prediction misses it, while NCP and Intave read the vector straight off the wire (NCP feeds it into the moving velocity model, Intave into its motion tracker).

checks.name: ExplosionHandler / AntiExplosion (Grim)
checks.purpose: Requires the client's simulated motion to include the explosion knockback vector, flagging players who ignore it.
checks.how_it_works: On the OUT explosion packet, applies the destroyed block records to the compensated world (with 1.21.2+ handling where blocks arrive via separate block-change packets) and records the knockback vector in a transaction-bracketed queue. On each prediction complete, the offset between the player's actual movement and the required explosion velocity is measured; offsets above the configured threshold flag with a setback, and knockback-overridden explosions are exempted by comparing transaction ordering.
checks.detects: Anti-explosion and velocity-cancel cheats that ignore explosion knockback, and world-desync from missing block destruction.
checks.variations: NCP and Intave read the vector directly; Grim additionally simulates the block destruction, which is unique in the corpus.

checks.name: VelocityAdapter (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Feeds the explosion knockback vector into NCP's moving velocity model so survivalfly and other movement checks allow it.
checks.how_it_works: ProtocolLib adapter on the OUT explosion packet: reads the three velocity floats (indices 1-3), skips packets with zero velocity, and adds the vector to the player's MovingData with the ORIGIN_EXPLOSION and ADDITIVE flags. The moving checks then know the player was legitimately pushed and subtract the explosion velocity from their expected motion.
checks.detects: Anti-explosion cheats are caught indirectly: without the recorded push, the movement checks treat the explosion's motion as impossible.
checks.variations: Grim requires the exact vector in prediction; NCP adds it to an expected-motion model that moving checks consume.

checks.name: ExplosionReader (Intave)
checks.purpose: Reads and rewrites the explosion knockback vector into the Intave motion abstraction for both simulation and mitigation.
checks.how_it_works: ProtocolLib reader over the OUT explosion packet: on pre-1.21.3 servers it reads velocity floats 1-3, on 1.21.3+ it reads the optional motion vector, converting either into a Motion value; setMotion writes the value back. The motion feeds Intave's fake-player simulation and its mitigation layer, which can resend corrected motion.
checks.detects: Anti-explosion and knockback reduction, detected through the simulation's motion comparison and mitigated by rewriting the sent vector.
checks.variations: NCP reads floats only; Intave supports both wire formats and can write the vector back, which NCP never does.

wiki_notes: The packet is sent for explosions from creepers, TNT and ghast fireballs, carrying center, strength, affected-block records and a per-player knockback vector.

MCP 1.8.9 S27PacketExplosion implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleExplosion; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readFloat, readInt.
1.8.9 callers: WorldServer.newExplosion sends new S27PacketExplosion (line 1019): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/world/WorldServer.java

packets.name: Effect
packets.desc: Plays a sound effect or particle effect at a position (without a named sound).

fields.name: disableRelativeVolume
fields.desc: If true, plays at full volume regardless of position

packets.notes: Effect IDs: 1000-1023 (sound events), 1500-2004 (particle events). Unlike S29 (named sound via resource location), S28 uses numeric IDs.

writeup.p: S28 is the numeric sound/particle effect packet: an int effect type, a BlockPos, an int data value, and a boolean that forces server-wide volume. Effect IDs are split into ranges: 1000-1023 for sound events (anvil, click, door) and 1500-2004 for particle/block events (smoke, portal, beacon, chest open particle). WorldManager sends it either to players near the position (64-block radius, volume-attenuated) or to every player when the server-wide flag is set (corpus lines 82/86).

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleEffect branches on the server-wide flag: isSoundServerwide routes to world.func_175669_a (global sound), otherwise world.playAuxSFX(type, pos, data), which maps the numeric ID to a sound or particle burst and plays it with position-based volume. The data int is effect-specific (block ID for break particles, pitch for sounds). There is no client feedback path; the packet is fire-and-forget.

Zero module hits in the 8-client corpus; the only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's script NetworkAPI registration. The packet metadata mentions ESP tracking record players and particles, but no module in these 8 clients implements it. The reason is redundancy: effect sounds and particles are transient and position-derived, and anything a module could learn (a chest opening nearby, a beacon activating) is already visible through block state or S24.

The exploitable direction is server to client: a malicious server can spam S28 with high-volume sound IDs or particle-heavy IDs to annoy or degrade the client (the classic record-spam or smoke-spam lag nuisance). The client applies each effect without rate limiting, which is why crash-patch modules bound effect rates. No corpus module does this for S28; Tenacity's AntiExploit covers the particle flood via S2APacketParticles instead, which is the named-particle equivalent.

implementation.overview: The numeric sound/particle effect packet with a server-wide volume flag. Zero modules in the 8 clients consume it; the only non-vanilla reference is Rise 6.x's scripting API registration. Transient, position-derived and fire-and-forget, it carries nothing a module needs that block state does not already provide.
implementation.server_handling: WorldManager.func_180439_a sends S28 to players within 64 blocks with serverWide=false; func_180440_b sends it to all players with serverWide=true (used for dimension-wide events like beacon activation or the wither spawn). The server never validates the effect ID or data against a whitelist, so any int in range goes through. No rate limit in vanilla.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: int effect type, BlockPos long, int data, boolean serverWide. The effect type is a raw int, unlike S29PacketSoundEffect which carries a resource location; this is the 'numeric' counterpart. The boolean is a plain byte on the wire (writeBoolean/readBoolean). The data int is interpreted per effect ID, so the same int means block ID for break particles and pitch for sounds.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not monitored. Effects carry no player state, and the only abuse is nuisance flooding, which anti-cheats handle by rate-limiting inbound effect packets rather than flagging players. Client-side crash patches treat S28 and S2A as the same threat class (audio/particle floods), but none of the 8 clients ships that guard for S28 specifically.
implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is available on all clients; no module registers for S28 in the corpus.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients keep the vanilla handler. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 register S28 in the script NetworkAPI table only. Tenacity's AntiExploit limits the S2APacketParticles flood but not the numeric S28 path.

anticheat.overview: The numeric world-effect packet has zero real hits in the corpus. The ac-mined file for S28 is dominated by keyword noise: the grep term 'Effect' surfaced potion-effect code (PotionEffectType, hasPotionEffect, banEffect) across Frequency, Negativity, Grim, Hydro, FlopAC and others, but none of those files reference S28PacketEffect or PacketPlayOutWorldEvent. No anticheat processes the packet, which is consistent with its role: a fire-and-forget clientbound sound or particle trigger carrying no player claim.

wiki_notes: The trailing boolean disables distance-based volume falloff so effects such as wither spawn, enderdragon death and end-portal opening play correctly, and record playback at one location overwrites any record already playing there.

MCP 1.8.9 S28PacketEffect implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleEffect; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBlockPos, readBoolean, readInt.
1.8.9 callers: WorldManager.playAuxSFX sends new S28PacketEffect (line 88): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/world/WorldManager.java

packets.name: Sound Effect
packets.desc: Plays a named sound at a world position with volume and pitch.

writeup.p: Server-to-client broadcast of a named sound at a fixed-point position. The server computes a delivery radius of 16 blocks, scaled by volume when volume exceeds 1.0, and fans the packet out through ConfigurationManager.sendToAllNear. The client handler converts the x8 fixed-point ints back to doubles and hands the call to World.playSound. Because the sound name is an arbitrary server-controlled string, the field is both a gameplay input and a data-injection surface for anything downstream that logs or parses it.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleSoundEffect does PacketThreadUtil.func_180031_a (main-thread marshalling) then World.playSound(name, x/8, y/8, z/8, volume, pitch/63, false). The pitch arrives as an unsigned byte with 63 meaning normal pitch; the client divides by 63.0F. Server side the packet is created by WorldManager.playSound and playSoundAtEntity, and by /playsound (CommandPlaySound), which converts double coordinates to the x8 int encoding. Netty reads the name with a 256-char cap via readStringFromBuffer(256).

Only two real handlers exist across the 8 clients, and neither is a sound-ESP. Rise 5.99's Disabler, in its HypixelSlime mode, cancels the mob.slime.big sound to strip the Hypixel double-jump slime indicator. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 route the packet through LoggerRCECheck, a security feature that matches the sound name against a ${...} pattern to catch Log4j RCE attempts (CVE-2021-44228): sound names are logged by the client logger, so a crafted name is an injection vector. No client in the corpus tracks sounds for ESP purposes.

The sound name string is the interesting field. It passes through String formatting and logger calls on both ends, which is exactly the Log4j RCE chain that LoggerRCECheck defends. Volume has no clamp on the wire, so a malicious server can send volume values far above 1.0 and inflate the client-side audio range beyond the 16-block visibility radius. The pitch byte is unsigned, so values above 127 encode negative pitches when interpreted as signed, a quirk modules rarely bother with.

implementation.overview: A pure world-effect broadcast: named sound, x8 fixed-point position, volume, pitch byte. The 8 clients barely touch it. The only module-grade hit is Rise 5.99's Disabler cancelling the Hypixel slime jump sound; Rise 6.x handles it as a Log4j RCE scan surface rather than as audio.
implementation.server_handling: WorldManager.playSound sends to all players within 16 blocks, or 16*volume when volume > 1.0F, on the same dimension. CommandPlaySound builds the packet from parsed coordinates (x*8, y*8, z*8) and clamps pitch to 0..255 before writing. The client handler marshals to the main thread, then plays the sound with pitch = raw byte / 63.0F. No server-side rate limit exists; sound spam is only bounded by the 256-char name cap and the per-packet cost.
implementation.protocol_notes: Encoding order: String name (max 256), int x*8, int y*8, int z*8, float volume, unsigned byte pitch. The y field is initialized to Integer.MAX_VALUE in the no-arg constructor as a sentinel for the client-side y-clamping fallback (field_149218_c). In 1.8.9 MCP this packet predates the generic Packet<T> signature, so it implements raw Packet and does a double dispatch through processPacket.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats do not flag sound packets; they are cosmetic. The abuse surface is the name string, and the relevant defense is client-side: Rise's LoggerRCECheck pattern-matches ${...} in the name to block Log4j RCE payloads that would otherwise execute through the client's logging pipeline. Because the packet is clientbound and server-trusted, there is no bypass trade-off: a compromised server can always send it, so the check is a pure filter.

modules.name: Disabler (HypixelSlime sound cancel)
modules.purpose: Cancel the mob.slime.big sound on Hypixel so the double-jump slime indicator never plays.
modules.how_it_works: In the HypixelSlime mode branch of the packet receive handler, every S29 is type-checked; if the sound name equals mob.slime.big the event is cancelled. The same mode also cancels SLIME-type S2APacketParticles and S1FPacketSetExperience, so the whole Hypixel double-jump visual cluster is stripped together.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Zero detection risk: cancelling a clientbound sound is invisible to the server. The only observable effect is the missing slime sound on the local client.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 do not carry this mode; their only S29 reference is LoggerRCECheck in the security pipeline.

modules.name: LoggerRCECheck (security)
modules.purpose: Block Log4j RCE payloads carried in the sound name string.
modules.how_it_works: A SecurityFeature registered in Rise's packet security chain. On every packet it checks the S29 sound name against the regex .*\$\{[^}]*}.*. A match returns true, which drops the packet before it reaches the game logic or any logging path. The same check also guards S02PacketChat text. It is a security component, not a toggleable user module.
modules.vanilla_hook: Security pipeline handle(Packet) invoked per received packet.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Not anti-cheat related. It defends the client against malicious servers; the cost is a regex match on every S29 and S02, which is negligible at server tick rates.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30 (com/alan/clients/security/impl/LoggerRCECheck.java). The packet class is also listed in Rise's NetworkAPI script bridge, which exposes it to JavaScript scripts but adds no game logic.

implementation.general_hooks: Both handlers sit on the packet receive path: Rise 5.99 uses PacketReceiveEvent, Rise 6.x uses the security chain that pre-filters every inbound packet before module dispatch.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 mutates/cancels via event.setCancelled on PacketReceiveEvent. Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 moved packet filtering into the SecurityFeature abstraction, which returns a boolean from handle(Packet) and lets the pipeline decide whether to drop.

anticheat.overview: The named-sound packet is the one sound packet in this family that a major anticheat actively intercepts. NoCheatPlus ships SoundDistance, a ProtocolLib listener on PacketType.Play.Server.NAMED_SOUND_EFFECT that cancels wither, enderdragon and lightning sounds when the player is too far from the sound origin, which removes fake distant-boss audio and reduces client noise. The rest of the corpus is registration plumbing: Artemis maps the packet name to a wrapper interface, and Negativity lists it in its packet-type registry. Bukkit playSound calls in Hydro, TruthfulAC and SafeguardAC are anticheat GUI sounds, not S29 handling.

checks.name: SoundDistance (NoCheatPlus)
checks.purpose: Cancel named sound packets for wither, enderdragon and lightning events when the player is beyond the configured audible radius of the sound origin.
checks.how_it_works: A ProtocolLib BaseAdapter registered at ListenerPriority.LOW on PacketType.Play.Server.NAMED_SOUND_EFFECT (S29). It maintains a hardcoded set of boss and weather sound names (pre-1.9 resource keys plus 1.9 and 1.21 enum names), matched against the packet's sound field via getStrings().read(0) on legacy servers or the Bukkit access matchSounds() on modern ones. For a match it computes the squared horizontal distance between the player and the packet's x8 fixed-point position and cancels the packet when that exceeds the configured soundDistanceSq limit, counting each cancel on the packet.sound.cancel counter.
checks.detects: Server-side sound spoofing where distant boss spawns or weather events are audible to players who should not hear them; the check doubles as client-noise reduction.
checks.variations: No other anticheat implements a sound-distance check. Artemis registers the packet family in its repository (PacketPlayServerSoundEffectNamed at SERVER_PLAY + 64, plus custom, entity and stop variants) and Negativity lists NAMED_SOUND_EFFECT in its PacketType registry, but neither reads sound payloads.

checks.name: Named sound wrapper registration (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Register the named sound effect packet in Artemis's packet repository so the abstraction layer can dispatch S29 to typed wrapper interfaces.
checks.how_it_works: PacketRepository maps SERVER_PLAY + 64 to PacketPlayServerSoundEffectNamed, a marker interface extending PacketServer. The packet generator's HardcodeMap associates the NMS name PacketPlayOutNamedSoundEffect with the same interface. The interface declares no fields or methods; Artemis only needs the packet to be recognized and routed.
checks.detects: Nothing. This is packet-library plumbing; no Artemis check consumes the sound name, position, volume or pitch.
checks.variations: Artemis registers the full S29 family: custom, entity, named and stop sound variants. Elikill58-Negativity maps NAMED_SOUND_EFFECT in its universal PacketType enum used by its packet listeners.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x29: sound name string max 256 chars, position ints at x times 8.
Followed by float volume and unsigned byte pitch where 63 means normal pitch.
Server fans out within 16 blocks, extended by volume above 1.0.

MCP 1.8.9 S29PacketSoundEffect implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleSoundEffect; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readFloat, readInt, readStringFromBuffer, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: CommandPlaySound.? sends new S29PacketSoundEffect (line 118) +2 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/command/CommandPlaySound.java

packets.name: Particles
packets.desc: Spawns particle effects at a position with offset, speed, and count.
packets.notes: Particle names: barriar, blockcrack, blockdust, bubble, cloud, crit, damageindicator, depthSuspend, drippingLava, drippingWater, droplet, enchantmenttable, endRod, explode, fireworkSpark, flame, footstep, happyVillager, heart, hugeexplosion, iconcrack, instantSpell, largeSmoke, lava, magicCrit, mobAppearance, mobSpell, mobSpellAmbient, note, portal, reddust, slime, smokeSpelling, snowballpoof, snowshovel, spell, suspended, sweepAttack, take, totem, townaura, wake, witchMagic.

writeup.p: Spawns a particle burst at a world position with random offset, speed, and count. The particle name is a String that the client maps to an EnumParticleTypes; a trailing varint array carries iconcrack/blockcrack item and block data. Server-side it is the workhorse of WorldServer.spawnParticle, which batches particles into a single packet and sends it with a long-distance flag when the emitter is far from the viewer. The client handler walks the count in a loop, so a large count is a direct CPU/GPU cost on the receiving machine.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleParticles marshals to the main thread, then calls clientWorldController.spawnParticle. When count is 0 the offset floats are treated as a single particle's velocity; otherwise the offsets are random spread and count particles are spawned. A Throwable around the spawn call logs 'Could not spawn particle effect' instead of crashing. The server path (WorldServer.spawnParticle) constructs one S2A per batch and uses sendToAllNear with a 512-block radius when longDistance is set.

Five distinct uses in the 8 clients. (1) Memeware 7.3 Disabler cancels every S2A unconditionally, an anti-lag/anti-crash blanket filter. (2) Rise 5.99 Disabler cancels only SLIME-type particles in its HypixelSlime mode. (3) Rise 6.x ParticleDistanceComponent, a performance component, drops any particle further than 6 blocks from the player. (4) Rise 6.x ParticleCheck, a security feature, token-buckets particle counts and drops floods. (5) Tenacity 6.0 AntiExploit cancels particles with extreme speed or count, and Sigma 4.11 Criticals skips S2A inside its own packet state machine so the crit-trigger logic is not disturbed.

Particle floods are a classic client-crash vector: a server sends one S2A with a huge count or repeated packets, and the client spawns thousands of entities per tick. Anti-cheat servers also use particle bursts as visual flags for cheaters (crit particles on KillAura, etc.). Client defenses range from blanket cancellation (Memeware) to rate limiting (Rise ParticleCheck: accumulate count, drain 6 per packet, cap 150, drop over 100) to heuristic drops (Tenacity: speed >= 1 or count > 1). The trade-off is visibility: aggressive cancellation hides legitimate gameplay effects.

implementation.overview: The particle broadcast packet, and the only one of the six where client defense depth actually shows: blanket cancel (Memeware), selective cancel (Rise 5.99 slime mode), distance culling (Rise 6.x performance component), flood rate limiting (Rise 6.x ParticleCheck), and crash heuristics (Tenacity AntiExploit). Sigma's Criticals skips it inside its packet state machine.
implementation.server_handling: WorldServer.spawnParticle builds one S2APacketParticles per batch with particle type, longDistance flag, x/y/z floats, three offset floats, speed, count, and a varint data array. It sends via ConfigurationManager.sendToAllNear (radius 512 when longDistance, else 32). NetHandlerPlayClient.handleParticles then loops count times through clientWorldController.spawnParticle, which is where a flood becomes a client-side hang. No server-side cap exists on count in vanilla 1.8.9.
implementation.protocol_notes: Encoding: String particle name, boolean longDistance, float x, float y, float z, float offsetX, float offsetY, float offsetZ, float speed, int count, then a varint-length int array of particle arguments used only by iconcrack and blockcrack. The name is read with readStringFromBuffer(64). Count 0 is special: offsets become velocity for a single particle. The packet was introduced in 1.8 with the EnumParticleTypes refactor that replaced the older string-only effect packets.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats use particles as a side channel rather than flagging the packet itself: critical-hit particles around a target are evidence for killaura checks on servers that render them. The client-side countermeasures here are defensive, not evasive. The interesting tension is Rise ParticleCheck's accumulator: it treats particle arrival as a budget (drain 6 per packet, cap 150, drop when the bucket exceeds 100), which keeps normal combat particles while killing flood attempts. Blanket cancels (Memeware) trade all particle feedback for stability.

modules.name: Disabler (particle cancel)
modules.purpose: Remove particle traffic client-side: blanket in Memeware, selective slime-only in Rise 5.99.
modules.how_it_works: Memeware's Disabler registers a PacketInEvent consumer that cancels every S2A it sees, unconditionally, regardless of mode. Rise 5.99's Disabler, in HypixelSlime mode, checks the particle type and cancels only EnumParticleTypes.SLIME. Nekoware's Disabler imports the class but ships no active particle handler in the file.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Invisible server-side: cancelled clientbound packets are never acknowledged. The cost is losing all particle feedback, which some servers use as hit indicators.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 restricts the cancel to SLIME particles in the HypixelSlime mode. Nekoware v1 private imports S2APacketParticles in its Disabler but has no handler using it (dead import).

modules.name: ParticleDistanceComponent (performance)
modules.purpose: Drop particle packets whose origin is more than 6 blocks away to save GPU work.
modules.how_it_works: A Component (non-module system) listening on PacketReceiveEvent. For each S2A it computes the squared distance from the player to the packet origin and cancels the packet when distanceSq >= 36, i.e. 6 blocks. Particles closer than 6 blocks pass through untouched.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat exposure; it is a pure client-performance filter. Aggressive distance culling can hide distant particle cues like explosions or beacon effects.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30 under com/alan/clients/component/impl/performance/.

modules.name: ParticleCheck (security)
modules.purpose: Rate-limit inbound particle volume so a malicious server cannot crash the client with a flood.
modules.how_it_works: A SecurityFeature. For each S2A it adds the packet's particle count to an accumulator, drains 6 per packet, and clamps the bucket at 150. The packet is dropped when the bucket exceeds 100, or when count is < 1, |count| > 20, or speed is negative or above 1000. Normal combat particles pass because their per-packet counts are small.
modules.vanilla_hook: Security pipeline handle(Packet) on the receive path.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Defends the client against particle-crash exploits. The drain rate and 100-threshold are tuned so that even heavy combat (crit, sweep, potion particles) never trips it.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30. Tenacity 6.0 AntiExploit implements the same idea with simpler heuristics (see its own entry).

modules.name: AntiExploit (particle flood)
modules.purpose: Cancel particle packets that look like crash attempts while logging the block.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent handler. For S2A it cancels and prints 'Blocked Exploit: Particles' when |particleSpeed| >= 1, or 'Blocked Exploit: Crash' when particleCount > 1. The module bundles several crash-vector filters (resource pack URLs, camera spectate, explosion strength) with a shared 100-packet-per-second counter.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The heuristic is aggressive enough that servers emitting unusual particle effects (custom enchant glints, heavy weather) get filtered. ChatUtil.print spam on each block is a minor DoS surface by itself.
modules.variations: Rise 6.x uses the token-bucket ParticleCheck instead; Tenacity's version trades precision for simplicity.

modules.name: Criticals (packet skip)
modules.purpose: Keep S2A out of the critical-hit packet state machine so it cannot reset the spoofed-position sequence.
modules.how_it_works: In the EventPacket branch of Criticals, an early return fires when the packet is S2A, so particle broadcasts never reach the transaction/position logic below. The handler's state machine tracks C0F transactions and C03 position packets to trigger criticals; particle noise would otherwise be type-checked pointlessly.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Skipping particles has no anti-cheat effect; it is a micro-optimization and a guard against future code paths that might misinterpret clientbound noise.
modules.variations: No other client in the corpus touches S2A from a combat module.

implementation.general_hooks: Every handler sits on the packet receive path: Memeware PacketInEvent, Tenacity and Rise 6.x PacketReceiveEvent, Sigma EventPacket, Rise security chain handle(Packet).
implementation.client_variations: Memeware cancels via event.cancel() on a custom bus. Rise 6.x components and security features use event.setCancelled() or pipeline drop. Sigma returns early inside a single handler. Tenacity combines cancel with a per-second packet counter shared across crash vectors.

anticheat.overview: The particle packet is the one clientbound cosmetic packet that anticheats actively generate. Kauri, FlopAC, Artemis, Daedalus and intave all construct and send S2A (or its PacketEvents equivalent) to draw debug overlays: hitbox cuboids, rays and collision boxes during testing and at flag time. Artemis additionally ships a full read/write wrapper so the packet can be parsed and re-emitted by its pipeline. No anticheat flags S2A as a cheat signal; the corpus treats it as an output channel, not an input.

checks.name: Debug particle visualization (Kauri / FlopAC / Daedalus / intave)
checks.purpose: Render hitboxes, rays and collision boxes to the player's screen by sending particle packets, so staff and developers can see exactly what a check computed.
checks.how_it_works: Kauri's Helper.drawRay and drawCuboid build a WrapperPlayServerParticle (the PacketEvents S2A equivalent) with the ray or box edge positions and send it to the player. FlopAC's MiscUtils does the same through its own WrappedPacketPlayOutWorldParticle wrapper, and its collision box types each implement a draw() that emits particles along their edges. Daedalus submits particle drawing for bounding boxes to a thread pool, and intave spawns villager-happy particles at waypoints via Bukkit spawnParticle, rate-limited per position. The packets are fired on flag, in debug mode, or from dedicated reveal handlers.
checks.detects: Nothing on its own. The visualization is an operator aid layered on top of reach, hitbox and phase checks; it exposes the geometry those checks reason about.
checks.variations: FlopAC MiscUtils.drawRay/drawCuboid mirror Kauri's Helper with its own tinyprotocol wrapper. Daedalus CollisionAssessment sends flame particles for bounding boxes. intave Particles.spawnVillagerHappyParticleAt rate-limits waypoint particles. Artemis BoundingUtil.drawBox uses its GPacketPlayServerWorldParticles wrapper for the same purpose.

checks.name: World particles wrapper (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Give Artemis a full read/write wrapper for the world-particles packet so the pipeline can parse inbound S2A and re-emit particle packets for debug drawing.
checks.how_it_works: GPacketPlayServerWorldParticles implements ReadableBuffer and WriteableBuffer. read() parses the particle type (with a BARRIER fallback on a bad id), the long-distance flag, position, offsets, speed, count and the per-type argument array; write() serializes them back, negating particle arguments on the wire. BoundingUtil.drawBox builds one of these packets per box edge to render debug bounding boxes, and the ProtocolGeneratorDirect registers the class in the generated protocol.
checks.detects: Nothing. The wrapper is bidirectional plumbing: inbound parsing feeds the packet pipeline, outbound construction powers the debug-box renderer.
checks.variations: Artemis also maps SERVER_PLAY + 93 to PacketPlayServerWorldParticles in its repository. FlopAC's WrappedPacketPlayOutWorldParticle covers the same packet for its 1.8 base, and Kauri uses PacketEvents' WrapperPlayServerParticle directly.

wiki_notes: The long-distance flag extends particle visibility from 256 blocks to 65536 blocks, and the offset fields are spread with gaussian random values around the source position.

MCP 1.8.9 S2APacketParticles implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleParticles; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBoolean, readFloat, readInt, readVarIntFromBuffer.
1.8.9 callers: WorldServer.spawnParticle sends new S2APacketParticles (line 1149): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/world/WorldServer.java

packets.name: Change Game State
packets.desc: Changes a global game state: rain toggle, gamemode change, credits, demo messages, elder guardian effect.

fields.name: value
fields.desc: Value associated with reason (gamemode ID, rain strength, fade value)

packets.notes: Reason 0: bed can't be set (respawn). Reason 1/2: rain toggle. Reason 3: gamemode change (value=0-3). Reason 4: credits. Reason 5: demo. Reason 6: arrow hitting entity. Reason 7/8: fade values. Reason 9: elder guardian effect.

writeup.p: A two-field state toggle: an unsigned byte reason and a float value. It is the server's mechanism for global client state that has no dedicated packet: rain start/stop and strength, gamemode changes, the end-game credits screen, the demo screen and its help messages, arrow-hit feedback, and the elder guardian mob-appearance effect. EntityPlayerMP sends reason 4 on end-game and reason 3 with the new GameType ID on gamemode change; WorldServer and ServerConfigurationManager drive reasons 1, 2, 7 and 8 for weather.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleChangeGameState switches on the reason. Reason 1 sets raining true, 2 sets raining false, 3 calls playerController.setGameType(GameType.getByID(value)), 4 opens GuiWinGame, 5 routes the demo screen (value 0) or demo help messages (101/102/103), 6 plays the successful-hit sound, 7 sets rain strength, 8 sets thunder strength, 10 spawns the mob-appearance particle and guardian curse sound. Reasons with a MESSAGE_NAMES entry also push a translated chat line.

Two Rise 6.x handlers, both defensive. Ambience, a render module, cancels reasons 1 and 2 whenever the user has forced a custom weather mode, so server rain toggles cannot override the client's chosen sky.
