DemoCheck, a security feature, drops reason 5 with value 0, which is the demo-mode screen: a malicious or griefing server can lock a player into the demo overlay, and the check removes that lever. No client in the corpus uses this packet for AutoGG-style game-end detection; reason 4 is ignored everywhere.

The demo screen (reason 5, value 0) is the abuse vector: it swaps the HUD and movement handling to demo mode, which hostile servers use to grief players. Rain reasons are a nuisance vector on weather-cycling servers, which is exactly why Ambience filters them. Reason 3 gamemode changes are server-authoritative and no client in the corpus fights them; overriding setGameType client-side desyncs the player controller and is a known crash/flag source, which is why it is absent.

implementation.overview: The catch-all state toggle: rain, gamemode, credits, demo, arrow feedback, guardian effect. The 8 clients use it only defensively: Rise 6.x Ambience filters rain toggles under forced weather, and Rise 6.x DemoCheck kills the demo-screen lockout. No game-end (credits) detection exists in this corpus.
implementation.server_handling: Server senders: WorldServer.updateWeather sends reason 7/8 (strengths) per dimension and reason 1/2 (rain stop/start) globally; ServerConfigurationManager sends reason 1 plus 7/8 on player join; EntityPlayerMP sends 4 on end-game and 3 with GameType.getID on gamemode change; EntityArrow sends 6 to the shooter on a successful hit; EntityGuardian sends 10 on the elder guardian effect; DemoWorldManager sends 5 with 0/101/102/103. The client handler applies each reason directly to client world state, with no validation of value ranges.
implementation.protocol_notes: Encoding: unsigned byte reason, float value. The value is only meaningful for reasons 3 (gamemode id), 5 (demo sub-state), 7 and 8 (weather strengths). Reasons 0, 4, 6, 9, 10 carry value 0.0F. MESSAGE_NAMES maps reasons 1, 3, 4, 5 to chat translations, so some reasons produce both a state change and a chat line. Reason 9 is defined but unused in 1.8.9; reason 10 is the elder guardian variant.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures this packet. Gamemode changes are server-authoritative and instant, so client-side gamemode spoofing is a desync crash rather than a cheat. The defensive angle is server trust: DemoCheck exists because a hostile server can emit reason 5 to disable normal gameplay, and Ambience exists because weather packets fight user-selected ambience. Both are filters on server-controlled state, not evasions.

modules.name: Ambience (weather override)
modules.purpose: Force a chosen weather and stop server rain toggles from overriding it.
modules.how_it_works: When the Weather mode is not Unchanged, the PacketReceiveEvent handler cancels every S2B whose reason is 1 or 2 (begin/end rain). A PreMotionEvent branch re-applies the forced state every 20 ticks via WorldInfo setters, and onDisable resets rain strength and weather flags to defaults.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Client-only state, invisible to the server. The 20-tick re-assertion matters because the server re-sends rain state on join and on weather ticks; without it the forced weather would flicker.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30 under com/alan/clients/module/impl/render/.

modules.name: DemoCheck (security)
modules.purpose: Drop the demo-mode packet so a server cannot lock the client into the demo screen.
modules.how_it_works: A SecurityFeature on the packet receive chain. It drops any S2B where reason is 5 and value is 0, which is exactly the packet DemoWorldManager sends to open GuiScreenDemo. The demo help messages (values 101-103) are not blocked, only the screen-opening state.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Server-trust defense, not anti-cheat. Only relevant on servers that abuse the demo state; on legit demo servers it changes nothing user-visible except skipping the overlay.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30. No other client in the corpus filters demo state.

implementation.general_hooks: Rise 6.x uses PacketReceiveEvent for module-level filtering (Ambience) and the security handle(Packet) chain for feature-level filtering (DemoCheck).
implementation.client_variations: Both Rise 6.x versions ship identical Ambience and DemoCheck files. Rise 5.99 has no S2B module reference at all; Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity only touch the packet in vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient code.

anticheat.overview: Server-side anticheats treat the change-game-state packet as authoritative world metadata, not as a cheat surface. Grim listens on the send path to keep its simulated gamemode and death-screen state transaction-ordered with the client, and feeds the rain reasons into the compensated world; Intave subscribes to the outbound game-state change to track the pending gamemode for its ability metadata. Artemis registers the packet in its wrapper repository. No anticheat uses it to flag the player, because the server controls both the reason and the value.

checks.name: GameState send listener (Grim)
checks.purpose: Keep Grim's simulated gamemode and death-screen state in sync with server-sent game-state changes.
checks.how_it_works: PacketSendListener on CHANGE_GAME_STATE. For CHANGE_GAME_MODE it sends a transaction and applies the new gamemode in a real-time task ordered after that transaction, clamping invalid plugin values (below 0 or past the enum) to SURVIVAL and notifying the spectate manager when leaving spectator. For ENABLE_RESPAWN_SCREEN (1.15+) it records whether the death screen is shown.
checks.detects: Gamemode desync between the server and the simulated player, plugin-sent invalid gamemode ids, and stale death-screen state that would corrupt the menu logic of BadPacketsM.
checks.variations: BadPacketsM (same repo) exempts the click-window menu check for one packet when a WIN_GAME reason arrives, since the client closes and reopens its menu on the credits screen. BasePacketWorldReader tracks the rain reasons (BEGIN_RAINING, END_RAINING, RAIN_LEVEL_CHANGE) into compensatedWorld.isRaining for the movement simulation.

checks.name: Gamemode tracking (Intave AbilityTracker)
checks.purpose: Track the pending gamemode on outbound game-state changes so ability metadata (flight, speed) matches what the client actually sees.
checks.how_it_works: PacketSubscription on outbound GAME_STATE_CHANGE with the GameStateChangeReader. If the reason is CHANGE_GAME_MODE, the value is mapped through GameStateChangeReader.GameState and stored as a pending gamemode on AbilityMetadata; the active gamemode only flips on the next tick feedback, which keeps ability state aligned with the client's processing order. The rest of the module consumes that metadata for the critical-flying-disallow mitigation.
checks.detects: Fly and movement cheats that exploit the one-tick window between a gamemode change and the client applying it, plus stale flight permissions after a mode switch.
checks.variations: GameStateChangeReader (src/main/java/de/jpx3/intave/packet/reader/GameStateChangeReader.java) resolves the reason index to the GameState enum and exposes the raw value; PacketReaders.java registers it under PacketId.Server.GAME_STATE_CHANGE.

checks.name: GameStateChange wrapper (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Register the outbound game-state packet in Artemis' packet abstraction so checks can listen to it.
checks.how_it_works: The packet API declares PacketPlayServerGameStateChange and PacketRepository maps SERVER_PLAY + 36 to it. This is framework registration only; no check in the corpus consumes the wrapper.
checks.detects: Nothing by itself; it exists so other Artemis checks can hook the packet.
checks.variations: Negativity (Elikill58-Negativity) lists the packet as GAME_STATE_CHANGE in its PacketType registry but has no handler on it.

wiki_notes: Reason 0 signals that no valid respawn block is available, reason 6 is sent when a player is struck by an arrow, and rain and thunder levels range from 0 to 1 with thunder rendering requiring active rain.

MCP 1.8.9 S2BPacketChangeGameState implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleChangeGameState; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readFloat, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: EntityGuardian.apply sends new S2BPacketChangeGameState (line 451) +5 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/monster/EntityGuardian.java

packets.name: Spawn Global Entity
packets.desc: Spawns a global entity visible to all players (lightning bolt).

writeup.p: Spawns a globally visible entity, in 1.8.9 exclusively the lightning bolt. The server broadcasts it to every player within 512 blocks of the strike (WorldServer.addWeatherEffect via sendToAllNear). The client handler converts the x32 fixed-point coordinates and, when the type byte is 1, instantiates an EntityLightningBolt in the client world. Because the entity is server-created and broadcast, it is the only lightning representation the client ever sees.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleSpawnGlobalEntity divides each coordinate by 32.0D and builds an EntityLightningBolt only when the type byte equals 1; any other type yields a null entity and is dropped. The bolt is then added to the client world, which drives its ambient light flash and thunder sound. Server-side the packet constructor derives entityId, coordinates and type from the Entity argument passed in by WorldServer.

Two module-grade consumers in the corpus. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 ship LightningTracker, an exploit-category module that prints the strike coordinates and distance to chat on every type-1 packet. LiquidSense Dev ships LightningCheck, a world-category module with the same read pattern: it divides the fixed-point coordinates back to blocks and posts them to chat, while also storing them in static x/y/z fields that other modules can read. Both are informational, not ESP. The remaining seven client dirs (Memeware, Nekoware, Rise 5.99, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity, November Recode 2.0) reference the packet only through vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient.

The packet is a broadcast with a server-chosen entityId and position, so a malicious server can spam it to fake lightning at arbitrary coordinates; there is no client-side validation beyond the type check. The 512-block broadcast radius means a strike far outside the client's render distance still spawns an entity. No client in the corpus abuses this for teleport hacks or lightning-based exploits, and none uses it for anti-cheat purposes.

implementation.overview: The lightning broadcast packet. Rise 6.x LightningTracker and LiquidSense Dev LightningCheck both print strike coordinates to chat on type-1 packets; LiquidSense additionally caches the coordinates in static fields. No ESP, no weather control, no exploit use: the 10 clients confirm this packet is near-invisible to module authors.
implementation.server_handling: WorldServer.addWeatherEffect calls ConfigurationManager.sendToAllNear with a 512.0D radius on the strike position, same dimension, constructing S2CPacketSpawnGlobalEntity from the EntityLightningBolt. The packet's constructor copies entityId, x*32, y*32, z*32 and type (1 for lightning) from the entity. NetHandlerPlayClient only materializes the bolt when type == 1, ignoring the entityId for lookup since the client creates the entity fresh.
implementation.protocol_notes: Encoding: VarInt entityId, int x*32, int y*32, int z*32, byte type. Coordinates are fixed-point at 1/32 block resolution, finer than S29's 1/8. The type byte is the only discriminator; in 1.8.9 only 1 (lightning) is ever sent. The packet predates the generic Packet<T> signature in the older clients (raw Packet with double dispatch) while Rise 6.x uses Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient>.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat touches this packet. Lightning is ambient weather; there is no cheat surface to measure. The only observable abuse would be server-side strike spam to distract or desync clients, which no module in the corpus defends against. The 512-block radius is worth noting for anyone building lightning-based radar: strikes beyond render distance still arrive.

modules.name: LightningTracker
modules.purpose: Print a chat message with the coordinates and distance of every lightning strike.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent listener. For each S2C it divides the x32 coordinates back to blocks, rounds to two decimals, and when the type byte is 1 calls ChatUtil.display with the position and the player's distance to the strike. It is an exploit-category module but performs no world manipulation.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Passive and read-only; nothing is sent or cancelled. No server can detect it.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30. Rise 5.99 has no equivalent module, and no other client in the corpus references this packet outside vanilla code.

modules.name: LightningCheck
modules.purpose: Report lightning strikes to chat and expose their coordinates in static fields for other modules.
modules.how_it_works: An @EventTarget onPacket handler on the LiquidBounce PacketEvent bus. For each S2CPacketSpawnGlobalEntity whose type byte is 1 it divides the x32 fixed-point coordinates by 32.0D, stores them in public static x/y/z fields, and prints a prefixed chat line with the strike position. The unused C07PacketPlayerDigging import is dead weight carried over from a copy-paste skeleton.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Read-only: nothing is sent or cancelled, so the module is undetectable server-side. Any abuse would live downstream of the static coordinate cache, which other modules consume.
modules.variations: Rise's LightningTracker computes the player's distance to the strike and formats a different chat line; LiquidSense prints raw coordinates and keeps the static cache. No other client in the corpus reads S2C.

implementation.general_hooks: Two consumers: Rise 6.x PacketReceiveEvent listener and LiquidSense Dev PacketEvent listener, both read-only.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 ship byte-identical LightningTracker files. LiquidSense Dev's LightningCheck uses the LiquidBounce event bus (@EventTarget onPacket) and static coordinate fields. The other seven clients touch the packet only in net/minecraft vanilla sources (NetHandlerPlayClient, EnumConnectionState, WorldServer).

anticheat.overview: No anticheat in the 50-repo corpus runs a check on the global-entity (lightning) packet. The only genuine packet references are framework registrations: Artemis wraps PacketPlayOutSpawnEntityWeather as GPacketPlayServerSpawnEntityWeather and registers it at SERVER_PLAY + 69, and Negativity lists the packet in its PacketType enum. Every other corpus hit is keyword noise from the search term Lightning: strikeLightningEffect ban-punishment visuals in PeyangSuperbAntiCheat KickUtil, TruthfulAC Check and SafeguardAC ViolationHandler, and lightning-rod block-shape comments in NoCheatPlus. Lightning is ambient server weather with no client-trust signal, so nothing measures it.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x2C: VarInt entityId, byte type, then X Y Z ints at times 32.
Type is always 1 in 1.8.9, meaning lightning bolt; other types are dropped.
Broadcast to players within 512 blocks of the strike position.

MCP 1.8.9 S2CPacketSpawnGlobalEntity implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleSpawnGlobalEntity; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readInt, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: WorldServer.addWeatherEffect sends new S2CPacketSpawnGlobalEntity (line 984): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/world/WorldServer.java

packets.name: Open Window
packets.desc: Opens an inventory GUI window (chest, crafting table, furnace, enchantment table, etc.) with window ID, type, title, and slot count.

fields.name: slotCount
fields.desc: Number of slots in the window

fields.name: entityId
fields.desc: Entity ID for EntityHorse type (only present for horse GUIs)

packets.notes: Inventory types: minecraft:chest, crafting_table, furnace, dispenser, enchanting_table, brewing_stand, villager, beacon, anvil, hopper, dropper, EntityHorse. RektSky B5 ChestStealer intercepts this packet for silent chest handling — it cancels the vanilla open, stores the window data, and manages the chest entirely via packet-level manipulation.

writeup.p: Opens an inventory window on the client. The server assigns a windowId (incrementing per player, wrapping at 256), picks a GUI type string, sends the title as a chat component, the slot count, and for EntityHorse windows the horse's entityId. The client switches on the type string: minecraft:container becomes a chest GUI, minecraft:villager a trade GUI, EntityHorse a horse inventory, anything else a LocalBlockIntercommunication GUI. The windowId must then be echoed back on every C0E click and C0D close.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleOpenWindow matches the type string and calls the matching display method (displayGUIChest, displayVillagerTradeGui, displayGUIHorse, displayGui), then stamps the windowId onto the player's openContainer. The horse branch looks up the entity by id and silently does nothing if the entity is missing. Server-side, EntityPlayerMP.displayGUIChest and openGui build the packet with the player's currentWindowId, which increments on every open.

Two Rise 6.x modules, both cancelling the packet for combat-adjacent reasons. WorldGuardRegen suppresses S2D while its regen burst is active (ticks <= 1) so a server-initiated window cannot interrupt the position-desync regen sequence. GodMode cancels every S2D unconditionally, which keeps the server's window state desynced from the client as part of the godmode attack-desync. The context's ChestStealer/AutoArmor/ServerCrasher open-window usage does not exist in this corpus; the 8 clients contain no inventory-stealing S2D consumer.

The windowId protocol is a state machine: the client must mirror every S2D with an open container and echo the id in later clicks. Cancelling S2D (Rise 6.x) leaves the server believing a window is open while the client never shows it, which is exactly the desync GodMode and WorldGuardRegen exploit. Server-side open-window spam (ServerCrasher style) is a client DoS: each S2D forces a GUI construction, and rapid-fire opens desync the container state. The EntityHorse branch's entity lookup is also a soft spot: a stale id silently drops the window.

implementation.overview: The window-open packet, and the desync hinge for two Rise 6.x combat modules: WorldGuardRegen suppresses it during regen bursts, GodMode cancels it permanently to keep the server-client container state split. No chest-stealing or shop-detection module exists in the corpus; the windowId echo contract is what makes cancellation useful.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.displayGUIChest/openGui increments currentWindowId, opens the container server-side, and sends S2D with the id, GUI type, display name, and slot count (plus entityId for horses). The client must echo the windowId in C0E clicks and C0D closes or the server container stays open with stale state. Vanilla performs no validation that the client actually opened the window, which is the desync window both Rise 6.x modules rely on.
implementation.protocol_notes: Encoding: unsigned byte windowId, String guiId (minecraft:container, minecraft:villager, EntityHorse, or a block interaction id), IChatComponent title, unsigned byte slotCount, then int entityId only when guiId is EntityHorse. windowId wraps at 256 and the client stamps it on openContainer.windowId. The type string is the discriminator; there is no numeric window-type enum on the wire in 1.8.9.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats track window state through the C0E/C0D echo trail, not through S2D itself. The Rise 6.x cancels create a server-side phantom container: the server keeps sending window updates (S2F, S30) to a window the client never opened, which is detectable if an anti-cheat correlates window items with click packets. The trade-off is why WorldGuardRegen only cancels during the short regen burst (ticks <= 1) while GodMode accepts the permanent desync.

modules.name: WorldGuardRegen (window suppress)
modules.purpose: Prevent a server-initiated window from interrupting the regen position-desync sequence.
modules.how_it_works: A Regen mode. Its PreMotionEvent handler drops the player y by 0.05 and holds yaw/pitch while health is below the threshold; the PacketSendEvent handler wraps attacks in a C04-teleport/attack/C04-return sandwich. The PacketReceiveEvent handler cancels any S2D while ticks <= 1, i.e. during the active regen burst, so the server cannot open a container mid-sequence and break the state machine.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The cancel is brief and purposeful: a phantom window for one or two ticks is below most anti-cheat window-state checks, which expect C0D echoes after a delay. Long cancels would desync window items.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30 under com/alan/clients/module/impl/combat/regen/.

modules.name: GodMode (window desync)
modules.purpose: Cancel every open-window packet so the server's container state permanently diverges from the client's.
modules.how_it_works: Cancels all S2D in PacketReceiveEvent. Combined with the module's core trick (drop y by 0.05 every pre-motion, wrap attacks in a position sandwich via PacketUtil.sendNoEvent), the server keeps an open phantom container while the client stays in normal movement. onEnable snapshots yaw/pitch for the desync frames.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: High detection risk by design: permanent window desync plus position desync is a classic godmode signature. Modern anti-cheats correlate C0E/C0D history with window ids and flag clicks against windows the client never opened.
modules.variations: Identical file in Rise 6.1.30. Rise 5.99 has no S2D reference in any module.

implementation.general_hooks: Both Rise 6.x modules filter S2D on PacketReceiveEvent; the surrounding exploit logic lives in PreMotionEvent and PacketSendEvent.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 ship identical GodMode and WorldGuardRegen files. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity reference S2D only in vanilla sources. No client uses S2D for chest stealing or shop detection.

anticheat.overview: The open-window packet is the state anchor for inventory anti-cheat: modern anticheats mirror the S2D open into a simulated window state and then validate every C0E click against it. Grim records the container id and type on the send side and rejects impossible click combinations, and its CompensatedInventory runs the full openWindowID state machine. Intave timestamps the open so its inventory-click-analysis check can measure click delay, and Artemis transaction-confirms the open to flip the inventory-open flag. Classic repos stop at wrappers (FlopAC WrappedOutOpenWindow, Kauri PacketHandler, Negativity PacketType).

checks.name: BadPacketsP invalid click (Grim)
checks.purpose: Reject crafted window-click packets whose button values are impossible for the click type.
checks.how_it_works: PacketSendListener records containerType and containerId from the S2D OPEN_WINDOW packet; PacketReceiveListener then validates every C0E click: button range per click type (PICKUP/QUICK_MOVE/CLONE 0-2, SWAP 0-8 or 40, THROW 0-1, QUICK_CRAFT a fixed set, PICKUP_ALL 0). The verbose line also reports whether the click's window id matches the container opened by S2D, and the packet is cancelled on repeated flags.
checks.detects: Crafted C0E packets used for packet-crash exploits and invalid-click lag machines, plus clicks that reference a window the server never opened.
checks.variations: CrashD in the same repo combines the S2D open with click parsing to drive crash checks; FlopAC WrappedOutOpenWindow and Kauri PacketHandler only wrap the packet.

checks.name: CompensatedInventory open-window state (Grim)
checks.purpose: Emulate the server-side inventory and open-window id so click, slot and item packets can be validated against client-visible state.
checks.how_it_works: On the S2D OPEN_WINDOW send it stores openWindowID from the container id (the horse-window variant is handled separately); the S2F set-slot and S30 window-items handlers then route updates to the player inventory (id 0) or the opened menu (id equal to openWindowID). Clicks against a mismatched window id are treated as invalid, and closeActiveInventory resets the menu, carried item and id.
checks.detects: Inventory desync, chest-stealer and inventory-manipulation that click windows the server never opened, and carried-item spoofing.
checks.variations: AbstractContainerMenu in the same repo replays valid click semantics on the emulated menu.

checks.name: Inventory click delay analysis (Intave)
checks.purpose: Flag chest-stealer and auto-inventory modules by measuring click timing and slot distance against the window open.
checks.how_it_works: The openWindowPacket subscription on outbound OPEN_WINDOW records lastWindowOpenTimestamp and marks the window open under tick feedback. The windowClickPacket subscription collects distance-time and slot-time samples per window; on close, if the sample count exceeds 30 it runs statistics (mean, variance, slope, Pearson correlation) and flags constant-speed item taking, excessive speed, and distance-indifferent patterns, nerfing the player's attack damage past 100 VL.
checks.detects: ChestStealer, inventory cleaners and refill modules that take items at uniform speed or ignore slot distance.
checks.variations: NotOpenCheck in the same package flags clicks when no window was opened; PacketEventDispatch.sentWindowOpen stores the slot count announced by S2D.

checks.name: WindowOpen wrapper and inventory-open flag (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Register the S2D packet and transaction-confirm the open so Artemis knows the player's inventory is open.
checks.how_it_works: GPacketPlayServerWindowOpen wraps PacketPlayOutOpenWindow with a readable buffer; EmulatorPreProcessor handles it by scheduling a transaction-confirmed PacketAction whose pre() stops item use and sets the inventory-open flag, so movement and click checks can distinguish windowed from normal play at the right tick.
checks.detects: Chest-stealer and window-state desync where clicks or movement are processed against a stale inventory state.
checks.variations: PacketExecutor registers the wrapper; PacketPlayServerWindowOpen is the API interface. Kauri (funkemunky-KauriV3) PacketHandler sets inventoryOpen(true) and resets lastInventoryOpen on a keepalive-confirmed OPEN_WINDOW.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x2D: unsigned byte windowId, type string, chat title, unsigned byte slot count.
Type strings include minecraft:container, minecraft:villager and EntityHorse.
Extra int entityId follows only for EntityHorse windows; ID is echoed in C0E and C0D.

MCP 1.8.9 S2DPacketOpenWindow implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleOpenWindow; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readChatComponent, readInt, readStringFromBuffer, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.displayGui sends new S2DPacketOpenWindow (line 758): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Close Window
packets.desc: Server forces the client to close an inventory window.

writeup.p: Server-initiated window close. It carries a single unsigned byte windowId and tells the client to tear down the open container and re-sync the held item. Server-side, EntityPlayerMP.closeScreen sends it when the server decides the player's window must close, which happens on death, teleport, dimension change, and anti-cheat interventions. The client counterpart C0DPacketCloseWindow is the player-initiated echo; the S2E path is always server-driven.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleCloseWindow calls thePlayer.func_175159_q(), which resets the carried item and closes the current screen. It does not check the windowId against the open container: any S2E closes whatever GUI is up. Server-side, EntityPlayerMP.closeScreen sends S2E with openContainer.windowId and closes the container. The asymmetry is the hook: a server can yank any GUI, and the client obeys blindly.

Two module families. NoGuiClose in Rise 5.99, 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 cancels S2E so servers cannot close the player's GUI; Rise 5.99 defaults the Chat Only setting on, meaning the cancel only applies while the chat screen is open, which preserves the ability to type while a container stays open. Rise 6.2.4 defaults it off, blocking every server close. LiquidSense Dev's KeepContainer uses S2E in the opposite direction: it reads the server's close to drop its cached container reference, and it cancels the client's own C0D close packets while the keep is armed. The other six clients (Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity, November Recode 2.0) have no S2E module reference at all.

The unguarded close is the surface: servers close windows to interrupt chest-stealing macros and inventory manipulation, and NoGuiClose defeats that by holding the GUI open. The cost is protocol desync: the server has closed its container while the client still shows it, so later clicks (C0E) reference a dead window. This is safe only while the player does not actually interact; the Chat Only mode exists precisely to limit the desync window to chat-while-looting use. Vanilla's failure to validate windowId on S2E also means a server can send a mismatched id to force-close anything.

implementation.overview: The server-driven window close. Rise ships NoGuiClose in all three releases to cancel S2E and hold the GUI open, with a Chat Only mode in 5.99 to limit the desync. LiquidSense Dev's KeepContainer listens to S2E to invalidate its cached container when the server closes it. The other six clients never touch the packet outside vanilla.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.closeScreen sends S2E with the current openContainer.windowId, then closes the server-side container and re-syncs the held item. NetHandlerPlayClient.handleCloseWindow runs func_175159_q() unconditionally: it resets the carried item and closes whatever screen is active, ignoring the packet's windowId entirely. Because the client never validates the id, the packet is a blind close lever from the server's perspective.
implementation.protocol_notes: Encoding: single unsigned byte windowId. It is one of the smallest packets in the play state. The client handler performs no id comparison against openContainer.windowId, which is the load-bearing detail for NoGuiClose: cancelling the packet has no side effects beyond keeping the GUI open. The windowId matters only for server bookkeeping, since the client close path is unconditional.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats flag the desync NoGuiClose creates: a window the server closed but the client keeps open will eventually produce clicks (C0E) against a dead windowId, which window-state checks flag as inventory manipulation. The Chat Only default in Rise 5.99 keeps the desync window small (chat open while looting); blocking every S2E (6.2.4 default) widens it and increases the flag surface. This is a utility module with a real anti-cheat cost, unlike the purely cosmetic filters elsewhere in this group.

modules.name: NoGuiClose
modules.purpose: Cancel server window-close packets so the player's GUI cannot be yanked away.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent handler cancels any S2E, gated by a Chat Only setting: when enabled, the cancel only fires while mc.currentScreen is a GuiChat. Rise 5.99 defaults Chat Only to true (onPacketReceive + event.setCancelled), Rise 6.2.4 defaults its chatonly value to false (Listener with event.setCancelled).
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (onPacketReceive override in 5.99; EventLink Listener in 6.x).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Clicks against a server-closed window are the flag surface. The chat-gated variant keeps the desync brief; the unconditional variant trades safety for convenience and is the one most likely to trip window-state checks on servers that close windows for inventory-macro protection.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 ship identical files (BooleanValue chatonly, default false). Rise 5.99 uses BooleanSetting chatOnly, default true, and the older onPacketReceive override style.

modules.name: KeepContainer
modules.purpose: Keep a formerly opened inventory container accessible anywhere: re-open it with the INSERT key and suppress close packets while armed.
modules.how_it_works: Stores the last non-inventory GuiContainer on ScreenEvent; pressing INSERT re-opens it via displayGuiScreen. On PacketEvent it cancels every C0DPacketCloseWindow and, for S2EPacketCloseWindow, clears the cached container when the packet's windowId matches the stored container, so the cache cannot be resurrected after the server closed it. Disabling the module sends the C0D close it had been suppressing.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling C0D while a window is open desyncs the client from the server's container state, the same flag surface NoGuiClose creates; the S2E listener bounds the desync by dropping the cached container as soon as the server closes it.
modules.variations: Rise's NoGuiClose keeps the live GUI open and never re-opens a closed container; KeepContainer instead re-opens a snapshot of a container the server believes is closed. The S2E handling is bookkeeping rather than a cancel.

implementation.general_hooks: Two patterns: Rise cancels S2E on the packet receive path, optionally gated by chat-screen state; LiquidSense Dev's KeepContainer reads S2E to clear its cached container and cancels C0D close packets instead.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 uses the Module.onPacketReceive override and BooleanSetting; Rise 6.x uses EventLink Listener fields and BooleanValue. Both default the Chat Only gate differently (true vs false). Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy, Tenacity and November Recode 2.0 reference S2E only in vanilla sources.

anticheat.overview: The server-close packet is consumed on the send side to reset simulated window state. Grim's CompensatedInventory closes the emulated inventory transaction-ordered after the S2E, and Artemis transaction-confirms the close to clear its inventory-open flag. Both anticheats do this so that later C0E clicks against the closed window are recognized as invalid. Intave and the classic repos only handle the client-side close (C0D) and are therefore not part of this packet's story.

checks.name: CompensatedInventory close handling (Grim)
checks.purpose: Reset the emulated open window when the server closes it, so clicks against a closed window are flagged.
checks.how_it_works: A send-side handler matches PacketType.Play.Server.CLOSE_WINDOW and schedules closeActiveInventory as a real-time task ordered after the last transaction; the reset restores isPacketInventoryActive, sets openWindowID back to 0, swaps the menu back to the player inventory and clears the carried item. Clicks that follow with the old window id no longer match openWindowID.
checks.detects: Chest-stealer and inventory desync where the client keeps clicking a window the server has closed.
checks.variations: None of Grim's other files reference the server close packet; BadPacketsP, CrashF and PacketOrderA act on the client-side C0E/C0D stream instead.

checks.name: WindowClose preprocessor (Artemis)
checks.purpose: Clear the inventory-open flag on the server close so downstream checks stop treating the player as windowed.
checks.how_it_works: fastHandle matches GPacketPlayServerWindowClose and schedules a transaction-confirmed PacketAction whose pre() sets the inventory-open flag to false. The same handler resets the flag on respawn, and handle() clears it on the client's own C0D close.
checks.detects: Window-state desync used by inventory-manipulation modules.
checks.variations: Kauri (funkemunky-KauriV3) PacketHandler wraps WrapperPlayServerCloseWindow and clears inventoryOpen on a keepalive action; Negativity lists CLOSE_WINDOW in both client and server PacketType sections.

wiki_notes: The server sends this when a window is forcibly closed, for example when a chest is destroyed while open, and window ID 0 refers to the player inventory.
MCP 1.8.9 S2EPacketCloseWindow implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleCloseWindow; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.closeScreen sends new S2EPacketCloseWindow (line 902): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Set Slot
packets.desc: Sets a single slot in an inventory window. Used for cursor updates, specific slot changes, and armor slot updates.

fields.name: item
fields.desc: ItemStack to place in slot (null = clear)

packets.notes: windowId=-1 special case: updates the cursor item (the item held by the mouse cursor). windowId=0: updates player inventory. S2F is sent for EVERY slot change — armor equips, hotbar changes, cursor picks up/drops. Inventory modules track S2F to detect armor swaps and item pickups.

writeup.p: S2FPacketSetSlot is the single-slot inventory sync packet, the fine-grained counterpart to the S30 full-window dump. The server emits it for every slot mutation: EntityPlayerMP.updateCraftingInventory pushes windowId/slot/stack on each container change, the cursor is synced with the (-1, -1) variant after clicks settle (lines 760, 774, 805), NetHandlerPlayServer line 554 re-sends the held hotbar slot after a swap, and ItemEditableBook pushes the signed book back into slot 0. windowId -1 means the cursor, 0 means the player inventory, anything else the open container.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleSetSlot resolves the target container from the window id: -1 sets the player's cursor stack, 0 and the player inventory window id write into inventoryContainer, otherwise the open container receives the slot. The matching GuiScreen is notified so the renderer updates. There is no validation: the client trusts the server's slot content unconditionally, which is exactly the trust that cancel-based modules exploit. The vanilla client never sends S2F; it is strictly clientbound.

Four distinct uses in the 8 clients. Rise 5.99 Auto sniffs S2F for the Redesky captcha item and clicks it with a crafted C0E. Rise 5.99 Scaffold and Spicy BlockFly cancel every S2F so the server cannot correct the hotbar while they place blocks. Tenacity 6.0 NoSlowModule cancels window-0 slot updates while using a non-sword item, keeping the ghost-item no-slow state alive. Rise 6.x AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent treats S2F as a significant packet that forces a HUD cache redraw, and PacketUtil exposes a wrapper for the script API.

Cancelling S2F is a local lie that only survives until the next window resync: the server owns slot state, and a rejected click (S32 accepted=false) triggers a full S30 dump that snaps the client back. That makes S2F cancellation a short-horizon trick, useful inside a single click loop, not a persistent desync. For inventory modules the packet is a cheap signal: an armor swap or a hotbar change arrives as one small packet, so AutoArmor-style logic can react without parsing a window. The trade-off is ordering: any module that cancels S2F upstream silently blinds every other module that reads it.

implementation.overview: The single-slot sync packet and the cheapest inventory signal on the wire. Rise's Auto reads it to click captcha items, Scaffold and Spicy's BlockFly cancel it to freeze the hotbar, Tenacity's NoSlow cancels window-0 updates to preserve a ghost item, and Rise 6.x treats it as a HUD-significant packet. The server always owns slot truth; cancelling only delays the client's view.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.updateCraftingInventory sends S2F(windowId, slot, stack) per slot change and the cursor variant (-1, -1) after click processing (lines 760, 774, 805 in the bundled sources). NetHandlerPlayServer line 554 re-sends the held item slot after a hotbar swap; ItemEditableBook line 116 pushes the signed book into slot 0. There is no rate limit and no client-side validation: handleSetSlot writes the slot into the resolved container and notifies the open GUI.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire layout: byte windowId, short slot, then a Slot encoding (short item id, byte count, short damage, optional NBT; item id -1 encodes null). windowId -1 (0xFF) targets the cursor, 0 the player inventory, other values the open container. S2F is PLAY-state only and always carries exactly one slot, which is what makes it the cheapest way for a module to detect an armor equip or hotbar change. The cursor variant pairs slot -1 with windowId -1.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures S2F: it is server-authoritative display state. The abuse is purely client-side view desync, and the detection surface is the eventual resync: a server that rejects a click re-sends S30, and any client that still behaves as if the old slot content exists is visibly desynced. Cancel-heavy movement modules (Scaffold, BlockFly) therefore risk inventory desync that manifests as phantom hotbar items rather than a flag.

modules.name: Auto
modules.purpose: Automated Redesky captcha solving: detect a captcha item in a container slot via S2F and click it before the server times it out.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent; on S2F, skip window 0 (player inventory), then check the item's display name case-insensitively for 'aqui'. On match, send C0EPacketClickWindow(windowId, slot, 0, 0, item, (short) 1919): button 0, mode 0, and an absurdly large action number the server ignores. Runs only while the redeskyAutoCaptcha setting is on.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Benign server automation; the fixed action number 1919 and the display-name scan are the only fingerprints, and no anti-cheat in the era flags them.
modules.variations: None in the corpus; the captcha logic is Redesky-specific and the rest of the module (auto register/login) works through chat packets.

modules.name: Scaffold
modules.purpose: Cancel all incoming slot sync so the server cannot correct the client's hotbar view during the block placement loop.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketReceive: if the packet is S2FPacketSetSlot, event.setCancelled(true). Every slot update is dropped while scaffolding, keeping the client's own view of the hotbar authoritative for the placement loop.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat flags the cancellation itself; the risk is long-horizon inventory desync, which surfaces when a rejected click forces an S30 resync.
modules.variations: None in the corpus; the file is 1042 lines of placement logic with this one receive-side cancel.

modules.name: BlockFly
modules.purpose: Block-fly movement that cancels S2F so the server cannot correct the fake block placement state.
modules.how_it_works: EventPacket pre-phase: if the packet is S2FPacketSetSlot, setCanceled(true), unless killaura has a target, in which case the handler returns early so weapon switching stays synced. The module also freezes yaw and pitch on C03 and EventMotion and places blocks below the player via onPlayerRightClick.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket (receive path), EventSendPacket, EventMotion, EventUpdate, EventSneaking, EventRender3D.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancels all slot updates while flying; same desync trade-off as Scaffold, with the added killaura guard that keeps combat state accurate.
modules.variations: None in the corpus; Spicy's other movement modules reference C00/C0F but only BlockFly touches S2F.

modules.name: NoSlowModule
modules.purpose: No-slow that preserves a ghost item by cancelling window-0 slot updates while using a non-sword item.
modules.how_it_works: Vanilla mode: on MotionEvent pre, if no ghost exists call sendBypass (C0D close window 0, then C0E shift-click of the held item into its own slot to create the ghost). Then on PacketReceiveEvent, cancel every S2F whose window id is 0 while the player is using a non-sword item with no screen open, so the server's slot corrections never remove the ghost. isItemGhost resets when the player stops using the item.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The ghost-item no-slow is a classic desync exploit; cancelling S2F is what keeps the ghost alive. It only survives until the next S30 or a transaction rejection.
modules.variations: The Watchdog mode branch is an empty stub; the corpus shows no other Tenacity module using S2F.

modules.name: AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent
modules.purpose: HUD performance component: S2F (and S30, chat, collect-item) mark significant events that force a GuiIngameCache redraw.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent: on S2F, reset the StopWatch and set the cache dirty so the next frame re-renders the HUD. PreMotionEvent re-evaluates dirty state every 100 ticks, on player-list/debug key changes, or while the component is disabled for a few ticks after health changes.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None; the component is cosmetic and only observes the packet stream.
modules.variations: Identical file in 6.1.30 (path com/alan/clients/component/impl/hud/). No other client has an equivalent.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the universal surface for S2F across the 8 clients. Tenacity pairs it with MotionEvent and SlowDownEvent, Spicy uses its monolithic EventPacket receive path with setCanceled.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 cancels via event.setCancelled on PacketReceiveEvent. Spicy cancels via setCanceled on EventPacket. Tenacity 6.0 cancels the event and toggles its own ghost-item state. Rise 6.x has no gameplay module for S2F; it reaches the packet through AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent and the PacketUtil wrapper used by scripts.

anticheat.overview: The set-slot packet is the server's single-slot inventory correction: window id, slot, and the item placed there. It is server-authoritative display state, so anticheats do not validate it, but simulation anticheats must consume it to keep their compensated copy of the player inventory honest. The only real corpus hits are Grim's replication listener, which reads S2F to detect held-item and offhand changes, and Grim's check listener, which manufactures S2F packets to resync the client after a cancelled interaction. Everyone else ignores it.

checks.name: SetSlot replication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Apply the server's single-slot corrections to the compensated inventory and end stale item-use state when the held item changes.
checks.how_it_works: PacketEntityReplication wraps SET_SLOT and, for window id 0 (the player inventory), schedules a transaction-sandwiched task: if the slot is the selected hotbar slot (36 + lastSlotSelected) or the offhand (45) and the item type differs from the compensated inventory, it clears the slowed-by-using-item state and resets item usage through the item reset handler. The task runs for the current and the next transaction to cover 1.8 clients that fail to send release-item packets.
checks.detects: Item-use desync after server-side slot corrections. It feeds NoSlow and item-use timing checks with accurate held-item state.
checks.variations: The only other anticheat that names the packet is Negativity, whose PacketType enum lists SET_SLOT as a clientbound constant; it is not consumed by any check there.

checks.name: SetSlot resync on cancelled place (Grim)
checks.purpose: Re-send the authoritative held-item slot to the client after a block place is cancelled, so the client's view cannot desync from the server.
checks.how_it_works: CheckManagerListener handles the block-place packet; when the placement is cancelled the server-side inventory no longer matches what the client predicted, so the listener sends a WrapperPlayServerSetSlot for the main hand (slot 36 + selected) or the offhand (slot 45) carrying the platform player's actual item. The code comment calls this 'stop inventory desync from cancelling place'.
checks.detects: Not a detection: a correction path that prevents ghost-item and desync artifacts from cancelled placements, which is what movement modules with inventory side effects tend to produce.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus writes S2F packets; Grim is alone in both consuming and producing set-slot traffic.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x2F: byte windowId, short slot, then Slot ItemStack encoding.
Window -1 with slot -1 updates the cursor item; window 0 updates player inventory.
Single-slot sync; full-window resync arrives separately via S30 Window Items.

MCP 1.8.9 S2FPacketSetSlot implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleSetSlot; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readItemStackFromBuffer, readShort.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.sendSlotContents sends new S2FPacketSetSlot (line 860) +2 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Window Items
packets.desc: Sends the full contents of an inventory window — all slots at once. Used for initial container opening and rejected transaction recovery.

fields.name: items
fields.desc: Array of all ItemStacks in the window, slot by slot

packets.notes: For windowId=0, this updates the entire player inventory (45 slots: 9 hotbar + 36 main). For chests, this is sent immediately after S2DPacketOpenWindow. When a C0E click is rejected (S32 accepted=false), the server re-sends S30 to force the client to revert its inventory.

writeup.p: S30PacketWindowItems is the full-window sync packet: an unsigned byte window id, a short slot count, then every slot encoding in order. The server sends it when a container opens (right after S2D PacketOpenWindow), when the player joins or respawns, and as the recovery path when a click transaction is rejected (S32 accepted=false). It is the server's authoritative statement of window contents, and the client applies it wholesale, replacing the container's slot list.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleWindowItems maps windowId 0 and the player inventory window to inventoryContainer and everything else to the open container, then overwrites every slot via putStacksInSlots. EntityPlayerMP.updateCraftingInventory (line 773) builds the list from inventorySlots and sends S30 on every full sync. Because the client trusts the dump completely, S30 is both the sync primitive and the revert mechanism: any client-side inventory manipulation is undone the moment the server decides to re-send.

Only Rise uses S30 as a module surface in the corpus. Rise 5.99 Stealer treats it as the go signal: gotItems flips true when the chest contents land, and the steal loop only starts clicking after that flag, with a randomized per-click delay and auto-close. Rise 5.99 Aura resets its blocking flag on S30, since a full window sync invalidates the client's assumption that the sword is still blocking. Rise 6.x AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent counts S30 among the significant packets that dirty the HUD cache.

S30 is the correction mechanism that makes S2F cancellation a short-horizon trick: one rejected transaction and the server pushes a full dump that reverts any ghost slot. For stealers the ordering constraint is the exploit surface: clicking before S30, or after a rejected click, races the resync and produces the visible pattern (clicking a slot whose content the server already changed) that chest-stealer heuristics flag. The packet is also the largest inventory packet on the wire, so a server that rejects transactions in a loop can force repeated full dumps, a bandwidth tax with no client-side mitigation in the corpus.

implementation.overview: The full-window sync and the revert path for rejected clicks. Rise 5.99's Stealer uses it as the trigger to start clicking chests, Aura resets its block state on it, and Rise 6.x treats it as a HUD-significant packet. Every other client in the corpus reaches it only through the vanilla handler.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.updateCraftingInventory (line 773) serializes the container's inventorySlots into a List and sends S30(windowId, list) on open, respawn, and after rejected clicks. NetHandlerPlayServer.processClickWindow validates the action number; on mismatch it calls updateCraftingInventory so the client receives a corrected dump. The client handler resolves the window by id (0 and the player window map to inventoryContainer, otherwise the open container) and overwrites all slots.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire: unsigned byte windowId, short count, then count Slot encodings (short id, byte count, short damage, optional NBT). Slots are ordered container-first, then player inventory 9-35, then hotbar 0-8. The cursor is not included; it is synced separately by S2F(-1,-1). A chest open produces S2D then S30 back to back, which is why inventory modules gate on S30 instead of the GUI opening event: the screen renders before the server contents arrive.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures S30 itself; it is authoritative recovery data. The heuristics that matter sit on the clicks around it: a stealer that fires before S30, or after a rejected transaction, clicks against stale content and produces the tell-tale sequence (C0E immediately followed by the server's S30 correction). Ghost-item exploits depend on S30 never arriving for the manipulated window, so cancel-happy modules trade durability: the longer the manipulation, the more likely a full dump reverts it.

modules.name: Stealer
modules.purpose: Chest stealer: use S30 as the sync gate, then click every whitelisted item with randomized delays and auto-close.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketReceive: if the packet is S30, set gotItems = true. onRender2DEvent: while GuiChest is open, wait a randomized decidedTimer (between min and max delay settings), then scan chest.inventorySlots and windowClick(chest.windowId, i, 0, 1, player) on the first whitelisted item, resetting the timer; auto-close via closeScreen once gotItems or ticksInChest > 10. gotItems resets whenever the player leaves the chest.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The randomized per-click delay and whitelist are the anti-heuristic layer; the pattern (one click per delay, immediate close) is still the classic chest-stealer fingerprint.
modules.variations: None in the corpus; Rise 6.x does not ship a chest stealer that touches S30, only the HUD component.

modules.name: Aura
modules.purpose: Reset the blocking state when a full window sync arrives.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketReceive: if the packet is S30PacketWindowItems, blocking = false. The Hypixel block mode keeps a blocking flag while the sword is held up; a full window sync means the server corrected the inventory, so the client must drop its assumption that the block is still active.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Purely a state resync; prevents false block states after inventory corrections. No anti-cheat signal.
modules.variations: None in the corpus; the file is 1145 lines of combat logic with this single S30 reference at line 190.

modules.name: AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent
modules.purpose: HUD performance component: S30 is one of the significant packets that force a GuiIngameCache redraw.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent: on S30, reset the StopWatch and mark the cache dirty so the next frame re-renders. Same component as the S2F entry; both packets are treated as inventory-significant events.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None; the component only observes the packet stream.
modules.variations: Identical file in 6.1.30.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent everywhere. Stealer additionally hooks Render2DEvent for the click loop and auto-close; Aura only the receive event; the Rise 6.x component only the receive event plus PreMotion and Render2D for cache management.
implementation.client_variations: Only Rise touches S30 outside vanilla in the corpus. Rise 5.99 has the gameplay modules (Stealer, Aura); Rise 6.x registers it in NetworkAPI for scripts and in AdaptiveRefreshRateComponent. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity 6.0 ship only the vanilla handler.

anticheat.overview: The window-items packet dumps the full contents of an inventory window, and for simulation anticheats it is the authoritative recovery data that resyncs the compensated inventory after rejected transactions or open-window changes. Grim consumes it in two places: the inventory mirror applies every server slot to its storage, and the entity replication listener uses window-id-0 dumps to detect held-item and offhand changes. Intave's nayoro stack models the same send as a WindowItemsEvent. No anticheat treats S30 as a detection surface on its own.

checks.name: Window-items inventory sync (Grim)
checks.purpose: Keep the compensated copy of the player inventory aligned with the server after every full window-items send.
checks.how_it_works: CompensatedInventory is a Check that listens on both directions. On WINDOW_ITEMS it wraps the packet, marks each server slot as corrected in the inventory storage, and when the window id is 0 (the player inventory) forces the packet-inventory mode back on and syncs the slot list. It tracks the open window id and the packet-sending inventory size, and falls back to the platform inventory for held item, offhand and armor reads when the packet stream is unsupported (modded menus).
checks.detects: Slot desync between the client's claimed inventory and the server's authoritative dump. The mirror is the basis for inventory-aware checks such as NoSlow and item-use validation.
checks.variations: PacketEntityReplication in the same repo consumes window-id-0 dumps to reset item-use state, and Artemis registers the packet in its repository (PacketPlayServerWindowItems) with a wrapper interface but no check logic.

checks.name: Window-items event (Intave)
checks.purpose: Model the server's window-items send as a typed nayoro event so Intave's inventory tracking can react to full window dumps.
checks.how_it_works: WindowItemsEvent carries the window id, the slot count, and a map of slot to item. It is one of the event types dispatched through the nayoro EventSink visitor, and the protocol layer registers it in the event registry. The class also handles item serialization for the nayoro wire format.
checks.detects: None directly: it is event plumbing that mirrors server inventory state into the monitoring stack that backs Intave's inventory and movement checks.
checks.variations: The only other named reference is Negativity's PacketType enum, which lists WINDOW_ITEMS as a clientbound constant; it is not consumed by any Negativity check.

wiki_notes: Clientbound 0x30: unsigned byte windowId, short slot count, then ItemStack per slot.
Window 0 dumps player inventory; container dump follows S2D open back to back.
Also sent as recovery when a C0E click is rejected, forcing client to revert slots.

MCP 1.8.9 S30PacketWindowItems implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleWindowItems; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readItemStackFromBuffer, readShort, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.updateCraftingInventory sends new S30PacketWindowItems (line 875): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Window Property
packets.desc: Updates a single property in a container (enchantment level, furnace burn time, brewing progress, etc.).
packets.notes: Property IDs vary by container type. Enchantment table: 0=top level, 1=middle, 2=bottom. Furnace: 0=burn time, 1=current item progress, 2=total cook time. Brewing stand: 0=brew time. Beacon: 0=power level.

writeup.p: S31PacketWindowProperty carries one container property update: unsigned byte windowId, short property id, short value. The meaning of the property id is container-type specific. The furnace uses 0 for burn time remaining, 1 for item cook progress, 2 for total cook time. The enchantment table uses 0-2 for the three level slots, the brewing stand 0 for brew time, the beacon 0 for power level. Tile entities push these through updateProgressBar whenever a field changes, typically once per tick while active.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleWindowProperty resolves the container by window id and calls Container.updateProgressBar, which writes into the container's progress array. The GUI renderers (furnace flame, enchant glint, brewing bubbles) read that array every frame. Server side, EntityPlayerMP.sendProgressBarUpdate (lines 783 and 788 in the bundled sources) forwards a single property and sendAllWindowProperties pushes every field when the window opens. The values are absolute, not deltas.

None of the 8 clients has a module for this packet. The only non-vanilla hits are the Rise 6.x NetworkAPI script registration table (both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4) and the vanilla handler files. Auto-enchant and auto-brewer style modules, which would read S31 to time clicks, do not exist in these corpora. The 8 clients concentrate their inventory effort on stealing, armor handling and transaction sync, not on container progress.

There is no exploit surface in this corpus. S31 is display-only state: the client renders the value and nothing else depends on it. A malicious server could flood S31 to churn the GUI renderer, but that is a server-side attack with no client counterpart, and no anti-cheat measures the packet because it carries no movement, combat or inventory-trust signal. Modules that needed progress data would have to parse the property stream themselves; none do.

implementation.overview: The container progress packet: furnace flames, enchant levels, brewing bubbles. Zero module hits in the 8 clients; the only non-vanilla reference is the Rise 6.x script API registration table. This is render data with no cheat value in this corpus.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.sendProgressBarUpdate constructs S31(windowId, var, value) and sends it whenever the open container's fields change; sendAllWindowProperties (line 788) pushes every field when the window opens. NetHandlerPlayClient.handleWindowProperty calls Container.updateProgressBar on the resolved container, which stores the value for the GUI to read. No validation, no rate limit, no client echo.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire: unsigned byte windowId, short property, short value. Property semantics are fixed per container class, not negotiated: furnace 0-2, enchantment table 0-2, brewing stand 0, beacon 0. Values are absolute ticks or levels so the GUI can render progress without keeping history. PLAY state only, and only while the corresponding container is open; the server stops sending once the player closes the window.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing to flag: S31 is server-authoritative display data, sent at most a few times per second per open container, and no movement, combat or inventory-trust check reads it. The only conceivable abuse is a server spamming S31 to load the GUI render path, a denial-of-service vector aimed at the client rather than something a cheat client would do.
implementation.general_hooks: No module hooks exist in the corpus. The packet reaches containers exclusively through the vanilla handler.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 register S31 in NetworkAPI so scripts can listen to it; that registration is the only non-vanilla reference in the corpus.

anticheat.overview: The corpus for this packet is empty: the mined index (data/ac-mined/S31PacketWindowProperty.txt) has no hits because the search terms were the MCP name S31PacketWindowProperty and the modern PacketPlayOutWindowProperty, while the 1.8 anticheats that know the packet call it WindowData. A direct grep of the anticheat root confirms the only references are registrations: Artemis maps SERVER_PLAY + 88 to PacketPlayServerWindowData and Negativity lists WINDOW_DATA in its PacketType enum. Neither runs a check on it. Container property updates are server-authoritative display data (furnace burn time, enchant levels, brewing progress) with no client-trust signal, so nothing flags them.

wiki_notes: The furnace uses four properties, not three: 0 is fuel left counting down, 1 is maximum fuel burn time, 2 is cook progress counting up, and 3 is maximum progress (always 200 on vanilla).

The enchantment table uses property 3 for the enchantment seed that drives the rune names shown clientside, and the beacon uses properties 1 and 2 for its first and second potion effect IDs (-1 means no effect).
The anvil uses property 0 for the repair cost in XP levels, and brewing-stand property 0 is a 0-400 countdown where 400 renders an empty arrow and 0 a full one.

MCP 1.8.9 S31PacketWindowProperty implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleWindowProperty; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readShort, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.sendProgressBarUpdate sends new S31PacketWindowProperty (line 886): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Confirm Transaction
packets.desc: Server confirms or rejects an inventory transaction from C0EPacketClickWindow. accepted=false causes client to revert inventory.

fields.name: actionNumber
fields.desc: Transaction action number from the click packet

fields.name: accepted
fields.desc: Whether the server accepted the click

packets.notes: If accepted=false, the client empties and refills its inventory by re-reading all slots from the server (C30PacketWindowItems is re-sent). This is how the server corrects desynced client inventory.

writeup.p: S32PacketConfirmTransaction is the server's reply to each serverbound C0F click confirmation: byte windowId, short actionNumber, boolean accepted. The action number is a per-container short counter the client increments on every click and echoes back; the server replies true when the number matches its own expectation and false when it does not. A false reply marks the window desynced and triggers a full S30 resync. The pair is also the de facto latency probe on post-2018 anti-cheats, which is why it is the most exploited clientbound packet in the Rise 6.x corpus.

NetHandlerPlayServer.processConfirmTransaction (lines 886-893 in the bundled sources) compares the echoed action number against the container's expected value: a match replies S32(windowId, action, true), a mismatch replies false and pushes S30 to force the client revert. NetHandlerPlayClient.handleConfirmTransaction resolves the container by window id and treats accepted=false as an order to re-read the window, which is how the server undoes any client-side inventory manipulation.

Seven distinct uses in the 10-client corpus. Rise 6.x WatchdogDisabler cancels negative-action S32 confirmations and replays the buffered C0F confirms a second later, a ping-spoof disabler. The 6.2.4 velocity modes (VulcanVelocity, WatchdogVelocity, WatchdogPredictionVelocity) cancel S32 on hit and answer with a deliberately corrupt C0F to desync transaction accounting around knockback. Timer queues S32 while its Watchdog timer mode runs behind a 9,999,999 ms ping spoof. InventorySync rewinds the container transaction counter from S32 values so spoofed clicks keep valid action numbers. Debugger prints every action number. November Recode 2.0's VelocityModule GRIM mode cancels S32 after a velocity cancel, queues the action numbers, and drops the matching C0F on send, a transaction-desync knockback bypass. LiquidSense Dev overwrites handleConfirmTransaction to auto-ack rejected windows through its own send-queue mixin.

The action counter is a short and the server only checks equality, so fabricating C0F replies is trivial; the subtlety is timing. Buffering C0F and cancelling S32 breaks the correlation the anti-cheat builds between server time and client time, which is the entire point of the Watchdog-era disabler. Cancelling an accepted=false S32 also prevents the inventory revert, which is what keeps ghost-item states alive. The cost is that the server's inventory truth diverges until a legitimate S30 lands, so the exploit is self-limiting.

implementation.overview: The confirmation half of the C0F/S32 transaction pair and the most exploited clientbound packet in the Rise 6.x corpus. WatchdogDisabler cancels and replays it, the velocity modes corrupt the transaction stream on hit, Timer queues it behind a ping spoof, InventorySync rewinds the action counter, and Debugger prints it. Spicy imports it and never instantiates it. November Recode 2.0 adds a GRIM transaction-queue velocity mode and LiquidSense Dev a handleConfirmTransaction overwrite.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerPlayServer.processConfirmTransaction (lines 886-893) replies S32(windowId, actionNumber, true) when the action matches the container's next expected short, otherwise false followed by updateCraftingInventory, which pushes S30. The container counter is per-window, starts at 0, and must be echoed exactly. The client handler resolves the container by window id; a false reply marks the window desynced and the server's S30 dump reverts the client's slot view.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire: byte windowId, short actionNumber, boolean accepted. C0F (serverbound) and S32 (clientbound) share windowId and actionNumber semantics; negative action numbers are legal and several anti-cheats use them as markers, which is why WatchdogDisabler specifically buffers transactions with actionNumber < 0. The pair doubles as a latency reference on Verus and Watchdog-class anti-cheats, so ping spoofers buffer C0F and S32 together with keepalives and flush them as one batch.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Verus and Watchdog-class anti-cheats fold C0F gaps into their latency model for movement checks. WatchdogDisabler's ping-spoof mode (cancel negative S32, replay all C0F confirms after 1s) and Spicy's Disabler (cancel every C0F, replay one every 500-1250ms) inflate measured ping and break that model. VulcanVelocity cancels S32 only when hurtTime == 10 and answers with a corrupt C0F, a Vulcan-specific knockback desync. The detection risk is not the packet itself but the divergence it causes: servers that resync on rejection eventually expose any client that keeps clicking stale windows.

modules.name: Debugger
modules.purpose: Print every S32 action number to chat as a development aid.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent; on S32, read the action number and push a chat message. Also prints S00 keepalive keys through the same handler.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None; the module only reads and prints.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 keep the same pattern (6.x checks transaction.getValue() and the packet type at line 109-110) with the same output.

modules.name: WatchdogDisabler
modules.purpose: Watchdog disabler mode: ping-spoof by cancelling negative-action S32 confirmations and replaying all C0F confirms after a one second delay; inventory mode re-wraps C0E clicks.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent: on S07 respawn, reset every queue and flag; if the ping-spoof value is on and S32 has a negative action number and the disabler is not already disabled, buffer the action, reset the stopwatch, and cancel the event. PreMotionEvent: when actions are buffered and one second elapsed, shuffle the list, send C0F(0, action, true) for each via sendPacket (bypassing the bus), and clear. PacketSendEvent: inventory mode cancels C0E for the player inventory when no GUI is open and re-sends it as C16 open-inventory, C0E, C0D close via sendUnregisteredPacket.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Negative-action transactions are the Watchdog marker; replaying them as confirms while cancelling the server's S32 keeps the server waiting on the client's timer, inflating the measured ping. The replay bypasses the event bus so it cannot be re-cancelled by another module.
modules.variations: The 6.2.4 version is a superset (278 lines) with the same core plus additional queues; 6.1.30 (104 lines) is the canonical minimal form.

modules.name: InventorySync
modules.purpose: Keep the client container transaction counter aligned with server confirmations.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent; on S32 for the player inventory container, store the action number; if 0 < action < container.transactionID, set transactionID = action + 1. This rewinds the client counter so the next C0E action number is a value the server has not seen yet, which matters when other modules (disablers, ping spoofers) have already consumed actions.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None directly; it is the repair module that keeps click sync valid while other modules spoof transactions.
modules.variations: Identical logic in 6.1.30 (same 34-line file under com/alan/clients).

modules.name: VulcanVelocity / WatchdogVelocity / WatchdogPredictionVelocity
modules.purpose: Velocity bypass keyed on S32 timing: cancel the confirmation on hit and answer with a corrupt C0F to desync the anti-cheat's transaction accounting.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent; on S32 when hurtTime == 10 (just hit), cancel the confirmation and send a fabricated C0F whose windowId and uid alternate between 1/-1 and -1/1 with the accepted flag toggling. Also cancels or scales S12 velocity and S27 explosion, with the Vulcan Speed mode check deciding between full cancel and 1.9x multiplication.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Vulcan-specific: the S32 gate ensures the spoof only fires during actual hit processing, and the corrupt transaction makes Vulcan's window accounting lose track of the knockback. A pure timing desync rather than a packet-rate abuse.
modules.variations: WatchdogVelocity (452 lines) and WatchdogPredictionVelocity (204 lines) implement the same S32-gated idea for Watchdog, the prediction variant replaying anticipated confirmations.

modules.name: Timer
modules.purpose: Watchdog timer mode that hides accelerated ticks behind a massive ping spoof.
modules.how_it_works: With the watchdog value on: PreMotionEvent forces onGround true; PreUpdateEvent calls PingSpoofComponent.spoof(9999999, ...) which buffers keepalives and transactions; PacketSendEvent intercepts S32 on ground, queues it into packetList and cancels the event; StrafeEvent flushes the queued packets via PacketUtil.queue and PingSpoofComponent.dispatch when the attempt flag is set (module key toggles attempt for 200 ms). S12 velocity and S08 teleport are cancelled on receive.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketSendEvent, PacketReceiveEvent, PreMotionEvent, PreUpdateEvent, TickEvent, StrafeEvent, JumpEvent, KeyboardInputEvent.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The 9,999,999 ms ping spoof makes the server's latency estimates absurd, which is how the timer acceleration hides. Queued S32 confirms are released on the next strafe cycle to keep the transaction stream alive.
modules.variations: None in 6.1.30; the 6.1.30 Timer (31 lines) does not reference S32.

modules.name: Disabler
modules.purpose: Hypixel disabler: buffer every serverbound C0F and replay them slowly to inflate measured ping.
modules.how_it_works: EventSendPacket: cancel every C0F and park it in a static list; EventUpdate: every 500-1250 ms send the oldest buffered C0F via sendPacketNoEvent; onEnable warns the user to relog. Also cancels C0C input on send and periodically re-sends C13 abilities with a random fly speed. The S32PacketConfirmTransaction import at line 30 is never used: the module's logic is purely serverbound C0F delay, with commented-out experiments in corrupting C0F fields.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The slow C0F stream keeps the server's transaction window open while the client stalls; the S32 import is vestigial. The module targets Hypixel and requires a relog to take effect.
modules.variations: None in the corpus; Spicy's other modules do not touch S32.

modules.name: VelocityModule (GRIM transaction queue)
modules.purpose: GRIM velocity bypass: after cancelling knockback, cancel the server's S32 confirmations and the matching outgoing C0F confirms to desync the anti-cheat's transaction-based movement timing.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent: on S12 for the local player, the CANCEL/GRIM/VULCAN modes cancel it and set funny. While funny, each S32PacketConfirmTransaction is cancelled and its action number queued. PacketSendEvent: an outgoing C0F whose uid is in the queue is cancelled (and removed from the queue); the EventUpdate listener clears funny once the queue drains. VULCAN mode instead cancels the next C0F after a cancelled S12.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.In / EventPacket.Out on the November event bus; EventUpdate for state reset.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The queue pairs each cancelled S32 with its own C0F so the server never sees the confirm it asked for, which breaks GRIM's transaction-gap timing without flooding. The comments mark VULCAN as working only on older Vulcan versions.
modules.variations: The Mode enum also carries INTAVE (unimplemented) and WATCHDOG_SAFE (applies partial motion manually); the S32 path is GRIM-only.

modules.name: MixinNetHandlerPlayClient (confirm overwrite)
modules.purpose: Re-implement handleConfirmTransaction so every rejected S32 is auto-answered with a true C0F through the client's own send-queue mixin.
modules.how_it_works: @Overwrite of handleConfirmTransaction: resolve the container by windowId (0 = inventoryContainer, otherwise openContainer), and when the packet says not accepted, addToSendQueue(new C0FPacketConfirmTransaction(windowId, actionNumber, true)) via Minecraft.getMinecraft().getNetHandler(). Semantics match vanilla; routing through getNetHandler().addToSendQueue means the confirm passes the class's own senpacket HEAD inject, which fires PacketSenEvent and lets modules cancel or delay it.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Behaviorally identical to vanilla, so no new detection surface; the point is that the confirm now travels through the LiquidBounce send event where Disabler-style modules can intercept it.
modules.variations: The same mixin class guards resource packs and fires EntityMovementEvent (see the C19 and S14 impl pages).

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the universal S32 surface in Rise. WatchdogDisabler adds PreMotionEvent and PacketSendEvent; Timer adds TickEvent, StrafeEvent, JumpEvent and KeyboardInputEvent; Spicy touches only the serverbound side via EventSendPacket. November Recode 2.0 uses EventPacket.In and EventPacket.Out on its own bus; LiquidSense Dev routes the auto-confirm through its send-queue mixin.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 has only Debugger. Rise 6.1.30 ships WatchdogDisabler, InventorySync and Debugger; 6.2.4 adds the velocity modes (VulcanVelocity, WatchdogVelocity, WatchdogPredictionVelocity) and the Timer watchdog mode. Spicy's Disabler imports S32 but processes only C0F. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma and Tenacity 6.0 carry only the vanilla handler. November Recode 2.0 is the only client cancelling S32 on the receive side (VelocityModule GRIM); LiquidSense Dev re-implements the handler rather than cancelling it.

anticheat.overview: S32 is the server's transaction confirmation, the oldest reliable latency probe in the protocol: the server sends a transaction id, the client echoes it back, and the round trip is the ping.
