Modern anticheats have turned the echo into a transaction clock (Grim sends a transaction before and after sensitive packets, Hydro schedules work on frames), while classic anticheats use it as a ping spoof detector by comparing transaction latency against keep-alive latency. Because the client must echo the exact id, S32 is also where ping-spoof disablers attack the anticheat.

checks.name: PacketPingListener (Grim)
checks.purpose: Runs the transaction clock: sends transaction ids the client must echo, tracks send and receive order, and fires the transaction events the whole anticheat schedules on.
checks.how_it_works: On the OUT side, records each sent window-confirmation (negative ids Grim generates, and the ping packet on modern versions) into a sent-map and increments lastTransactionSent. On the IN side, only accepts replies whose id was actually sent, marks the transaction valid, cancels the echo to keep packet limiters happy, and fires the send/receive events that checks, setback teleports and velocity handlers all schedule against.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof disablers that echo fake transaction ids, and any client that reorders or drops transaction confirmations.
checks.variations: Hydro's TransactionTracker uses Pledge frames for the same two-phase confirmation; Frequency keeps a simple id-to-timestamp map.

checks.name: PingSpoofA (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Flags ping spoofing as a divergence between the transaction-measured ping and the keep-alive-measured ping.
checks.how_it_works: On each flying packet, reads the transaction ping (from the ConnectionManager echo map) and the keep-alive ping. If the transaction ping exceeds the keep-alive ping by more than 50ms outside lag, teleport, tps and chunk exemptions, and after the first 10 ticks, the check fails.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof modules that inflate only the transaction clock while the keep-alive clock stays honest.
checks.variations: Azure's PingSpoof sends its own random transaction ids and compares the echo delay to the reported NMS ping; both detect the same divergence.

checks.name: PingSpoof (Azure)
checks.purpose: Sends its own random transaction probes and compares the echo delay against the reported ping to expose spoofed latency.
checks.how_it_works: On the first flying packet after a transaction, sends a server-bound transaction with a random id and sets the sent flag. When the client echoes it, the check compares the round-trip delay against the player's reported NMS ping: if the reported ping is more than 2.75 times the measured delay plus 50ms, it flags with the spoofed millisecond difference.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof modules that inflate the reported ping while the real transaction echo stays fast.
checks.variations: Frequency compares two independent clocks; Azure compares the transaction clock against the server's own reported ping field.

checks.name: TransactionTracker (Hydro)
checks.purpose: Schedules anticheat work on the transaction confirmations using Pledge frames, and kicks on frame errors.
checks.how_it_works: Registers pre and post actions against Pledge frame ids: confirmPre schedules work on the first id of a frame, confirmPost on the second. When a transaction frame arrives, the tracker runs every action scheduled for that id; missing or incomplete frames are handled as error events that kick the player.
checks.detects: Transaction desync and confirmation manipulation: a client that drops or reorders confirmations produces missing or incomplete frames.
checks.variations: Grim implements the same two-phase ordering natively; Hydro outsources it to Pledge and turns frame errors into kicks.

wiki_notes: Server reply to C0F click: byte windowId, short actionNumber, bool accepted. Accepted=false rejects the click and the client reverts its inventory view.
After a reject the server pushes a full S30 WindowItems resync so client slots match server truth. Action numbers are per-window short counters echoed exactly.

MCP 1.8.9 S32PacketConfirmTransaction implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleConfirmTransaction; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBoolean, readShort, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: NetHandlerPlayServer.processClickWindow sends new S32PacketConfirmTransaction (line 1031): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/network/NetHandlerPlayServer.java

packets.name: Update Sign
packets.desc: Updates a sign's text for all nearby players.

writeup.p: S33PacketUpdateSign carries one sign's text: a BlockPos (packed long) plus four chat components. The server sends it to every player tracking the chunk when a sign is placed or edited, including the editing player, so the client replaces the tile entity's lines and re-renders. The content is formatted text, not raw strings, so formatting codes and component metadata survive the trip.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleUpdateSign looks up the tile entity at the packet position, copies the four lines into TileEntitySign.signText, and if the local player is editing that sign, overwrites the GUI's text fields with the server's canonical text. TileEntitySign.func_145912_a (line 116 in the bundled sources) builds the packet from the raw lines. The client trusts the content completely; there is no length or content validation beyond the component format.

None of the 8 clients has a module for this packet. The only non-vanilla hits are the Rise 6.x NetworkAPI script registration table (both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4) and the vanilla handler files. NameProtect-style modules, which would rewrite sign text to hide player names, do not appear in any of the 8 corpora. The packet has no movement, combat or inventory value, so cheat clients have no reason to intercept it.

The content is untrusted server data rendered directly into the world, so the only theoretical abuse is component injection: a malicious server can embed hover and click events in sign lines. The client renders them, and none of the 8 clients sanitizes components. That is a server-side attack vector, not a cheat surface. No anti-cheat measures S33 because it carries no gameplay-trust signal.

implementation.overview: Zero module hits in the 8 clients. Sign text is display-only world data with no cheat value, and NameProtect-style rewriting is absent from all 8 corpora. The only non-vanilla reference is the Rise 6.x script API registration table.
implementation.server_handling: TileEntitySign.func_145912_a (line 116) constructs S33(world, pos, lines) from signText, and the server broadcasts it to every player tracking the chunk. NetHandlerPlayClient.handleUpdateSign finds the tile entity, writes the four components into signText, and if the player is editing that sign, pushes the canonical text into the editor GUI. No validation of line content or length beyond the chat component format.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire: BlockPos packed as a long (x 26 bits, y 12 bits, z 26 bits), then four IChatComponent JSON strings, each VarInt length-prefixed UTF-8. Lines are chat components, so formatting codes survive. PLAY state only. The placing player receives the packet back, which is how the editor confirms the server accepted the write.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing to flag: S33 is authoritative world data sent once per sign change, and no movement, combat or inventory check reads it. The only conceivable issue is rendering-injection via crafted components from a malicious server, a client-side rendering decision no anti-cheat polices.
implementation.general_hooks: No module hooks exist in the corpus. The packet reaches tile entities exclusively through the vanilla handler.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 register S33 in NetworkAPI so scripts can intercept it; every other client in the corpus reaches it only through the vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient handler.

anticheat.overview: No anticheat in the corpus runs a check on the sign-update packet. The only real server-side reference is Artemis, which registers PacketPlayServerUpdateSign at SERVER_PLAY + 82; the rest of the mined corpus is keyword noise from the search term Sign: client-side sign-editing handling (C12PacketUpdateSign in Grim ExploitB and Vrekt-Arc PayloadFrequency, MC|BSign payload checks in Truthful CrasherA and Grim, Intave ItemCrashTracker.checkSign on Client.UPDATE_SIGN), sign block physics and placement in NoCheatPlus AutoSign, Kauri Materials and ThotPatrol UtilBlock, and unrelated JVM method-signature code in Intave's bundled ASM library. Sign text is authoritative world data the client renders, so server-side anticheats have nothing to measure.

wiki_notes: BlockPos packed long plus 4 sign lines as JSON chat components. Server broadcasts it to chunk trackers when a sign is placed or edited.
Client writes the lines into TileEntitySign and re-renders; the placing player gets it back as the edit confirmation.

MCP 1.8.9 S33PacketUpdateSign implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleUpdateSign; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBlockPos, readChatComponent.

1.8.9 callers: TileEntitySign.getDescriptionPacket sends new S33PacketUpdateSign (line 128): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/tileentity/TileEntitySign.java

packets.name: Maps
packets.desc: Updates a map item's data (pixels, colors).

writeup.p: S34PacketMaps delivers a map item's data: VarInt map id, byte scale, a collection of Vec4b map decorations (type, x, y, rotation), a short patch width, a short patch height, and the patch bytes, each a 4-bit palette index into the map color table. MapData builds it from the dirty column region; a full refresh goes out every fifth tick, incremental patches in between.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleMaps looks up MapData by map id in the player's inventory, applies the column patch into the colors buffer, updates scale and decorations, and marks the map for re-render. MapData.func_176101_a (lines 244-246 in the bundled sources) constructs the packet; the 5-tick full refresh keeps the renderer honest when no patch traffic flows. The client trusts the patch dimensions and writes them into the render buffer directly.

None of the 8 clients has a module for this packet. The only non-vanilla hits are the Rise 6.x NetworkAPI script registration table (both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4) and the vanilla handler files. No ESP, no map exploit, no minimap integration consumes S34 in these corpora. Map pixels are world render data with no entity, inventory or movement signal, so cheat clients have nothing to gain from it.

The only theoretical abuse is server-side: a malicious server can send patch dimensions that exceed the map buffer and stress the client renderer. That is a denial-of-service vector against the client, not a cheat surface, and no client in the corpus defends against it. No anti-cheat measures S34 because it carries no gameplay-trust signal.

implementation.overview: Zero module hits in the 8 clients. Map pixel patches are pure render data; no ESP or map-exploit module consumes S34 in these corpora. The only non-vanilla reference is the Rise 6.x script API registration table.
implementation.server_handling: MapData.func_176101_a (lines 244-246) produces S34(mapId, scale, visible decorations, colors, minX, minY, width, height); a full refresh is emitted every fifth tick (field_176109_i % 5 == 0) and dirty-column patches in between. NetHandlerPlayClient.handleMaps resolves the MapData by id from the player's inventory, copies the patch into the colors array, refreshes scale and decorations, and triggers a re-render. The client applies the patch without validating dimensions.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire: VarInt mapId, byte scale, VarInt icon count, then per icon a byte type, byte x, byte y, byte rotation, then short patch width, short patch height, then width x height bytes of 4-bit palette indexes. The patch is a dirty-column region; the full 128x128 refresh is a single patch with 16,384 bytes of indexes. PLAY state only, delivered to players who hold the map or stand near it.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat touches S34: it is render data delivered to map holders and nearby players. The only risk is a malicious server sending oversized patches to load the client renderer, a server-side attack with no client cheat counterpart.
implementation.general_hooks: No module hooks exist in the corpus. The packet reaches MapData exclusively through the vanilla handler.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 register S34 in NetworkAPI for scripts; the other six clients carry only the vanilla handler.

anticheat.overview: No anti-cheat consumes S34. The corpus sweep for S34PacketMaps and PacketPlayOutMap returns only keyword noise from the chunk family: Artemis' HardcodeMap generator and its GPacketPlayServerChunkLoad and GPacketPlayServerChunkLoadBulk wrappers match on the PacketPlayOutMapChunk class names, and Kauri's BlockUpdateHandler Javadoc mentions a wrapped map-chunk packet. None of these read map item data. S34 is pure render state for players holding or standing near a map, with no movement, combat or inventory signal, so no check in any cloned anticheat references it.

wiki_notes: Scale runs 0 to 4, where 0 is fully zoomed in at 1 block per pixel and 4 is fully zoomed out at 16 blocks per pixel.
Each map icon carries a type plus X and Z in map coordinates (-128 for the far edge to +127) and a direction of 0-15, where 0 is a vertical icon and each step rotates 22.5 degrees.

MCP 1.8.9 S34PacketMaps implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleMaps; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readByte, readByteArray, readUnsignedByte, readVarIntFromBuffer.
1.8.9 callers: MapData.getPacket sends new S34PacketMaps (line 270): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/world/storage/MapData.java

packets.name: Update Tile Entity
packets.desc: Updates NBT data for a tile entity (sign, skull, beacon, command block, etc.).

writeup.p: Server-pushed NBT updates for tile entities: a BlockPos, a one-byte action type, and an NBT tag. The action discriminates the tile entity class (1 mob spawner, 2 command block, 3 beacon, 4 skull, 5 flower pot, 6 banner), and the client applies the tag only when the loaded tile entity at that position matches the action. It is the per-block complement to the block change packets: S22 and S23 carry block ids and metadata, while S35 carries the full compound for the entity attached to a block. Sign line edits, skull owner changes, beacon effect retunes and spawner entity swaps all arrive here.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleUpdateTileEntity dispatches on the main thread (PacketThreadUtil), checks isBlockLoaded(pos), fetches the tile entity, and calls readFromNBT only when the action matches the tile entity class; an unloaded position or a mismatched type is silently dropped, so a forged packet cannot create tile entities out of thin air. The producers are the tile entities themselves: TileEntityMobSpawner emits action 1, TileEntityCommandBlock 2, TileEntityBeacon 3, TileEntitySkull 4, TileEntityFlowerPot 5, TileEntityBanner 6.

In this corpus they do not. The mined grep across all 8 clients returns only the vanilla handler, the EnumConnectionState registration, the INetHandlerPlayClient declaration and the tile entity producers; the only non-vanilla hit is Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 NetworkAPI.java registering S35PacketUpdateTileEntity.class for the script engine. There is no SignESP, chest tracker or beacon ESP module referencing S35 in Memeware, Nekoware, Rise, Sigma, Spicy or Tenacity. The metadata drafts for Tenacity 6.0 ChestESP and SpawnerFinder fail corpus verification and are deliberately not listed.

Because the handler requires a loaded chunk and a matching tile entity class, the packet is a poor injection surface and no anti-cheat measures it. The realistic module use would be read-only: sniffing sign text players type, or tracking spawner and beacon changes for ESP. Their absence in these clients is a corpus fact rather than a protocol limitation; nothing about the wire format stops a client from observing the stream.

implementation.overview: The tile entity state channel: the server pushes NBT diffs for signs, spawners, command blocks, beacons, skulls, flower pots and banners, and the client applies them only when the loaded tile entity matches the action byte. None of the 8 clients ships a module that reads or cancels this packet; the corpus holds only vanilla handler and producer hits plus Rise 6.x script API registration.
implementation.server_handling: The server never validates the payload beyond construction: each tile entity builds its own packet from its NBT via getUpdatePacket, and the server sends it to the relevant players. The readFromNBT gate on the client is the only enforcement point. The action byte is read as unsigned, so the vanilla set of 1-6 is a convention rather than a wire constraint; modded servers reuse the channel for custom tile entities.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire layout: BlockPos (a packed long, x << 38 | z << 12 | y in the 1.8.9 encoding), an unsigned byte action, then a length-prefixed NBT compound. The NBT payload dominates the size: a banner pattern list or a long command block command can push the packet past the server compression threshold. Frequent beacon or spawner updates are a known bandwidth cost on chunk-heavy servers.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat watches S35; it is server-trusted data flowing clientbound. The only abuse vector is a malicious server shipping crafted NBT to crash or lag clients, which is a server-side concern outside module scope. Clients gain nothing by spoofing it because the direction is clientbound and the handler discards mismatches, so the packet contributes nothing to detection or evasion.
implementation.general_hooks: The natural hook surface is PacketReceiveEvent, but no module in the 8-client corpus registers one for S35; Rise 6.x additionally exposes the class through its script NetworkAPI whitelist.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 let scripts match S35 through the script API packet registry; the other six clients carry only vanilla references.

anticheat.overview: No anti-cheat consumes S35. Every corpus hit matches the TileEntity keyword rather than the packet: Grim's chunk readers and CompensatedWorld pass TileEntity arrays embedded in map-chunk data, NCP's BlockCache implementations call world.getTileEntity to read server-side block state, Kauri's BlockUpdateHandler forwards the same chunk-embedded array, Photon's WorldDownloaderSentinel writes a disable-tile-entity-saving option into the WorldDownloader channel, and intave's EntityTypeDataRegistry is a misnamed entity-type hitbox table. The only direct packet references are plumbing: Negativity's TILE_ENTITY_DATA constant, and Artemis' PacketRepository entry with the PacketPlayServerTileEntityData wrapper interface. Tile-entity policing runs on the commit side of sign edits instead: NCP AutoSign and Intave ItemCrashTracker.checkSign watch C12PacketUpdateSign, because S35 is server-trusted NBT the client applies only when the loaded tile entity matches the action byte.

wiki_notes: BlockPos, unsigned-byte action, full NBT compound. 1.8.9 actions: 1 spawner, 2 command block, 3 beacon, 4 skull, 5 flower pot, 6 banner.
Client applies NBT only if a matching tile entity is loaded at the pos; mismatches and unloaded positions are silently dropped.

MCP 1.8.9 S35PacketUpdateTileEntity implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleUpdateTileEntity; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBlockPos, readNBTTagCompoundFromBuffer, readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: TileEntityBanner.getDescriptionPacket sends new S35PacketUpdateTileEntity (line 98) +5 more: https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/tileentity/TileEntityBanner.java

packets.name: Sign Editor Open
packets.desc: Opens the sign editor GUI for a specific sign position.

writeup.p: One field, one purpose: the BlockPos of a sign the player may edit. The server sends it when the player right-clicks an edit-eligible sign (EntityPlayerMP.openEditSign), and the client opens GuiEditSign over that position. It is the request half of the sign edit flow; the committed text returns as C12PacketUpdateSign. It is the only play-state packet that forces a GUI open purely from coordinates, which makes it the canonical trigger point for sign automation.

handleSignEditorOpen dispatches on the main thread, reads the tile entity at the position, and if it is not a TileEntitySign it fabricates one, attaches the world and position, then calls thePlayer.openEditSign. Because the handler constructs the tile entity, the packet works even when the sign block is not client-loaded, a quirk automation could lean on. Server side the producer is EntityPlayerMP.openEditSign, which sends S36 built from the sign's position.

Zero module hits across all 8 clients. The mined grep returns only the vanilla handler, the EntityPlayerMP producer, the EnumConnectionState registration and the packet class, plus Rise 6.x script API registration. Auto-sign modules that auto-fill shop or claim signs would hook exactly this packet and answer with C12PacketUpdateSign, but none exists in Memeware, Nekoware, Rise, Sigma, Spicy or Tenacity. The metadata draft for an AutoSign module has no corpus backing and is omitted.

The packet is clientbound and only changes GUI state, so there is no exploit surface worth the name. A server can spam it to force the editor open, which is an annoyance rather than an exploit; the client honors it only while in game. Nothing validates, rate-limits or acknowledges it, and no anti-cheat measures it. The practical module use is benign: observing when the server grants edit rights, then answering with a pre-filled C12.

implementation.overview: The sign edit prompt: one BlockPos that makes the client open GuiEditSign. It is the request half of the sign flow, with the text committed separately via C12PacketUpdateSign. No module in the 8-client corpus hooks it, so the impl is a vanilla-only story about a GUI state transition with no exploit surface.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.openEditSign sends it with no validation beyond the right-click interaction; the server never tracks whether the client opened the editor. The sign text is only committed when C12PacketUpdateSign arrives, so S36 is a prompt rather than a lock: the server cannot tell an auto-filled response from a typed one.
implementation.protocol_notes: A single BlockPos encoded as the 1.8.9 packed long. PLAY state only. The packet implies a stateful client transition (GUI open) but carries no transaction id, so duplicates or reordered packets simply reopen the editor. This is also why modules cannot correlate a specific S36 with a specific C12 without tracking the position themselves.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Irrelevant to anti-cheats: no movement, timing or combat signal. Servers that police auto sign filling do it by pattern-matching C12PacketUpdateSign text and measuring the latency between open and commit against human behavior. No module in the corpus exists to trigger such heuristics anyway.
implementation.general_hooks: The natural hook surface is PacketReceiveEvent, but no module in the 8-client corpus registers one for S36; Rise 6.x only adds the class to its script NetworkAPI whitelist.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients carry the byte-identical vanilla handler; the only non-vanilla reference anywhere in the corpus is the Rise 6.x script API registration.

anticheat.overview: The sign editor open packet has an empty corpus: the sweep for S36PacketSignEditorOpen and PacketPlayOutSignEditorOpen returns zero hits across all 50 anticheats. The packet only flips GUI state, so anticheats police sign interaction on the commit side instead. NCP's AutoSign times the gap between the server granting edit rights and the C12PacketUpdateSign commit, and Intave's ItemCrashTracker.checkSign validates the returned sign lines; the open prompt itself carries no abuse signal and nothing in the corpus reads it.

wiki_notes: Single BlockPos of a sign the player may edit. Client opens the GuiEditSign editor over that position.
Prompt only: text is committed separately via serverbound C12 UpdateSign, so the server cannot tell typed text from auto-filled.
MCP 1.8.9 S36PacketSignEditorOpen implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleSignEditorOpen; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readBlockPos.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.openEditSign sends new S36PacketSignEditorOpen (line 744): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Statistics
packets.desc: Updates statistic values (walk distance, damage dealt, items crafted, etc.).

writeup.p: The stats and achievements channel. The server ships a map of StatBase to integer value on join and after each stat change, and the client folds it into its StatisticsFile and triggers the achievement toast for positive achievement values. The payload mixes plain counters with achievements, so a module cannot silence the toast without also discarding the counters unless it rewrites the map.

handleStatistics iterates the entry set and calls the stat file writer's readStat per entry, then triggers the toast sequence for achievements with a value greater than zero. Server side, StatisticsFile.sendStats dumps the full file on join and sendUpdate pushes a delta after each change, both via S37. It is the only path by which the client learns its own stats, which makes it the interception point for any stats-related module.

Exactly one real module in the corpus: Rise 5.99 NoAchievements cancels every S37 on receive, killing the toast at the cost of stale local counters. The other seven clients have zero module hits; their corpus entries are the vanilla handler, the StatisticsFile producers, the registry and the Rise 6.x script NetworkAPI registration. The metadata draft for a StatSpoof module has no corpus backing. The landscape is thin because stats are cosmetic: they grant no combat, movement or rendering advantage.

The entire surface is the client-side cancel, and it is invisible: there is no serverbound stats packet, so the server never learns the client discarded the data. Anti-cheats ignore the packet entirely. The engineering subtlety is collateral: S37 bundles achievements with counters, so NoAchievements trades accurate local stats for a quiet toast; a surgical implementation would rewrite the map instead of cancelling the packet.

implementation.overview: The stats and achievements channel, normally invisible to cheat clients. Exactly one corpus module touches it: Rise 5.99 NoAchievements cancels the packet on receive to silence the achievement toast, accepting stale local counters as the price. Everything else in the corpus is vanilla handler and producer code.
implementation.server_handling: StatisticsFile.sendStats (join, full dump) and sendUpdate (per-change delta) both push via playerNetServerHandler.sendPacket. There is no rate limit, no acknowledgment and no retry: the server pushes and forgets, and the client applies whatever arrives. On join the packet is part of the login burst alongside S38 and S39.
implementation.protocol_notes: Encoding: VarInt count, then per entry a VarInt stat id and a VarInt value. Stat ids resolve against the client's own StatList tables; unknown ids are skipped silently. A full join dump is dozens of entries but each is compact, so the packet rarely matters for bandwidth. The values are absolute rather than deltas even in sendUpdate: the map holds the new totals.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not measured by any anti-cheat: no serverbound counterpart exists, so nothing about client behavior can be inferred from this stream, and the client-side cancel produces zero server-visible signal. Modules face no detection risk from S37 handling, which is why the only module in the corpus uses it as a blunt UI toggle.

modules.name: NoAchievements
modules.purpose: Suppress the achievement notification toast by cancelling the entire statistics packet.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent handler checks the packet type and calls event.setCancelled(true) on every S37PacketStatistics. Because the packet bundles plain stat counters with achievements, cancelling it also kills the toast trigger inside handleStatistics; the local counters simply never update.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Zero detection risk: the cancel is client-only and the packet has no serverbound counterpart, so the server sees no signal at all. The only cost is stale local statistics and achievement state.
modules.variations: Single implementation in the corpus. Rise 6.x ships no NoAchievements module; it registers S37 for its script API instead.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on the client event bus; only Rise 5.99 registers one for S37.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 cancels the live packet via event.setCancelled(true); Rise 6.x has no module but whitelists the class in the script NetworkAPI.

anticheat.overview: No anti-cheat reads the statistics packet. The corpus hits all match the Statistic or Statistics keyword, not the packet: Photon's DoubleStatistics and batch-processing math, TruthfulAC's Statistics utilities, Artemis' DescriptiveStatistics in the autoclicker checks, intave's CheckStatistics bookkeeping, Kauri's Interval summary statistics, Hydro's violation-message Statistics line, Shard's Bukkit Statistic enum reads in ProfileCommand, MC-Jinky's statistics key message and NCP's comment noise are all statistical infrastructure. The only direct packet references are registrations: Negativity's STATISTIC constant, FlopAC's NMSObject STATISTICS string, and Artemis' PacketRepository entry with the PacketPlayServerStatistic wrapper. S37 is pure server-authored display state with no serverbound counterpart, so nothing about client behavior can be inferred from it.

wiki_notes: The client can explicitly request its statistics through the Client Status packet, which the server answers with this packet.

The statistic map covers block-mining, item crafting, use, breakage, pickup, and drop counters, entity kills and deaths-by-entity, plus custom counters such as play time, distances traveled, damage dealt and taken, deaths, mob kills, and player kills.

1.8.9 callers: StatisticsFile.func_150876_a sends new S37PacketStatistics (line 227): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/stats/StatisticsFile.java

packets.name: Player List Item
packets.desc: Adds, updates, or removes entries from the tab player list. Used for player join/leave, gamemode changes, ping updates, and display name changes.

fields.name: players
fields.desc: List of AddPlayerData entries (UUID, name, profile properties, gamemode, ping, display name)

encoding: UUID + String + Property[] + VarInt + VarInt + ChatComponent
packets.notes: Action 0 (ADD_PLAYER): UUID, name, skin properties, gamemode, ping, display name. Action 4 (REMOVE_PLAYER): just UUID. Action 2 (UPDATE_LATENCY): UUID + ping. This is how the client builds the tab list and gets player skins.

writeup.p: The tab list state machine: one VarInt action plus a list of per-player records. ADD_PLAYER (0) ships UUID, name, the skin property map, gamemode, ping and an optional display name; UPDATE_GAME_MODE (1) and UPDATE_LATENCY (2) carry a UUID plus one field; UPDATE_DISPLAY_NAME (3) a UUID plus an optional chat component; REMOVE_PLAYER (4) a bare UUID. ServerConfigurationManager broadcasts ADD on join, REMOVE on leave, and every 600 ticks it broadcasts UPDATE_LATENCY for the whole list, which is how ping reaches the tab GUI.

handlePlayerListItem branches per action and mutates the player info map: ADD builds a NetworkPlayerInfo from the AddPlayerData, UPDATE_LATENCY overwrites the ping field, UPDATE_DISPLAY_NAME swaps the display name, REMOVE drops the entry. The ADD path doubles as the skin pipeline: the textures property is consumed by the player renderer. Server side, the packet constructors snapshot each EntityPlayerMP's profile, ping, gamemode and tab display name into records.

Four modules across three clients. Rise 5.99 Denicker intercepts ADD_PLAYER, decodes the base64 textures property from the GameProfile and compares the embedded profileName against the displayed name to reveal nicked players, pairing results with S02PacketChat join lines. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 StaffDetector keep a hardcoded staff list, but the S38 handler is commented out in both builds, leaving only the PreMotion decay counter live. Sigma 4.11 AntiVanish reads UPDATE_LATENCY and REMOVE_PLAYER to catch vanished players, and FriendAlert notifies when an ADD_PLAYER name matches the friend list.

The ADD_PLAYER payload is the richest unencrypted metadata stream in the protocol: the full GameProfile including signed skin properties, which Denicker turns into an identity oracle that nick plugins do not scrub. UPDATE_LATENCY is a ping heartbeat that enables vanish detection: a vanished player stops appearing, and AntiVanish also flags latency updates for UUIDs absent from the player info map. No anti-cheat polices the packet; the countermeasures are tab-list plugins that strip or re-sign properties.

implementation.overview: The tab list state machine and the most information-dense clientbound metadata channel: ADD_PLAYER carries full GameProfiles with signed skin properties. Four corpus modules live on it: Rise 5.99 Denicker decodes skin payloads to un-nick players, Rise 6.x StaffDetector carries a disabled S38 hook, and Sigma 4.11 AntiVanish and FriendAlert track the latency heartbeat and join records.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager sends ADD to everyone when a player joins and REMOVE on quit; the joining player additionally receives ADD records for everyone already online. onTick broadcasts UPDATE_LATENCY for the whole list every 600 ticks. The channel is broadcast-only: the server never validates what the client does with the data, and there is no clientbound acknowledgment.
implementation.protocol_notes: The action is a VarInt enum. Record layout depends on action; the widest is ADD_PLAYER: UUID, name capped at 16 chars, VarInt property count, then per property name, value and optional signature strings with a boolean flag, then gamemode VarInt, ping VarInt and an optional chat component. Property strings cap at 32767 bytes. UPDATE_LATENCY entries are only UUID plus ping VarInt, which is why ping refreshes stay cheap.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not a detection surface; no anti-cheat measures tab list traffic. The realistic risks are social and structural: Denicker's un-nicking fails when servers strip profileName from the textures payload, and vanish alerts are defeated by networks that keep vanished players in the tab list, which is exactly why Sigma hard-disables AntiVanish on hypixel, hive and mineplex via a server-IP check.

modules.name: Denicker
modules.purpose: Reveal the real identity of nicked players by decoding the signed skin texture payload from ADD_PLAYER records.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, an ADD_PLAYER S38 is read: the first AddPlayerData's GameProfile is taken, the textures property is base64-decoded into JSON, and the embedded profileName is compared with the displayed name. Mismatches are queued as realName=nickedName pairs; S02PacketChat join messages are then scanned on a background thread, and a matching nick triggers a notification plus a log4j chat rewrite when overlay support is on.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat involvement; the countermeasure is server-side property scrubbing. Servers that strip or re-sign the textures property defeat the decode, which is why the module only works on networks that leave profileName intact.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 only; no other corpus client ships an S38-based denicker.

modules.name: StaffDetector
modules.purpose: Detect staff on the server by matching tab list names against a hardcoded staff list, then auto-leave via /hub.
modules.how_it_works: The module keeps a hardcoded comma-separated staff name list and a PreMotion counter that decays each tick. In both corpus builds the actual packet handling is commented out: the S38 ADD_PLAYER and S3EPacketTeams branches that would count staff sightings and send /hub at count 6 are dead code. Only the name list and the decay counter remain live.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat risk; the feature is a reconnaissance countermeasure. The hardcoded list is per-network and rots quickly, which is presumably why the hook was disabled in the shipped builds.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 carries the same file under com/alan/clients/module/impl/exploit with the same commented-out S38 branch.

modules.name: AntiVanish
modules.purpose: Detect vanished players by watching UPDATE_LATENCY and REMOVE_PLAYER records that reference UUIDs absent from the tab list.
modules.how_it_works: On EventPacket (incoming), UPDATE_LATENCY records are checked against mc.getNetHandler().getPlayerInfo(uuid): a latency update for a UUID with no player info entry is flagged as a vanished player and added to a watch list. On the update event, any watched UUID that later gains a player info entry is reported as un-vanished. A REMOVE_PLAYER branch prints the removed display name. A server-IP guard auto-disables on hypixel, hive and mineplex.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat risk; the module is pure tab list observation. Its practical weakness is structural: any server that keeps vanished players listed (Hypixel-style) defeats the oracle, which is why the module refuses to run there.
modules.variations: Sigma-only. Rise 6.x attempts the inverse (staff detection) with a name list; no other client watches the latency heartbeat.

modules.name: FriendAlert
modules.purpose: Notify when a friend joins by matching ADD_PLAYER profile names against the friend manager.
modules.how_it_works: On incoming EventPacket, an ADD_PLAYER S38 is iterated and each AddPlayerData's profile name is checked with FriendManager.isFriend; a match posts a Friend Alert notification with the name. The module reads only the name field and ignores the skin properties.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No detection surface; join alerts are indistinguishable from passive tab list rendering to the server.
modules.variations: Sigma-only in the corpus; Rise 5.99's Denicker pairs ADD_PLAYER with S02 join messages instead of relying on the friend manager.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent / incoming EventPacket is universal; Rise 6.x adds its component system on top of the same receive bus.
implementation.client_variations: Sigma reads fields through the MCP accessors (func_179768_b, func_179767_a, field_179964_d); Rise 5.99 uses the same MCP names; Rise 6.x uses renamed accessors (getMatches-style). None of the four modules mutate the packet; all are read-only consumers.

anticheat.overview: The player-list packet manages tab list entries: add, remove, and updates of game mode, ping and display name. Server-side anticheats almost never validate it, and in this corpus only Grim consumes it: one listener rewrites game modes to hide spectators, and the entity replication listener stores the UUID-to-profile mappings that checks use to resolve entity identities. The keyword noise in the corpus is tab-complete and math-table code, not player-list handling.

checks.name: Spectator hiding in the player list (Grim)
checks.purpose: Prevent spectators on Grim's spectate system from leaking through the tab list with spectator game mode.
checks.how_it_works: PacketHidePlayerInfo is a HIGHEST-priority send listener. For PLAYER_INFO (pre-1.19.3) it walks the player data list and, for entries that should be hidden, rewrites SPECTATOR game mode to SURVIVAL, cancels the packet when every entry was hidden and the action was a pure game-mode update, and marks the packet for re-encoding otherwise. The 1.19.3+ PLAYER_INFO_UPDATE path does the same per entry, removes the UPDATE_GAME_MODE action from a cancelled packet, and re-encodes modified entries.
checks.detects: Not a cheat detection: it hides the anticheat's own spectators from other players' tab lists, which also removes the game-mode tell that would expose staff spectating.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus touches player-list packets; the rest of the S38 corpus hits are tab-complete (C0B) or table-name keyword noise.

checks.name: Player-list replication (Grim)
checks.purpose: Record the UUID-to-profile mappings announced on the player list so entity and profile lookups in checks resolve correctly.
checks.how_it_works: PacketEntityReplication wraps PLAYER_INFO and PLAYER_INFO_UPDATE sends and, transaction-sandwiched, puts ADD_PLAYER game profiles into compensatedEntities.profiles and removes them on REMOVE_PLAYER. The profile map feeds checks that need the game profile behind an entity id or uuid.
checks.detects: None directly; it is state replication that keeps the compensated entity model consistent with the tab list.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus reads player-list packets; Grim's SpectateManager is the only consumer of the stored profiles besides the checks themselves.

wiki_notes: Tab-list ping icons follow fixed thresholds: negative (unknown) ping shows the no-connection icon, under 150 ms shows 5 bars, under 300 shows 4 bars, under 600 shows 3 bars, under 1000 shows 2 bars, and anything slower shows 1 bar.

packets.name: Player Abilities
packets.desc: Server updates the player's capabilities (flying, invulnerable, creative, fly speed, walk speed).
packets.notes: This is the SERVER→CLIENT version. The server sends this when the player's abilities change. The CLIENT→SERVER version is C13PacketPlayerAbilities (which only carries the isFlying flag).

writeup.p: Server-to-client capability sync: one flags byte (0x01 invulnerable, 0x02 flying, 0x04 allowFlying, 0x08 creative), then fly speed and walk speed floats. The server pushes it on join, on every capabilities change, and as part of the login burst alongside S01, S37 and S38. Its serverbound mirror C13PacketPlayerAbilities carries only the isFlying flag, so S39 is the only place the client learns the full authoritative set.

handlePlayerAbilities copies all four flags and both speeds into thePlayer.capabilities, and the movement code then obeys them: fly speed scales creative flight, walk speed scales ground speed. Server side, processPlayerAbilities (C13) flips only isFlying and only when allowFlying is true, so the server stays authoritative and re-broadcasts the corrected state via S39 whenever it disagrees with the client. The client handlers are behaviorally identical across all 8 corpus clients.

Three Rise 6.x surface areas. CreativeFlight, a mode of the Flight module, rewrites the received packet in place: wrapper.setFlying(mc.thePlayer.capabilities.isFlying) so the server's flying flag can never desync the client while the mode force-flies the player at timer speed 3. Debugger carries an Abilities toggle that prints fly speed, allowFlying and isFlying to chat for protocol inspection. PingSpoofComponent classifies S39 as a teleport-class packet, so when a spoof window is active, held S39 packets flush together with S08 teleports and S09 held-item changes rather than being held with regular traffic.

The packet is clientbound, so the server cannot see mutations; the risk is desync rather than detection. CreativeFlight's rewrite makes local capabilities authoritative and hides the server's corrections, viable only while the server does not re-send S39 faster than the module rewrites it. The packet also constrains packet-holding systems: because S39 arrives on gamemode and flight changes, holding it across an S08 teleport would leave the client's flag state and position inconsistent, which is why the component groups the three packet classes.

implementation.overview: The authoritative capability sync packet: flags byte plus fly and walk speeds, mirrored by a single-flag serverbound C13. Three Rise 6.x surface areas in the corpus: CreativeFlight rewrites the received S39 to claim flying, Debugger prints its fields for protocol inspection, and PingSpoofComponent treats it as teleport-class traffic so held S39 flushes with S08.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP re-sends S39 whenever the capabilities setter path detects a change, and ServerConfigurationManager sends it once on join. C13 processing is the only serverbound input and it gates flying on allowFlying; the server's S39 responses are the corrective loop that keeps the client honest about permission.
implementation.protocol_notes: One flags byte then two raw 32-bit IEEE floats with no quantization: 0.05 default fly speed, 0.1 default walk speed. Bit 0x02 is current flying, 0x04 is permission to fly; creative players get both set, survival players neither unless a plugin grants flight. The same byte layout is reused by C13, which zeroes the unused fields.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats infer flight from movement and C13, not from S39, but the packet is a synchronization oracle for them: a client that never confirms flying while the S39 stream says flying is on is not mirroring state, and the movement that follows is what actually flags. CreativeFlight's rewrite exists to keep that mirror consistent. Holding components treat S39 as teleport-adjacent because a held S39 crossing a held S08 desyncs flags and position, a failure mode that correlates with timer and fly flags.

modules.name: CreativeFlight
modules.purpose: Force creative-style flight on survival servers by keeping the server's flying flag in sync with client-forced capabilities.
modules.how_it_works: A mode of the Flight module. On enable it sets capabilities.isFlying and jumps; on pre-motion it force-flies with timer speed 3 and motion scaling. In the receive handler, every S39PacketPlayerAbilities is rewritten in place: wrapper.setFlying(mc.thePlayer.capabilities.isFlying), so the server's corrections can never desync the local flying state. PreUpdateEvent arms PingSpoofComponent.spoof(300000, ...) to hold all stateful traffic while the mode runs.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The mutation is invisible to the server, but the movement it enables (timer 3, 9.5x motion scaling) is a textbook fly flag on any serious anti-cheat; the S39 rewrite only prevents the flag-state desync that would compound the detection.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 carries the same mode with an identical S39 branch (wrapper.setFlying(mc.thePlayer.capabilities.isFlying)); the 6.2.4 build adds the Render3D interpolation scaffolding.

modules.name: Debugger
modules.purpose: Developer tool that prints protocol traffic to chat, including a dedicated Abilities readout for S39.
modules.how_it_works: The receive handler branches by packet class: S32 transactions, S00 keepalives, S08 teleports, S12 velocity, S27 explosions and S39 abilities each print their fields. The S39 branch logs fly speed, allowFlying and isFlying via the MCP accessors. The send side only fires while Client.DEVELOPMENT_SWITCH is set, but the receive side is live in release builds.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent; PacketSendEvent gated on the development switch.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None; the module only reads packets and prints text. It is a diagnostic tool, included here because it is the only corpus code that consumes S39 purely for inspection.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4 ships the same module under Client-release2/Client/src/main/java with an identical S39 branch.

modules.name: PingSpoofComponent (packet holding)
modules.purpose: Hold and replay latency-sensitive packets; S39 is classified as teleport-class so it flushes together with S08 rather than with regular traffic.
modules.how_it_works: The component owns five class tuples (regular, velocity, teleports, players, blink, movement) plus per-tuple enable flags set by spoof(). While enabled, matching packets are cancelled on send or receive and queued as TimedPacket entries; on PostMotion, entries older than the spoof amount are replayed via PacketUtil.queue. S39PacketPlayerAbilities sits in the teleports tuple with S08PacketPlayerPosLook and S09PacketHeldItemChange.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Holding S39 is not itself detectable, but the desync it prevents is: a held S39 crossing a held S08 would leave flag state and position inconsistent, a correlation anti-cheats can use. The teleport grouping exists to keep that ordering intact.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4 ships the identical component under Client-release2/Client/src/main/java; both versions are driven by the same spoof() and blink() entry points.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the common surface; CreativeFlight mutates the packet object on the event, Debugger reads it, PingSpoofComponent cancels and queues it.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 6.x uses the component system for holding; the 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 trees are functionally identical. The other six clients carry only the vanilla handler and have no S39 modules.

anticheat.overview: The abilities packet is the server's flight permission broadcast: it carries allow-flight, invulnerable, creative, and the fly and walk speed factors, and it is the synchronization oracle anticheats use to validate the client's own abilities packet (C13). Checks pair the two directions: the server send sets the player's canFly and isFlying state, and the client send is checked against that state, so a flying flag without a server grant is a spoof. Grim runs a dedicated both-direction check plus a fly-flag spoof check; older anticheats fold the client abilities packet into their packet dispatch to feed movement physics.

checks.name: Abilities state sync (Grim)
checks.purpose: Keep the player's flight capability and flying flag in sync with what the server last sent on S39, so every other movement check reasons about the same flight state the client was granted.
checks.how_it_works: PacketPlayerAbilities listens on both directions. On the client abilities packet (C13) it sets player.isFlying to the packet's flying flag gated on player.canFly. On the server send (S39) it opens a transaction, remembers the last sent allow-flight value, and if flight was just revoked schedules a netty task that fires a setback when the client's transaction has not confirmed receipt within max-ping-out-of-flying (default 1000ms). A real-time task then applies canFly and isFlying from the server packet. The comment in the source explains the ordering hazard: Mojang's netcode lets ability packets arrive out of order, so state is applied one tick late to stop a client from flying for a tick before the anticheat knows.
checks.detects: Clients that fly while the server has not granted flight, and clients that keep flying after the server revokes the ability. This is the S39-side half of fly-cheat detection.
checks.variations: Artemis mirrors the server abilities packet into its emulated entity capabilities in EmulatorPreProcessor (GPacketPlayServerAbilities), and BetterAnticheat's PlayerCapabilities reads WrapperPlayServerPlayerAbilities into isFlying, canFly and flySpeed fields; both are the same S39-as-oracle pattern.

checks.name: Fly flag spoof (Grim BadPacketsI)
checks.purpose: Flag a client abilities packet that claims flying while the server has never granted flight on S39.
checks.how_it_works: A PreVia packet receive listener: when the packet type is PLAYER_ABILITIES, the wrapper reports isFlying true, and player.canFly is false, the check flags and cancels the packet. canFly is only ever true after the server sent allow-flight on S39, so this is a direct cross-check of the client's C13 claim against the S39 grant.
checks.detects: Spoofed flying flags, creative-fly hacks that send the flying bit without permission, and clients that desync their abilities state from the server.
checks.variations: AutoEye reads the same client packet in its netty channel handler and pushes the flying bit into the movement physics, so its fly checks run with the client's claimed flight state; Observer's Move check tracks a creativeFly boolean from C13PacketPlayerAbilities and exempts movement while it is set.

checks.name: Abilities dispatch (AutoEye)
checks.purpose: Route the client abilities packet into the movement physics state so fly and timer checks see the client's claimed flight mode.
checks.how_it_works: The channel handler switch matches PacketPlayInAbilities and writes the wrapper's flying bit into the player's physics state via setFlying. It is the C13-side counterpart to the S39 grant: AutoEye has no server-side abilities reader, so it trusts the client bit and lets the movement checks decide whether the resulting motion is possible.
checks.detects: Fly cheats that move with the flying flag set. The state feeds the movement check pipeline rather than flagging directly.
checks.variations: The dispatch pattern is shared by the 1.8 anticheat generation: the abilities packet is folded into per-player state, and flight permission is either trusted from the client or not tracked at all. Grim is the outlier that validates the claim against the server send.

wiki_notes: If the Flying flag is set while Allow Flying is unset, the player cannot stop flying, so the two bits must stay consistent.
The third float doubles as a field-of-view modifier tied to movement speed, which is why the vanilla server sends the same 0.1 default as the movement-speed attribute.

packets.name: Tab Complete
packets.desc: Server responds to C14PacketTabComplete with a list of matching commands/player names.

writeup.p: The server's answer to C14PacketTabComplete: a VarInt count followed by the matching command and player-name strings. The vanilla GUI feeds them into GuiChat.onAutocompleteResponse to cycle suggestions on Tab. Because Bukkit forks populate the server command registry from plugins, the response leaks plugin names as colon-prefixed commands (/plugin:subcommand), which is the entire basis of the plugin-enumeration features in the corpus.

NetHandlerPlayServer.processTabComplete asks the command dispatcher for matches and echoes them back as S3APacketTabComplete with no rate limit and no length guard beyond the request's own string cap. Client side, handleTabComplete dispatches on the main thread and, only when the current screen is a GuiChat, calls onAutocompleteResponse; any other screen means the payload is silently ignored, a detail modules must remember when they fire requests outside chat.

Five corpus features consume the response. Rise 5.99 Plugins sends C14 with '/' in Normal mode or '/a' through '/z' in Bypass mode, then parses every S3A response, splits on ':' and filters '/minecraft' to print the plugin list; Bypass defers the printout to onDisable. Sigma 4.11 PluginFinder is a command doing the same with a 20-second listen window, its own dedupe and a cancel of the event. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 Chat reimplements the chat screen and consumes S3A for autocomplete cycling: it stores the matches on receive, rotates through them on Tab, and fires C14 itself with the typed text and an optional targeted BlockPos. LiquidSense Dev's Plugins module fires a single C14 on enable and auto-disables after printing the sorted, deduped list. November Recode 2.0's PluginsCommand runs the same enumeration as a chat command and additionally regex-parses bare-word suggestions and accepts a custom completion seed.

The enumeration trick is the exploit: a server that does not filter tab completion inventories its own plugins, which names the anti-cheat and its version for targeted research. Bypass modes blast up to 26 requests in one burst, which is a clean rate signal; servers that rate-limit C14 or strip plugin-prefixed commands from the registry kill both modes. The GUI dependency is the subtle constraint: S3A only reaches the vanilla autocomplete when a chat screen is open, so UI-less requesters must hold their own state.

implementation.overview: The tab-completion response channel and the backbone of plugin enumeration: Bukkit leaks plugin names as colon-prefixed commands. Five features across the corpus consume it: Rise 5.99 Plugins (Normal and Bypass modes), Sigma 4.11's PluginFinder command, the Rise 6.x Chat module, LiquidSense Dev's Plugins module, and November Recode 2.0's PluginsCommand.
implementation.server_handling: processTabComplete resolves matches from the server command registry and player list, then sends S3A. There is no server-side rate limit in vanilla; rate limiting lives in plugins. The response is a snapshot, one S3A per request in order, and nothing invalidates a previous response, which is why burst enumeration is reliable.
implementation.protocol_notes: VarInt count, then count strings, each VarInt-length-prefixed UTF-8, bounded by the 32767-byte frame limit per string. The request may carry an optional targeted BlockPos that enables coordinate-aware completions, but the response carries no position data back. Results arrive in registry order, which is why cycling modules rotate through the array instead of assuming alphabetical order.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats do not flag S3A; they flag the request side. A burst of 26 C14 packets inside one tick is a clean rate signal, which makes Rise 5.99's Normal mode (one request, one parse) the safe variant and Bypass the risky one. Servers defeat enumeration server-side by filtering S3A responses or hiding plugin-prefixed commands, both invisible to the client.

modules.name: Plugins
modules.purpose: Enumerate server plugins by parsing the colon-prefixed commands leaked in tab-completion responses.
modules.how_it_works: Normal mode sends one C14PacketTabComplete("/") on enable and parses the S3A response immediately, splitting each command on ':' and filtering the '/minecraft' namespace; results print to chat as they arrive and the module toggles off. Bypass mode fires 26 requests ('/a' through '/z') and defers the deduped printout to onDisable. Timeouts (5s Normal, 2.5s Bypass) disable the module when the server returns nothing.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Normal mode is low-risk: one request, one parse. Bypass mode fires 26 C14 packets back to back, a clean rate signal for servers that rate-limit tab completion; the responses themselves are never flagged.
modules.variations: Sigma 4.11 implements the same idea as the PluginFinder command; Rise 6.x moved the mechanics into the Chat module's autocomplete.

modules.name: Chat
modules.purpose: Replacement chat screen with custom autocomplete: S3A responses feed the Tab cycling and the module sends C14 requests itself.
modules.how_it_works: On PacketReceiveEvent, every S3A is stored into a matches list and each match is printed to chat. On the Tab key, if matches is empty the module sends C14PacketTabComplete with the typed text and an optional targeted BlockPos (the looked-at block), then cycles the stored matches on subsequent Tab presses. The dot-prefix guard skips requests for client command input, and the matches list is nulled when the input closes.
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketReceiveEvent (S3A storage), GuiKeyBoardEvent (Tab cycling and C14 send).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: No anti-cheat surface; the module is a UI replacement. The C14 traffic it generates is identical to vanilla autocomplete traffic.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30 ships the same module under com/alan/clients/module/impl/render/chat with an identical S3A branch.

modules.name: PluginFinder (command)
modules.purpose: Command-driven plugin enumeration: send one C14 for '/', listen for a single S3A, print the deduped plugin list.
modules.how_it_works: fire() resets a timer, registers the command object with the event system and sends C14PacketTabComplete("/"). The event handler waits for S3A, splits each command on ':', dedupes plugin names, filters 'minecraft' and 'bukkit', prints the list, unregisters and cancels the event. A 20-second timer self-unregisters if the server never answers.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket via a self-registered command listener; C14 sent through NetUtil.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: A single C14 request is indistinguishable from vanilla autocomplete, making the command the stealthiest enumeration variant in the corpus.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99's Plugins module covers the same ground with Normal and Bypass modes; PluginFinder is the one-shot command form.

modules.name: Plugins (LiquidBounce)
modules.purpose: Enumerate server plugins from a single tab-completion response, print the deduped list and turn the module off.
modules.how_it_works: onEnable sends one C14PacketTabComplete("/") through mc.getNetHandler().addToSendQueue and resets a TickTimer; onUpdate disables the module with a timeout chat message after 20 ticks if the server never answers. The PacketEvent handler catches S3A, splits every command on ':', strips the leading '/', dedupes into a list, sorts it and prints count plus names via ClientUtils.displayChatMessage, then setState(false).
modules.vanilla_hook: PacketEvent (receive side) and UpdateEvent; the request goes through addToSendQueue.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: One request, one parse, auto-disable: the least aggressive enumeration variant in the corpus. The single C14 is indistinguishable from vanilla autocomplete traffic.
modules.variations: Same role as Rise 5.99's Plugins and November Recode 2.0's PluginsCommand, but the LiquidBounce module sorts the result and self-disables instead of holding a burst mode or a long listen window.

modules.name: PluginsCommand
modules.purpose: Command-driven plugin enumeration: dispatch fires one C14 with a custom completion seed and a subscribed packet listener parses the S3A response.
modules.how_it_works: dispatch builds the seed string ('/' plus joined args, or '/' alone), resets a 10-second timeout timer, sets listening and sends C14PacketTabComplete through mc.thePlayer.sendQueue.addToSendQueue. The EventPacket.In listener returns while listening is false, aborts with a chat message after 10 seconds, then on S3A splits colon-containing suggestions on ':', strips whitespace and the '/' and filters 'minecraft'; non-colon suggestions are matched against a [A-Z0-9]\\w+ regex and added when they do not start with '/'. Results print through Printer as a joined, deduped list.
modules.vanilla_hook: EventPacket.In listener subscribed on the November event bus; the request goes through the player's sendQueue.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The custom seed can probe completion beyond the root '/', and the one-shot listen window keeps the request count at exactly one; responses are never flagged.
modules.variations: The command form mirrors Sigma 4.11's PluginFinder. Unlike LiquidSense Dev's module and Rise 5.99's, it accepts an argument to seed completion and parses bare-word suggestions that carry no colon.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent on every client; the request side is a raw C14 construction, and Sigma sends it through NetUtil while Rise uses PacketUtil. LiquidSense Dev and November Recode 2.0 send through addToSendQueue; November listens via its own EventPacket.In bus event.
implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 parses responses live and toggles off; Sigma registers and unregisters a one-shot listener; Rise 6.x keeps the matches as GUI state for Tab cycling. LiquidSense Dev auto-disables after one parse; November Recode 2.0 routes through a subscribed EventPacket.In listener with a timeout flag. None of them rely on the vanilla GuiChat path, which is exactly what the vanilla handler requires.

anticheat.overview: S3A is the tab-completion response channel, and the flagging half of the domain runs on the request side: Grim's ChatA and CrashH and BetterAnticheat's ImpossibleCompletionCheck read the inbound WrapperPlayClientTabComplete (C14) and are documented on that packet's page. Only Intave consumes the outbound response, and both consumers are suggestion filters rather than flaggers: CommandFilter strips Intave's own commands out of the completion list and VanishFilter removes hidden players' names. The rest of the corpus is plumbing and noise: FlopAC's WrappedInTabComplete and WrappedOutTabComplete wrappers, Artemis' PacketRepository entry with the GPacketPlayServerTabComplete wrapper, Negativity's TAB_COMPLETE constants, SafeguardAC's compiled-only TabComplete check, and Bukkit TabCompleter implementations in every anticheat's own command system.

checks.name: CommandFilter (Intave)
checks.purpose: Keeps Intave's own commands out of tab-complete responses so players without the intave.command permission cannot discover them by pressing Tab.
checks.how_it_works: Subscribes to TAB_COMPLETE_OUT (S3A) and reads the response's string array. For players without the intave.command permission it rebuilds the array, dropping every suggestion that contains /intave or /iac, and writes the filtered array back into the packet only when something was removed. The same filter's inbound method rewrites /iac and /intave chat and tab-complete requests into a forwarder command; that half runs on C14 and is documented on that page.
checks.detects: Leakage of Intave's commands through tab completion; it also hides the anticheat's presence from players probing with Tab.
checks.variations: The only anticheat that rewrites outbound tab-complete suggestions. VanishFilter is the sibling filter in the same module that strips hidden player names instead of commands.

checks.name: VanishFilter (Intave)
checks.purpose: Removes hidden players from tab-complete responses so vanished staff do not leak through name completion.
checks.how_it_works: Subscribes to TAB_COMPLETE_OUT (S3A) at MONITOR priority, reads the response's string array, and rebuilds it without the names of online players whose UUIDs are not in the viewer's shownPlayers set. The set is maintained by the same filter's PLAYER_INFO (S38) handler, which hides and shuffles the viewer's tab list.
checks.detects: Vanished players exposed by tab completion; the filter is a privacy measure for staff, not a cheat flag.
checks.variations: CommandFilter is the sibling filter that strips command suggestions; both run on TAB_COMPLETE_OUT.

wiki_notes: Reply to C14 TabComplete: VarInt count then that many completion strings (commands and player names).
On Bukkit servers plugin commands leak as colon-prefixed entries, so one C14 '/' request enumerates server plugins.

packets.name: Scoreboard Objective
packets.desc: Creates or removes a scoreboard objective (the scoreboard itself, not individual scores).

writeup.p: The scoreboard objective lifecycle packet. A byte action drives it: 0 creates an objective, 1 removes it, 2 updates its display name and render type. Wire fields are the objective name (16-char cap), the action byte, then conditionally for actions 0 and 2 the display name (32-char cap) and the render type string ('integer' or 'hearts'). Objectives are containers; the visible rows arrive separately via S3CPacketUpdateScore and the display slot binding via S3DPacketDisplayScoreboard. ServerScoreboard broadcasts S3B to all players on objective creation, removal, and display-name change.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleScoreboardObjective creates a ScoreObjective with the DUMMY criteria on action 0, sets display name and render type, removes the objective on action 1, and applies display name and render type on action 2. The client scoreboard is the only consumer: the HUD sidebar renders whatever objective the S3D binding points at, populated by S3C rows. Because S3B never carries row data, cancelling it produces an objective-less board, not a blank one.

The landscape is thin across the 8 clients. Spicy's HideName imports the class but its EventPacket handler never branches on it: the import is dead weight from a name-hiding feature that actually rewrites S3C rows. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 register the class in the script API NetworkAPI table so JavaScript scripts can construct or match it. No client cancels S3B. The scoreboard-blocking modules that exist in the wider ecosystem (Gugustus Scoreboard, AntiScoreboard) sit outside this corpus, so none of the 8 reference clients carries an objective-blocker.

Cancelling S3B is client-visual only. Blocking action 0 leaves rows orphaned, which renders as a sidebar with no header; blocking action 1 freezes a stale objective. The server never learns, because S3B is one-way clientbound and the server does not track which objectives a client holds. Anti-cheats in the corpus never measure scoreboard packets: they carry display strings and no timing or movement state. The only abuse value is a clean HUD, and none of the 8 clients bothers.

implementation.overview: The objective lifecycle packet. Across the 8 reference clients it is only an import (Spicy HideName) and a script API registration (Rise 6.x). Nobody cancels or mutates it, because the visible rows travel in S3C and the slot binding in S3D.
implementation.server_handling: ServerScoreboard emits S3B on objective creation (action 0), removal (action 1), and display name or render type updates (action 2), fanned out with sendPacketToAllPlayers. The server never reads S3B back; the packet is strictly clientbound in PLAY state, registered in EnumConnectionState alongside the rest of the scoreboard family. There is no client-to-server scoreboard acknowledgement in the protocol.
implementation.protocol_notes: readPacketData reads the objective name with a 16-char cap, then the action byte, then only for actions 0 and 2 the 32-char display name and the render type string, mapped through EnumRenderType.func_178795_a. writePacketData mirrors this, so a create packet missing the trailing fields desyncs the stream. Action 1 sends name plus action byte only.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat in the corpus inspects S3B. It carries display strings only, no timing, position, or movement content. The only measurable effect of tampering is client-side rendering, which server-side anti-cheat cannot observe. Any module touching it is doing cosmetic work with zero detection risk.

modules.name: HideName
modules.purpose: Hide the player's real username from server-rendered name surfaces. For this packet the class is only imported; the shipped onEvent branches on S02PacketChat and S3CPacketUpdateScore, never on S3BPacketScoreboardObjective.
modules.how_it_works: Imports S3BPacketScoreboardObjective at the top of the module file. The EventPacket pre handler has no S3B branch; the module's real work sits in the S3C branch, which rewrites score names to a chosen alias. The S3B import is a leftover from the same name-hiding feature.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. A dead import carries no detection risk and no packet is mutated for this packet class.
modules.variations: None. The same file is the corpus hit for S3CPacketUpdateScore and S3DPacketDisplayScoreboard; the S3C branch is where the alias logic actually runs.

modules.name: NetworkAPI (script API)
modules.purpose: Expose the packet class to Rise's JavaScript scripting API so scripts can construct, read, or match it from the clientbound table.
modules.how_it_works: NetworkAPI.java holds a static Class array of clientbound packets that includes S3BPacketScoreboardObjective. The API maps packet ids to classes for script-side instantiation and inspection; it is an API surface, not a runtime module.
modules.vanilla_hook: None directly. Script-level packet handling sits on top of this table.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. It is a class registry, not runtime packet logic.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4 ships the byte-identical file with the Client-release2/Client/src/main/java path prefix.

implementation.general_hooks: Spicy uses EventPacket pre; Rise 6.x script packets run through the NetworkAPI table.
implementation.client_variations: Spicy mutates packet objects inside its EventPacket pre-phase. Rise 6.x routes packet awareness through the script API rather than module code.

anticheat.overview: S3B carries scoreboard objective lifecycle state, and only Shard touches it. The monitor HUD system consumes and emits the packet family: ScoreboardSlotObserver reads S3B REMOVE actions and S3D display binds to detect when its claimed sidebar slot is displaced, and ScoreboardPacketBridge builds the S3B objectives, S3D display binds and S3C score rows that render the monitor sidebar. Everything else in the corpus is plumbing or sibling-family noise: Negativity's SCOREBOARD_OBJECTIVE constant and Artemis' four scoreboard wrapper interfaces with their PacketRepository entries register the family, intave's ScoreboardAccessor and EntityCollisionDisabler build and read PacketPlayOutScoreboardTeam (S3E), NCP's CollisionUtil uses the Bukkit scoreboard API for team-collision lookups, and BetterAnticheat's ReloadCommand hits on a comment.

checks.name: ScoreboardSlotObserver (Shard)
checks.purpose: Watches the scoreboard objective and display streams so the monitor HUD notices when its claimed sidebar slot is taken over or its objective is removed by the server or another plugin.
checks.how_it_works: MONITOR-priority PacketSendEvent listener active only while the slot registry holds claims. packets.name: Update Score
packets.desc: Updates a single scoreboard entry (add, remove, or change score value).

writeup.p: Single-row scoreboard mutation. Fields are the score name (40-char cap), an action enum (CHANGE or REMOVE), the objective name (16-char cap), and for CHANGE a VarInt value. The server emits one S3C per row update: value change, row removal, removal scoped to one objective, and full replay during objective creation and on join. It is the most frequently emitted scoreboard packet: a 15-row sidebar refresh is 15 packets.

handleUpdateScore resolves the objective by name, then either sets the score points (CHANGE) or removes the row (REMOVE). A REMOVE with an empty objective name removes the row from every objective. The client scoreboard then re-renders whichever slot binds the objective. The value field is only present for CHANGE, so the read path is action-dependent.

Two Spicy files rewrite this packet, both for name visibility. HideName replaces the session username with a chosen alias in both the objective name and the row name fields, so sidebar kill feeds and stats boards stop showing the real name. Account.java does the inverse for alt accounts: it appends the real account name in green so the user can tell which identity is live. Both mutate the decoded packet inside EventPacket pre, before the vanilla handler runs. Rise 6.x only registers the class in the script API.

Name rewriting here is invisible to the server: S3C is clientbound, and the rewrite happens after decode and before the client scoreboard consumes it. Anti-cheats never see the mutation. HideName stays consistent by applying the same alias to chat (S02PacketChat) and scoreboard rows, so the client-side story matches everywhere. There is no server-side state to desync because the scoreboard lives only on the client.

implementation.overview: The only scoreboard packet the 8 clients actually mutate. Spicy's HideName swaps the player's username for an alias in score rows; Spicy's Account.java appends the real alt name in green. Both rewrite the decoded packet before the vanilla handler, which the server cannot see.
implementation.server_handling: ServerScoreboard emits S3C on score value changes, row removal, and removal scoped to one objective, plus full replays during objective creation and join. All sends go through sendPacketToAllPlayers. The packet is clientbound only; the server never validates or receives score state back from the client.
implementation.protocol_notes: readPacketData order: score name (40-char cap), action enum via readEnumValue, objective name (16-char cap), then the VarInt value only when the action is CHANGE. REMOVE rows omit the value, keeping the packet short. The enum has exactly two members, CHANGE and REMOVE; there is no separate add action.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing flags S3C abuse in the corpus. It carries display strings and a display integer, no timing or movement content. Rewriting name fields is purely cosmetic client-side work that server-side anti-cheat cannot detect.

modules.name: HideName
modules.purpose: Stop the player's real username from appearing in scoreboard rows: sidebar stats, kill feeds, and per-player objectives.
modules.how_it_works: In EventPacket pre, when the packet is S3CPacketUpdateScore, it strips the invisible joiner character (׼) from both name fields and checks whether the objective name or the score name contains the session username. On a match it replaces the username with the selected alias via setObjective and setName. The same handler rewrites S02PacketChat for chat surfaces.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. Pure client-side string rewrite after decode; the server never sees the mutation.
modules.variations: Account.java reuses the same rewrite pattern but appends the real account name in green instead of hiding it.

The same treatment applies to S02PacketChat. It also polls the SpicyClient.info API per player to map alt names to real accounts.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. The rewrite is client-side after decode; the server only ever sent the alt username.
modules.variations: HideName performs the same two-field rewrite with a fake name; Account.java uses the real account name from the login session.

anticheat.overview: S3C is the single-row scoreboard mutation, and no anticheat flags it. The only live consumer is Shard's monitor, which renders its status sidebar by emitting the scoreboard family itself, including the S3C row updates. The rest of the corpus is registrations (Negativity PacketType SCOREBOARD_SCORE, Artemis PacketRepository SERVER_PLAY+57 with the PacketPlayServerScoreboardScore wrapper and HardcodeMap) and keyword noise: intave's hits handle the sibling S3E team packet and matched on the Scoreboard search term, NCP's CollisionUtil reads the Bukkit scoreboard API for team collision predicates, and amnoah's ReloadCommand mentions BetterScoreboard in a comment.
