packets.name: Display Scoreboard
packets.desc: Sets which scoreboard objective is displayed in a position (sidebar, list, below name).

fields.name: objectiveName
fields.desc: Objective to display (empty string to clear)

writeup.p: Binds an objective to a display slot: a position byte (0 sidebar, 1 player list, 2 below name) followed by the objective name string. An empty name clears the slot. The packet is tiny and is sent by ServerScoreboard whenever the display binding changes and during full replays on objective creation and removal. The HUD reads the bound objective each frame and renders its rows from the client scoreboard.

handleDisplayScoreboard sets or clears the objective in the given slot. The visible sidebar depends on the combination of S3B (objective definition), S3C (rows), and S3D (binding): S3D alone paints nothing, it only points the renderer at an objective.

Almost nothing across the 8 clients. Spicy's HideName imports the class (line 15) but its handler has no S3D branch, mirroring the dead S3B import. Rise 6.x registers the class in the script API. No module cancels the display binding; a cancel would freeze the previous objective in the slot, a HUD artifact none of the 8 clients bothers to produce.

Nil for anti-cheat. The slot byte is not validated: values outside 0-2 are stored in the client's 19-entry slot array and render nowhere. Cancelling S3D only affects local rendering. The packet carries no timing or movement state, so no anti-cheat in the corpus measures it.

implementation.overview: Display slot binding. In the 8-client corpus it is an import in Spicy's HideName and a script API entry in Rise 6.x; no module binds, clears, or blocks the slot.
implementation.server_handling: ServerScoreboard sends S3D in setObjectiveInDisplaySlot (both the set and clear paths) and during full replays on objective creation and removal, with a null objective serialized as an empty name string. The server never reads the binding back from the client.
implementation.protocol_notes: Two fields: position byte then objective name string. An empty name clears the slot. The position byte indexes the client's 19-slot display array directly, so out-of-range values are stored but never rendered.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not monitored. S3D carries a slot index and a display string, no state an anti-cheat validates. Tampering is client-visual only.

packets.name: Teams
packets.desc: Create/update/remove a scoreboard team. Manages team name, prefix/suffix, players, friendly fire, and nametag visibility.

writeup.p: Scoreboard team management. The action byte drives five modes: 0 create, 1 remove, 2 update info, 3 add players, 4 remove players. Info fields for actions 0 and 2 are display name (32-char cap), prefix (16), suffix (16), a friendly-fire byte, the nametag visibility string (32), and a color byte indexing EnumChatFormatting. Player lists follow for actions 0, 3, and 4 as a VarInt count of 40-char names. Team color drives the nametag color in the client renderer, which makes this packet the surface for team-colored nametag features.

handleTeams creates or fetches the team by registered name, applies the info fields for actions 0 and 2, then adds or removes memberships for actions 3 and 4. The client stores teams in its scoreboard; the nametag renderer reads team color and visibility per player each frame. ServerConfigurationManager replays existing teams to a joining player with action 0.

Only Rise 6.x. StaffDetector carries a fully commented-out S3EPacketTeams branch that would scan team members for staff names and trigger an auto-leave (/hub) after six hits; the live module relies on the S38 player-list scan instead. The commented block proves the teams surface was tried and abandoned in favor of S38. Rise also registers the class in the script API. No client colors ESP by team here: nametag coloring is left to vanilla rendering.

The color byte is server-controlled; a client cannot push team colors back because S3E is clientbound. Nametag-visibility abuse (hiding tags via team properties) is a server-side decision. The interesting angle is staff detection: team rosters leak staff membership on servers that place staff in teams, and the Rise staff list plus a six-hit counter is the pattern. It is entirely client-side reading and undetectable.

implementation.overview: Team management and nametag color. Rise 6.x StaffDetector contains the only module reference, and it is commented out: the teams scan was replaced by the S38 player-list scan. Everything else is vanilla plus the script API table.
implementation.server_handling: ServerScoreboard broadcasts S3E on team create (0), remove (1), info update (2), player add (3), and player remove (4). ServerConfigurationManager sends a create replay to each joining player so the client knows existing teams and their colors before the world settles. All sends go through sendPacketToAllPlayers or the per-player handler.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire order: team name (16-char cap), action byte, then for actions 0 and 2 the info block, then for actions 0, 3, and 4 a VarInt count of 40-char member names. The packet constructors throw IllegalArgumentException for player actions with empty member lists, and the read path trusts the action byte to choose which trailing fields exist.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not monitored. The team color byte feeds EnumChatFormatting.func_175744_a, so a malformed color renders garbage but cannot crash. StaffDetector's commented branch is the only staff-detection use of teams in the corpus, and it never runs.

The counter decays each PreMotion tick. The block is dead code in both 6.1.30 and 6.2.4.

anticheat.overview: S3E is the one scoreboard packet anticheats actually consume and produce. Grim reads the outbound team stream into per-entity team state that its collision predicates use; intave rewrites the collision rule on outbound team packets and emits team packets to hide fake-player nametags; Shard's monitor emits team packets to render the target name tag and watches for conflicting team traffic. Photon's Teaming is the only flagging check in the domain and it is driven by Bukkit events, not the packet. The rest of the corpus is noise: Rammelkast and AntiCheatPlus match the 'AntiCheat Team' license header on every file, NCP's CollisionUtil reads the Bukkit scoreboard API, and Negativity plus Artemis only register the packet class.

checks.name: TeamHandler (Grim)
checks.purpose: Keep a transaction-ordered mirror of the client's team state so entity checks know the collision and push rules between players and entities.
checks.how_it_works: TeamHandler is a PacketSendListener on PacketType.Play.Server.TEAMS. On each S3E it wraps the packet, reads the team name, and schedules a real-time task at the last transaction id so the update applies at the same tick the client processes it. CREATE builds a new EntityTeam, REMOVE drops it, and the other modes update the stored team with the collision rule from the packet. EntityTeam maps members to the team by UUID, and MovementTicker plus EntityPredicates consult it to decide whether an entity can push the player.
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It feeds collision semantics: team-based collision rules are read consistently because the mirror is transaction-ordered, so push-based exploits cannot desync it.
checks.variations: CheckManager registers the handler per player (CheckManager.java line 119). No other anticheat mirrors team state for physics; the collision-rule consumers are unique to Grim's simulation.

checks.name: Teaming (Photon)
checks.purpose: Flag UHC players who cooperate by clustering, the teaming cheat domain that S3E team membership normally exposes.
checks.how_it_works: Every 5 seconds the check builds a 3D RTree of eligible players (adventure or survival mode, out of combat, outside configured safe zones and WorldGuard no-PVP regions), then clusters players within a configurable proximity range who can see each other. Any cluster larger than the allowed size flags every member with a violation level equal to the surplus. The corpus hit is the team domain: the check never parses S3E and never reads Bukkit team state.
checks.detects: Players teaming in UHC-style gamemodes: two or more players who move together and avoid PVP.
checks.variations: None in the corpus. Photon's ModuleManager registers the module, and Placeholders exposes its violation level for alert messages.

checks.name: EntityCollisionDisabler (intave)
checks.purpose: Patch outbound team packets so the monitored player stops colliding with entities, a server-side no-collision service.
checks.how_it_works: A HIGHEST-priority ProtocolLib subscription on the outbound SCOREBOARD_TEAM packet rewrites the collision-rule string field to 'never' before the packet reaches the client. Version-dependent field indexes handle the 1.13 and 1.17 wire changes, and on 1.17+ the rule is read from the optional internal structure instead of the top-level string list. Active only on 1.9+ servers where the team packet carries a collision rule.
checks.detects: Nothing cheat-related. It is the anticheat applying a collision exemption through the vanilla team mechanism instead of a per-player flag.
checks.variations: Same anticheat, opposite direction: ScoreboardAccessor and FakePlayerBody emit S3E team packets to hide the fake-player nametag (see the next check).

checks.name: ScoreboardAccessor fake-player nametag (intave)
checks.purpose: Hide the nametag of intave's fake-player bait entities so ESP and nametag features cannot distinguish them from real players.
checks.how_it_works: sendScoreboard builds a PacketPlayOutScoreboardTeam with action 3 (ADD_PLAYERS) that places the fake player profile in a dedicated team, then, when hiding is requested, sends a second team packet with action 2 (UPDATE) that sets nameTagVisibility to NEVER. FakePlayerBody invokes it at spawn (FakePlayerBody.java line 318).
checks.detects: Nothing. The team packets are the bait infrastructure behind the aura and reach checks; the nametag must vanish or the fake entity is trivially spotted.
checks.variations: FakePlayerBody.java owns the spawn flow and FakePlayerEventService loads the accessor by class name for the 1.8 pipeline.

checks.name: Monitor nametag team bridge (Shard)
checks.purpose: Render the monitored target's name tag by emitting its own S3E team packets, and keep that rendering valid against other plugins' team traffic.
checks.how_it_works: ViewTeamPacketBridge builds WrapperPlayServerTeams packets (CREATE, UPDATE, ADD_ENTITIES and REMOVE) whose prefix and suffix carry the rendered tag, with the collision rule and nametag visibility forced to ALWAYS so the monitor's tag never interferes with physics. Its companion ViewTeamConflictObserver listens for outbound S3E at MONITOR priority and, when the session renders above the name, marks the target's tag for rebind whenever another plugin creates a team or adds the target to one.
checks.detects: Nothing. The name-tag rendering is the monitor output channel; the observer exists so a server plugin that manages its own teams does not break the view.

package ac.shard.monitor.view

import ac.shard.monitor.core.ComponentCache
import com.github.retrooper.packetevents.PacketEvents
import com.github.retrooper.packetevents.wrapper.PacketWrapper
import com.github.retrooper.packetevents.wrapper.play.server.WrapperPlayServerTeams
import net.kyori.adventure.text.Component
import net.kyori.adventure.text.format.NamedTextColor
import org.bukkit.entity.Player

internal class ViewTeamPacketBridge(private val componentCache: ComponentCache) {
  fun createTeam(viewer: Player, teamName: String, playerName: String, rendered: RenderedTag) {
    val wrapper =
      WrapperPlayServerTeams(
        teamName,
        WrapperPlayServerTeams.TeamMode.CREATE,
        createTeamInfo(rendered),
        listOf(playerName),
      )
    sendPacket(viewer, wrapper)
  }

  fun updateTeam(viewer: Player, teamName: String, rendered: RenderedTag) {
    val wrapper =
      WrapperPlayServerTeams(
        teamName,
        WrapperPlayServerTeams.TeamMode.UPDATE,
        createTeamInfo(rendered),
        emptyList(),
      )
    sendPacket(viewer, wrapper)
  }

  fun rebindEntity(viewer: Player, teamName: String, playerName: String) {
    val wrapper =
      WrapperPlayServerTeams(
        teamName,
        WrapperPlayServerTeams.TeamMode.ADD_ENTITIES,
        null as WrapperPlayServerTeams.ScoreBoardTeamInfo?,
        listOf(playerName),
      )
    sendPacket(viewer, wrapper)
  }

  fun removeTeam(viewer: Player, teamName: String) {
    val wrapper =
      WrapperPlayServerTeams(
        teamName,
        WrapperPlayServerTeams.TeamMode.REMOVE,
        null as WrapperPlayServerTeams.ScoreBoardTeamInfo?,
        emptyList<String>(),
      )
    sendPacket(viewer, wrapper)
  }

  private fun createTeamInfo(rendered: RenderedTag): WrapperPlayServerTeams.ScoreBoardTeamInfo {
    return WrapperPlayServerTeams.ScoreBoardTeamInfo(
      Component.empty(),
      componentCache.component(rendered.prefix),
      componentCache.component(rendered.suffix),
      WrapperPlayServerTeams.NameTagVisibility.ALWAYS,
      WrapperPlayServerTeams.CollisionRule.ALWAYS,
      NamedTextColor.WHITE,
      WrapperPlayServerTeams.OptionData.NONE,
    )
  }

  private fun sendPacket(viewer: Player, packet: PacketWrapper<*>) {
    PacketEvents.getAPI().playerManager.sendPacket(viewer, packet)
  }
}

packets.name: Custom Payload (Plugin Message)
packets.desc: Sends a plugin channel message from server to client. Used for mod/plugin communication.
packets.notes: Common channels: "MC|Brand" (server brand), "MC|AdvCmd" (command block update), "MC|TrList" (villager trades), "MC|RPack" (resource pack).

writeup.p: The clientbound plugin message. A channel name string (20-char cap) plus a raw PacketBuffer payload capped at 1048576 bytes. Vanilla channels include MC|Brand (server brand, sent once at join), MC|TrList (villager trades), MC|BOpen (book opening), and MC|AdvCmd (command block updates). handleCustomPayload dispatches by channel name; unknown channels are ignored. This is the standard bus for server-to-client mod and plugin communication.

handleCustomPayload branches on the channel: MC|TrList decodes the merchant recipe list into the open GuiMerchant, MC|Brand stores the brand string on the player, MC|BOpen opens the written-book GUI. The buffer is released in a finally block. Channel length is capped at 20 and the payload at 1MB, with an IOException on overflow.

Rise 5.99 PacketDebugger logs the channel name of every S3FPacketCustomPayload to chat via Rise.addChatMessage, as part of anti-cheat fingerprinting: the module also times keepalives and transactions. Reading MC|Brand is the standard server-identity read: brand strings identify Paper, Purpur, BungeeCord, and plugin stacks before a bypass picks a mode. Rise 6.x registers the class in the script API. The dedicated BrandDetector modules of the wider ecosystem (Flux, Lycoris) sit outside this corpus, so PacketDebugger is the only real consumer here.

Purely observational. The payload is server-controlled; a malicious server can send oversized or malformed payloads, but the 1MB cap and try/finally release keep the vanilla path safe. Clients read the channel and payload for fingerprinting, and nothing is sent back, so servers cannot detect the read. The detection value is the brand string itself, which identifies the server stack before a disabler selects a mode.

implementation.overview: The clientbound plugin channel. Rise 5.99's PacketDebugger logs every channel name to chat for anti-cheat fingerprinting, and the MC|Brand channel is the standard server-identity read. Rise 6.x only registers the class in its script API.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager sends MC|Brand once per join with the server mod name. EntityPlayerMP sends MC|TrList when a player opens a merchant and MC|BOpen when opening a written book. The channel table is per-connection; the vanilla client only receives S3F and never echoes it. The wire payload length is the remaining readable bytes, capped at 1MB.
implementation.protocol_notes: readPacketData reads the channel (20-char cap), then takes the remaining readable bytes as the payload buffer, rejecting anything over 1048576 bytes with an IOException. writePacketData writes the channel then the raw buffer bytes. The payload is channel-specific; parsers must know the channel before reading fields from the buffer.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Passive surface. The brand and channel names fingerprint the server stack; anti-cheats that send their own channels (version checks, telemetry) leak their presence through this packet. Clients never echo S3F, so the read is undetectable server-side. No anti-cheat in the corpus flags the packet itself.

modules.name: PacketDebugger
modules.purpose: Fingerprint the server's anti-cheat and network behavior by logging plugin channels and packet timing to chat.
modules.how_it_works: onPacketSend logs C0FPacketConfirmTransaction window id and uid with inter-arrival milliseconds, C00PacketKeepAlive key with inter-arrival milliseconds, and S3FPacketCustomPayload channel name via Rise.addChatMessage. The S3F branch catches clientbound payloads as they pass through the event.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Logging only, no mutation, nothing flaggable. The timing output doubles as a manual check of server keepalive/transaction behavior.
modules.variations: None in the corpus. Rise 6.x drops the module and exposes the class through the script API instead.

modules.purpose: Expose the packet class to Rise's JavaScript scripting API.
modules.how_it_works: S3FPacketCustomPayload is listed in the clientbound Class array of NetworkAPI.java (line 106).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. Registry only.

implementation.client_variations: Rise 5.99 logs the packet through its event bus; Rise 6.x exposes the class to scripts. No client in the corpus cancels or forges S3F.

anticheat.overview: S3F is the outbound plugin channel, and the corpus splits by direction. The inbound machinery dominates the keyword matches: brand recognition (Grim ClientBrand, Shard ClientBrand, Truthful BrandListener, Photon BrandChannelData, intave PayloadInReader and SettingsTracker, LightAntiCheat ClientBrandRecognizer), payload frequency (Arc PayloadFrequency), payload exploits (Grim ExploitA and ExploitB), and badpackets (Frequency BadPacketsD, Hydro BadPacketsC, FlopAC BadPacketsF and BadPacketsG) all consume the client-to-server payload and appear here because the search terms overlap. The genuine S3F consumers are the anticheats' own outbound payloads: Photon rewrites the outgoing brand so clients cannot fingerprint the server, intave emits a brand-channel mark to authenticate its companion client, and Negativity sends FML handshake probes to enumerate Forge mods. Artemis and Negativity register the packet classes (SERVER_PLAY+21, CUSTOM_PAYLOAD_IN and CUSTOM_PAYLOAD_OUT).

checks.name: BrandHider (Photon)
checks.purpose: Stop clients from fingerprinting the server: rewrite every outbound brand payload to a configured fake brand.
checks.how_it_works: Two PacketAdapterBuilder listeners hook the outbound PLUGIN_MESSAGE packets (Configuration.Server and Play.Server, the S3F path) with onSendingRaw. When the channel is the brand channel (MC|Brand or minecraft:brand), the payload data is replaced with createBrandPayload of the configured brand ('Some Spigot' by default) and the packet is marked for re-encode. On join, and at an optional refresh rate, the module also pushes an empty brand payload so the adapter has something to rewrite.
checks.detects: Clients and disablers that read the server brand to pick a bypass mode; the rewrite keeps the advertised stack generic.
checks.variations: Photon's inbound twin is BrandChannelData, a ParsedPluginMessageListener that records the client brand into the user object; MessageChannel.MC_BRAND_CHANNEL is the shared channel constant.

checks.name: Sibyl brand authentication (intave)
checks.purpose: Mark the server for the Intave companion client: emit an S3F brand payload carrying the Intave identifier so the Sibyl client can authenticate.
checks.how_it_works: On join, and again on every restart broadcast and whenever a player is not yet authenticated, the service calls authentication.sendMessageToClient(player, 'MC|Brand', 'INTAVE', null), which writes the payload into an outbound custom payload packet (SibylAuthentication.java builds the ProtocolLib container around line 251). The companion client recognizes the mark and replies over its own channel.
checks.detects: Nothing cheat-related. It is the anticheat's outbound identification channel; the brand mark also lets the anticheat tell its own clients from vanilla ones.
checks.variations: The inbound side of the same system is PayloadInReader, a CUSTOM_PAYLOAD_IN reader that intave's SettingsTracker, CustomClientSupportService and LabymodClientListener consume for brand and LabyMod detection.

checks.name: FML mod probe (Negativity)
checks.purpose: Detect Forge clients by sending FML handshake payloads and reading the mod-list reply.
checks.how_it_works: initMods sends three FML|HS plugin messages (bytes {-2,0}, {0,2,0,0,0,0} and {2,0,0,0,0}) to the player when the outgoing FML channel is registered, the standard FML handshake sequence that makes Forge reply with its mod list. ChannelEvents handles the incoming FML data (the C17 side) and stores the result in the player's mod map, which feeds the mod-based cheat checks.
checks.detects: The presence and version of Forge and its mods; server owners use the result to allow or block modded clients.
checks.variations: Negativity's PacketType declares CUSTOM_PAYLOAD_IN and CUSTOM_PAYLOAD_OUT for both directions. No other anticheat probes FML; the modern anticheats read the brand channel instead.

wiki_notes: Channel string capped at 20 chars plus raw payload capped at 1048576 bytes (1MB); larger payloads throw IOException.
Vanilla channels: MC|Brand sent once at join, MC|TrList villager trades, MC|BOpen written book. Unknown channels are ignored.

packets.name: Disconnect (Play)
packets.desc: Kicks the player from the server during gameplay with a JSON chat component reason message.

fields.name: reason
fields.desc: Kick/disconnection reason displayed to the player

packets.notes: This is the PLAY-state disconnect (vs S00PacketDisconnect for LOGIN). When received, the client immediately closes the network connection and displays the disconnect screen with the reason.

writeup.p: The play-state kick. One IChatComponent reason, serialized as a chat component. Sent by NetHandlerPlayServer and NetworkSystem when the server closes a PLAY connection with a reason; the client's handleDisconnect closes the channel and the onDisconnect path unloads the world and shows GuiDisconnected with the reason. It is the play-state counterpart of the login-state S00PacketDisconnect, and it is the last packet on the wire before the server tears the connection down.

handleDisconnect calls netManager.closeChannel(reason), which triggers the disconnect cascade: world unload, then GuiDisconnected with the reason. The kick is one-way; there is no acknowledgement. Modules see the packet in PacketReceiveEvent before the vanilla handler runs, which is the only window for reacting to it.

Sigma 4.11 Ranking inspects the reason text: if it contains 'ban' and the player has been alive more than 15 seconds, it reports a ban stat into its kill and death ranking telemetry. Rise 5.99 StaffAlert imports S40PacketDisconnect but never branches on it; the module's real work polls the Hypixel punishment API over HTTPS. The classic AutoReconnect and AntiKick modules of the wider ecosystem (Tenacity 5.1, Gugustus) sit outside this corpus, so none of the 8 reference clients cancels the kick. Rise 6.x registers the class in the script API.

The kick cannot be meaningfully cancelled: the server has already dropped the connection after sending the packet, so cancelling it only skips the disconnect screen and leaves a dead connection. The real value is reading the reason: ban detection for telemetry (Ranking) and staff-ban awareness. Reason parsing is the only client-side logic, and it is invisible to the server. Anti-cheats use S40 as the enforcement channel, not as a measurable signal.

implementation.overview: The play-state kick. Sigma's Ranking reads the reason text for ban telemetry; Rise 5.99's StaffAlert imports the class but never uses it. None of the 8 clients cancels the kick, because the connection is already dead by the time the packet arrives.
implementation.server_handling: NetHandlerPlayServer and NetworkSystem both send S40 with a GenericFutureListener that closes the channel after the packet flushes, so the kick is fire-and-forget. The reason is built from translated chat components. The server removes the player from its world state regardless of whether the client ever processes the packet.
implementation.protocol_notes: Single field: a chat component serialized via writeChatComponent, which embeds the full JSON chat tree including formatting and translations. The reason string is attacker-controlled, so clients parsing it must handle arbitrary text. Registered clientbound in PLAY state; the login-state equivalent is S00PacketDisconnect at id 0x00.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats use S40 as the enforcement channel: a flagged player receives one and is gone, so there is nothing to bypass inside the packet. Client-side modules can only observe it. Ranking's use is the only corpus example of reacting to the reason text, and it is telemetry, not evasion.

modules.name: Ranking
modules.purpose: Track kills and deaths and report ban kicks to the client's ranking telemetry.
modules.how_it_works: onEvent handles EventPacket; for S40PacketDisconnect it checks func_149165_c().getUnformattedText().toLowerCase().contains("ban") and ticksExisted greater than 15*20, then calls sendStat("ban", ""). The module also correlates S0B animations, S02 chat, S06 health, and S13 destroy-entity packets to attribute kills and deaths.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Telemetry only. The check reads the reason after the kick is already in flight; nothing is mutated or blocked.
modules.variations: None in the corpus. The module is auto-enabled and hidden.

modules.name: StaffAlert
modules.purpose: Alert when staff ban players on Hypixel by polling the punishment API. The S40 import is unused.
modules.how_it_works: Imports S40PacketDisconnect at the top of the file, but the shipped handlers only process S02PacketChat (API key capture) and a periodic HTTPS poll of api.hypixel.net/punishmentstats that shows a notification when staff_total grows. The import is leftover from a planned disconnect-aware feature.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. The module makes outbound HTTPS calls, not packet manipulation; the S40 import never executes.
modules.variations: None in the corpus.

modules.name: NetworkAPI (script API)
modules.purpose: Expose the packet class to Rise's JavaScript scripting API.
modules.how_it_works: S40PacketDisconnect is listed in the clientbound Class array of NetworkAPI.java (line 107).
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. Registry only.
modules.variations: 6.2.4 ships the byte-identical file with the Client-release2 path prefix.

implementation.general_hooks: Sigma: EventPacket. Rise 5.99: PacketReceiveEvent and UpdateEvent on StaffAlert. Rise 6.x: script API table.
implementation.client_variations: Sigma reads the reason text inside its event bus; Rise 5.99 imports the class without using it; Rise 6.x registers it for scripts. No client in the corpus cancels S40.

anticheat.overview: No anticheat parses the play-state disconnect packet. The only real packet references are plumbing: Artemis registers PacketPlayServerKickDisconnect (PacketRepository SERVER_PLAY+39, the GPacketPlayServerKickDisconnect wrapper, ProtocolGeneratorDirect and HardcodeMap) and Negativity declares the KICK_DISCONNECT PacketType constant. The rest of the corpus is the anticheats' own kick enforcement matched on the Kick keyword: NCP KickCommand and DenyLoginCommand, intave FaultKicks, Arc PunishmentManager and PlayerPendingKickEvent, Negativity KickCommand and PlayerCheatKickEvent, Peyang Kick, KickUtil and BanAnalyzer, CheaterDeleter TeleportVerifierCheck, Rammelkast and AntiCheatPlus PlayerListener, NESS MiscEvents, proton Kick, ThotPatrol, Daedalus, Kauri JoinListener, AutoEye AutoEyePlayerList, network-dev AlarmUtil and MenuUtil, and Bubble bubble.sk. All of them kick through Bukkit's player.kickPlayer; the server crafts S40 itself when it flushes the connection, so the packet is the enforcement channel, never a measured signal.

wiki_notes: Play-state kick: a single JSON chat component reason. Client closes the channel, unloads the world and shows the disconnect screen.
Fire-and-forget last packet before teardown; no acknowledgement. Login-state kicks use S00 instead.
MCP 1.8.9 S40PacketDisconnect implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleDisconnect; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readChatComponent.

packets.name: Server Difficulty
packets.desc: Informs client of the server's difficulty setting.

writeup.p: Join-time world metadata: the server announces its difficulty once, inside ServerConfigurationManager.initializeConnectionToPlayer, alongside the other world-state packets (S05 spawn position, S03 time of day, S44 world border INITIALIZE). The payload is a single unsigned byte 0-3 mapped to EnumDifficulty. Vanilla never re-broadcasts it: the /difficulty command mutates the server WorldInfo without notifying clients, so the value learned at join stays stale for the whole session.

The client handler handleServerDifficulty writes the value into WorldInfo (setDifficulty and setDifficultyLocked) and nothing else; gameplay code reads it later via world.getDifficulty(). Note the asymmetry: the packet has a difficultyLocked constructor field and getter, but neither readPacketData nor writePacketData ever touches it, so the wire format is one byte and the locked flag is permanently false on the client.

None of the 8 clients contains a module that references S41. The only non-vanilla hits are Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 NetworkAPI.java, which registers the class in the list of packet types exposed to the JavaScript scripting bridge; no shipped script uses it. The reason is functional: difficulty only scales vanilla survival math (mob damage, hunger drain, regeneration), and cheat modules replace that math with their own logic, so no module output depends on the server's difficulty setting.

The value is trust-on-receive. readPacketData feeds the raw byte to EnumDifficulty.getDifficultyEnum, which in 1.8.9 clamps with a modulo (difficultyEnums[p % 4]), so out-of-range bytes wrap instead of crashing: 4 maps to peaceful, 5 to easy, and so on. The handler stores the enum without validation. That is the entire surface: a hostile server can only lie about difficulty, which changes nothing a client-side cheat relies on.

implementation.overview: One-byte join-time announcement of the world difficulty, written straight into WorldInfo by the client handler. In the 8 clients it is invisible: no module references it, the locked flag is dead on the wire, and out-of-range bytes wrap modulo 4. The only non-vanilla trace is Rise's script API registering the class for JS packet filtering.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager.initializeConnectionToPlayer sends new S41PacketServerDifficulty(worldinfo.getDifficulty(), worldinfo.isDifficultyLocked()) (line 136 in the Rise 6.x bundled sources, 163 in the MCP builds). It is sent exactly once per join, before the initial S08 teleport completes the login sequence. Nothing else on the vanilla server constructs the packet; /difficulty changes WorldInfo directly and does not broadcast.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format in 1.8.9 is a single unsigned byte (writeByte / readUnsignedByte) despite the packet metadata table listing a difficultyLocked boolean. The boolean exists as a constructor argument and getter but is never serialized, so clients always see difficultyLocked == false. EnumDifficulty.getDifficultyEnum applies difficultyEnums[p % 4], so any byte value is accepted. Play state only; sent once during join before the player is fully active.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures this packet. It is clientbound, unidirectional, sent once, and carries no timing or state information that movement or combat checks could use. Spoofing or cancelling it would only change the client's local mob-damage math, which is irrelevant to server-side validation.

anticheat.overview: The difficulty announcement is invisible to the anticheat corpus. The single hit is Artemis HardcodeMap, which maps PacketPlayOutServerDifficulty to its wrapper class for the packet generator (line 60). One unsigned byte sent once at join with no serverbound counterpart, so there is nothing to validate, spoof, or time; the value only scales vanilla survival math that server-side checks never see.

wiki_notes: Join-time announcement: one unsigned byte, 0 peaceful, 1 easy, 2 normal, 3 hard. Sent once during login.
The difficultyLocked constructor flag is never serialized in 1.8.9, so the client always sees it false; /difficulty changes are never rebroadcast.

MCP 1.8.9 S41PacketServerDifficulty implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleServerDifficulty; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readUnsignedByte.

1.8.9 callers: ServerConfigurationManager.initializeConnectionToPlayer sends new S41PacketServerDifficulty (line 145): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/server/management/ServerConfigurationManager.java

packets.name: Combat Event
packets.desc: Server sends combat-related events: enter combat, end combat, entity dead with death message.

writeup.p: Combat tracker state machine. The server announces combat tag transitions through ENTER_COMBAT and END_COMBAT, with a third variant ENTITY_DIED defined for death broadcasts. EntityPlayerMP sends ENTER_COMBAT from func_152111_bt when combat starts and END_COMBAT from func_152112_bu when it ends; END_COMBAT carries the fight duration in ticks and the tracked entity's ID. Only the clientbound direction exists: the client never acknowledges combat state.

The client handler func_175098_a resolves the tracked entity by ID and feeds Twitch streaming metadata: END_COMBAT becomes a MetadataCombat with a negative timestamp derived from the duration (1000 * duration / 20), and ENTITY_DIED becomes a MetadataPlayerDeath carrying the victim, the killer entity and the death message. Nothing in the handler touches the death screen, the health bar or the tab list; those are driven by the client's own entity state.

No module in the 8 clients references S42. This is the natural home for death-event hooks (AutoGG, kill counting, KillAura target cleanup), yet the corpus shows none: AutoGG modules in these clients key off S02PacketChat death-message patterns instead, and KillAura cleanup keys off S13PacketDestroyEntities. The structural reason is that the vanilla server never sends ENTITY_DIED: EntityPlayerMP.onDeath broadcasts the death message through ServerConfigurationManager chat (becoming S02PacketChat on the client), and only ENTER_COMBAT and END_COMBAT are ever constructed. The ENTITY_DIED branch of the client handler is dead code in vanilla 1.8.9.

readPacketData dispatches on a VarInt enum; an out-of-range value deserializes to null (readEnumValue returns null past the last ordinal) and the handler's event comparisons then NPE. The death message is read as a length-prefixed UTF-8 string capped at 32767 bytes, not a chat component, so no JSON component parsing happens here. END_COMBAT writes the tracked entity ID as a plain 4-byte int while ENTITY_DIED writes the killer as a VarInt and the victim as an int: the mixed widths are a known 1.8 protocol quirk.

implementation.overview: Combat tag transitions from the server's CombatTracker. ENTER_COMBAT and END_COMBAT are the only variants the vanilla server constructs; ENTITY_DIED exists on the wire but is dead code in vanilla 1.8.9, which is why none of the 8 clients hooks it. Client-side the handler only feeds Twitch streaming metadata.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.func_152111_bt and func_152112_bu wrap the combat tag transitions and send the packet with the current CombatTracker; END_COMBAT fills the duration from CombatTracker.func_180134_f and the tracked entity ID from func_94550_c. Player deaths do not produce this packet: onDeath routes the death message through ServerConfigurationManager chat broadcast, so the ENTITY_DIED variant is only reachable from plugin or modded servers that construct it directly.
implementation.protocol_notes: Event enum is a VarInt (readEnumValue). END_COMBAT: duration VarInt plus tracked entity ID as a full int. ENTITY_DIED: killer entity ID as VarInt, victim as int, then a String (not IChatComponent, despite the metadata table) capped at 32767 bytes. ENTER_COMBAT carries no payload. readEnumValue returns null for out-of-range values, which reaches the handler as a null eventType.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats do not use S42 for validation: it is clientbound, and combat tag state is tracked server-side from attack packets (C02) and damage events. Server plugins that expose combat tags rely on ENTER_COMBAT and END_COMBAT, not on client acknowledgements, so there is nothing to spoof or cancel from the client.

anticheat.overview: The combat event packet carries combat tag transitions: enter combat, end combat, and entity died. Server-side anticheats do not use it for reach or killaura validation, because combat state is tracked from attack packets, but two anticheats consume it for state: Grim reads the death combat event to track whether the client's death screen is showing, which anchors its respawn-alive check, and Intave registers a packet reader that exposes the two entity id fields for substitution. Artemis and Negativity only name the packet in registries.

checks.name: Respawn alive / death screen state (Grim BadPacketsM)
checks.purpose: Flag a PERFORM_RESPAWN status request sent while the player is alive and no death screen is showing.
checks.how_it_works: BadPacketsM listens on both directions. On the server side it wraps DEATH_COMBAT_EVENT and COMBAT_EVENT (ENTITY_DEAD) for the player's own entity id and, transaction-sandwiched, marks the menu state from showsDeathScreen. On the client side, a PERFORM_RESPAWN action while the compensated self is not dead and no menu is recorded flags the player. Change-game-state win events and respawns grant short exemptions for the client's own menu toggling.
checks.detects: Respawn-while-alive exploits, death-screen spoofing, and clients that send respawn without the server having announced their death.
checks.variations: No other anticheat in the corpus runs a death-state check keyed to this packet; Negativity and Artemis only register the packet name.

checks.name: Combat event reader (Intave)
checks.purpose: Expose the combat event packet's two integer entity fields to Intave's packet pipeline so they can be read or substituted.
checks.how_it_works: CombatEventReader is registered in PacketReaders for COMBAT_EVENT. It reads the first two integers of the packet through a substitution iterator: the iterator writes back to the same integer fields, which lets the pipeline rewrite entity references carried by combat events.
checks.detects: None directly; it is packet plumbing that lets entity-tracking code see and optionally rewrite the entity id fields carried by combat events.
checks.variations: Artemis's PacketRepository maps SERVER_PLAY + 18 to PacketPlayServerCombatEvent and ships a marker interface, and Negativity's PacketType enum lists COMBAT_EVENT('CombatEvent'); neither runs a check on it.

wiki_notes: VarInt enum: ENTER_COMBAT (no payload), END_COMBAT (duration VarInt in ticks plus tracked entity id), ENTITY_DIED (killer id, victim id, death message).
Vanilla 1.8.9 never sends ENTITY_DIED; player deaths broadcast via chat S02 instead. Client handler only feeds Twitch stream metadata.

MCP 1.8.9 S42PacketCombatEvent implements Packet<INetHandlerPlayClient> dispatching to INetHandlerPlayClient.handleCombatEvent; wire serde is readPacketData/writePacketData via readEnumValue, readInt, readStringFromBuffer, readVarIntFromBuffer.

1.8.9 callers: EntityPlayerMP.sendEnterCombat sends new S42PacketCombatEvent (line 257): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/entity/player/EntityPlayerMP.java

packets.name: Camera
packets.desc: Sets the player's camera to spectate a specific entity (spectator mode teleport).
packets.notes: Only works in spectator mode. Used by servers when a player enters spectator and clicks on an entity. Freecam modules may use this to switch camera target. No module in the examined client sources directly targets this packet.

writeup.p: Spectator camera switching. EntityPlayerMP sends it whenever its spectatingEntity changes (line 1084 in the MCP builds, 1057 in Rise), which happens when a spectator clicks an entity, cycles targets, or returns to their own body. The single VarInt entity ID is resolved client-side against the entity list, and the handler then reparents the render view to that entity. It is the only packet that moves the camera independently of the player's own position.

The client handler func_175094_a calls packet.func_179780_a(world) to resolve the entity ID, and only if the entity is non-null calls gameController.func_175607_a (setRenderViewEntity). The null guard means a bogus ID silently leaves the camera unchanged. The server side only ever sends the packet in spectator mode, after validating the target through EntityPlayerMP's spectator logic.

Exactly one module in the 8 clients: Tenacity 6.0's AntiExploit (dev/tenacity/module/impl/misc/AntiExploit.java) cancels S43 when the local player is not a spectator. The rationale is the classic 1.8 camera exploit: a malicious server can force the render view onto an arbitrary or fast-moving entity even while the player is in survival, producing unusable camera motion or a client crash. The check mirrors the server's own precondition, so legitimate spectator flow is never blocked.

The packet is one VarInt with zero client-side validation of game state. The abuse is a server-side precondition failure: vanilla only sends it to spectators, so any S43 arriving at a non-spectator client is by definition hostile. Beyond Tenacity's check, none of the 8 clients rate-limits or sanity-checks it. Freecam-style modules move the render view locally and never touch this packet, which is why no Freecam or spectate module appears in the corpus.

implementation.overview: Spectator-mode camera reparenting: one VarInt entity ID, resolved and applied by the client handler with a null guard. Only Tenacity 6.0's AntiExploit touches it in the 8 clients, cancelling the packet for non-spectators to block the camera crash exploit.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP tracks a spectatingEntity field and sends new S43PacketCamera(spectatingEntity) on every change. The server-side precondition is spectator game mode; the client cannot verify that, so it must trust or filter. The packet is also sent to restore the camera to the player when spectating ends.
implementation.protocol_notes: Single VarInt entity ID. The client resolves it with WorldClient.getEntityByID; a missing entity yields null and the camera is left untouched thanks to the handler's null check. 1.8.9 uses readVarIntFromBuffer. Play state only; no ordering constraints beyond the entity's spawn packet having arrived, otherwise the resolve fails silently.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Not an anti-cheat surface. The packet is clientbound and carries no data the server re-validates. Server-side plugins that support spectator mode do not measure camera behaviour. The relevant threat model is malicious-server-to-client, which is exactly what Tenacity's AntiExploit addresses; cancelling it cannot produce a flag because nothing serverbound is modified.

modules.name: AntiExploit
modules.purpose: Block high-risk clientbound packets, including S43PacketCamera when the local player is not a spectator, to prevent the camera crash exploit.
modules.how_it_works: A PacketReceiveEvent listener walks instanceof checks over a set of high-risk clientbound packets. For S43 it tests mc.thePlayer.isSpectator(); when false it prints a chat notice and calls event.cancel(), so the vanilla handler never runs. The same listener validates S48PacketResourcePackSend URLs, rate-limits S2APacketParticles, S27PacketExplosion and S11PacketSpawnExperienceOrb, and bounds-checks S18PacketEntityTeleport coordinates.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. Cancelling a clientbound packet is invisible to the server; the server never learns whether the camera switch was applied, and no serverbound data is altered, so no anti-cheat can flag it.
modules.variations: The other 7 clients have no S43 handling at all; Tenacity is the only one with a camera-related guard. The same AntiExploit module appears in other client bases (Flux, Lycoris, Raze), but those are outside the 8-client corpus.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent with instanceof dispatch is the pattern; Tenacity registers an IEventListener on the event bus in the module constructor.

anticheat.overview: The camera packet is clientbound and server-authoritative, so anticheats see it only on send. Exactly two consumers act on it: Grim's CompensatedCameraEntity records which entity the server ordered the client to spectate, and intave's AbilityTracker marks the player as having a view entity so its movement checks treat spectator camera motion as legitimate. The rest of the corpus is keyword noise: Photon's CanSee family and TruthfulAC's AimB mention cameras in the ESP raycast and aim domains without touching the packet, and Artemis and Negativity only register the packet type.

checks.name: CompensatedCameraEntity (Grim)
checks.purpose: Track the spectated entity id from the camera packet so entity checks keep measuring against the right body.
checks.how_it_works: A PreVia packet send listener on the CAMERA packet. It reads the camera entity id from the S43 packet, sends a transaction, and on the next real-time task resolves the id against the compensated entity map, keeping a single-entry queue of possible camera targets. isSelf() reports whether the view is back on the player's own body and getPossibilities() exposes the candidates to other checks.
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It is state sync: the spectated entity becomes the reference body for entity-dependent checks while the player's view is attached elsewhere.
checks.variations: intave AbilityTracker.receiveCamera is the only other consumer, and it stores a view-entity boolean instead of the entity itself.

checks.name: AbilityTracker.receiveCamera (intave)
checks.purpose: Record when the server moves the player's view onto another entity, so movement checks exempt spectator camera motion.
checks.how_it_works: A CAMERA packet subscription on the abilities tracker module. receiveCamera reads the entity id from the packet and schedules a tick-synchronized update that sets hasViewEntity to true when the id differs from the player's own entity id. AbilityMetadata.isSpectatorLike() (line 311) returns true for a player whose game mode is spectator or whose hasViewEntity is set, which movement checks use to skip flags that would otherwise fire for spectator motion.
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It prevents false positives: the view-entity flag keeps spectator camera movement out of the normal movement checks.
checks.variations: Grim CompensatedCameraEntity keeps the spectated entity itself and reports whether the view is on the player, instead of a boolean flag.

wiki_notes: Spectating certain mobs loads dedicated post shaders: creepers, spiders and cave spiders, and endermen each apply their own shader, which unloads when the camera returns to anything else.
Control returns to the player by sending the packet with the player's own entity ID, and the packet is ignored when the target entity is not loaded by the client.

packets.name: World Border
packets.desc: Updates the world border (center, size, warning distance/buffer, damping).

writeup.p: World border state machine with six actions: SET_SIZE, LERP_SIZE, SET_CENTER, INITIALIZE, SET_WARNING_TIME and SET_WARNING_BLOCKS. ServerConfigurationManager broadcasts the five change actions to all players on border mutation (lines 245-261 in the MCP builds) and sends INITIALIZE to each player on join (line 786). INITIALIZE is the only action carrying the full state: center, current and target diameter, transition time, and both warning values.

The client handler func_175093_a delegates to packet.func_179788_a(worldBorder), which mutates the single WorldBorder object owned by the client world: setCenter, setTransition, setWarningDistance and setWarningTime. The border then feeds the renderer's red vignette and the camera clamp in EntityRenderer. It is one of the few packets whose handler mutates shared world state instead of copying values into local fields.

No module in the 8 clients references S44. Border tracking would matter for movement modules pathing around a shrinking border or for border-bypass claims, but none exists in the corpus. The border is server-enforced: EntityPlayerMP movement validation and WorldBorder.intersects run server-side and teleport or damage players who cross it, so the client's copy is purely cosmetic and modules gain nothing by intercepting it.

All six actions deserialize doubles and a VarLong transition time with no sanity bounds; a hostile server can inject NaN or extreme diameters into the client WorldBorder, which the renderer then lerps against, producing visual glitches (the classic NaN border). Because enforcement is server-side, corrupting the client border changes nothing gameplay-relevant. The notable quirk is LERP_SIZE's VarLong time field, which is milliseconds server-side, not ticks.

implementation.overview: Six-action world border state machine, broadcast on change and fully initialized on join. Server-enforced, so the client copy is cosmetic; none of the 8 clients has a module that references it. The interesting wire details are the mixed field widths and the VarLong transition time.
implementation.server_handling: ServerConfigurationManager registers a WorldBorder listener that broadcasts SET_SIZE, LERP_SIZE, SET_CENTER, SET_WARNING_TIME and SET_WARNING_BLOCKS to all players on mutation (lines 245-261, MCP numbering), and sends INITIALIZE in initializeConnectionToPlayer (line 786). INITIALIZE serializes the whole border: center X/Z doubles, diameter and target doubles, VarLong transition time, warning distance and warning time ints.
implementation.protocol_notes: Action is a VarInt enum; payload depends on action. SET_SIZE: one double (target diameter). LERP_SIZE: old diameter double, target double, VarLong transition time in milliseconds. SET_CENTER: two doubles. SET_WARNING_TIME and SET_WARNING_BLOCKS: one int each. INITIALIZE: center doubles, both diameters, VarLong, and both warning ints. readEnumValue can return null on an out-of-range action, which NPEs in the read switch.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures border packets. The server enforces the border in its own movement pipeline (EntityPlayerMP position validation against WorldBorder.intersects), so client-side border state has no bearing on any server-side check. The only client-visible effect of tampering is rendering artifacts.

anticheat.overview: The world border packet is the one clientbound world-state packet anticheats genuinely consume. Grim decodes all five actions into a border state and feeds it into the collision pipeline so phase checks treat the border as a solid wall, and intave decodes the same actions into the border model its movement simulation runs against. NCP and Artemis implement the border-as-wall idea too, but they read Bukkit's server-side WorldBorder instead of the packet. Negativity and Artemis also register the packet type.

checks.name: PacketWorldBorder (Grim)
checks.purpose: Mirror the server's world border state on the compensation side so collision and movement checks know where the border is.
checks.how_it_works: A PacketSendListener that wraps the five border packet forms (WORLD_BORDER action packet, INITIALIZE_WORLD_BORDER, WORLD_BORDER_CENTER, WORLD_BORDER_SIZE, WORLD_BORDER_LERP_SIZE) and mutates a BorderExtent: SET_SIZE and WORLD_BORDER_SIZE set the diameter, LERP_SIZE and WORLD_BORDER_LERP_SIZE build a moving extent with the transition duration, SET_CENTER and WORLD_BORDER_CENTER move the center, and INITIALIZE fills the whole state plus the portal teleport boundary. Each update is transaction-bracketed and applied on the next real-time task, and tickBorder() advances the lerp on movement ticks.
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It is the data foundation for the border collision check.
checks.variations: intave WorldBorderReader performs the same decode on intave's event bus; Artemis PacketRepository (SERVER_PLAY + 91) and Negativity PacketType only register the type.

checks.name: Border collision (Grim Collisions)
checks.purpose: Treat the world border as an axis-aligned collision wall so phase and clipping checks cannot move a player through it.
checks.how_it_works: Collisions.addWorldBorder computes the border's min and max X/Z from the PacketWorldBorder check state and, when the player is within 16 blocks of the border, appends four thin collision boxes (one per side, infinite in Y) to the box list the collision resolver tests against. getCollisionBoxes calls it first, so any movement that would place the player across the border collides like a wall.
checks.detects: Phase and border-bypass cheats that move through or beyond the world border.
checks.variations: NCP CollisionUtil.addWorldBorder (line 1074) and Artemis NMS_v1_8 (lines 139-206) add the same border-as-wall boxes to their collision resolvers, but both read Bukkit's server-side WorldBorder and never parse the S44 packet.

checks.name: WorldBorderReader (intave)
checks.purpose: Decode the border packet family into the immutable border model that intave's movement simulation runs against.
checks.how_it_works: A packet reader registered for all seven border packet ids (WORLD_BORDER, SET_BORDER_CENTER, SET_BORDER_SIZE, SET_BORDER_LERP_SIZE, SET_BORDER_WARNING_DELAY, SET_BORDER_WARNING_DISTANCE, INITIALIZE_BORDER). updated() maps the packet type to an UpdateType, reads the doubles and longs out of the ProtocolLib container (with legacy 1.8 offset handling for the action packet), and returns a new WorldBorder: center updates rebuild with a new center, size updates set the diameter, lerp updates build a MovingWorldBorder with the transition time, and INITIALIZE applies all four. MovementDispatcher.sentWorldBorderUpdate (lines 803-812) feeds the result into the movement metadata, and the simulation environment exposes it through border().
checks.detects: Nothing directly. It keeps the simulation's boundary in sync so movement checks simulate against the correct border.
checks.variations: The decoded model is split into StaticWorldBorder and MovingWorldBorder under de.jpx3.intave.world.border; the simulation environment views (ImmutableSimulationEnvironmentCopy, MutableSimulationEnvironmentView, MockSimulationEnvironment) each carry a WorldBorder field with border() accessors.

wiki_notes: Warning time is measured in seconds and warning distance in blocks, matching the units of the worldborder warning time and warning distance commands.

packets.name: Title
packets.desc: Displays titles/subtitles on screen with animation timing. Actions: TITLE, SUBTITLE, TIMES, CLEAR, RESET.

writeup.p: Screen title display with five actions: TITLE, SUBTITLE, TIMES, CLEAR and RESET. The vanilla server produces it from the /title command (CommandTitle), and plugins use it for game announcements. TITLE and SUBTITLE carry an IChatComponent, TIMES carries three ints (fade-in, stay, fade-out in ticks), and CLEAR and RESET carry no text. The client handler routes everything into GuiIngame.displayTitle, which owns the fade state machine.

handleTitle reads the type, formats the component text, and calls ingameGUI.displayTitle(title, subtitle, fadeIn, displayTime, fadeOut). GuiIngame stores the strings plus the three timings and animates alpha over ticks. RESET clears both text slots and restores default timings (10/70/20); CLEAR hides immediately. The packet is clientbound-only and stateless server-side: the server tracks nothing about what the client currently displays.

Two module hits in the corpus. Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 ship RueSessionStats, a SessionStats HUD mode that listens on PacketReceiveEvent, strips control codes from the title message, and increments its wins counter when the text equals 'VICTORY!' (Hypixel game-win detection). November Recode 2.0's AutoPlayModule pattern-matches S45PacketTitle inside its packet-in handler but only null-checks the message; the branch carries no behaviour, so the title serves as a guard against a null component rather than a signal. Anti-title modules that suppress or rewrite titles are common in other clients, but none of the 10 reference clients has one: the corpus shows no cancel-based title handling.

The text is a full IChatComponent parsed client-side, so it shares the component-parsing attack surface of S02PacketChat, including formatting codes and arbitrarily nested JSON. The handler calls getFormattedText() with no length limit beyond the component parser's own. For module authors the useful property is that titles are a timing-accurate game-state signal: Hypixel sends VICTORY! exactly once per win, which is why the win counter keys off it rather than chat.

implementation.overview: Screen title state machine fed by /title and plugin announcements. Rise's RueSessionStats HUD mode uses the VICTORY! title as a win signal for its session stats counter; November Recode 2.0's AutoPlayModule pattern-matches S45PacketTitle with a null-message guard only. No anti-title module exists in the 10 clients.
implementation.server_handling: CommandTitle constructs the packet per /title syntax: TIMES from three parsed ints, TITLE and SUBTITLE with a ChatComponentProcessor-processed component, CLEAR and RESET with a null component. The server keeps no per-client title state; each packet is fire-and-forget. Plugins such as Hypixel send titles directly with their own timing sequences, typically TIMES followed by TITLE.
implementation.protocol_notes: Type is a VarInt enum. TITLE and SUBTITLE append an IChatComponent (JSON); TIMES appends three ints; CLEAR and RESET append nothing. readPacketData reads the component only for TITLE and SUBTITLE and the three ints only for TIMES. The component is null on the wire for TIMES, CLEAR and RESET, and handlers must tolerate that; RueSessionStats and November's AutoPlayModule both null-guard the component before use.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat involvement: titles are cosmetic, clientbound and unacknowledged. Suppressing or rewriting them cannot affect server-side validation. The only measurable behaviour is client rendering, which is invisible to the server.

modules.name: RueSessionStats
modules.purpose: Session stats HUD overlay that counts kills and wins; uses S45PacketTitle to detect Hypixel game wins.
modules.how_it_works: A Mode<SessionStats> render module. onPreMotionEvent refreshes the elapsed-time string every 20 ticks; onKill increments the kill counter; onPacketReceiveEvent checks each S45PacketTitle, strips control codes from getMessage().getUnformattedText(), and increments wins on an exact 'VICTORY!' match. onServerJoin resets the session; the overlay draws through the client's layered render system with a draggable position.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None. The module only reads clientbound state and draws HUD text; nothing serverbound is altered, so there is no flag surface. A false-positive win count is a client-side cosmetic issue, not a detection risk.
modules.variations: Rise 6.2.4 ships the identical file under Client-release2/Client/src/main/java with the same package path. Rise 5.99 has no S45 reference at all; the module exists only in the 6.x component-based module tree.

modules.name: AutoPlayModule (play again)
modules.purpose: Automatically re-queue for the next game after a Hypixel or BlocksMC match; the S45PacketTitle branch only guards against a null title component.
modules.how_it_works: An EventPacket.In listener on November's event bus. In HYPIXEL mode it parses S02PacketChat siblings for a 'Click here!' RUN_COMMAND click event after a win or death message, stores the command, and sends it via addToSendQueueSilent after the configured delay. The S45PacketTitle branch is a match with a null-message guard and no further action, so the title path is effectively inert; the module's real signal is chat.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: None for the title branch. The module sends a legitimate chat command after a real delay, indistinguishable from a player typing it manually; the silent send queue bypasses the client's own event pipeline but not server validation.
modules.variations: Rise's RueSessionStats reads titles as a win counter; November's AutoPlayModule matches S45PacketTitle but performs no title-driven action. No other client in the corpus references S45.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent with an instanceof check and a null-message guard is the pattern RueSessionStats uses; no client in the corpus cancels or rewrites the packet.

anticheat.overview: No anticheat processes the title packet. The corpus is 'Title' keyword noise: inventory GUI titles (Hydro menus, TruthfulAC GUI menus, NCP InventoryListener, Arc InventoryListener, MinecraftAntiCheat MenuEvents), scoreboard and sidebar output (Shard), discord webhook labels (Negativity, FlopAC), and book-inventory code (Grim ExploitB, Peyang Books). The only packet-shaped hits are Artemis's five wrapper interfaces (PacketPlayServerTitle, TitlesClear, TitlesSetAnimation, TitlesSetSubtitle, TitlesSetText) plus its PacketRepository registration (SERVER_PLAY + 75), and the Negativity PacketType TITLE constant; none of these consume or validate the packet. Titles are cosmetic, unacknowledged and carry no timing or state the server re-checks, so there is nothing to flag.

wiki_notes: The fade-out value is the number of ticks spent fading out, not the time at which fading starts, mirroring the fade-in and stay semantics.

1.8.9 callers: CommandTitle.processCommand sends new S45PacketTitle (line 83): https://github.com/Marcelektro/MavenMCP-1.8.9/blob/master/src/main/java/net/minecraft/command/CommandTitle.java

packets.name: Set Compression Level
packets.desc: Changes the compression threshold mid-game. Same as S03 but for PLAY state.

writeup.p: Mid-connection compression threshold change. The client handler reads the VarInt threshold and, only for real network connections (isLocalChannel() false), reconfigures the Netty pipeline: it updates the threshold on the existing decompress decoder or inserts one, and symmetrically for the compress encoder. In vanilla 1.8.9 compression is negotiated once during the login state, so this play-state packet is effectively a modded-server feature.

func_175100_a guards with 'if (!netManager.isLocalChannel())' and calls netManager.setCompressionTreshold(threshold). NetworkManager.setCompressionTreshold mutates the pipeline handlers in place: NettyCompressionDecoder for incoming data and NettyCompressionEncoder for outgoing, inserting the handlers when absent and removing them when the threshold is negative. From that point every packet larger than the threshold is zlib-compressed on the wire.

No module in the 8 clients references S46 beyond the vanilla handler, the packet registry, and Rise's NetworkAPI script-bridge class list. A disabler has no use for it: compression changes do not alter packet semantics, timings, or the ability to spoof data, and the threshold is a server policy the client cannot exploit. Anything that cares about compression (packet-size spoofing) operates on payload construction, not on this control packet.

The packet arrives mid-stream and the client applies it immediately, so a hostile server could toggle the threshold repeatedly; each change reconfigures the pipeline, but the cost is negligible and the result is simply a different compression ratio. A negative threshold disables compression. There is no length validation: an enormous threshold effectively disables compression for the session, which is only a bandwidth concern. The change applies to the next packet in flight, not retroactively.

implementation.overview: Play-state compression threshold control, handled entirely inside the Netty pipeline: the vanilla handler reconfigures the decompress and compress handlers only for non-local channels. None of the 8 clients has a module for it; it is invisible to gameplay and to anti-cheat logic.
implementation.server_handling: The server-side counterpart is NetworkManager.setCompressionTreshold, which the client handler invokes after receiving S46. Vanilla 1.8.9 negotiates compression once during login (the login-state S03PacketEnableCompression) and never sends S46; the packet exists for modded and plugin servers that change the threshold after the play state begins. The threshold applies to both directions from the moment the pipeline is reconfigured.
implementation.protocol_notes: Single VarInt threshold; any negative value disables compression. The client skips the whole operation for local channels (singleplayer and LAN), so the handler is a one-line guard around a pipeline mutation. Because the packet is processed inline in the receiving thread, the new threshold takes effect for the very next packet the encoder writes, with no handshake or acknowledgement.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Invisible to anti-cheats. Compression level is transport policy, not gameplay data; no movement, combat or timing check reads it. The only observable effect of a changed threshold is packet sizes on the wire, which server-side proxies handle transparently.

anticheat.overview: Compression level is transport policy, not gameplay data, and the corpus reflects that: the only hit is Artemis's packet generator HardcodeMap, which maps the name PacketPlayOutSetCompression to the PacketPlayServerCompression interface for the protocol generator. That is build infrastructure, not a check. No anticheat reads the threshold; changing it only changes wire sizes, which proxies handle transparently, so there is no flag surface.

wiki_notes: Single VarInt threshold applied mid-game to the Netty pipeline; a negative value disables compression. Takes effect on the very next packet.
Vanilla 1.8.9 negotiates compression once at login via S03; S46 exists for modded servers that change the threshold during play.

packets.name: Player List Header Footer
packets.desc: Sets text above and below the tab player list.

writeup.p: The server paints arbitrary text above and below the tab list. Two IChatComponent JSON strings (header, footer) arrive whenever the server wants to update the display: restart notices, rules, game-state text. The packet is clientbound-only, PLAY state, and generates no reply. It is pure presentation state pushed from the server, with no client-controlled round trip.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handlePlayerListHeaderFooter writes the header and footer into GuiPlayerTabOverlay; when the formatted text is empty the field is set to null, which hides that line. Nothing is sent back, so there is no packet the client can influence, delay or spoof.

None of the 8 clients ships a module that intercepts S47. The only non-vanilla reference in the corpus is the Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 script API (NetworkAPI), which registers the class in the packet list exposed to JavaScript so user scripts can attach receive handlers. Memeware, Nekoware, Sigma, Spicy and Tenacity touch only the bundled net/minecraft handler. The packet offers no timing, state or spoofing advantage, which is exactly why module authors ignore it.

The content is untrusted server JSON rendered into the tab GUI. Malformed JSON is caught by the chat-component reader, but very long header or footer text and deep component nesting stress the client renderer. No client in the corpus exploits or defends against this; the packet is not a cheating surface.

implementation.overview: A pure presentation packet with zero module coverage in the 8 clients: modules is empty because no module file in the corpus references S47. The only non-vanilla hit is the Rise 6.x NetworkAPI script registry listing the class so user scripts can hook it.
implementation.server_handling: Server side, the packet is constructed from chat components and pushed via sendPacket; there is no server-side processing of a reply because none exists. The header and footer are typically rebuilt by plugins on a timer or on state change.
implementation.protocol_notes: Two chat components read via readChatComponent (VarInt length prefix plus JSON UTF-8). The vanilla handler nulls a field when its formatted text length is 0, so an empty string hides the line instead of rendering blank space. Wire cost is the two JSON strings and their length prefixes.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: No anti-cheat measures this packet: it has no timing value and no client response. The only related concern is client-side stability under hostile JSON, which is a client defense topic rather than an anti-cheat one.
implementation.general_hooks: Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 expose S47 to scripts through NetworkAPI's packet registry; no event bus in any of the 8 clients has a module handler for it.
implementation.client_variations: Only Rise 6.x differs from vanilla: its NetworkAPI packet list includes S47PacketPlayerListHeaderFooter.class. All other clients carry the unmodified NetHandlerPlayClient handler.

anticheat.overview: The corpus for this packet is entirely 'Tab' keyword noise across 2087 lines, with zero references to the packet, its wrapper, or its header and footer fields. The noise splits into tab-complete (C14) processing (Grim ChatA and CrashH, FlopAC WrappedInTabComplete, Artemis TabComplete packet wrappers and registrations, BetterAnticheat ImpossibleCompletionCheck, Photon TabCompleteSupplier), tab-list rendering (Shard TabListOutput, intave TablistMutator for fake players), command tab-completion handlers (NCP commands, Photon InternalCommand, Rammelkast and AntiCheatPlus config tables), and math table code (Hydro ApacheMath and SensitivityTable, intave's ASM library). The packet is pure presentation with no reply and no timing value, so no anticheat measures it.

wiki_notes: The vanilla server never sends this packet; it exists for custom servers and plugins to paint extra information above and below the tab list.
Clearing a line is done by sending an empty text component, which the client renders as a hidden line rather than blank space.
